THE SCIENCE OF KNOWLEDGE

BY

G. TIBERGHIEN DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY. — ORDINARY PROFESSOR AT THE UNIVERSITY OF BRUSSELS

PART ONE

GENERAL THEORY OF KNOWLEDGE

ITS ORIGINS, ITS LAWS, ITS LEGITIMACY

PARIS

LIBRAIRIE INTERNATIONALE

13, RUE DE GRAMMONT, 13 A. LACROIX, VERBOECKHOVEN & C ie , PUBLISHERS

IN BRUSSELS, LEGHORN AND LEIPZIG

1865

PDF 4

Philosophy is decomposing. Little schools are forming, more and more insignificant and disheartening. M. Cousin had opened a broad path to speculation in France by calling the attention of the educated public to the great systems of the successors of Locke and of Kant, and had given minds a powerful impulse toward historical and psychological studies. That movement has ceased; eclecticism is dying, and now produces scarcely anything but literary or declamatory works. Everything that is happening before our eyes attests its insufficiency in the face of the logical necessities of thought and the practical necessities of the age. The grossest materialism, under the generous protection of the natural sciences, the most shameless atheism, under pretext of progress, the most pretentious skepticism, under the guise of criticism, occupy the stage. Auguste Comte and his school, MM. Colins, Poulin, Proudhon, Taine, Moleschott, Büchner and a host of others, however diverse their tendencies, join hands and agree on one point: the radical impotence of reason before the problem of human destiny, the impossibility of any future metaphysics.

Logic. — I. 1

PDF 5

M. Renan himself once fell into this fault. There is theology well avenged for the attacks of rationalism.

We are told everywhere and in every tone that the soul is matter, that man is composed of molecules, endowed with senses, deprived of reason, and that there is no longer any line of demarcation in the scale of beings. The animal is perfecting itself, man is degrading himself; the quadrumana are to take the place of the bimana, their degenerate sons. No more trace of rational life in the activity of our fellows: the ideal, liberty, duty, religion are pompous and empty names. Instead of God, man; instead of a moral world, nature; instead of principles, phenomena. The infinite and the absolute withdraw before facts. Such is the teaching of contemporary sensualism and materialism, decked out with a new title, positivism.

This system already has its logic, the logic of sensation, the logic of Epicurus and of Condillac, restored by physiology and enlarged by induction. It suffices to cite the pedagogical school of Dr. Beneke for Germany, M. Renouvier for France, Mr. Stuart Mill for England. To be sure, I do not accuse these thinkers of adopting all the extravagances put forth by Aug. Comte; but I maintain that their theories are the logical expression of the positivist current of our age, and that they can only favor its development, by the denial of all general truth and the pretension of reducing reality to the phenomena of sensibility.

PDF 6

Strengthened by this unexpected support, positivism becomes a serious embarrassment for philosophy. There is no question of sparing it because it too combats the supernatural and incomprehensible dogmas; it must be attacked openly as an error that debases human nature and takes no account of the moral interests of society. Is it even an ally in the struggle of thought against ignorance and [PDF 6] superstition? I doubt it; with one hand it raises what it throws down with the other, and by the deplorable weakness of its arguments it compromises the very cause that it wishes to defend. It is not merely the abuse, but the use of reason that it proscribes. If on one side it stands with rationalism against the prejudices of the Middle Ages, on the other it stands with theology against every rational doctrine founded on principles. I forget even its own cult, the adoration of humanity, an inconsistency already repudiated by the most intelligent of its adherents: humanity, no more than God, is a phenomenon that falls under the senses. Its blows go beyond traditional beliefs and strike at the very idea of religious belief. Metaphysics in its eyes is a new form of idolatry; the supra-sensible is no less condemnable than the supernatural. And since religion is after all a need of the heart and of thought, what support remains for the moral convictions of man, once they have been withdrawn from the authority of reason, if not blind faith or historical revelations? A doctrine is never abolished except by a more complete doctrine.

PDF 7

In this disarray of philosophical systems in which we find ourselves, it falls to logic to repair the breaches made in human reason. Logic is the science of knowledge. We must show to blinded minds in what knowledge consists, what are its conditions, its laws, its extent, its value, how it differs from truth and from certainty, and how it arrives at its perfection, that is to say, at science. We must, in other words, set forth methodically the general theory of knowledge, insisting on its rational elements and on its legitimacy, and the theory of the organic forms of thought, which has been too much lost from view. We must oppose, finally, the logic of reason to the logic of the senses. Whoever shall be able to resolve, or even merely to understand, this problem will return to the feeling of the [PDF 7] dignity of man, and will no longer fall, through want of intellectual culture, into the snares set for his good faith by the apostles of materialism, of positivism, and of atheism.

Logic needs to be made over, not only as a theory of human knowledge, but even as the organic form of science, as Organum, in the way in which it has generally been treated since Aristotle. The Stagirite is still our master in the analysis of reasoning and particularly of the syllogism and of demonstration, that is to say, of deduction, the method of the geometers. But his teaching has been so decried since Bacon extolled experience and induction, that Aristotle is more and more ignored and misunderstood, and a man who, like William Hamilton, has not lost the sense of dialectical traditions could be pointed out as a rare phenomenon. The Abbé Gratry, in his work on Logique, or rather on the occasion of logic, observes, not without reason, that for seven hundred years there has not been in Europe a century as ignorant as our own in the matter of the forms of reason. And he is himself a sad proof of the truth of his words. It is a matter, then, first of reinstating Aristotle in his claim to universal esteem, as the editor of the laws of thought; it is a matter next of completing him, by bringing within the frame of logic the whole fruit of the philosophical movement of modern times, in one of its most original tendencies, all that is called observation, generalization, induction, analogy, in a word, the experimental method. To be sure, the procedure of the natural sciences had not escaped the author of the Analytics, but his views in this matter are less sure, and the capital importance of induction could be revealed only in our own day, thanks to the labors of scientists, so well appreciated in the System of Logic of Mr. Stuart Mill.

PDF 8

It is important here to keep within the just limits of the truth [PDF 8] and to avoid the faults of exclusive minds, who exalt either deduction to the detriment of observation, or observation at the expense of deduction. Science can dispense with neither of these two instruments. To disparage experience would be nonsense in the presence of the marvels of our industry and of our whole material civilization; but to conclude from this that experience suffices for the needs of reason, that man has only senses and should concern himself only with matter, is that not nonsense too, in the presence of the moral and religious aspirations of our time, nay, in the presence of that group of sciences which are placed in the first rank for certainty and which are wholly foreign to all empiricism, in the presence of mathematics? Let us beware of these extreme parties; let us distrust authors who perceive only one point of view of things, who are always ready to sacrifice the rights of the intellect to their individual prepossessions and to make of truth a question of party. “Let us take nothing away from the human mind; to suppress is bad. We must reform and transform.” The poet’s maxim applies to logic as to social science. Let us suppress neither Aristotle nor Bacon; let us disown neither deduction nor observation; let us not mutilate thought, let us accept at once the syllogism and induction.

A complete treatise on logic that does justice to all the forms of reason does not exist, to our knowledge. Details of it are found scattered through a multitude of writings, mingled with gross errors; but the organization of knowledge, considered as a whole, is certainly not to be met with either in France or in England, even after the considerable labors of Mr. Mill, and setting aside the exclusive character of that author’s theories.

PDF 9

What will it be, then, if to the logic of the Schools, to Organics, we add the general theory of human knowledge, [PDF 9] considered in its various species, in its laws, and in its legitimacy? We shall have to go back as far as the Recherche de la vérité and the Essais sur l’entendement humain of Malebranche, of Locke, and of Leibniz, or at the very least as far as the Origine des connaissances humaines of Condillac, in order to discover a few fragments, in order to have at least some views on the value of rational ideas and of sensible perceptions, according to the spirit of Cartesianism and of sensualism. Need it be said, none of these doctrines goes to the bottom of things or can withstand the skeptical arguments of Hume or of Kant. And what has been done since? The eclectic school, without compass and without metaphysics, has scarcely touched on the problem of knowledge. M. Javary’s book on Certitude proves that the most serious talent, when it lacks direction, does not suffice to resolve such questions; the secret of philosophical method seems lost in the native land of Descartes.

PDF 10

M. Renouvier, in his Essais de critique générale, has at least understood that we were on the wrong road, that to reach the goal we must hasten to retrace our steps and seek first to get our bearings in science, by taking up again the work of the philosopher of Königsberg. He has made praiseworthy and laborious efforts to carry out this fine project, and he has miserably failed from the outset. Instead of beginning with a severe analysis of the soul, based on observation, and of scrutinizing the whole of our faculties before engaging in the operations of thought, he approaches the problem of knowledge directly and takes it by one of its most secondary elements, confusing the whole with the part. Knowledge, for him, is representation, representation with limit and number, that is to say, sensible representation. Phenomena are therefore the only elements of knowledge, and the objects of reason are idols [PDF 10] that must be banished from science. That is all there is to it. The conclusions of the author must be those of sensualism and of positivism, since the principle is the same. But this is not a serious study of human knowledge. M. Renouvier has not seen that logic has its roots in psychology, and that psychology well developed is something quite other than a pure phenomenology, as I have demonstrated elsewhere. Had he gone deeply into the question of the starting point of science, as one is bound to do after Descartes in a critique of the human mind, or had he merely understood the scope of reason, failing consciousness, by profiting from the labors of the eclectic school, he would have arrived at results less disheartening to our dignity, he would have found that thought affirms no phenomenon at its initial point and at its final point, since it affirms the self and God, and he would not have voluntarily condemned himself to skepticism and to atheism. Everything is relative, says the author, copying Protagoras; every absolute is a chimera; “theology, as well as psychology, vanishes in the presence of criticism, whose true name in this respect would be atheism, if, confined to the domain of pure science, that word did not exclude any legitimate belief and did not serve to cover doctrines as vain as those that it claims to disavow.” The conclusion of science is therefore that there is no science, that all truth is relative, true for some, false for others, according to circumstances. Here we are, from progress to progress, back in the fine days of the sophists of Greece.

PDF 11

Circumstances, unfortunately, are rather favorable to M. Renouvier. The reaction against the abuses of speculation continues everywhere in Europe. Many scientists without philosophical culture lay claim to the title of philosopher, and repeat on all sides that principles are going away with divine right, with the supernatural, with systems, and that nothing remains [PDF 11] but facts, henceforth the sole object of the adoration of men. Statistics governs the world. Let us no longer speak of liberty, of right, of duty, of God; these are not facts. Give us the number of crimes, a positivist will say, and we will give you in return the nature of man and the destiny of society. A fact contains everything, mind and matter, war and peace, time and eternity. M. Janet has described this subject with eloquence in the introduction to his Études sur la dialectique de Platon et de Hegel; M. Caro returns to the charge in his book on l’Idée de Dieu; but that is not enough, a complete and methodical work is needed to rehabilitate philosophy at least in the minds of the new generations who will wish to study it without prejudice. To stop this flood of unwholesome errors which pervert rational life and poison all the moral relations of man, we must return to the theory of knowledge, which is still unknown in its essential parts and which alone, nevertheless, can serve as a measure between the incontestable rights and the absurd pretensions of criticism. The theory of knowledge needs to be made over, elucidated, and completed after the warnings of Kant, and finally to be discussed with maturity in its basis and in its legitimacy.

PDF 12

Does the Logique of Hegel, translated into French and annotated by M. Véra, relieve us of carrying out this plan? Quite the contrary, it requires it. Hegel’s method has been judged and condemned. The sumptuous edifice which has seduced so many imaginations is overthrown; there remains only the genius of the architect, which is not in question. The most vaunted part of this system is logic. What does it teach us on the theory of knowledge? Nothing. From the very first proposition it confounds the question of the starting point of science with the question of the principle, thought with reality, logic with metaphysics. Hegel does not analyze knowledge in itself, impartially, as a manifestation of [PDF 12] our consciousness; he makes it appear in the series of his deductions, as one of the moments of the development of the Idea; after the theory of being and of essence, between life and the absolute idea, the last term of the process. What he says of it resembles a riddle whose answer no sensible mind can find. Let the reader judge by the beginning.

“The idea exists in a state of liberty and for itself only when the universal is its element, when the object and the notion are but one, or, what comes to the same thing, when the idea takes itself for object. Here the subjective form of the idea, which determines itself in order to attain the universal, is only a simple distinction produced within itself, an intuition in which the idea maintains itself in its state of identity and universality; but as there is here a determinate difference, we find ourselves again in the presence of a judgment in which the idea separates itself from itself and at first presupposes itself as an external world. There are here two judgments which are identical in themselves, but which are not yet posited as such. The relation of these two ideas, which in themselves, or as life, are identical, forms the relative and consequently finite side of this moment of the idea. It is a reflected relation, in that the differentiation of the idea is here only a first judgment; it is a presupposition, and not a position, and, consequently, in the presence of the subjective idea there is posited an immediate objective world, or rather, the idea as life, appearing in the form of individual existence. But this judgment is produced in the bosom of the idea itself. Consequently, while doubling itself, the idea preserves its unity and the conviction of its identity with the objective world, an identity which is here only in the immediate state. Reason applies itself to the knowledge of the world with the absolute belief of realizing this identity; it feels the need of making the contradiction disappear and of giving to this belief the form of truth. This process of the idea constitutes knowledge.”

PDF 13

Happy are those who can understand such a deduction and who know how to convince themselves that it applies to knowledge rather than to love, to virtue, to becoming, or to vegetation. As for me, in spite of the twenty or so years that I have devoted to the study of knowledge since my first Essay, I must confess that in this moment of the absolute idea I discover absolutely no idea at all, and that I do not even grasp why one should not put in place of each term the contrary term. What difference would there be in the demonstration of the thesis, if one said: the idea exists in a state of necessity and outside itself only when the particular is its element, when the object and the notion are two, or when the idea takes itself for subject, etc.? Let the reader compare, and he will avow that the notion of knowledge is not at all obscured by this substitution. That Hegel took himself seriously, I believe; his doctrine, after all, is a natural phase in the evolution of German idealism; but this doctrine, which consists in realizing our thoughts without first consulting the real world subject to our observation, can assume as many forms as there are possible combinations among our thoughts; every poet, every dreamer is an idealist, and Hegel is not the least fanciful. It is time for the jest to cease; this is not logic, it is a caricature of logic.

PDF 14

Knowledge is already the idea for Hegel. But before the idea becomes idea, it manifests itself as object in mechanics, in chemistry, and in teleology; why not in the plant, in the animal, and in man? And before passing to the state of object, it is subject in the notion, in judgment, and in the syllogism. Here one might ask the author why he treats of the manifold operations of thought before speaking of knowledge in general. Are not the notion, the judgment, and reasoning [PDF 14] particular cognitions, determinate forms of knowledge, or does deduction not proceed from the more to the less, from the general to the particular? Doubtless; but Hegel calls notion what everybody calls knowledge; this suits better the march of the idea. Be it so, that is his least fault, provided that this maneuver can teach us something about the notion, the judgment, and reasoning. These organic forms of thought have a perfectly determinate value, given by theory and by tradition since Aristotle. Kant declared them perfect, though he had no prejudices in favor of the ancients. To be sure, it is permitted to criticize or even to refute what is established, but on the condition that we be told why and that something better be done. Let us therefore put absolute idealism to the test, let us see how the triads are applied to the formal logic of the Schools. We should look in vain, they are not applied. Hegel gives no theory of the notion, of judgment, and of reasoning, but a very superficial explanation of a few notions, of a few judgments, of a few reasonings. The rest does not enter into the movement of the idea, and that is often the essential. The author has not given himself the trouble of understanding formal logic, he disdains it. He confounds the syllogism with reasoning in general and induction with the syllogism; but he takes care to conceal his errors under the pretentiousness of his terms. For the rest, no spirit of observation or of analysis, no explanation that the intellect can assimilate and reproduce; in place of science, logogriphs:

PDF 15

“The notion is truly concrete existence, because individuality, which is the negative unity, determinate in itself and for itself, contains also a relation with itself, that is to say, universality. The moments of the notion cannot, consequently, be separated. Reflected determinations can each be separated from its contrary, and, thus [PDF 15] isolated, can be understood and have a value. But as in the notion their identity is posited, each of the moments of the notion can be grasped only with and by the other.”

“The judgment constitutes the moment of finitude; for the finitude of things consists precisely in this, that they are judgments, that is to say, that in them are united both their own existence and their general nature, their body and their soul; without this they would not be; but these two moments are distinct, and can be separated. In the abstract judgment: the individual is the universal, the individual, as negative term and one that is in relation with itself, is the immediately concrete term, and the predicate is the abstract and indeterminate term, the universal. But as they are united by the copula is, the predicate must contain, in its universality, the determinability of the subject. The universal thus determined is the particular, which posits the identity of the subject and of the predicate; and since it is in a state of indifference with regard to the form of both, it constitutes the content of the judgment.”

PDF 16

“The syllogism is commonly represented as a form of rational thought, but as a subjective form which has no intimate connection with the content of reason, for example, with the principle of an action conformable to reason. People speak much and often of reason, and appeal to it without determining what it is, and without thinking at least of the faculty it has of reasoning. If the formal syllogism, which is the instrument of reason, seems to offer nothing rational, it is because it is separated from the content of reason. And yet this content has a rational character only by virtue of the determination which gives to thought itself that character; and this determination is the syllogism, which is nothing other than the notion posited with all its real elements (but which is at first only notion [PDF 16] in the formal sense). Consequently, the syllogism is the essential foundation of all truth, and therefore the absolute is a syllogism; a definition which might be stated also in this proposition: all things are a syllogism. The notion is, in fact, at the bottom of all things, and their existence expresses the difference of its moments. For its universal nature gives itself an external reality through the particular, whence, by a negative return upon itself, it posits itself as individual, which, inverting the terms, can equally be expressed thus. The real is the individual which through the particular rises to the general, and thereby attains its identity. The real is one, but in such a way as to give, so to speak, passage to the different moments of the notion; and the syllogism is as it were the circular movement of these moments, by the aid of which the real posits its unity.”

Verba et voces. This is beneath all criticism. Philosophy must hasten to repudiate such verbiage, on pain of discrediting itself.

PDF 17

Such, then, is the logical situation at this moment. On the one side, Mr. Stuart Mill and M. Renouvier, England and France, considered in their most lively tendencies, favor the recrudescence of sensualism that results from the exclusive development of the physical studies, join hands with positivism, and reduce science to a catalogue of phenomena. On the other side, Hegel, the representative of Germany in its idealist tendency, develops pantheism and reduces science to pure speculation, under the pretext that the ideal is the true reality and that the beings of the world are notions. These two contrary currents end in two extremes equally disastrous, the negation of the absolute and the negation of contingency. The one sets God aside, misunderstands reason, and provokes the abdication of the moral dignity of man. The other sets facts aside, misunderstands sensibility, and takes no account of common sense. As methods, [PDF 17] the first rejects deduction and contests the value of the syllogism, Mr. Mill at least pushes logic that far. The second rejects observation and refuses all authority to induction. Both do violence to human nature, lead to skepticism by different paths, and call for a serious reform in the theory of knowledge. To the narrow and arrogant observation of the positivist schools we must oppose the laws and conditions of a legitimate observation, and show that experience can do nothing without reason, and that consequently it pronounces its own condemnation by eliminating every a priori element from scientific researches. To the arbitrary and unregulated speculation of the pantheistic schools we must oppose a methodical and prudent speculation, and show that the impartial analysis of the facts that appear to us in intuition must precede synthesis, and that consequently deduction, without the support and control of observation, is as powerless to engender certainty as observation without the guarantee of deduction. Analysis and synthesis, developed in isolation, in opposition to one another, cast upon objects only a doubtful light, which hides from us one face of their nature and brings out the other. Every exaggeration brings about a reaction in the contrary direction. Thus the aberrations of the sensualist schools are the excuse of absolute idealism, and the extravagances of the idealist schools become in their turn a warrant for positivism. It is important for the honor of philosophy to pass beyond the circle of these narrow and paradoxical notions. We must at last demonstrate that the construction of science requires the concurrence of all our intellectual forces, the testimony of all our sources of knowledge, the employment of all our procedures of investigation, that exclusive solutions are necessarily errors, and that truth is above the conflict of contrary opinions and alone can unite and reconcile them.

PDF 18

Eclecticism was on this road, but it did not rise high enough to face the difficulties of the moment. The name of science is not eclecticism, for that doctrine lacks unity, but organism, that is to say, organization of the intellectual life, of the moral, social, and religious life, on the basis of reason and of observation, of philosophy and of history, of authority and of liberty.

PDF 19

One philosopher alone is equal to the situation. Krause is still little known in France, because he does not belong to the movement set going by Kant and ended by Hegel, which alone has fixed attention in this country, and because he took up afresh the institution of science according to the Cartesian method. Starting point, principle, method, system, organization of science, considered in its conditions, in its laws, in its forms, in its legitimacy, everything has been subjected by Krause to a severe examination and treated with a sureness of view that can defy criticism. M. Renouvier has recognized the importance of a table of categories, as laws of thought, for the upbuilding of science; he rightly points out the imperfections in the labors of Aristotle and of Kant on this matter and proposes a new list which is not worth the old ones; he did not know that this work has long been accomplished in Germany and that it has been carried out with a talent to which even adversaries have paid a brilliant tribute, as may be seen from the work of Dr. Erdmann on the History of Modern Philosophy. Although the doctrine of Krause no longer bears, like those of his predecessors, the pure stamp of the German school, it has not yet had the luck to meet a translator in France. Spain has taken the initiative in this regard, thanks to M. Sanz del Rio, professor at the University of Madrid. Only some parts of this doctrine, concerning psychology, right, and society, have been presented to the French public by MM. Ahrens, Bouchitté, Pascal [PDF 19] Duprat and Darimon. Others have spoken with praise of the moral and religious conceptions of the author. I propose in the present work to reproduce, in complete freedom of mind and on a new plan, his logical theories on the whole body of human knowledge. The logical works of Krause are quite numerous and followed one another over a long space of time. They are:

Grundriss der historischen Logik, Jena, 1803;

Abriss des Systemes der Logik, Göttingen, 1825, 1828;

Vorlesungen über die Grundwahrheiten der Wissenschaft, Göttingen, 1829;

Die Lehre vom Erkennen und von der Erkenntniss, Göttingen, 1836; a posthumous work edited by M. Leonhardi, accompanied by a new and complete annotation for all the organic forms of knowledge.

PDF 20

But logic is not an isolated science. To set forth the theory of knowledge, we must rest upon the analysis of the soul which produces knowledge and which knows that it knows. Logic is to psychology what physiology is to anatomy. Psychology ascertains by inner sense the organs or faculties of the mind, will, feeling, thought, and decomposes thought in turn into sensibility, imagination, memory, understanding, and reason. Logic takes hold of these data and shows the action of the intellectual faculties in the formation and the organization of knowledge. I therefore warn the reader that the logic which I publish today and the psychology which I published in 1862, under this title: The Science of the Soul within the Limits of Observation, form but one and the same whole. The close relations which unite these two sciences, and the developments which I have given to the primitive fact of consciousness, to the nature and life of the mind, to its properties and its faculties, spare me from dwelling on the antecedents of logic. Whoever should take no account [PDF 20] of my earlier labors would rightly regard as rash the first pages of the logic, in which I simply set forth the results obtained by psychological analysis. The explanation and the justification which one has a right to ask of me are to be found elsewhere.

Logic and psychology are both a preparation for metaphysics, regarded as a science. Nothing less is needed than the thorough study of the self and of its intellectual capacity to take from metaphysics the character of a series of hypotheses, and to give it the form and the value of geometry, which is itself a branch detached from pure philosophy. Kant had well understood this necessity of a critique of our means of knowing in order to approach the problems of metaphysics with fruit, but he had gravely mistaken the scope of reason. This subject will be treated with all the developments it admits of. We shall see that the legitimacy of our knowledge can be decided only by the solution of the capital question of thought, that of the existence of God; no science without a principle, and the principle of all that is, whether outside us or within us, the principle of existence and of knowledge, is the being of all reality whom we call God. Logic then has its end in the affirmation of God, as the principle of science, and this principle, recognized in the full light of consciousness, when the mind is in possession of all its forces, becomes thereafter the basis on which metaphysics rises. The notion of God is for metaphysics what the notion of space is for geometry. If the notion of God is certain, the science of God can unfold by the sole effect of reasoning, in a manner as regular, as systematic, as the science of space. All the effort of thought must bear on this point. This is what psychology and logic tend to. These two sciences, from the point of view of method, belong to analysis;

PDF 21

Logic. — I. 2 [PDF 21] they are a gradual elevation of the mind to the infinite and absolute being, a march of thought which goes from the starting point to the principle, from the self to God; metaphysics constitutes synthesis, the definitive construction of science as a whole. Synthesis will follow analysis and conform to it, while enlarging the frame of the inquiries.

PDF 22

I. THE NOTION OF LOGIC

Every science is a body of knowledge, invested with the character of truth and certainty, set forth with method and presented in systematic form. The study of nature and mathematics, history and philosophy, deserve the name of science only on this condition. Isolated affirmations, without relation to one another, are apophthegms or aphorisms, like the sayings of the Sages of Greece; judgments passed in haste, probable indications, individual opinions, are prejudices, paralogisms or common knowledge. Something other than error and hypothesis is needed, something more than disconnected maxims, however just, to constitute science; truth and certainty are needed, method and system are needed. Science, whatever its object, is an organic whole, a body of doctrines whose members are regularly linked together, whose parts explain one another, in which everything holds together, is concatenated, and relates to everything else, as in a living body.

p. 24

Science is the organism of knowledge, or knowledge organized.

There are therefore general conditions for all the sciences. Physics and metaphysics, chemistry and ethics, zoology and algebra, differ from one another in their object; but all the sciences, however diverse they may be, present the state of our knowledge; all of them develop the knowledge acquired by the efforts of successive generations, and strive to render it true and certain, to set it forth with method by induction or by deduction, and to unite it in a well-coordinated whole, in which the parts are grouped in order, and the theories throw light upon one another. All the sciences, in a word, have common properties, which are united in the very idea or in the definition of science.

p. 25

The common properties of all the particular sciences are the object of a new science, which is neither less extensive nor less important than any other branch of human learning. This science is Logic. It is, in the intellectual system of the world, what physics is in the group of sciences that deal with nature, and what right is for the social sciences. Physics studies the general properties of bodies; right, the general conditions of the life of rational beings; logic, the general attributes of science. But logic has a higher character of universality than any other branch of knowledge, since it fixes the qualities common to all the sciences, not excepting physics or natural right. It was born after the other sciences in the progressive march of society, when the mind, after many fruitless efforts, and already given over to doubt, felt the need of turning back upon itself and of asking itself seriously whether science is possible, and under what conditions it can be acquired. This moment of thought, in which it attains consciousness of itself and raises the question of its own legitimacy, in order to give itself an account of the extent of its means and of the success of its later activity, corresponds in Greece to the movement of the Socratic philosophy, illus-illustrated [p. 25] by Plato and by Aristotle. An analogous event had taken place in the East, at the period when the speculative genius of the Hindu people reached its maturity, though no direct relations can be established between the labors of the preceptor of Alexander and those of Gotama (1). One and the same inspiration gave birth to logic at the zenith of the intellectual culture of two distinct races, under the sway of two independent civilizations.

Logic is therefore the science of knowledge in general, and especially of scientific knowledge, that is to say, the science of science. Starting from this definition, we can easily account for its domain and its relations.

p. 26

Logic has its roots in psychology, and depends on the faculty of thinking; it is the theory of the complete and normal development of the intelligence. But it leaves to the science of the soul the task of analyzing thought in its various applications, as memory, as imagination, as reason; it reserves to itself the consideration of thought in its spontaneous and voluntary activity, as the cause of knowledge. This side of the intellect is the understanding or reflection. Logic does not treat of sensibility or of reason as a whole, as faculties of the soul, but only as sources of intuitions. Its proper object is knowledge; it is the science of knowledge considered in itself and in all its determinations. The understanding is subject to error and to doubt in interpreting the data of the senses and of reason—in referring, for example, a sensation to one object rather than to another, and in judging the shape, the size, the distance of the object by the impression of the moment, without taking account of the physical and physiological laws of the phenomenon. Reason and the senses are not deceived, whatever may be said, for the very simple reason that they do not judge; it is we who deceive ourselves on the occasion of sensations or of ideas, it is the understanding that is at fault when we wrongly appreciate the intuitions of our receptive faculties. The conviction of this infirmity [p. 26] of the human mind can weaken our confidence in the most legitimate judgments, and, as it grows firmer, can even take from us the belief in the possibility of knowing the truth. Such is the foundation of logic. Sensibility and reason demand no rule, because they are the same in all men capable of observation, and because their testimony is involuntary. The scientist has no better eyes, nor more reason, than the ignorant man; but he knows better how to turn to account the revelations that these organs furnish him concerning the visible world and concerning ideal things. The superiority of minds depends on the power of reflection (1). Logic is the regulator of the understanding; to guide thought, it sets forth the rules that must be followed in order to avoid error and doubt, or the principles that must be applied in order to arrive at truth and certainty. It is, in short, the Discipline and the Canon of the intellect, if it is granted that discipline is a curb which limits activity to keep it from going astray, and that the canon is the ensemble of the positive principles that determine the legitimate use of the faculty of knowing (2).

(1) Ch. Waddington, Essais de logique, III. Paris, 1857.

p. 27

Knowledge is true or false, truth is certain or doubtful. Error and doubt are the two reefs of thought, the posts which skepticism has seized and which science must retake. Logic, as the theory of knowing, is therefore the science of knowledge, of truth, and of certainty. Knowledge is the first product of thought; truth is its aim; and certainty, its term or conclusion. The intellect begins by knowing; but knowledge has as yet only a subjective value, relative to the subject that possesses it; is it an opinion or a truth? Knowledge attains its destination, it is what it ought to be, when it conforms to the object; truth, which expresses this equation between thought and reality, has an objective validity; it is no longer a fugitive representation of [p. 27] things, but a universal and divine principle. Yet the intellect in possession of truth has not exhausted the circle of its activity; error has disappeared, doubt remains; is it not a hypothesis? Is truth accessible to the human mind? How can we know whether things are in themselves such as we think them? What reply can be made to the objections raised against the legitimacy of our knowledge? We need, then, more than truth in order to be at peace with ourselves; we need certainty. Certainty is truth recognized as such after examination: it is the consciousness of truth; it brings back into the subject the absolute principle that has been discovered; it is the harmony of the subjective activity of the intellect and the objective reality of the world. Knowledge, truth, and certainty are the successive stages in the development of thought. The first supposes only a subject, an object, and some relation or other between the subject and the object; the second expresses in addition the equation of this relation, being a determinate relation, an exact correspondence between thought and things; the third, finally, adds to this the consciousness of the exactness of that relation.

(1) La Science de l’âme dans les limites de l’observation, 2nd part, ch. ii. Brussels, 1862.

(2) Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, transcendentale Methodenlehre.

p. 28

Logic embraces all the questions that relate to knowledge, to truth, and to certainty. It concerns itself with knowledge in general, with its origin, its various species, its legitimacy, and its organization, as notion, as judgment or proposition, and as reasoning. The notion, in fact, is the knowledge of an object considered in itself; the judgment, the knowledge of the relations that exist between things; reasoning, the knowledge of the relations that are found anew between relations or propositions. It is always knowledge that is determined and organized in these operations. Logic is therefore also the science of the organic forms of thought; it is even by this title that it has long been understood as the Organum, and that it is still sometimes treated in France and in England (1); but syllogistic, which is then its highest expression, is not [p. 28] more than one of its parts. The syllogism, and reasoning in general, abstract from the matter of the judgments they combine, as grammar neglects the meaning of the propositions it subjects to analysis; both syllogistic and grammar regard only formal truth, the relation of words and notions, whereas logic must study knowledge from the twofold point of view of matter and form, in its legitimacy as well as in its organization. It concerns itself with real truth, with its species, its possibility, and its contrary, error. It concerns itself, besides, with certainty, with its characters, its sources, the signs by which it is recognized, and its contrary, doubt.

True and certain knowledge is scientific knowledge. Logic is therefore also the theory of science. It inquires first into the particular forms of each scientific cognition: definition, division, and demonstration. These operations are expressed in the form of judgments and of reasonings, but they go beyond formal logic, because they have regard to matter, and have value only through their conformity with the things they express. A false judgment is still a judgment, but cannot be a definition or a division; a false reasoning may be excellent as reasoning, but instead of being received as a demonstration it will be treated as a sophism, or at the very least as a paralogism, if the error is involuntary. Definition determines the comprehension, or the attributes, of objects; division sets forth their extension, or their species; demonstration binds notions to one another by the ties of causality or of sufficient reason, showing that they stand to each other as principle and consequence.

(1) Dr. Whately, Elements of Logic. 1826.

p. 29

This is not all. As each particular thought has its scientific form, the whole of science has its own. Science, in its entirety, forms a system, an organic whole which develops from within like living bodies, not by mechanical aggregation, but by intussusception. There is no system without unity, without variety of parts, without harmony [p. 29] The unity of each science is expressed in the definition of its principle; the variety is stated in the division of its object; the harmony, finally, results from the relation of all the parts, effected by demonstration. Logic is therefore also the science of systems, the theory of systematization, or, as it is also called, the Architectonic of thought. Science, finally, has means of research for reaching its end, for discovering truth, and means of exposition for making it known. These procedures constitute the methods. Must we employ analysis or synthesis to determine the objects of thought? May we content ourselves with observation and generalization in all kinds of speculation? Must we rely on induction or on analogy to arrive at some probable or certain result? All these questions, too, belong to the science whose object is science. Logic is therefore, in the last analysis, the science of methods, Methodology; it is at once Heuristic for investigation and Didactic for the expression of truth (1).

Such is the framework of logic. This science extends at once to the Dialectic of Plato, the theory of ideas or of rational knowledge, to the Analytic of Aristotle, the theory of the understanding or of discursive thought, and to the Canonic of Epicurus, the theory of sensation or of sensible knowledge, Aesthetic in the exact sense of that word. Logic is the science of knowledge, rather than the art of thinking and of knowing, as it is still commonly described. Art is a regulated activity, inspired by feeling and developed by the imagination, according to the principle of the beautiful. Logic has for its principle the true; it can indeed also unfold itself in life as an art, by formulating itself in language; this art must rest on the science of thought and depends upon it, but it does not constitute it. The art of thinking is to logic what the art of speaking is to the science of language, what rhetoric is to grammar.

(1) Duval-Jouve, Traité de logique ou Essai sur la théorie de la science. Paris, 1844.

p. 30

However extensive it may be, logic is one, like truth, like science. There are no more two logics, the one practical, for the use of the ordinary people, the other theoretical, for the use of scientists, than there are two moralities, one for private life, the other for public life. All rational beings, at all ages and at all stages of culture, follow the same laws in the operations of the intellect, as they obey the same laws in their moral activity. Logic is regulated neither by race, nor by climate, nor by temperament, but by the nature of the mind, which is immutable. The logic of Aristotle is the logic of the human race. The learned are mistaken like men of the world, and men of the world meet with truth like the learned, but all are mistaken and recognize truth in the same manner. All logical theories, all the conditions of science, are common to them. The only difference that can be made between them is that some think, judge, and reason according to laws of which they are not conscious, or which they have not analyzed, whereas the others apply laws which they have recognized as legitimate.

I I . T H E R E L AT I O N S O F L O G I C

From the notion of logic its relations with the other sciences are easily deduced. Is it a formal or a material science, historical or philosophical, particular or general? What, finally, is its place among the various kinds of sciences?

p. 31

If we call material the sciences that deal with beings or substances, such as mineralogy, botany, zoology, anthropology, and theology, and formal those that deal with the properties or qualities of a substance, with the relations that exist between things, with the actions and manifestations of beings, such as mathematics, ethics, right, and philology, there is no doubt that logic is a formal science; for its [p. 31] object is not the mind, the substance that thinks, but the property of thinking which that substance possesses. Yet it must not be forgotten that this property is itself a real and not an imaginary object, comprised in the totality of things, as are space, time, motion, and other qualities, and that logic must study it in its essence and in all its applications, considering it apart, in an abstract manner, as geometry, chronometry, and mechanics do with regard to the forms of nature.

p. 32

It is in another sense that logic is ordinarily called a formal science, or the science of the formal laws of thought. By this is meant that this science applies only to the connection of thought, to the sequence or consequence that must be found in notions, in judgments, in reasonings, in abstraction from their objective validity (1). This conception dominates the whole school of Kant. It is very true that the theory of the operations of thought does not consider the matter of which they are composed, or at least that any matter is good enough for them; a judgment, whether borrowed from astronomy or from astrology, from chemistry or from alchemy, remains none the less subject to all the laws of the intellect, and falls exactly within the framework of the division of judgments. This part of logic may rightly, apart from a few details, be called formal or subjective logic. But it is a mistake to confine the whole of logic within these narrow limits, or to judge of the whole by the part. The syllogism is a two-edged weapon, which can serve sophistry as well as science. “Most of the errors of men come much more from their reasoning on false principles than from their reasoning badly according to their principles (2).” There is no other cause for the discredit into which logical studies have fallen in France than the pretension [p. 32] to continue, in spite of progress, the work of the schoolmen, and to see in logic only the art of reasoning, or still less, the science of the laws of reasoning. Logic is the science of knowledge, and since knowledge expresses a relation between the subject and the object, it must be determined from this double point of view, and consequently studied in its truth and in its certainty, as well as in thought, as a psychological phenomenon. Knowledge is legitimate and scientific only at this price. The theory of truth and of certainty escapes the subjective forms of thought, and constitutes a real logic as opposed to syllogistic. The theory of science unites these two faces of knowledge, and composes a logic at once formal and real.

(1) William Hamilton, Fragments de philosophie, translated by Peisse. Paris, 1840.

(2) Arnauld, Logique de Port-Royal, 3rd part. 1662.

p. 33

What may have given rise to this misunderstanding is that logic does not leave the generalities of knowledge, or that it itself makes no application of its principles to this or that domain of reality. It is distinguished in this from the particular sciences. Chemistry and mechanics develop the knowledge that we possess concerning the combination of bodies and the laws of motion, and seek truth and certainty in that part of the world. Logic confines itself to setting forth the general theory of knowledge, the general theory of truth, the general theory of certainty. It is no more the science of truth in the natural order than the science of truth in the moral or religious order; it is both at once, since it treats of truth in general. If it left this elevated region, if it wished, according to the counsels of Hegel, to determine knowledge in all its details, it would stifle the other sciences and would itself be the universal science. Such is not its scope. It skirts the particular sciences without stopping at them, and hastens to arrive at the principles that dominate the whole labor of thought. The particular sciences in this respect depend on logic, but they are subject to it in one respect only. Logic has no right of control or of censure over the propositions they contain, considered in their objective validity, but [p. 33] it can verify the manner in which these propositions have been obtained, and pronounce upon their relation of conformity or opposition to the general conditions of method, of systematization, and of science. The logician has no infused knowledge, but he has the right to criticize everywhere what is contrary to the principles of scientific knowledge. Has a physicist failed in the rules of observation or of induction? logic notes it, but makes no new observations upon facts that are not within its competence. Is a definition faulty in geometry, a demonstration incomplete in geology? logic points them out, but proposes no others, for lack of arguments in these matters. Logic, in a word, as the general science of human knowledge, is the normal science, which must serve as guide and as ideal to all the others. It is by this title that it is called the preparatory science, Propaedeutic, and the instrument or organ of all the sciences. We do not yet know whether logic itself is possible as a science, but assuredly no science would be possible if logic were not. The impossibility of logic would overthrow the legitimacy of our knowledge in general, and would render vain thenceforth all hope of grasping truth in whatever order of things it may be.

Logic is not the general science, without restriction, but a general science, the general science of knowledge. It need not inquire into the objective validity of all our cognitions, but into knowledge in general. It does not divorce itself from reality, but neither has it to demonstrate the truth of all things. It is important to define these points exactly, in order to find one’s bearings in logical speculations, and to recognize what is well founded and what is illusory in the objections which a certain school raises against the old logic (1).

p. 34

Hegel, who reproaches logic with having separated itself from metaphysics, by abandoning all inquiry into the ground of things in order to keep to the pure forms of thought, [p. 34] falls itself into the opposite excess, and ends by confounding two distinct parts of knowledge. If we divide the sciences into historical and philosophical, the former dealing with the facts or phenomena of life, the latter with principles or with general and eternal truths, logic is before all else a philosophical science; for it is the general science of knowledge, considered in its immutable essence, in its conditions and its universal laws. It abandons to experimental psychology the study of the facts that mark the becoming of thought, of imagination, of memory, and takes hold only of that product of thought which is called knowledge, in order to examine it in its essential characters. But logic is not on that account the whole of philosophy. Philosophy has for its objects God, the world, and humanity, whereas logic has for its object only knowledge.

The first principles of philosophy constitute metaphysics, the general science of being, ontology. The object of logic belongs to the science of man and to the science of God, inasmuch as human knowledge proceeds from the self and is grounded in the divine knowledge, inasmuch as our science, in other words, has its ultimate reason in omniscience. Psychology and metaphysics are in this respect the auxiliary sciences of logic, for they furnish to all our knowing its starting point and its absolute principle. But logic results from another point of view, which better indicates its relations with metaphysics. Principles, in fact, may be considered either as they exist, or as they are known, according to the distinction that is made between thought and things. Logic rests on that particular kind of principles which are called principles of knowledge (principia cognoscendi). Metaphysics, on the contrary, is the science of principles in general, as they exist (principia essendi). Now these two aspects mutually presuppose each other without being confounded: thought must accord with reality, and reality is destined to be known by minds. Hence the reciprocal dependence of logic and metaphysics.

(1) A. Véra, Logique de Hegel, Paris, 1859.

p. 35

Logic depends on metaphysics, since the science of principles in general is also the science of the principles of logic, as they exist. This is why logic can be treated as a branch of metaphysics, in the synthetic part of science, as the deduction of the absolute principle (1). But metaphysics in its turn depends on logic, since the science of the general conditions of scientific knowledge is also the science of the possibility of metaphysics as a science. Metaphysics must satisfy the laws of thought, as logic must satisfy the laws of reality. When both are exact, they necessarily agree; but in the contrary case they contradict each other, and have the right to check each other mutually. Logic then attacks metaphysics, by demonstrating that it fails in the rules of method or of systematization; and metaphysics refutes logic, by proving in its turn that the principles which serve it as a basis are illusions, hypotheses, without foundation in the nature of things, and that the axioms which it rejects, or which it applies only in one sense, are in every respect the most incontestable truths, witness the law of contradiction.

III. THE UTILITY OF LOGIC

p. 36

The advantages of logic are those of philosophy: as a general science, it elevates, extends, and ripens thought, and tends to exert the same influence upon feeling and upon will. Philosophy, by giving to the faculties of the human soul the elevation, the extension, and the maturity which distinguish us from the lower beings of creation, by directing the spiritual forces toward the whole of things and toward the absolute principle, the ideal of reason, forms the character and gives to man the salutary conviction of his dignity, of his [p. 36] moral worth, of his freedom, at the same time that it inspires in him, with the feeling of his limitation, the virtue of tolerance and the desire of impartiality toward all doctrines. Logic has a large share in this influence of philosophy upon the culture of the mind. It contributes to it above all by disengaging the intellectual side of human life, by pointing out the part of thought in the work of our destination.

Science is beyond dispute the first guarantee of the improvement of man. It is not only mistress of the mind, but also of the heart and of the will, for psychology teaches that our affections and our resolutions are gradually regulated by our convictions and are modified along with them. Now there are no serious convictions without logic. A right judgment commands rectitude in conduct; a false judgment accommodates itself to every deviation from duty, to every capitulation of conscience. The rigor of acts corresponds to the rigor of individual opinions, and our opinions, whether conformable or contrary to reason, are strengthened or set right only by science (1). Moreover, man can accomplish only what he understands; to whatever labor he applies himself, he must know in order to succeed. The science that teaches the use of thought is therefore of the highest importance for the success of our efforts; and what is true in private life remains true in social life. The progress of society is in direct proportion to the intellectual culture of its members. Art and industry, morality and religion, rise or fall according to instruction. The average of capacities is the exact measure of the prosperity of States.

(1) Krause, Abriss des Systemes der Logik, Göttingen, 1828.

p. 37

But science is not only a condition for the realization of the ends of life; it is itself an essential part of our destiny. Truth is the aim of thought; certainty is the reward of our constancy in the pursuit of that aim. Man is restless, agitated, exposed to every sort of disappointment, as long as he has not attained [p. 37] self-evidence. The mind can enjoy the goods of this world in security only when its convictions are formed. Certainty is therefore an element of the very happiness that is allotted to us. Now it is logic, once again, that teaches us wherein truth and certainty consist, how they are acquired, and how science is formed. If science is necessary to man in order to realize his destiny as a whole, if science is useful in itself, as an integral part of the rational life, can it seriously be asked what use the science of science is?

The criticisms directed in our day against the study of logic proceed only from an incomplete notion of that science. A distinguished author complains bitterly of the abandonment of logic in philosophical teaching in France. Whose fault is it, if not that of the authors who have treated only the forms of thought, and who have not even understood that in these forms the general laws of knowledge are still to be found? Raise again the lofty questions of science, of truth, of certainty, of method; set them forth in their organic relations, as the development of the theory of thought; show that our knowledge is legitimate under certain conditions and that skepticism has finished its mission, and the educated public, I am convinced, in spite of the discouragement and indifference that prevail in our day, will follow you and support you.

Logic, it is said, does not create specialists. Doubtless, and the reason is simple: logic is a general science. It teaches neither chemistry, nor calculus, nor law, nor physiology; it makes neither mathematicians, nor jurists, nor physicians; but it teaches what is common to all the sciences. It is indispensable to all scientists; does it follow that it is useful to no one? People think today that they have said everything when they have pronounced the word specialty. They do not notice that specialties pushed to the extreme destroy the harmony of the soul and themselves become contrary to the scientific spirit, by restricting more and more the horizon of the intellect. That social labor must be divided as the various

(1) Ph. Damiron, Cours de philosophie, logic; preface, 1836.

p. 38

Logic. — I. 3 [p. 38] branches of human activity are perfected and their applications multiply, no one denies; but specialization has its limits, beyond which it becomes a defect. Let us not forget that man is man before all else, and that he has the duty of developing as such in every aspect of his nature. Specialties should reveal themselves only on the broad basis of the general culture of the mind. No one disputes that education is a good and an advantage for all careers, even the humblest. Well, then, logic is for the intellect, to whatever science one may devote oneself, what education is for the whole soul. Logic, by discussing the theory of knowledge in the whole range of its applications, trains the understanding; it strengthens and nourishes thought, it gives it the consciousness of its worth and of its resources, and this acquired strength is not a burden but a benefit to the scientist.

p. 39

The domain of human knowledge is still far from being exactly circumscribed. How many questions, how many controversies, how many hypotheses hover to this day over the various parts of science! Theologians are at grips with philosophers, naturalists with metaphysicians; nay, thinkers with thinkers in every class! And what is the dispute about? About the competence of faith and of reason, about the scope of observation and of synthesis, about the part played by the senses and by consciousness, about the origin, the formation, the value, about all the details of human knowledge. These questions, which should be put by all who give themselves to intellectual work, since one must know the instrument one handles, are almost foreign to everyone. How many misunderstandings in the sciences, for want of a preparatory study of the faculties of the mind, or of a sufficient criticism of the whole of our knowledge! Take a few authors at random and compare! Here is an abbé who, in the very midst of the nineteenth century and in the very midst of logic, comes to speak to us of supernatural light, of infused knowledge, and of inspired intellectual virtues. Reason, he says, makes us know that God is, but in order to know God in himself, [p. 39] faith is needed. And faith teaches us that “Jesus Christ is at once wisdom itself, personal wisdom, entire wisdom, divine and human wisdom. He is the source of all wisdom; he is the model and the type of our wisdom; he is its means, its way, its right way, and, if I dare say so, its method. As for science, he is its term, the truth; he is its way, he is its principle and its life (1).” Here is a new logic, unknown to Aristotle, for the use of believers.

Scientists, on the other hand, exalt observation, and, without suspecting that there are other procedures for thought, they forget the limits of their method and ceaselessly confound it with intuition, with induction and analogy, with deduction itself. Other thinkers respect only a priori cognitions, despise experience, and do not perceive that they are constantly at war with themselves in order to keep as far as possible within the bounds of universal experience. Then come the theorists who, hoping to reconcile sensualism and idealism, wishing to spare both observation and speculation, award the palm successively to these two tendencies of the soul, distinguishing between the logical order of thought and the chronological order of our knowledge. Where is the truth in all this? Are Descartes and Bacon right against theology, Locke against Descartes, Leibniz against Locke, Kant against Leibniz, or Krause against Kant? The authority of the great critic still stands, and it is neither the ambitious propositions of the Hegelians nor the timid observations of the eclectics that will dethrone it. A new analysis of the faculties of knowing is required to undo the work of Kant. As long as it has not been proposed, discussed, and adopted, skepticism will reign in pure psychology, in rational cosmology, and in metaphysics. If the immortality of the soul and the existence of God rest only on moral arguments without value for theoretical reason, how can we seriously think of combating materialism and atheism, which are again invading men’s consciences?

(1) A. Gratry, Logique, bk. v, ch. iii. Paris, 1858.

p. 40

This is what ought to occupy logicians, for all this concerns only the scope and the limits of human knowledge. Let us not disdain the syllogism, but let us agree that the question of God and of the moral order of the world takes precedence over that of the forms of thought.

Bossuet was quite right when he said that logic is one of those sciences which tend to action, and which are called practical (1). To think is to act; the activity of thought is the activity par excellence, which accompanies and enlightens all the other tendencies of the soul. If logic had no other result than to give a suitable direction to this activity, to rid us of our prejudices, and to make us contract by exercise good intellectual habits, its study would still have to be recommended. “All the generations that have honored and cultivated logical studies have recognized that they contributed to the progress of the intellect, and that, for example, they introduced into our ideas and into our language order, clearness, precision, solidity, and exactness. In truth, there is not an intellectual quality that these studies cannot maintain and develop in those who have the germ of it. Wise precepts, if joined with assiduous practice, can instill deeply in us all the scientific virtues: exactness of definitions, rigor of reasoning, considered either in its form or in the objects to which it relates, the regular use of the inductive method, a just and exact measure of freedom and of deference to the authority of testimony, clearness of ideas, precision of terms, subtlety in unraveling difficulties of every kind, sagacity in inventing arguments, etc., etc. I stop; it would take too long to enumerate all the advantages that may be drawn from a good logical discipline (2).”

(1) Bossuet, Logique, introduction.

(2) Ch. Waddington, Essais de logique, I. Paris, 1857.

p. 41

I V. T H E D I V I S I O N O F L O G I C

The division of a science must issue from its very definition. The definition sets forth the object under study; the division indicates the various points of view from which that object can be considered. These points of view reduce to three: the whole, the parts, and the relation of the parts to the whole.

The object of logic is knowledge. It is therefore knowledge itself that we must consider successively in its totality and in its manifold determinations in order to obtain a complete division of logic.

The first part of logic is concerned with knowledge in general. What is it to know? What do we know? What are the sources of our knowledge? How do we know things, or what are the conditions and the laws of our knowledge? Is our knowledge legitimate, or can it be? Such are the principal points that concern the theory of knowledge as a whole.

The second part of logic treats of knowledge considered in its content. We know objects and relations, and we perceive new relations between these relations. These three determinations of thought are called notion, judgment, and reasoning. They are the object of Formal Logic. But to form is opposed matter. Do we know things and their relations as they are? These questions, which regard truth and error, belong to Real Logic. Matter and form, object and subject, unite in the consciousness that we have of truth. Hence certainty and its contrary, doubt.

p. 42

The third part of logic studies, finally, knowledge fully developed in all its elements, true and certain knowledge, in a word scientific knowledge. It therefore sets forth the theory of science, combining knowledge, as the product of thought, with truth, which is its ideal, and with certainty, which completes it. What are the various forms of our scientific knowledge; in [p. 42] other words, what become of our judgments and our reasonings when they join real truth to the formal truth of the operations of the understanding? Definitions, divisions, and demonstrations. How are these scattered cognitions to be grouped in a single whole, in a body of doctrines which possesses at once, like organized beings, unity, variety, and harmony? By system. And what means have we to constitute or to set forth science as a system of true and certain knowledge? Method, which comprises analysis and synthesis, that is to say, observation and generalization, induction and analogy, deduction and construction.

Such is the regular division of logic. But as it is important today to insist on the first part, which is almost entirely new, I am persuaded that it will be preferable to modify this division slightly by giving a common title to the last two parts. The theory of knowledge as a whole is, in fact, the general part of logic, that which goes back to principles, stops at generalities, and demands no thorough study of the various operations of thought. On the other hand, the theory of notions, of judgments, and of reasonings, the theory of truth, of certainty, and of their contraries, the theory of definition, of division, and of demonstration, the theory of systems and of methods, is the special part of logic, the only one which has been the object of sustained inquiries since the origin of this science, and which enters into the detail of the questions set down in its program.

Apart from this change, the second division coincides perfectly with the first, and moreover falls within the idea of logic as the science of human knowledge.

The general part treats of knowledge considered as a whole, in its species, its laws, and its legitimacy. It concerns itself, therefore, with the formation, or the generation, of knowledge and with the constitution of science.

p. 43

The special part, which embraces the whole content of traditional logic, everything that belongs to the Organum [p. 43] of Aristotle and of Bacon, treats precisely of the organization of knowledge. What, in effect, are notion, judgment, and reasoning in formal logic? The organic forms of thought, the operations in which knowledge is molded, according as it has for its object beings or relations, whatever its intrinsic value may otherwise be. What are definition, division, and demonstration? The organic forms of scientific knowledge, of knowledge arrived at its term, clothed with the characters of truth and of certainty. What is system, if not the organic form of the whole of science? Every organism is a system, and every scientific system is the faithful reproduction of an organized body under the conditions of intelligence. What, finally, is method, if not the very organ of science, that is to say, the instrument by whose aid science is formed and developed?

GENERAL PART

THEORY OF KNOWLEDGE

PDF 45

BOOK ONE

THE NOTION OF KNOWLEDGE

p. 48

Psychology teaches that the human mind possesses three fundamental faculties, irreducible, always distinct from one another, never separated in life: thought or intellect, feeling, and will. Two of these faculties, feeling and will, are foreign to logic—not that we can think without performing an act of will or without experiencing some emotion, but thought has its own laws and must not be diverted from its end by the influence of the other faculties of the soul. Science is not an affair of feeling and does not conform to our desires: we must see things as they are, and not as they please us or as we would wish them to be. Feeling and will can sustain, fortify, and warm thought, but they must not weigh upon it or lead it astray. The intellect alone has the mission of acquiring truth and certainty. It is therefore the intellect that we shall have to study [p. 48] apart in logic, sheltering it from the suggestions of the heart and the caprices of the will, without forgetting, however, that our three faculties are intimately united in all the manifestations of the soul. The possibility of this abstraction, on which all the sciences rest, is itself a property of thought.

p. 49

Thought is the faculty of knowing. To think is to have consciousness of an object, and when we have consciousness of an object, we distinguish it, we see it, we know it in some manner or to some degree. But this act of consciousness is itself manifold: at one time it concerns a prior fact that we wish to recall, at another a present fact or a principle that we approach for the first time. In the first case thought shows itself as memory; in the second, as imagination, as reflection, or as reason. Memory is not, properly speaking, a faculty of knowing, but of recognizing what we have already known; its function is to preserve the cognitions acquired, and not to acquire new cognitions: in this it is opposed to the other applications of thought. Imagination and the senses are in turn opposed to reason, as the fact is to the principle, or the image to the idea: sensibility and reason are the receptive organs of the mind that furnish us the matter of our cognitions; but the one puts us in relation with individual objects, completely determined in time or in space, of which it gives us a representation, a sensible intuition, whereas the other opens to us the higher world of laws, of causes, of universal and necessary principles, of which it procures for us an intellectual intuition. Imagination and reason, finally, are opposed to reflection or the understanding, as receptivity to spontaneity or as the matter to the form of knowledge, according to the testimony of Kant. The understanding is thought active, attentive, personal, which directs its activity upon the data of the senses and of reason, which interprets them, judges them, analyzes them in order to draw cognitions from them. Such is the system of the intellectual faculties of the mind that results from the psychological study of the [p. 49] thought and that will guide us in the theory of knowledge (1).

1. Will. Mind. 2. Feeling.

1. Conservation of cognitions: Memory.

1. External: Senses.

1. Sensibility.

3. Thought. 2. Formation 1. Matter. 2. Internal: Imagination.

of cognitions. 2. Reason.

2. Form: Reflection or understanding.

Thought, like feeling and will, is at once faculty, activity, force, and tendency. As faculty, it can know; it is the source of all our possible cognitions; as activity, it knows; it is the cause of our actual cognitions, present or past; as force, it increases or diminishes the number of our cognitions, it extends or restricts the horizon of the intellect, it makes our perceptions livelier or slower, more penetrating or more confused, richer or more incomplete; as tendency, finally, it marks our individual preferences, it inclines us toward certain orders of truths, it characterizes our dispositions or our aptitudes for this or that part of the vast domain of the sciences.

p. 50

Thought is to knowledge as cause is to effect. All our acquired cognitions are produced by intellectual activity, and our future cognitions can be realized only by the same energy. But in considering thought as the cause of knowledge, we must not abstract from the mind. The faculties of the soul are not beings having an existence independent of the self; they are only properties or distinct points of view of one and the same substance. It is the mind itself that is the cause of all spiritual acts, and consequently [p. 50] of acts of knowledge as well. Only, in so far as it knows, the mind is called thought. In saying that knowledge is an effect or a product of thought, we therefore mean to imply that our cognitions derive their origin from the mind considered not as an affective or voluntary being, but as an intelligent being, as a thinking thing, according to the expression of Descartes.

This being laid down, what is knowledge? Is it a substance or a property; in other words, is it a being endowed with a proper existence, or some quality of a being? The Greeks might have answered: it is a divinity, it is Minerva or Apollo; but the reign of hypostases is past, and knowledge is now no more than a property, a property of the mind. Is it a simple property, which presupposes only a single term, like unity, form, existence, or a relative property, which expresses a relation between two things, like cause or condition? It is a relative property, for it contains an antithesis. For there to be knowledge, two things are needed, the one that knows, the other that is known; an intelligent being and an intelligible object are needed. Knowledge is therefore a property of the mind, considered in its relations with things. This definition does not exclude self-knowledge, for the word “thing” embraces all possible objects, without excepting the self. By virtue of the consciousness and the feeling that it has of itself, by virtue of its personality, the mind has internal relations with its own essence, as it has external relations with foreign things. It exists, it acts, it has rights and duties for itself, and thus becomes the object of its own thought.

(1) Psychologie, la science de l’âme dans les limites de l’observation. Bruxelles, 1862.

p. 51

Knowledge therefore has a threefold content: two terms and a relation. The two terms are called the subject and the object of knowledge. Knowledge properly expresses the relation between what knows, as subject, and what is known, as object. The relation presupposes at once the distinction and the union of the two terms.
