They are distinct and opposed to each other, since they are two: what knows is not identical with what is known; the mind is not successively [p. 51] all the objects of which it thinks. It is quite possible that the laws of thought are the same as the laws of reality, but this certainly does not mean that the intellect is the same thing as the substances or the properties of every sort with which it is occupied. It is not in this sense that the proposition of some ancient philosophers can be justified: the same can be known only by the same. But if thought and reality remain distinct in knowledge, they are also united. Knowledge bears witness to a remarkable phenomenon, namely that the subjective world of thought and the objective world of things are not separated by any barrier, do not remain strangers to each other, but penetrate each other mutually. Whatever the cause of this fact may be, we must admit it.

p. 52

In knowledge, the object passes into us, gives itself to the mind, without changing its nature or its position, and becomes present to consciousness. Who says relation says union; in knowledge, the union is established between the subject that thinks and the object that is thought. There is in this some reflection of the relations that anthropology observes between soul and body, things profoundly distinct and yet intimately united. However strange the fact may appear, however difficult its explanation, if we go back to the reason of things, mind and matter, whatever Malebranche and Leibniz may say, are not isolated in man, but influence and modify each other reciprocally. A union of the same kind is effected in knowledge: the mind has consciousness of the object as it has consciousness of itself, and if we call intimate the relation of a being with itself, when it has consciousness and feeling of itself, we may say that the subject and the object of thought are intimately united in the self. There may be an intermediary between the intellect and the external world; bodies may pass through the channel of the senses and affect our nerves in order to penetrate to the mind; but the result remains the same: from the moment they are known, external objects exist in us, in our imagination, such as they appear to us in space, and present themselves to thought as often and as soon as we will; we have consciousness of them [p. 52] then as of ourselves, in whatever manner we may have discovered them.

To determine this notion of knowledge, we must analyze it in the three elements it contains, as subject, as object, and as relation.

CHAPTER ONE

THE SUBJECT OF KNOWLEDGE

The subject of knowledge is thought, that is to say, the mind as an intelligent being. Intellect and thought are synonymous for us. And as the mind is one and its intellect is one, the subject of knowledge is always the same for each of us. The objects of thought may vary to infinity; the subject does not vary. However manifold our cognitions may be, they are always our cognitions, that is to say, the manifestations of one and the same individual substance. The whole sum of things can thus be reflected in each intellect; each self is a mirror of the world. Here again we see an image of human nature. Anthropology teaches that man is an epitome of the entire creation, that all the forces of the physical world and of the spiritual world are balanced in humanity and show themselves there at their highest power. The part is like the whole. The thought of rational beings reproduces, it seems, the universal organization, or becomes, as Leibniz said of his monads, representative of the entire universe.

p. 53

The subject of knowledge is the self. It is from the self that all our thoughts proceed; it is to the self that they belong and are referred as phenomena; it is in the self that they abide and are grouped into a whole. However [p. 53] manifold our cognitions may be, they are united into one in the unity of consciousness. It seems, then, that the self has a perpetual and incontestable consciousness of itself. In effect, the self affirms itself in all its particular affirmations; the thought I does not leave the field of the intellect, whatever object we think of, whether we know it or are ignorant of it. When we speak of the external world, we set it over against the self, and we grasp both terms at once, for the world is external only in relation to the self. When we think of our fellow men, we turn back upon ourselves, for it is to the self that other men are like. As soon as we discover thought, activity, or freedom by psychological analysis, we attribute them as qualities to the self, and each of us will say: my thought, my activity, my freedom. The thought I is therefore beneath all our other thoughts; these presuppose it and complete it, while it presupposes none of them and accompanies them all. This is why the thought I is the primitive fact of consciousness and the starting point of science (1).

The thought I is a simple notion, which affirms the self without affirming anything of the self. It cannot therefore be expressed in the form of a judgment, for judgment requires two terms. The first proposition that, in the logical order, follows upon the intuition of oneself is this: I think; the second is I know. At the initial point, the self is still indeterminate; now it determines itself successively and recognizes itself in consciousness as a thing that thinks and that knows. What is the value of these two judgments? Often they are taken as synonymous, and this equivalence is grounded on the fact that we cannot think without an object, and that there is knowledge as soon as there is a subject, an object, and a relation. To think of God is to know him to some degree, it is to distinguish him from what is not himself. We do not think in a void, although we sometimes say, to stop an indiscretion: I was thinking of nothing. Whoever is willing to observe himself will find that his thought always has an object, trivial or grave, chimerical

p. 54

Logic. — I. 4 [p. 54] or real. We can think of the impossible, no doubt; but the impossible is also something: it is the limit of the possible, and as such an important and difficult object of science; if it has no objective existence, it still exists in us, in our imagination. The search for the quadrature of the circle, for example, may be a vain attempt, but it is not an empty thought, for it has for its object the relation of curved lines to straight lines. The reading of marvelous tales often leads the mind astray, but may also give rise to ingenious combinations that are perhaps realized on some globe. Fables, legends, and stories, considered as elements of the education and instruction of the people, give no fewer lessons than experience. Every thought, then, has an object, and in this sense to think is to know.

We do not say with the sensualists: to think is to sense; for sensation is never a thought. Nor do we say: to think is to represent or to imagine something; for if representation by the imagination is an act of the intellect, it is not the whole intellect; to think is also to generalize, to comprehend, to judge, to conclude: every reflection, every conception, in a word every act or combination of the understanding, is a manifestation of thought, whether its object be sensible or non-sensible.

(1) La Science de l’âme dans les limites de l’observation, 1st part, ch. II.

p. 55

But if, instead of considering thought in its acts and in its products, where it is identified with knowledge, we regard it in its source, as a property of the mind, the propositions I think, I know cease to be equivalent. We are then concerned with thought and not with a thought, and if a thought can signify a cognition, it is no longer so with thought. Thought is a faculty of the soul, knowledge is an act, a determinate state of the understanding. Thought is to knowledge as potency is to actuality: it is the property of the mind that produces knowledge. This distinction leads to a second. Thought is permanent, continuous in life; knowledge is fugitive, transitory, always in the course of development [p. 55] and transformation; the one is, the other becomes, according to the ancient value of these words.

The mind thinks without ceasing, whether it will or not, because thought is one of its attributes, or because it is of its essence to think. Observation, it is true, does not suffice to establish the continuity of thought in all the states and at every instant of life; but it establishes that there exists no situation of the soul from which the intellect is positively excluded, and that thought presents itself to consciousness as soon as we observe ourselves. Incoherent and disconnected thoughts, as in dream and madness, are not meditations, no doubt, but they are still thoughts. The stages of culture offer in this respect the same phenomenon as the periodic and abnormal states of life. Thought persists at all ages, now confused and slow, now clear and lively. The child thinks before speaking, whatever Viscount de Bonald may say, and must think in order to learn to speak. We have no recollection of a first act in the series of our thoughts, no presentiment of a final act. As far as inner sense extends into the past and into the future, as memory and as foresight, we have always thought and we shall not cease to think.

p. 56

Is it the same with knowledge? No; our cognitions are formed and unformed, are born, ripen, and sometimes die, according to the ages and situations of the soul. The child in the cradle knows nothing as yet of the society of which he is a member, of the family he is entering, of the external world that will be the theater of his activity, of the very body that is to be the companion and the instrument of his soul in its earthly existence. Perhaps the soul has lived already before appearing on this globe, but assuredly it has lost all recollection of its previous life when it enters, through language, into communication with its fellows. Whether through ignorance or through forgetfulness, it has therefore everything to learn in order to come up to the level of its age. Such is the aim of the social function of instruction. Thanks to teaching, new cognitions are constantly deposited in young minds and are transmitted with new increases [p. 56] to future generations. Study or personal training perfects the notions acquired; want of application drives them out and abolishes them. Human knowledge is therefore in a state of perpetual fluctuation: every day we learn something, every day we forget something. In the ascending period of life, gains exceed losses; the contrary takes place in the declining period. Apart from this law, everything depends on circumstances and on individual dispositions. What one knows, another is ignorant of; what one retains, another loses.

p. 57

But if cognitions are essentially variable as to their objects, are they not fixed at least in another respect? Do we not always know something, and is not knowledge then a permanent property of the soul? Granted; but knowledge in this sense is no more than the act of thought in general, in abstraction from this or that object, and we come back to the identity of the judgments I think, I know. Every man, in effect, though he were deaf and dumb or an imbecile, knows something, and is a man only on this condition. He distinguishes the objects that surround him, he finds his bearings in the external world, he has opinions about his fellows, he knows himself. Even the child, before being initiated into conventional language, is not destitute of all knowledge; for if speech rests essentially on the signification of sounds, that is to say, on the correspondence established by usage between the series of sounds and the series of acts of the mind, it is manifest that, in order to learn to speak, we must already have consciousness of the spiritual acts that the sounds express. Without self-knowledge, sounds would remain sounds and would never become words. Moreover, before speaking our languages, the child already possesses in his gestures and in his cries natural signs for the expression of his thoughts, his feelings, his desires, and knows very well how to make his parents obey him. It seems, then, that knowledge is innate like thought: who, then, remembers the precise moment when he acquired a first cognition? Can the primitive fact of consciousness have an origin in time? Yet, as our [p. 57] memories do not reach back to the first year of our earthly existence, it is impossible to decide by way of observation whether our cognitions have or have not a beginning in this world. All that can be affirmed with some likelihood is that knowledge is to the mind what light is to the eyes, that intelligible light has its dawn as physical light has, that we do not pass abruptly from the darkness of ignorance to the clearness of science, that knowledge, in short, is at first in us only in the state of a vague glimmer, and that it emerges insensibly and continuously, by a movement more or less rapid, according to the energies of the soul, the organic dispositions, and the circumstances without.

CHAPTER TWO

THE OBJECT OF KNOWLEDGE

The object of knowledge is as manifold as reality: it embraces first of all everything that is known, then everything that is intelligible; and is not the intelligible everything that is? To be sure, we do not yet know everything that exists in space, in time, in the entire world; but what we do not know at present, shall we not know one day, and do not some of our fellows know it already? By intelligible I mean what is accessible to the thought of rational beings, and I take care not to confound the limits of my own knowledge with those of human knowledge. Is there an object that is not intelligible, that cannot be known in some manner or other, true or false, complete or partial? It would be impossible to decide the question without trespassing on metaphysics, but it is important, at least, to understand its meaning.

p. 58

An object that was not intelligible would have this peculiarity, that, unlike all the others, it would sustain no relation to thought. It would exist in itself, but not for consciousness; it would be for us as if it were not. No one would ever have suspected its existence, and consequently it would have received a name in no language. For everything that is named is an object of thought and can be known; everything that is affirmed or denied in a proposition is intelligible. Languages are therefore a public criterion of the intelligibility of things: what is not found in a lexicon might well exist without being known, but what is found there is certainly known, whether it exists or not. Here is an important point, and beyond all dispute, if we leave out of account the scientific character of knowledge; this simple observation, drawn from common sense and from the value of all languages as the expression of human thought, is already enough to set aside the numerous objections that many authors raise against the possibility of knowing certain parts of reality. That these objections should arise concerning truth and certainty, I can conceive; but concerning knowledge itself, whatever its value may be, they are no longer admissible. If we knew nothing of substance, of the infinite, of the absolute, of God, of the essence of things, how would these terms be found in our languages? Who would have created them? Was it God? But then they correspond to something real. Was it man? But then they represent at least our thoughts and exactly register the state of our knowledge.

p. 59

The object of knowledge is therefore any thing whatever, finite or infinite, possible or real, simple or composite, spiritual or physical. For an object to be known, it need not present itself in this or that part of time; it suffices that it be able to be. Knowledge excludes no mode of existence, neither the possible, nor the real, nor the necessary. Even impossibilities are determinable in science. Nor is there any reason for confining all human knowledge within the limits of the world, for suppressing [p. 59] the infinite and the absolute as objects of thought. One could not pronounce this elimination with any semblance of reason without relying at least on the notion of knowledge. But what is knowledge, if not a relation between thought and an object? What object? Any object whatever. Why one rather than another? Why should the human mind be in relation only with finite things? Because it is itself finite, we are told: the finite cannot comprehend the infinite. There is the argument: the infinite is incomprehensible! One moment! If by incomprehensible you mean inaccessible to the senses, I grant it; but besides the senses we have reason. If by that you mean inexhaustible, I agree: it takes an infinite intelligence to exhaust the infinite. But if by incomprehensible you mean inaccessible to thought, unintelligible in every respect, I deny it, and I place you in contradiction with yourself. When you say that the infinite is incomprehensible to a finite being, have you not present to thought two notions, that of the finite and that of the infinite, and do you not judge that the second infinitely surpasses the content of the first? Now this judgment attests that you know at once the finite, the infinite, and their relation, and that, moreover, you know them in truth, for you rightly affirm that it is not the finite that contains the infinite, but the infinite that envelops the finite. You are misled only by the meaning of the word “comprehend,” which you apply to knowledge. To comprehend is sometimes to contain, sometimes to know; but beware of concluding from this juxtaposition that knowledge demands a relation of containment between subject and object; otherwise you would arrive at this idealist consequence, that all that is intelligible subsists in the self, that the self is all and contains all, as Fichte asserts. The object of knowledge is present to consciousness, no doubt, but it does not cease to exist in itself, and remains what it was before being known. Knowledge implies simply a relation between subject and object; this relation is possible and perhaps necessary between the finite and the infinite, and in this sense the infinite is no more incomprehensible than the finite. How could one discourse on the infinite, whether [p. 60] to establish or to contest its reality, if the infinite were not an object of thought? But the theologians, you will say, write treatises on the dogmas, and nevertheless declare them incomprehensible. I do not undertake to present the defense of theology, nor to demonstrate the existence of the dogmas inscribed in all the religious systems; but I repeat that a thing need not exist really outside us in order to become an object of thought, for we can imagine the impossible and reflect on our own creations; the question of objective existence concerns science; what is now in question is not the value of our thought, but its reach, or the objects it can attain. Besides, if the objection is pressed, I shall add by anticipation that there is no absolute error, that the dogmas themselves have a reasonable and intelligible meaning that can be accepted by the adversaries as well as by the partisans of divine revelations (1).

p. 61

It does not appear easy to divide the objects of knowledge, for they embrace all that is, and how is the whole of things to be partitioned? The problem, however, becomes simpler if we are willing to stop at a few great lines of demarcation and have recourse to the dichotomic procedure. There are first of all things or beings (that is the most general thought we possess); there are things that subsist in themselves and others that have no proper existence, that have only a relative existence or exist only in relation to something else: we call the former substances, and the latter properties, modes, accidents, in a word, determinations of substance. Space, time, motion, spiritual and physical forces, for example, do not exist apart from the beings to which they are attributed; they can indeed be conceived in isolation and analyzed in turn, but that is an abstraction of the mind which does not conform to reality. Every property supposes a substance, but does not constitute it. How can we help thinking that there is something that supports the qualities and the [p. 61] modes; and how can we admit that substance is only the simple union of properties, a pure aggregate of things none of which could subsist without a subject to which it adheres? It may be, no doubt, that there are no more substances without attributes than attributes without substances; we do not claim that these two points of view must be separated, but they must be distinguished, as we distinguish between an organ and its functions. The first question to be put concerning a thing that we propose to determine is therefore this: is it a substance or not? Is God the order of the world or the being that exists in itself ? Is time that which changes or the quality of what changes? It is thus that we have fixed the notion of knowledge. To take a property for a substance is to hypostatize.

(1) J. Reynaud, Philosophie religieuse, Terre et Ciel. Paris, 1854.

p. 62

Some modern authors, adopting the point of view of Kant, think that we know substances only by their manifestations. Mr. Stuart Mill is of this opinion. But he speaks of knowledge only incidentally, in connection with the terms of language. Qualities, like substances, he says, are known to us only by our sensations or by other states of consciousness, including our thoughts. The author, moreover, does not appear disposed to suppress substances (1). Another writer goes further. Substance is an idol, says M. Renouvier; there is no such thing as substance, because substance is the thing in itself, stripped of every quality and every relation; it is nothingness. Substance, he adds, is known only by its attribute; the self, for example, is represented only by thought, as a thinking being; and the attribute itself is manifested only by its modes; we in no way know our thought, or thought, but only our thoughts. In short, “we know only phenomena (2).” If this last proposition, which is the author’s principle, were exact, we should have to renounce every scientific conception, [p. 62] for no science can resign itself to describing phenomena, that is to say, appearances, variable and contingent facts. The mathematical sciences claim to determine, without even having recourse to observation, the eternal and necessary properties of space, of motion, of quantities; the natural sciences seek the invariable properties of organized bodies and of matter in general; the philosophical sciences study the essence or the nature of things. What is the use of grasping fleeting phenomena, if knowledge must stop there, if beneath the passing fact nothing stable and permanent can be fixed? A droll story indeed, if the scientists, instead of saying, bodies attract one another, carnivores feed on flesh, were to proclaim gravely that they have seen some bodies falling, that they have heard tell of some cats that ate mice, and if they added, for fear of compromising themselves, that these phenomena prove absolutely nothing regarding the properties attributed by the metaphysicians to these so-called substances, to these phantoms that they call bodies and cats. The animals, in that case, would be as clever as we. For the brute, indeed, there are only phenomena or sensible manifestations; for man there is something else, there are general elements, principles, laws, which are formulated in science. Phenomena themselves have their essence, and M. Renouvier, just like the dogmatists, aspires to analyze them in themselves, although nothing, in his view, can be known in itself. How can a thinker maintain so paradoxical a system? What! Mind and thought are a collection of modes, a perpetual flux of ever-different phenomena, and you think of making a book, and you heap proposition upon proposition to define this appearance that is called the self, to determine in an immutable manner the conditions and the limits of thought, of all human thought! Do you not see, then, that you are writing against yourself, that all the principles you lay down are the condemnation of your thesis? We know only phenomena, and you set forth the laws of phenomena as ends of the [p. 63] knowledge! Is a law, then, also a phenomenon? And if we know laws, and if there are, besides, categories that invariably preside over the activity of the intelligence, how can phenomena be the sole elements of our knowledge? There is some misunderstanding underneath this. In fact, the phenomenon changes its meaning as soon as it comes into the presence of the law. There now exist “general phenomena,” “composite phenomena constantly produced,” a thing “which may seem odd, says the author, to those who restrict the name of phenomenon to the mere data of sensible and divided experience (1).” Well and good! Phenomena are no longer phenomena; but then what becomes of the consequences deduced from real phenomena? If there are general and constant phenomena, which are called laws, why should there not also be phenomena of phenomena, which would be named substances? If the epithet phenomenon can be applied “to abstractions and to ideas of genus,” why should it not equally suit absolute ideas (2)?

(1) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, bk. I, ch. III, General results. 5th ed. London, 1862.

(2) Ch. Renouvier, Essais de critique générale, I, § 13. Paris, 1854.

p. 64

Here is the question. Do we know phenomena? Yes. Do we know only phenomena? No; we know also the laws of phenomena, we know the essence or the properties of things, which do not change, whereas phenomena change ceaselessly; and as phenomena suppose properties of which they are the variable manifestations, properties in their turn suppose a substance to which they belong. All scientists are agreed on this point. Phenomena, says one of them, are modifications or changes introduced into a substance; they are the passage from one state or manner of being to another. If, for example, a body liquefies, the phenomenon is not fusibility, but fusion, that is to say, the operation by which the solid becomes [p. 64] liquid or passes from one state to another. There is no phenomenon without a property or without a substance. Every phenomenon is a property in act, every property is a phenomenon in potency (1). Physics and chemistry, says another, know matter only by properties that are the immediate or remote causes of all the phenomena it presents to our observation (2). But if it were true that we knew only phenomena, should we be authorized to conclude that there is no substance? Doubtless not: knowledge is not existence, and the limits of our knowing might not coincide with the modes of reality.

These elucidations suffice for the moment. To the question posed, what do we know? we answer: substances and properties, and by properties we understand all the modifications that can affect substances. Hence the division of the sciences into material sciences, which deal with substances or beings, and formal sciences, which treat of the properties or relations of things.

(1) Essais de critique générale, § 18.

(2) La Science de l’âme dans les limites de l’observation. Introd., ch. II, and Part I, ch. III.

p. 65

What substances do we know? The self and the not-self. Hence a new division, very important for logic. The knowledge of the self is called immanent, because all its elements, subject, object, and relation, reduce to the self. The knowledge of the not-self, on the other hand, is transcendent, because its object surpasses the sphere of individual consciousness. The first has this remarkable feature, that object and subject are one and the same being, and that the relation of subject to object consists, consequently, in an internal relation of the self with itself. It does not seem that serious objections can be raised against the validity of this sort of knowledge. It is otherwise with the second kind, where the object is no longer enclosed in the subject, where the [p. 65] knowledge expresses henceforth a relation between two things foreign to one another and constituted, perhaps, according to different or contrary laws.

What substances, in turn, does the not-self contain? Bodies, spirits, beings formed by the union of a spirit and a body, that is to say, animate or living beings. Hence the physical sciences, the psychic sciences, and the biological sciences. Man, subject for himself and object for others, belongs to each of these groups of substances, as body, as spirit, and as a being of harmony formed by the union of the soul with matter. How does the thought of these different objects develop in us? At first we know only a small number of bodies, celestial and terrestrial, organized and inorganic, accessible to our senses; but the study of astronomy, of geology, and of physics, by ceaselessly multiplying distances, periods, and numbers, leads us to pass beyond the limits of observation and makes us suppose, rightly or wrongly, that all bodies, distributed in solar systems, form only a single whole, called Nature or the corporeal world, and that this whole might well be infinite in its kind, infinite in space, in time, and composed of an infinity of stars or bodies. The thought of the spiritual world, which we oppose to the physical world, follows the same progression; we unite in one whole the souls with which we are in relation on this earth, and we arrive gradually at suspecting that creation contains an infinity of like substances, that the moral world, in other words, has no less fullness or perfection than matter, and that it is equally infinite in its kind. Spirits and bodies unite with one another, and perhaps in various degrees: human nature presents this union in its most complete and most intimate form; animals perhaps realize it under more imperfect conditions and in an unconscious manner. Be that as it may, among the beings that are neither pure spirits nor pure matter, we distinguish men, and the thought of humanity follows the same phases of development as the preceding objects.

(1) L.-A. Gruyer, Essais philosophiques, vol. I, ch. I, on phenomena in general. Paris, 1855.

(2) M.-E. Chevreul, Lettres sur la méthode en général et sur la définition du mot fait, IV. Paris, 1856.

p. 66

We rank in humanity all the men who live either on the earth or on other habitable globes in space, and although we can observe only a certain number of our fellows, we are led to believe that humanity is infinite in its kind, like the physical world and the spiritual world, of which it offers the synthesis, or that there exists in creation an infinity of rational beings at different stages of culture. We recognize, then, three orders of transcendent substances: material, immaterial, and mixed substances, and we classify these substances in three genera, the genus nature, the genus spirit, and the genus man, which we consider as each infinite in its own domain. These three genera together form the world or the universe, the cosmos, the object of cosmology.

Do we not know still other substances? We perceive none other within the limits of the world; but considering that spirits, bodies, and men are finite beings, and that a genus, even if it extended to infinity, is never more than a genus, that is to say, a part of reality, we are obliged to rise above the world and to conceive a fourth object, the infinite and absolute substance or the being of all reality, which we call God. A collection of genera cannot satisfy reason in its search for causes; we affirm that everything is brought back to unity and that there exists, outside the series of limited beings, a being who is the cause of all things, who is no longer enclosed in a genus nor opposed to any other essence, who is, in short, the infinite and absolute being in every respect. We may doubtless be mistaken on this subject, but most assuredly we have knowledge of God, and all peoples that have a worship are in the same situation.

p. 67

Such is the whole of the substances that present themselves to our thought, whatever, moreover, may be the objective validity of the notions we form of God, of nature, of spirit, and of humanity. All the substances that have ever been pointed out fall into one or other of these [p. 67] categories. Mr. Mill, who likewise set himself to search out all the kinds of things expressed by names, cites only two substances, bodies and souls. What, then, does he think of God (1)? Let us now take the second term of the division.

Everything that is not substance is a determination of a substance. Among these determinations, we distinguish on the one hand properties, qualities or attributes, and on the other, acts, states, phenomena or accidents: properties are the invariable manners of being of substance; phenomena, its variable, and therefore temporal, manners of being; both express the essence, although this word is ordinarily reserved to designate the fundamental attributes of things. The essence is manifested in the qualities, the qualities in the acts, and the being is at once the whole of its acts and of its qualities. If I make, for example, a right triangle whose sides measure 15, 20, 25 millimeters, the properties of this figure will consist in the determinate relations that exist between the angles as well as between the squares of the sides; the accidents, in the magnitude of the two acute angles and in the length of the sides; the first characters belong to the essence of the right triangle in general, the second to the essence of the individual triangle that has been constructed. In this sense, accidental states form part of the essence and are themselves properties, contingent properties, mere possibilities that have been realized. It is a property of each triangle to have sides of such a length rather than of another; it is a property of the self to find itself at this moment in this or that determinate situation.

p. 68

Every substance has properties in relation to its essence, or rather constituting it: a finite substance has finite properties, an infinite substance infinite properties. I do not know how an author could have imagined that immaterial substances are distinguished from one another only [p. 68] by the properties of the bodies to which they are united, and that they would necessarily be confounded together if they lived separated from matter (1). Psychology teaches the properties of the soul; physics, chemistry, mineralogy, the properties of bodies. Individuality makes it possible to discern from one another substances of the same species.

There are various orders of properties. The principal divisions concern simple and relative properties, fundamental and derived properties, generic and individual properties, universal and particular properties.

(1) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, bk. I, ch. III. Things denoted by names. London, 1862.

p. 69

The simple properties are those that affect substances considered in themselves, apart from all external relation; such are unity, identity, activity, force, time, space. The relative properties are those that belong to beings in so far as they are in relation to one another, and which consequently suppose at least two terms; such are causality, utility, knowledge, union, motion. Let us see some applications of this division. The modes of existence are relative properties; a thing is not possible or impossible, necessary or contingent, in itself, but only for this or that being. Possibility, reality, and necessity indicate how a thing exists in relation to another; if the relation is unique, it is necessary; if it admits several cases, it is possible; if it is effected, it is real. The length of the circumference, for example, is necessarily determined by that of the radius; the length of chords is arbitrary; in drawing a circle and a chord, we shall realize at once a necessity and a possibility. But the length of the circumference is by no means necessary in itself; it is independent of the idea of the circle in general and has a unique and constant relation only with the given radius. — Another interesting question concerning relative properties is the one that was raised by Origen on the subject of the origin of the world. This great thinker remarked that we generally grant to God certain [p. 69] attributes that imply a relation with the universe, and demonstrated that, given the eternity of God and of his attributes, the eternity of the world follows rigorously. God is cause and providence, for example. Now cause supposes an effect, and providence is conceived only with an ensemble of beings subject to a higher direction, as paternity is inseparable from filiation. The divine causality and providence therefore entail the existence of the world and of finite beings. But God did not become cause and providence at a determinate moment; he is the eternal cause and providence, otherwise he would have received an increase of qualities, which is in contradiction with the nature of the all-perfect being. If now there is no cause without an effect, no eternal cause without an eternal effect, we must admit that the world had no beginning in time. To combat this conclusion one must contest the premises. — To the relative properties there is still attached the theory of judgment and of reasoning. These operations, indeed, have no other object than to determine the relations of substances to one another, of properties to one another, and of properties to substances. Some parts of grammar can be explained by the same distinction. The substantive is the word that expresses substances or hypostatized qualities. The adjective designates properties; this general definition suffices, for it embraces all cases. The division that is made of the adjective into qualificative and determinative corresponds to the division of properties into simple and relative. The qualificatives give the simple properties, inherent in the object or considered as such; the determinatives indicate the more or less accidental and variable relations of the object spoken of, whether with the self as possessing subject, or with the position of the subject in space, or with objects of the same species from the point of view of number and rank; the numeral adjectives manifest this relation in a precise manner; the indefinite adjectives in a vague or indeterminate manner.

There are next fundamental and secondary properties, material and formal properties, constitutive

(1) P. Poulin, Qu’est-ce que l’homme? Qu’est-ce que Dieu?

p. 70

Logic. — I. 5 [p. 70] and consequent properties. The fundamental properties are commonly called essential, in opposition to the secondary qualities, which are called accidental. One must be on guard against the use of these terms; to avoid all equivocation it would be well to replace them by the words generic and individual. The fundamental attributes, in fact, inseparable from the object, are common to the entire genus, whereas the secondary attributes or modes are found only in individuals, accompanied by particular traits that distinguish each being from its fellows; but at bottom both belong to the essence, and mark the difference between the essence of the genus and that of individuals. The anatomical characters of the horse, for example, belong to the essence of this species of pachyderms; stature, strength, color, defects belong to the individual essence, realized in time according to the circumstances or accidents that mark the life of a finite being. Thought, feeling, and will are fundamental faculties inherent in all rational beings: generic properties; errors, passions, vices, on the contrary, are variously shared among persons: individual properties. The former are immutable, indelible, eternal; the latter variable, temporal, and susceptible of modifications. Errors are effaced, passions are calmed, vices are lost, as man perfects himself; but if the individual is a completely determinate being, who must with limited means strive to attain an ideal of absolute perfection, he will in all likelihood always have the property of being mistaken and of doing evil, and this possibility will still have to be realized in some manner in all the phases of his existence. Individual properties seem therefore to be only original manifestations of generic properties, or singular and accidental appropriations of the qualities that belong to the whole genus. In this sense there would be no purely individual properties; in other words, these properties would be only modes, manners of being of general and common properties. All the more reason [p. 71] for not isolating phenomena from properties, as we have already pointed out. What are the size, the agility, the special dispositions of an animal, if not the individualization of the qualities found in its species? Facts are properties in act.

p. 72

Material and formal properties concern the matter and the form of things. If by matter we understand the essence, the what, and by form the how or manner of being, everything, whether substance or property, appears to have a form, as it has an essence, and can then be considered at once in its material and formal qualities. Space and time, for example, are fundamental properties, but what kind of properties? They are forms; space is the form of matter as continuous; time is the form of all beings as they are active or as they are modified. Eternity is the form of what is immutable. Will is a material property of the mind, of which the form is liberty. Science in its turn is a property of the soul and a material property, like art; but science again has a form and a matter. The matter of science is knowledge, and knowledge must be true and certain in order to have scientific virtue. The form of science is system, and system has for its conditions unity, variety, and harmony, which are the elements of all organization. The material properties of science, considered as a whole, are therefore knowledge, truth, and certainty; its formal properties are unity, variety, and harmony. Harmony implies union and distinction, it excludes confusion and separation; hence this formula of organization: to unite without confounding, to distinguish without separating (1). The same distinction holds in the details of logic: judgment and reasoning require only a formal truth, vis formæ, resulting from the concatenation of notions and not from their intrinsic value; definition, division, and demonstration require in addition [p. 72] a material truth, vis materiæ, arising from the agreement of each notion with its object.

Properties have their properties also. Knowledge, for example, is a property of thought; responsibility, a property of will; continuity, a property of time and of space, and divisibility a property of continuity. The immediate or primitive properties in this case are called constitutive, and the properties of properties, which constitute the attributes they qualify, are simply consequent with respect to the substance to which they are attached. Responsibility, for example, is a consequent attribute of the soul, and a constitutive one of liberty.

There are, finally, common or universal properties, which appear to suit all things, and proper or characteristic attributes, which belong to a single class of objects only. Self-consciousness, for example, with the personality, the liberty, the perfectibility, and the rational life that depend on it, is a proper attribute of man among finite beings; unity, identity, activity, causality are common properties that are met with in some degree in all living beings. This is a distinction of the highest interest for logic and for metaphysics. To define things, we must give their properties, but which? Common properties alone would not allow us to distinguish the object; proper characters alone would not allow us to classify it: we must therefore combine common and proper attributes. But has not every object an innumerable quantity of properties? We must therefore make a choice. Now logic has a very sure method of summing up in a few words all the fundamental, constitutive, common, and proper attributes of an object: by virtue of the theory of extension and comprehension, the properties of the species include also the properties of the genus, of the family, of the order; the latter can therefore be omitted, and all the common properties indicated by designating the proximate genus. When we say, for example, that the dog is a carnivore, there is no longer any need to state that it is a mammal, a vertebrate, an animal, an organized being.

(1) Esquisse de philosophie morale. Introduction. Brussels, 1854.

p. 73

It suffices to add to the genus the particular character that distinguishes the object in order to give a definition at once simple and complete. Thus we shall say of the circle: a curved line whose curvature is homogeneous or always the same; the first term indicates the genus; the second the difference.

p. 74

In metaphysics, one may ask whether there truly exist universal attributes and proper attributes. We are not in a position to resolve this question. Proper attributes might well be, like individual qualities, an appropriation of more general characters; yet this very appropriation would have to have its reason in the proper essence of each object, and would already be a sufficient element of distinction. There would thus always be, if not proper attributes, at least particular manifestations of common attributes. Here is the bearing of the problem: if there are proper attributes, they are added to the common attributes; if there are none, or if they are only the common attributes manifested in a certain manner, to this or that power, all things, spirits or bodies, men or beasts, have an equal number of properties, without ceasing to be distinct. What is called inner sense in the mind, for example, would be at bottom the same thing as cohesion in matter: both properties would indicate the relation of a being with itself, but this relation would be determined, on the one hand, according to the essence of mind, and on the other, according to the essence of matter. Likewise thought and light, feeling and heat, will and motion, love and affinity would be analogous expressions of one and the same property, realized under two different forms in the physical world and in the moral world. Mind and body themselves would be equivalent terms, homologous organisms that represent, under two opposite aspects, like the sexes, one and the same nature. In a word, all beings would proceed from being and would have its properties to some degree, each according to its own essence. Such is at bottom the theory of the unity of substance, which it would be wrong to confound with pantheism, since it only expresses this religious thesis that [p. 74] everything has its cause in God and bears the traces of its origin. “Ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia.”

Let no one be astonished that this question of common properties throws us into the current of metaphysics: it is the question of the categories, or, if you will, of universal analogy, which has seduced all the great minds. The categories, in fact, designate, since Aristotle, who created the term, the common attributes of all things, that is to say, the points of resemblance that exist among all the objects of thought. Everything is like everything, if there really are categories, at the same time that everything differs from everything: things resemble one another by their common properties, and are distinguished by their proper essence, which modifies these same properties. The attributes of God are reflected in the world, finite beings are made in the image of the infinite being, thought itself corresponds to reality, and the laws of knowledge are in conformity with the general laws of creation. All is built on the same plan, and hence everything can be faithfully reproduced in consciousness. The categories contain the secret of method: whoever possesses them can know everything, by analyzing all things in order according to the evolution of the simplest and most fundamental elements of thought. Science is acquired when an object is completely determined in all respects. How are we to proceed to this determination so as to forget nothing essential? By examining the object successively from the point of view of each category. The categories, finally, are a logical topic: they are the “commonplaces” of philosophy, that is to say, a basis and a means for the scientific development of thought. The commonplaces themselves are an application of the categories to the art of oratory, an application which must await its further perfecting from the progress of logic.

p. 75

The first well-known system of categories is that of Aristotle. Words, according to the Stagirite, can express only ten kinds of things. There are therefore ten genera of being, or ten points of view under which reality must be regarded. And as the first aspect embraces the others and applies [p. 75] to all that is, the categories are truly universal or common attributes. For the rest, Aristotle follows no methodical procedure in discovering the categories. But, however incomplete they may be, they opened the way, they nourished thought throughout the Middle Ages, they are still a work worthy of admiration. Here are the ten categories:

οὐσία, essentia, essence;

ποσόν, quantitas, quantity;

ποῖόν, qualitas, quality;

πρὸς τί, relatio, relation;

ποῦ, ubi, space;

πότε, quando, time;

κεῖσθαι, situs, situation;

ἔχειν, habitus, manner of being;

ποιεῖν, actio, action;

πάσχειν, passio, passion.

p. 76

The first category is that of being or essence, which lies at the bottom of all the others, because there is being everywhere, and of which the others are only the accidents; it alone exists in itself and serves as the common subject of all the attributes that the understanding can affirm. These ten genera, says Aristotle, are not resolved into one another, but are united simultaneously in one and the same subject: quality has no quantity, time is not space, but every object possesses a quantity and a quality and manifests itself at once in time and in space. The categories are the simplest elements of thought and of language; they are irreducible, they have no higher genus and consequently cannot be defined; but they have their affections, their accidents, which differentiate them in the various subjects in which each is realized. All of them, too, have their oppositions, which are expressed in the form of contradiction, by affirmation and negation, or in the form of contrariety. The contraries (τὰ ἐναντία) which affect all the categories are being and non-being, the one and the many, [p. 76] the same and the other, the like and the unlike, the equal and the unequal. Potency and act, other contraries, relate to quality, to quantity, and to space (1).

It is easy to see what this table of categories lacks as method, as unity, and as concatenation or combination of ideas. Aristotle’s power of abstraction dominates it: the categories are not united with one another, as Plato’s ideas are. It would be equally easy to criticize the details of the system: the first four categories are fundamental and will be taken up again later; the others are more or less accessory and betray Aristotle’s preoccupation with regarding the individual as the basis of all reality. Passion, situation, manner of being apply only to finite beings; space suits only the world of bodies.

To the ten categories (prædicamenta) may be added the five categorems (prædicabilia), which complete them. They are: the genus, γένος, the species, εἶδος, the difference, διαφορά, the proper, ἴδιον, and the accident, συμβεβηκός. These universal terms comprise the various orders of relations that exist between two things, subject and attribute. Animal, for example, is a genus in relation to man, and man is a species in relation to animal. Reason is the difference that distinguishes this species from the others: it is the excess of the comprehension of the species over that of the genus. To state the genus and the difference of a species is the aim of definition, which makes known the essence of the object. The proper derives from the essence; the accident is foreign to it: the one will be, for example, for man the faculty of speech, the other color (2).

p. 77

Kant’s table is better coordinated. The categories are there represented as the forms of the understanding, that is to say, of the faculty of judging. They correspond therefore to the [p. 77] various kinds of judgments and are themselves supra-sensible concepts, implied in all the complex operations of thought. Kant's error on this point consists in relying on the common division of judgments, without even seeking to complete and reform it, in order to discover the simplest elements of the intelligence. The categories are not posterior but anterior to judgment. Here first is the table of judgments:

1. Quantity. 2. Quality.

Singular judgment, Affirmative judgment,

” particular, ” negative,

” universal. ” infinite.

3. Relation. 4. Modality.

Categorical judgment, Problematic judgment,

” hypothetical, ” assertoric,

” disjunctive. ” apodictic.

Here now are the categories that correspond term for term to the various forms of judgment:

1. Quantity. 2. Quality.

Unity, Affirmation,

Plurality, Negation,

Totality. Limitation.

3. Relation. 4. Modality.

Inherence (substance and accident), Possibility and impossibility,

Causality (cause and effect), Reality and non-existence,

Community (action and reaction). Necessity and contingency.

(1) F. Ravaisson, Essai sur la métaphysique d’Aristote, vol. I, part III, bk. III, ch. I. Paris, 1837. — Barthélemy Saint-Hilaire, la Logique d’Aristote, vol. I; Paris, 1838.

(2) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, bk. I, ch. VII, 5th ed. London, 1862. — Th. Reid, A Brief Account of Aristotle’s Logic.

p. 78

There are therefore four fundamental categories, each of which comprises three others. The first two classes contain the mathematical categories; the last two, the dynamical categories. The former are simple, the latter are double or possess correlative terms. Kant also [p. 78] points out, besides, that the third category in each class results from the combination of the two preceding ones, which are opposed to each other as members of a dichotomous division. Thus totality is plurality reduced to unity; limitation is reality united with negation; community or reciprocity expresses the causality of substances that depend on one another; necessity, finally, designates real existence deduced from pure possibility.

p. 79

The correspondence between the categories and the judgments of quantity is easily understood. Quality presents a difficulty with regard to the third element that it contains in the two tables. It seems strange that Kant should make the category of limitation correspond to the infinite judgment. But the error lies rather in the terms than in the things. The author calls an infinite judgment a proposition that is positive in one respect, as to the verb or the relation, and negative in another, as to the subject or the predicate. He gives as an example: the soul is not-mortal, which means that the soul is positively included in the unlimited extension of the things that are not perishable. All equivocation would disappear if we distinguished between the positive or negative character of the terms and that of the relation established between them, and if we called limitative judgments the propositions in which affirmation and negation are found together. The third class is exposed to graver objections. Why does Kant distinguish only three kinds of relations? Apparently to preserve the symmetry of the table. But the classification itself is arbitrary, and the correspondence between the categories and the judgments is forced. The categorical judgment expresses between the subject and the predicate a pure and simple relation, which has nothing in common with substance. The hypothetical judgment indicates that the two terms are united by a relation of conditionality rather than of causality. The disjunctive judgment, which represents the division of the subject into its various species, offers only a remote analogy with the idea of reciprocity. Kant founds this analogy on the coordination that exists between the [p. 79] species of one and the same genus and on the reciprocal determination of these species, each of which excludes the others; but there is nothing here that recalls action and reaction as dynamical categories. The fourth class does not have the same defects, but the modalities of existence, so important for metaphysics, have been badly determined by Kant, as postulates of empirical thought (1).

Kant's categories are still generally adopted. It has been proposed in France to reduce them to two, substance and causality; but such an attempt is not serious, for the point is to discover the whole of the universal attributes rather than the common root of all ideas; otherwise substance would suffice, since all properties, the cause included, can be only attributes of substance or of being. Another author, who follows in Kant's footsteps while exaggerating his defects, has set forth a new system of categories, as general laws of representation:

Categories. Thesis. Antithesis. Synthesis.

Relation. Distinction. Identification. Determination.

Number. Unity. Plurality. Totality.

Space

Position. Point (limit). Extent.

(interval).

Instant Time

Succession. Duration.

(limit). (interval).

Quality. Difference. Genus. Species.

Becoming. Relation. Non-relation. Change.

Causality. Act. Potency. Force.

Finality. State. Tendency. Passion.

Personality. Self. Not-self. Consciousness.

p. 80

The first category of M. Renouvier is therefore relation. It had been thought hitherto that relation presupposed at [p. 80] least two terms, namely the things that are united, “fundamentum relationis,” and that it was impossible in knowledge to abstract from beings; but the author claims that the sole object of thought is the phenomenon and that the phenomenon is a relation. The function of thought therefore consists in uniting and separating relations by synthesis and by analysis, and such also is the evolution undergone by the category of categories, relation. The sensible representations that make up all human knowledge are governed by the laws of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis: they manifest themselves in two terms that exclude each other, under the character of antinomy, but instead of leading to contradiction, they are brought back to unity in the synthesis of the third term, as Hegel teaches.

(1) I. Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, Elementarlehre, II Theil, I Abth., I Buch, I Hauptst. und II Buch, II Hauptst.

p. 81

Determination is the synthesis of distinction and of identity, which are contraries. To determine, says the author, is to limit: all the supra-sensible objects of thought, the infinite, the absolute, substance, are therefore necessarily eliminated from phenomenology; one determines by distinguishing and by identifying, that is to say, by uniting. Totality, which is a number, is the one of the many or the many of the one, the synthesis of unity and plurality. Extent is the synthesis of point and space, a limit with an interval or a limited interval; infinite space is therefore a contradictory notion. Duration is the synthesis of the instant and of time; it is a limited time, and there is no other. Quality shows itself in species, which is the synthesis of genus and difference; it is the genus of the difference or the difference of the genus. After number, position, succession, and quality come the categories of unstable relations. Becoming, or the change of states, is the non-relation of the relation or the relation of the non-relation, that is to say, the synthesis of the same and the other, or of being and non-being, at two successive instants that representation distinguishes, although experience does not separate them. Force is the act of potency or the potency of the act; it is, in other words, the synthesis of two phenomena, the one real, the other possible, which are considered as cause and effect with respect to each [p. 81] other; for causes are reduced to relations of succession, as Hume maintained. Tendency is an interval between two states, as potency is an interval between two acts, but the former has only a single direction, which is its end; two definite states that limit the tendency form a synthesis that may be called passion. Passion is therefore the state of the tendency or the tendency of the state, the synthesis of the means and the end. Finality is a category as universal as life and becoming: one lives for something; becoming implies tendency and end, as well as potency and cause. To the law of finality are attached good and evil, the beautiful and the ugly, which provoke in us desire and repulsion, hope and fear, pleasure and pain, love and hate, and which reveal themselves throughout the whole of nature, now by appetite or instinct, now by affinities or by attraction. Starting from relation in general, all the categories end finally in that particular relation which is personality. Of any object represented in space or in time, one may ask in whom it manifests itself. Personality is completed, like the other categories, by the synthesis of a limit and a corresponding interval. The limit is the self, a sphere of internal phenomena; the interval is the not-self, the whole of external phenomena. The synthesis of the self and the not-self is consciousness, the person: consciousness, in other words, is the self of the not-self or the not-self of the self. The relations between persons constitute rights and duties. The person offers us, realized to an eminent degree, the character of individuality that belongs to beings (1).

p. 82

The peculiarity of this system is to reduce all the categories to relation, excluding the very terms that every relation supposes, that is to say, beings or substances; to confine science within the world of representations or phenomena, eliminating the infinite and the absolute; and finally to apply to nature the psychological categories of finality and personality, summed up in passion and [p. 82] in consciousness. This is not the moment to pronounce on these various hypotheses, which are as bizarre as those of Hegel and more obscure. We shall remark only that these logical constructions, which proceed by general conceptions a priori, have nothing in common with the science of phenomena, and that the skeptical conclusions to which they lead are justified only by arbitrary definitions. It is certain that the infinite is not an object of science if thought has the function of determining things, and if to determine is to limit. But why this definition? It is equally evident that divine personality must be rejected if personality is confounded with individuality, and if the self can arrive at consciousness of itself only through the opposition of a not-self. But why this confusion? There is not even any discussion on these points. Nothing is more dogmatic than such a criticism (1).

(1) Ch. Renouvier, Essais de critique générale, 3rd and 4th parts. Paris, 1854.

p. 83

It remains for us to set forth one last system, that of Krause, in which the categories appear for the first time in their logical connection, as laws of thought, and in their ontological order, as constitutive attributes of beings, without logic being absorbed by metaphysics, as in the absolute idealism of Hegel. All the categories rest, as Aristotle had recognized, on the idea of being, which is the simplest and the most universal, since being lies at the bottom of every thought and at the bottom of every thing. Whatever is, substance or property, self or not-self, has being, is something. Being is the first and the last word of all science, since all science has for its object to determine, that is to say, to explain a thing, finite or infinite, the soul, the body or God, space, motion or quantity. The analysis of being is the whole of science. But how are we to proceed to this analysis? By regarding being from all the points of view that are given by observation: in itself, in its content and in its relations with its content; in other words, as [p. 83] whole, as an ensemble of parts, and in the relations of the whole with the parts. These three faces of being correspond to the thesis, the antithesis, and the synthesis. Being is first posited in itself: as such it is one; it is next posited as a variety of things, if we consider all that is contained in its essence: as such it is manifold, and each element of the variety is in antithesis or in opposition to the others; finally, being is posited in the union of the whole and the parts, as an organism: as such it is the harmony of the whole and the parts. Such are the fundamental principles that preside over the determination of being.

(1) La Science de l'âme dans les limites de l'observation, Part I, ch. II, and Part III, ch. III. Brussels, 1862.

p. 84

Hegel and other authors likewise have recourse to the laws of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, but they employ them in an entirely different manner. The thesis, according to them, posits an object, the antithesis denies it, and the synthesis reconciles both the object and its negation: thesis and antithesis are therefore the two terms of a contradictory opposition which, in spite of the contradiction, flow into one another, and which are found again intact in the synthesis after having been destroyed. It is thus that the absolute idea passes into nature, which is the negation of the idea, and rises to spirit, where it is identified with nature. In the same way, being is transformed into non-being and with this nothingness composes becoming. This procedure is violent and arbitrary. The antithesis requires a coordinate opposition between two contrary terms, one of which is not the pure and simple negation of the other, but a new affirmation; it results from the analysis of the posited object, and so does not overthrow the thesis but decomposes it into two elements coordinated with each other and both subordinated to the unity of the object; in a word, the antithesis is not opposed to the thesis, but contains two terms opposed to each other. The synthesis, in its turn, is not a higher idea that raises thesis and antithesis together to a higher power, but simply the union or harmony of the two members of the antithesis. Let us take an example from anthropology: man is one: that is the thesis; this unity manifests itself through two opposed beings, mind and body: that is the antithesis or the variety; the mind is united to the body without being confounded [p. 84] with matter and remains distinct from it without being separated from it: that is the harmony or synthesis. The antithesis does not exist between man and mind, nor between man and body, but between the two parts of human nature.

Here is the whole of the categories of being from these three points of view:

I. Being considered in itself: the Thesis.

Being

Essence Form

Existence.

Categories of essence. Categories of form.

Unity of essence. Unity of form.

Proper essence. Whole essence. Direction. Containment.

Harmony of essence. Harmony of form.

Categories of existence.

Unity of existence.

Substance. Modalities.

Harmony of existence.

II. Being considered in its content: the Antithesis. Categories of contraries.

Opposition or the coordinate relation of the parts: Determination and exclusion. Identity and difference. Unity and multiplicity. Affirmation and negation. Interior and exterior. Limit and magnitude. Beginning and end. Condition and complement.

Evolution or the inner relation of being with the series of phenomena that constitute becoming: Being and non-being. Change and immutability. Time and eternity. Potency and actuality. Action and reaction. Force and tendency. End and means. Good and evil.

III. Being in relation with its content: the Synthesis.

Transcendence or the subordinate relation: Superiority and inferiority. Whole and parts. Container and contained. Similarity and contrast. Principle and consequence. Cause and effect. Law and fact.

Being completely constituted as whole and as parts: the organism. Relation of whole with whole. Plenitude. Perfection. Beauty.

p. 85

A few definitions will suffice to make the value and the applications of this table understood; it makes no claim, moreover, to be complete.

1. The fundamental category is that of being, which suits every thing and expresses what is, whether substance or property. The first distinction to be made with respect to being is that of ground and form. The ground designates the essence or the nature of things: essence belongs to being, it is what being is, it embraces the whole of its qualities or attributes. Essence is one; it is purely and simply what it is, nothing else. But this unity manifests itself through two opposed qualities, as proper essence (proprium, idem), and as whole essence (omne, totum). Being, on the one hand, is itself what it is, it is identical with itself, it is its own essence, and on the other hand, it is all that it is, it is its whole essence. Selfhood and wholeness are the principle of all opposition in the world and in God. All the differences that can be pointed out between bodies and souls are summed up in these two points of view. In bodies the idea of wholeness predominates, of the interlinking of everything with everything, of continuity, of necessity; in mind the idea of selfhood predominates, of spontaneity, of will, of liberty. In the human mind, the category of the proper, of original and independent activity, again characterizes consciousness or thought; the category of totality and of connection is the distinctive character of feeling. In the human body the same antithesis is drawn between organic life and animal life, between the heart and the brain, which correspond to feeling and to thought. The sexes in the series of living beings are constituted according to the same attributes, applied to all the manifestations of essence. God himself is not a stranger to this law. The first propositions of metaphysics, developed methodically, can only reproduce the categories in their logical order: God is being, God is essence, God is one, and finally God is infinite and absolute. These two coordinated attributes, which all theology grants to God and which so many thinkers declare incomprehensible

p. 86

Logic. — I. 6 [p. 86] are only other terms for designating whole essence and proper essence: God is infinite inasmuch as he is all reality or whole essence; he is absolute inasmuch as he is himself and he alone all that is. The contrary terms are the conditioned and the finite. As sole and unique being, God is without limits and without conditions.

To essence is opposed form, to each material category a formal category which says how it is. How is being? It is posited, it has a position, it is positive. Position is the form of being, of every being, mind or body, finite or infinite thing. Position first of all is one, like essence: formal unity is numerical unity; each being is a single being, it is unique. Unity of number corresponds to unity of essence; proper essence has for its form direction, whole essence containment. What is spontaneous declares itself, asserts itself, tends to move: the mind, which is free, directs itself or turns sharply back upon itself in inner sense; matter, whose activity is fettered, obeys the same direction in cohesion. To these interior movements are added, for finite beings, exterior movements: they direct themselves toward their center in the form either of gravitation, if bodies are in question, or of religion, if souls are. On the other hand, what forms a whole contains parts or is determined internally: the soul encloses in its essence a series of acts or states, matter is divided into molecules, the infinite contains all. Formal unity, like unity of essence, therefore embraces a variety of things, and this variety, reduced to its simplest expression, reveals itself as duality: two poles, two sexes, two orders of things, the physical world and the spiritual world. But unity is maintained in spite of this variety and, combining with it, engenders harmony, the accord of everything with everything, under the double character of distinction and of union. The fault of pantheism is to absorb the variety of things in unity or to confound what is distinct; the fault of dualism is to suppress unity for the benefit of variety or to separate what is united.

p. 87

Essence and form combined constitute existence. Everything whose essence is posited exists. If the essence of an object takes form only in our imagination, existence is purely imaginary or subjective; if the essence is realized in external space or in the world, being has an objective existence, independent of our thought. Existence is one, like essence and like form: unity is always the first aspect and the higher point of view of all things, but within this unity analysis next discovers two distinct elements. The principal opposition with regard to existence is that of what exists in itself and what exists in something else, according to the categories of selfhood and of relation. What exists in itself, what has a proper and independent existence, is called substance; what exists in something else is called the qualities or affections, the modes and accidents of substance, in a word the modalities of existence. Kant was gravely mistaken with regard to this category. He makes of modality a separate class, set apart from substance, and opposes to substance only the accident. Possibility, reality, and necessity are the general modes of relative existence, and the accident is only one of the terms of this relation. The necessary is what exists in relation to something else under the character of unity, what can be only in one single manner; the possible, what exists in relation to something else under the character of plurality, what can be in several manners. Contingency is one of the cases of this possibility, which is realized in time. The real is not opposed to the possible or to the necessary; it applies to both and expresses simply what is, whatever may have been the mode of this existence in the first place.

p. 88

2. When we analyze being in its content, we obtain new categories, which may be called, with Aristotle, the categories of contraries, and which suit only the various parts or determinations of being considered in their reciprocal relations. Here antithesis or opposition predominates, that is to say, the relation of two coordinated terms. Let us take mind and body in man as types of this [p. 88] kind of relation. Each of these substances, considered in itself, possesses all the preceding categories: it has its essence, its form, and its existence; it is one and whole, one and the same, one and simple; it has its direction and its containment; but it is still indeterminate so long as it does not enter into comparison with something else. Let us now place it in the presence of the other substance, let us examine the one with the other, and at once each determines itself and finds its contrary: each is what it is and is only that; the mind is identical with itself, but it is the other of the body, and the body in its turn is the other of the mind; the mind is not what the body is, and the body is not what the mind is; spirituality excludes materiality; to affirm the one is to deny the other, as in contrary judgments. The coordinate relation therefore manifests itself as determination and exclusion. Let us continue the analysis of the two opposed terms: each taken in itself is one, together they are two: whence unity and plurality or multiplicity, the basis of judgments of quantity. Moreover, each term in itself, inasmuch as it is posited, is positive, since it is something, but in relation to the opposed term it is negative, since it is only what it is or is deprived of all the reality that belongs to its contrary: whence affirmative and negative judgments, which are called judgments of quality.

p. 89

Determination, number, and negation, which necessarily affect the two terms of an antithesis, lead us to the category of the limit, which is equally inherent in being considered not in itself, but in its content. Each member of the opposition, mind or body, has its interior, since it has a containment, but as it is not alone, as it is not all, as it is deprived of some reality, its content stops where that of its contrary begins; each therefore has also an exterior. For everything that is limited or determined there is an inside and an outside, an interior world and an exterior world. The limit is precisely the line of separation between the interior and the exterior. The infinite has no exterior; the infinite is alone, without [p. 89] a second, without opposition, without negation, the infinite has no limits. The limit affects only the parts of the whole, inasmuch as they mutually exclude one another; but these parts with their limits are contained in the whole or in the infinite. The limit is determined anew as beginning and as end, as initial point and as final point, according as the object is regarded from without inward or from within outward. The finite is properly what has an end, but it is commonly taken for the limit in general. The confusion, moreover, is easily understood: no end without a beginning, no beginning without an end. The content of the limit, what is circumscribed on all sides between extreme points, what is susceptible of more or less, is called quantity or magnitude. Magnitude is to the limit as ground is to form.

p. 90

Considering further the relations of the parts to one another, from the point of view of their coexistence, we obtain a new category, that of conditionality. Two things like mind and body, which are with one another in one and the same whole, are necessary to one another, and the more necessary the more opposed or heterogeneous they are, so that if the one comes to suffer or to fail, the other likewise suffers or fails: this relation is called condition; it expresses the mutual or bilateral dependence of two coordinated terms, the solidarity of the parts, whereas causality designates a unilateral relation, the dependence of the part upon the whole. The idea of condition applies to all finite beings that are together in the same world: each species finds its conditions of existence and development in neighboring species; man above all has need of the cooperation of his fellows in society: whence the just and the unjust, for right is only the expression of certain conditions that are indispensable for the realization of our end. From the idea of condition there derives further that of complement. What needs external conditions in order to live is incomplete and must be completed by the cooperation of others. This category does not apply to the infinite considered in itself, which, as [p. 90] such is alone, without conditions, and has no need of complement.

p. 91

We have just analyzed being in relation with another being, its contrary; let us now consider it in its evolution, where it presents a new opposition with itself.
