Here we find the distinction between being itself and the series of acts, states, or phenomena by which being realizes its essence inwardly. The phenomenon is the accident of substance. Its place must be marked out for it in the table of the categories, without exaggerating its importance: it is neither the first nor the sole object of thought, as the positivists teach today. Beings change by passing from one determinate state to another determinate state; minds and bodies, everything is modified, everything manifests itself by phenomena that are always distinct; but the essence and the properties of beings are not lost on that account. There is therefore a double face in things, the one variable, the other immutable; each being, in other words, has two opposed attributes, change and immutability, of which the one relates to the passing phenomena, the other to the permanent essence. Becoming is the continuous series of the states that flow away; it reconciles being and non-being, as Hegel says, in the sense that each completely determinate state excludes the others, that one cannot be at once in two different situations, that if the one exists, the other does not exist, and conversely. What becomes is not yet, and yet it is after a fashion: it begins to be, it passes gradually from possibility to reality. All these states that exclude one another coexist in the same essence. This apparent contradiction is resolved by time, by succession, which contains the categories of before and after. Being is not at the same instant in two states that exclude one another, but it advances successively from the one toward the other. Time is the form of change; eternity, the form of the immutable. If phenomena are mobile and transitory, essence is eternal. Time is a real category that concerns all beings, inasmuch as they change or become other. It is not the same with [p. 91] space, which is only the form of one species of beings, bodies, inasmuch as they exist under the character of extension and continuity, unless one assimilates the intelligible space of the imagination to the external space of nature. Time and space combined give motion, as the direction of finite beings toward one another, under the condition of translation and of duration.

p. 92

To the immutable and eternal face of things is attached potency; to their variable and temporal face, act. This distinction of Aristotle relates to everything, considered in its inner evolution, inasmuch as it becomes or constantly realizes the possible states enveloped in its essence. The possible exists in potency, the real exists in act. In their application to the soul, the potencies are the faculties; the acts, produced in the form of a series in time, are activity. Every substance is active; the materialists are now in agreement on this point with the spiritualists, and if the substance is finite, it manifests this property by a double current of which it is the subject and the object, by action and passion, by spontaneity and receptivity. Every action received provokes a reaction. Appreciated from the point of view of quantity, activity is determined as force: force is the degree or the quantum of activity displayed by beings, spiritual or physical. Combined with potency, activity becomes tendency or inclination. Each being has tendencies, marked by the possible states that are contained in its nature and that must be realized by its activity. The unconscious tendencies are, in inorganic matter, the affinities, in organized bodies, the instincts and dispositions; the conscious tendencies in rational beings are the desires. Inclinations indicate the end, the aim or the destination of beings: attractions, in other words, are proportional to destinies. Every being has an end, a final cause, as it is improperly said, which forms part of the general teleology of creation, and this end manifests itself in the whole of its forces and dispositions. Every being that has an end [p. 92] finds in its nature the means of attaining it. Beings that have their end in themselves, that are conscious of their destiny and recognize themselves as responsible for the manner in which they fulfill it, are persons. Personality is a characteristic attribute of man within the limits of the world. The being that fulfills its mission, that acts according to its nature, does good; he who acts in opposition to his essence or contrary to the nature of other beings does evil. Good and evil are met with everywhere in the universe; moral good and moral evil, done with intention, as meritorious and culpable acts, belong only to the life of rational beings, endowed with personality and as such members of the moral world.

p. 93

3. Let us now combine the two preceding aspects, let us consider being at once in itself and in its content, and let us see what new properties are revealed in this synthesis. Between a being and its content there no longer exists a relation of opposition, but of transcendence, that is to say, of subordination or of superiority. There is therefore no longer any occasion to apply, as before, the principle of contradiction. We have on the one hand the whole, on the other the parts; for example, man, in the unity of his nature, and mind and body, as expressions of his duality. Man is neither pure mind nor pure matter; he is the one and the other and he is more than their sum or their aggregation, for he is also the union of mind and body; we shall therefore say: man is mind and is not mind, man is matter and is not matter; the whole is also each of its parts, but no part is the whole; the parts are subordinated to the whole, the whole is above the parts. The whole is the container, the parts the contained. All that is in the contained is also in the container, but not all that is in the container is for that reason in the contained: all that is affirmed of mind and body, such as thought and extension, can be affirmed of man, but not all the qualities of man are either qualities of the mind or qualities of the body. Only, by virtue of the unity of essence or of human nature, each part is similar to the whole, and consequently the mind and the [p. 93] body are also similar to one another: the human soul and the human body are, in fact, homologous organisms which correspond in their whole and in their parts, whatever contrasts there may be between their proper essence, as anthropology demonstrates. Analogy may even extend to all things, and would be proved if it were certain that the categories with which we are concerned had universal validity.

The containment and subordination of the parts expresses the relation of reason or of foundation, that is to say, the relation of principle to consequence, on which all demonstrative reasoning rests. The parts are founded in the whole; the whole is the reason of each of its partial manifestations. Causality adds to these relations a new relation, the relation of determination or of production: causality is the bond between two things of which the one is produced or determined by the other: the latter is called cause, the former effect. The cause is therefore a determining or sufficient reason. It is now seen that this category is essentially distinguished from those of condition, means, and end, with which it is often confounded: conditioning cause, instrumental cause, final cause. The true cause is the determining or efficient cause, which indicates that one thing determines another according to its essence. For the rest, the preceding relations apply equally to the causal connection: the effect is in the cause, under the cause, similar to the cause. As the cause, so the effect. Inasmuch as being by its causality constantly realizes its essence, which is one and the same, there are elements common to the whole series of phenomena that mark its becoming: these common and invariable characters are the laws of activity, founded in the nature of things.

p. 94

A whole together with the sum of its parts, constituted according to thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, gives us the idea of an organism. In the organism all the preceding relations are reproduced, coordinative as well as subordinative, for the organized being is itself the being completely achieved in itself and in its interior determinations: everything is [p. 94] summed up, everything blossoms in the organism, as in the highest expression of being: to the whole apply the categories of essence, form, and existence; to the relations of the parts among themselves, the categories of contraries; to the relations of the parts with the whole, the categories of subordination. The idea of organization itself appears capable of being adapted, in certain respects and under various forms, to everything that is, to physical or spiritual beings, to the finite or the infinite: man, animal, plant, as living beings, are organized; thought in the whole of its functions and operations, light with its colors, space with the possible combinations among its dimensions, though pure properties, nevertheless have an organization conformable to their essence. All the manifestations of rational life, society with its organs, art with its manifold forms, right with its applications, science with its parts, everything is susceptible of organization. Organized science is the system of knowledge, in harmony with the system of things. The fundamental properties of the organism are plenitude, perfection, and beauty. The conditions of beauty are precisely the same as those of organization: unity, variety, harmony. If we are willing to admit, provisionally, that there exists neither absolute void, nor absolute imperfection, nor absolute ugliness, we shall recognize that there are in all things some traces of organization, and we shall seek the cause of it in the infinite and absolute organism (1).

p. 95

Such is the table of the categories as a whole. A subject of this kind would require a special work; but on the one hand, I do not wish to repeat what I have said in psychology on the properties of the soul, and on the other, I shall return to the ideas that will be indispensable for the completion of logic. The essential thing for the moment is to embrace the categories in their real order and in their relations, in order to rectify [p. 95] the errors that arise from an exclusive point of view cast upon the objects of thought. It is needless to add that in setting forth the categories as universal attributes we do not pretend to have demonstrated that they all apply to every thing. This question will present itself in connection with the laws and the legitimacy of our knowledge, and cannot be resolved without the aid of the deductive or synthetic part of science.

CHAPTER THREE

T H E R E L AT I O N B E T W E E N S U B J E C T A N D

OBJECT IN KNOWLEDGE

We know what the subject is and what the possible objects of knowledge are; but knowledge is constituted only by a certain relation between subject and object. What is this relation? The object offers itself to thought, either because it imposes itself on the mind, if it is present, or because it waits to be discovered, if it lies beyond our horizon. How is it given to us? Knowledge, finally, has a twofold aspect, the one subjective, the other objective; how is it determined from these two points of view? That is what we must inquire into in order to complete the notion of knowledge in general.

(1) Krause, System der Philosophie, 1828. — Vorlesungen über die Grundwahrheiten der Wissenschaft, 1829. — Die Lehre vom Erkennen und von der Erkenntniss, herausgg. von Leonhardi, 1836.

p. 96

Feeling as well as thought puts us in relation with things; but the relations differ, although in both cases it is a matter of the same soul in the presence of one and the same object. The soul, as affective, is stirred, agitated, impassioned, in the widest sense of that word: it suffers, it experiences some emotion; as intelligent, the soul is calm, indifferent, and retains all its freedom of action and of appreciation; on the one hand, it undergoes an external influence, whether it will or no; on the other, it remains impassive. The same opposition appears in the object, according as it speaks to the heart or to the mind: it presents itself to feeling [p. 96] as an undivided whole, in the totality of its qualities and relations; to thought, as a thing apart, which detaches itself from the surrounding reality and must itself be studied apart in each of its properties, its parts, and its relations. This difference could not be better expressed than by the two opposite categories that are inherent in the unity of essence, the ideas of selfhood and of wholeness. The soul, as thought, remains what it is and tends to grasp the object as it is, whereas the soul, as feeling, is impressed in its whole manner of being, which results from all its antecedent activity, and tends toward the object considered in its totality. The relation indicated by knowledge is therefore a relation of proper essence, in which the two terms, the subject and the object, maintain their distinction and are opposed to one another without undergoing any reciprocal influence. The subject and the object of knowledge are independent of each other and preserve their independence even while uniting; both remain what they are, and the union they contract in consciousness in no way alters their originality. In feeling, on the contrary, the subject is affected by the object, and the union of the two terms prevails over their distinction. That is why thought, conscious of itself and disengaged from feeling, abstracts, in the work of knowledge, from every personal motive of hope or fear, from every consideration of pleasure or interest, from every prejudice of family or nation. Thought well developed secures the freedom of the mind; it withdraws it from the empire of the passions and the tyranny of traditions, and requires that it show itself in knowledge as it is in itself, and not as the habits that prevail in the milieu in which it develops have made it. That is why the object, in its turn, must be known as it is in itself, outside of us, without adding anything to it or taking anything from it, without modifying any of its properties.

p. 97

Knowledge expresses a relation of distinction, an analytic relation between subject and object. If this relation is determined, we arrive at exact, incontestable consequences, which demonstrate its value. For, indeed, the faculties [p. 97] OBJECT. of a limited being such as man are necessarily affected with negation: they may attain their end or fail to attain it. Let us examine thought from this point of view. Its end is to grasp the proper essence of things. What happens when it accomplishes this, and when it does not know how to accomplish it? In other words, how does it manifest itself according as it stands to the proper essence of things in a positive or in a negative relation? In the one case it is in the true; in the other, it is in the false. Truth is precisely that relation in which thought adapts itself to the object and recognizes it as it is, and error is exactly the contrary situation, in which the mind does not recognize the object as it is, whether we give to the object properties that do not belong to it or deny it properties that it possesses. Truth is the end of thought, error its deviation. These definitions offer nothing new, but are drawn, for the first time, from the very definition of knowledge, and justify it: knowledge is the relation of thought to the proper essence of things; this relation, for us, as finite beings, may be positive or negative: the positive relation gives truth, the negative relation gives error. Truth and error are therefore the two determinations of knowledge, considered in its quality. The comparison of thought and feeling renders this result still more manifest. Appraised from the same point of view, as positive or negative, feeling is determined as pleasure and as pain, according as the object, taken as a whole, is in harmony or in opposition with the present situation of the soul. Pleasure and pain therefore explain the relation of whole essence, the concrete and synthetic relation, which feeling establishes between the soul and things, as truth and error account for the contrary relation indicated by thought. Hence new comparisons which mark the difference between thought and feeling, between knowledge and emotion: thought is to feeling as truth is to pleasure, as error is to pain.

p. 98

We now see how knowledge differs from truth: the one is a genus in relation to the other, truth is [p. 98] a species of knowledge. Not all knowledge is true, but all truth is knowledge for us or for God. Knowledge is the relation of thought to the proper essence of the object in general, positive or negative; truth is a determination of this relation, the affirmative relation between thought and its object. The other relation is knowledge also; it is the knowledge contrary to truth, it is error, which must not be confounded with ignorance. Knowledge is the most extensive or the most indeterminate, but not the most comprehensive, relation between thought and its object; it is an analytic relation, no doubt, but any relation of this kind whatever, an adequate relation or not. We must therefore range under the title of knowledge everything that is a product or a state of thought: truth and error, certainty and doubt, are of this number. Certainty is a species of truth; it is conscious truth, the truth that we know to be true and can maintain against every contrary affirmation. Doubt is a hesitation about truth, not about knowledge. All the varieties of error and of doubt, opinions, prejudices and beliefs, conjectures, hypotheses and probabilities, are still cognitions, for all denote a situation of thought in relation to an object, present or future, possible or real, contingent or necessary. The operations of the intellect are other determinations of the same act of consciousness. Hence the circumscription of logic. This science embraces only the theory of knowledge, but it sets it forth entire in its generality and pursues it in all its fundamental manifestations.

Knowledge is the product of intellectual activity, which rests on the distinction of subject and object. The conditions of knowledge are drawn anew from this definition. For there to be knowledge, there must be a subject, an object, a relation between the two terms. But analysis demands more: what are the functions of the subject, and how is the object given to us in knowledge?

p. 99

The functions of thought, or the various moments of intellectual activity [p. 99] OBJECT. considered in itself, apart from its object, are attention, perception, and determination: the internal or subjective conditions of knowledge. To know an object, whatever it may be, finite or infinite, substance or relation, thought must first of all turn toward it; this first movement of the mind, which belongs indeed to thought, although the will joins in it, is called attention: without attention, no knowledge, whether it be a matter of a phenomenon or of absolute being. In vain should we receive some sensation from the objects that surround us or some impression from a higher world; if thought is not present, if the soul is distracted or preoccupied, we know nothing of what passes within us or without us. To this direction of the mind, which tends toward the object, there succeeds a second act by which thought grasps or perceives the object that calls for its attention; this higher degree of intellectual activity is called perception, or sometimes apperception: without perception, no knowledge. To understand is to grasp; we know nothing of a thesis that we have not grasped. The first two functions of the understanding are often simultaneous and may then be confounded: an object that is within our reach is perceived as soon as we apply some attention to it; but the distinction is manifest when the object presents difficulties: in that case attention may be prolonged for a very long time without perception following in its train. On one and the same point, one man will grasp and another will not grasp, although the attention is equal, and the same person may, in spite of his good will, grasp a fact and not grasp a principle, or the reverse, according to the turn of his mind. When estimable authors come and tell you, as is generally the case in England, that they do not comprehend the infinite, the absolute, God, they are in good faith, but they are singularly mistaken if they believe that they have thereby fixed the limits of human knowledge. The fact finds its explanation in the nature of the soul: perception varies according to the subjects, according to the intellectual dispositions and habits of peoples. An infirmity of this kind attests an important [p. 100] gap in public education, but proves nothing against the capacity of the human mind; it would doubtless suffice, in order to cure it, to denounce the traditional compromise between reason and faith, or to recognize that the principles which it is customary to abandon to faith belong to the domain of reason. In any case, it is an illusion to think that we in no way grasp supra-sensible objects when we admit them in the name of religion. There is no religion without a certain knowledge of God.

p. 101

Attention and perception are the subjective conditions of all knowledge, determinate or not. And since these functions are inherent in thought and not in objects, it is already evident that knowledge comes from us and is formed in us by our own activity, contrary to the claims of all the externalist doctrines which, under the name of sensualism, of traditionalism, or of pantheism, place the origin of our knowledge in matter, in society, or in God. Determinate or analytic knowledge requires one condition more, determination. To know an object in some of its properties or relations, we must combine attention and perception unceasingly, directing them successively upon one point and upon another, until we obtain a clear and sufficient knowledge of the object; thus science is formed: this combination of attention and perception constitutes the third function of the understanding. To determine an object is not to limit it, as M. Renouvier asserts, although the word lends itself to this equivocation; it is to analyze it, to decompose it into its qualities and its relations, to refer it to its cause, considering each element apart, in an abstract manner, and applying to it the functions of the intellect. The better an object is determined, the more adequate or complete is the knowledge. It appears probable that each thing is determinable without end by thought, that is to say, that knowledge is always susceptible of new increase. It is therefore interesting to know whether there exists some method for the scientific determination of objects. This method exists; it has been brought to light [p. 101] OBJECT. by Kant and consists in the application of the categories, as we shall see when we treat of the laws of knowledge.

Attention, perception, and determination are the internal conditions of knowledge. Let us now see the conditions that concern the object. Our cognitions are eminently variable; they vary in clearness and in perfection according to the functions of thought, according to the strength of the attention, the vividness of the perception, the method of determination employed; they vary in kind or in nature according to the objects that we wish to know. The knowledge of a sensible object, which presents itself to our organs, is other than the knowledge of a supra-sensible object, which addresses itself to reason alone. Nevertheless, in both cases it is a question only of objects, and the knowledge of an object considered in itself, whether it be sensible or not, is called notion. If, instead of a single object, we wish to know a relation between two things, whether between two substances, or between two properties, or between a substance and its properties, the knowledge takes another name and is called judgment. If finally, instead of a simple relation, we wish to combine several relations and draw from them a new proposition, the knowledge changes its denomination once more and becomes a reasoning. All these points of view are founded in the nature of things; for if there are objects in the world, there also exist, independently of us, whether we know it or not, relations between these objects, and there exist again relations between these relations, were they only relations of equality or of difference. The activity of the intellect, regarded under this aspect, as it is determined by the objects, is called operation. Operations are opposed to functions as object to subject, although both apply to active thought or to the understanding.

The theory of the operations of thought gives rise to a new division of knowledge, which it is important to point out from this moment, because it determines the notion of method and sheds a vivid light on certain obscure or contested parts of our knowing. How

p. 102

Logic. — I. 7 [p. 102] do we have notions, or how do we know objects considered in themselves? By seeing them, whether with the eyes of the body or with the eye of the mind, which is reason; that is to say, by observing or contemplating them with attention. As soon as a fact falls under our senses, we grasp and observe it, and if we recognize that it is real and not illusory, we admit it among our cognitions, even though it should be in contradiction with received opinions: it is an intuition, an intuitive knowledge, or knowledge of simple view, as Locke expresses it. We have no need whatever of reasoning to ascertain a fact: it suffices to see. In like manner, as soon as a principle enlightens reason, we grasp and contemplate it, and we may again admit it among our cognitions, with the ordinary chances of error. It is impossible for us, for example, not to think of space, of eternity, of humanity, of God, although these objects do not appear to the senses: these also are intuitions, intuitive cognitions. Every time we perceive an object in itself, without deriving it from its cause, the knowledge is intuitive, whether it be a question of a fact or of a principle. Only, in the first case the intuition is sensible, in the second it is intellectual.

p. 103

Now how do we have judgments and reasonings, or how do we know the relations of things? Sometimes in an intuitive manner, sometimes in a discursive manner. When the relation is evident, intuition suffices, with no distinction of sensible or supra-sensible elements. Thus we judge that an animal is white or black, that lead is heavier than iron, that the whole is greater than the part, that God is infinite. But it often happens that the relation between two objects or two thoughts is difficult to grasp at first sight, by a rapid intuition: it is then that we look for a common measure, a middle term, an intermediary between the two things submitted to examination; it is then that we reason, and that knowledge becomes discursive or demonstrative. What relation is there, for example, between the alternate interior angles [p. 103] OBJECT. formed by the cutting of two parallel lines? Their equality is not immediately manifest, but it becomes so if we compare the two angles in question with a third angle which, added to each of the first two, makes two equal sums.

Our cognitions are therefore intuitive or discursive, according to the manner in which we know things, in themselves or in their cause. On this distinction rests the division of method into analysis and synthesis. Analysis is content with intuitions; synthesis proceeds only by reasonings and deductions. There is no difficulty here, and Locke on this point is in perfect agreement with Descartes. But what must be remarked is that intuitive knowledge bears as well on the objects of reason as on those of the senses. Locke admits this with regard to the truths called axioms. The general propositions, what is, is, and it is impossible for one and the same thing to be and not to be, are no less evident in themselves than these particular propositions, what is white is white, red is not blue (1). Such is the foundation of supra-sensible knowledge.

The operations of thought will be discussed in what follows. In the general theory of knowledge, a single question concerns the conditions of knowing: how is the object, substance or relation, known in intuition? On the condition that it be given to us. The object is the matter of knowledge, according to Kant's terminology. This matter exists outside of us, independent of our activity, whether we know it or not, and must be known as it is, without addition or diminution. Thought does not change things or their relations, but accepts them and has only to take them as they are. If the object is not a creation of thought, how then is it given to us? Sometimes in an immediate manner, sometimes in a mediate manner.

p. 104

The self is revealed immediately to thought: each one has [p. 104] direct consciousness and feeling of himself. Between the self as subject and the self as object of knowledge there is room for no intermediary. The phenomena and the properties of the soul are therefore the object of an immediate apperception. The same holds of certain parts of our body, of the affections of the cerebral nervous system to which the mind is intimately united. The soul has the consciousness and the feeling of the modifications undergone by the nerves of animal life, which extend into the sensory organs, as vividly and as rapidly as of itself. That is why sensations, although they are accomplished outside of the soul, are often regarded as acts of consciousness.

External objects, or bodies, are given to us by the senses and are revealed to thought only in an indirect manner. When they are the object of knowledge, they reach the subject only by passing through an intermediary; without organs or without nerves, we should not even suspect their existence. If we close our eyes, one face of bodies escapes us; if we stop our ears, another class of phenomena disappears in its turn; if we had no senses, we should have, in our present condition, no perception of the external world. Our own body does not differ in this respect from foreign bodies; its form, its movements, its vibrations fall under our senses; sensation alone is perceived directly by thought.

(1) Locke, Essai sur l’entendement humain, bk. IV, ch. II and VII.

p. 105

Bodies are therefore given immediately to our senses, mediately to the mind that has to know them. From this the role of sensibility, as a condition of the knowledge of the external world, is easily deduced. Nervous matter, the most delicate part of the organism, has the property of receiving impressions from everything that surrounds it, of resonating, if you will, at the contact of light, caloric, sound, and electricity; the soul, like the spider at the center of its web, according to an ancient comparison, perceives and feels these nervous vibrations and must by this means judge of the spectacle of nature, explain to itself the phenomena [p. 105] OBJECT. which unfold there, and try to understand the value and the relations of things. In sum, the soul is reduced to itself and must read in the organs to which it is intimately united what passes outside, with the conviction that the senses give it in miniature an exact representation of the material universe. The common attribute of the senses is receptivity, the capacity of being affected and modified by the various impressions that proceed from the action of bodies; one undergoes the influence of light and colors, another is sensible to vibratory motion; each has its special properties, but all are receptive and are destined to transmit to consciousness the modifications that they undergo. A nerve that should lose this property, that should become insensible by paralysis or by the effect of an anesthetic substance, would be of no further help to the soul. The receptivity of the senses is therefore a fundamental condition of the knowledge of the external world.

p. 106

Let us not stop now at the ulterior consequences that are deduced from this fact. Let us remark only that if the knowledge of bodies is exposed to doubts, the difficulties do not fall upon the testimony of the senses, but upon the interpretation that thought gives to sensations. Bodies are really revealed to the senses; their action upon the organs is a purely physical phenomenon, altogether foreign to the life of the soul; we can therefore no more suspect the fidelity of the senses than the veracity of a mirror that reflects the rays of light. Thus we distinguish perfectly the real objects that are given to us by the senses from the fantastic objects that are represented to us by the imagination in dream or in reverie. But if bodies manifest themselves to our senses as they are, does thought, which can grasp them only in a roundabout way, through our organs and in our organs, know them also as they are in themselves? Here doubt is permitted: it may be supposed that the intermediary which is placed between subject and object falsifies the object or conceals it from thought; and we have in fact no means of experimental verification to decide whether external things are in themselves such as [p. 106] they offer themselves to us in our senses; for we can observe them only with the aid of our organs. Deduction alone is capable of grasping them in their cause, as they must be.

p. 107

The knowledge of the external world is accompanied by an intuition or a representation of objects. This is what is called a sensible intuition. Whence does it come? From the imagination. As soon as we perceive an external object, we form an image of it, and this image, endowed with the three dimensions of extension, subsists and maintains itself in us even when the object has disappeared. If we do not succeed in representing to ourselves the object that has struck our organs, we do not know it. This image is not a product of our senses, otherwise it would vanish with the sensation; and besides, the retina of the eye, which alone offers some analogy with the phenomenon of psychological intuition, could furnish, like a mirror, only the two dimensions of the surface. The representation of objects results from the work of the imagination: this is the proper function of that faculty in the generation of our knowledge. This cannot be doubtful to anyone who has reflected on the composition of dreams, on the creation of a work of art, or merely on the images that succeed one another in us when we read a poem. It is the imagination that draws, that figures, that paints, that gives a body to thought in all these circumstances. Sensible intuition is therefore a condition of the knowledge of the external world. Thus far we are in agreement with Kant and with his imitators. But we part from them when they affirm that sensible intuition is the condition of all human knowledge, or that all our knowledge is nothing but representations, as M. Renouvier expresses it. Representation may well suit a part of our knowledge, that which has for its object limited things, capable of being figured in the imagination; but it by no means embraces our supra-sensible knowledge, the objects of which exceed the limits of observation and the capacity of fancy. To identify knowledge with representation is to shut oneself up as if at will [p. 107] OBJECT. in the circle of phenomena, and to exclude without discussion the infinite, the absolute, metaphysics as a whole, from the sphere of thought. This skepticism has its source in an arbitrary definition of knowledge, borrowed from the sensualists, and proves only that the psychological theory of the intellect, and above all the scope of reason, are still unknown to those very persons who ought to be most thoroughly imbued with them.

p. 108

Bodies are given to thought in a mediate manner and are perhaps not in themselves such as they appear to us in representation. The same holds of our fellow men, considered as minds. We do not know spiritual substances any more directly than the physical substances that are foreign to the self. Everyone can convince himself of this on the spot by asking himself whether he knows the thoughts, the feelings, or the projects of another as he knows his own: the consciousness that suffices in the latter case is evidently insufficient in the former. It is a truth of common sense that we judge others by ourselves. Indeed, we must have consciousness of ourselves, as a mind united to a body; we must know how the acts of our spiritual life express themselves outwardly in language, in the attitudes and movements of the organism, in order to assure ourselves, by ascending from the effect to the cause, that the gestures and the voice of our fellow men correspond, as in ourselves, to an interior activity, or are the manifestations of a soul. Minds are revealed to observation only in their union with matter; it is language that makes us suspect their existence, and language, in its oral or written form, is perceived only by our senses. Nervous sensibility thus serves anew as intermediary between the subject and the object of knowledge, between the mind and its fellows, thanks to the intimate relations of soul and body; for the mind itself does not fall under the senses. Minds are therefore given to us in an indirect manner like bodies and with bodies, and we can then represent them to ourselves in our imagination, because they are, like bodies, only determinate beings. We figure to [p. 108] ourselves the affections, the desires, the character of our fellow men; we even create minds and social relations in poetry or in dream; but we distinguish with certainty the persons who present themselves to us in knowledge from those who are only a product of our fantastic activity.

Minds, bodies, men: this is almost the whole world; all this is given to us indirectly, with the exception of our own mind and of the nervous phenomena of animal life, of which we have immediate consciousness. But above these determinate objects we conceive nature, humanity, space, time, which we regard, rightly or wrongly, as infinite each in its kind; and above these kinds we admit still the one and whole Being that is called God. How do these supra-sensible objects come to the mind? Since we speak of them, they are objects of thought, they are intelligible; and since we attribute to them the character of infinity, they are given to us. The infinite, which so many authors today take pleasure in rejecting, has precisely this peculiarity, that it can appear to consciousness only on the condition that it gives itself to us, and consequently that it exists. When a limited being presents itself to our senses, we may hesitate, in certain situations of the soul, to grant it an objective existence, because we ourselves produce in ourselves analogous representations in our hallucinations and even in our apparent sensations; but is it the same with the infinite? A bounded being such as the human mind is capable of creating bounded things; but how could it invent that which has no bound, which exceeds all the limits of observation and refuses all representation in the imagination? Let it be well considered: there is here a manifest impossibility; it is no less absurd to suppose that the infinite emanates from the finite than to affirm that the effect surpasses the cause and that man is about to become God.

p. 109

If the soul has some notion of the infinite, of the absolute, of the perfect, as things radically distinct from what it is itself and from all that it knows of the finite, of the imperfect [p. 109] OBJECT. and of the relative, these things must be given to it. Given how, and by what? By the spectacle of the world, by the earth or the sun, which are in space and strike our senses? That is impossible, for all bodies on earth and in heaven are limited, and nothing infinite appears to our eyes. By education, by tradition or language, by intercourse with our fellow men? That is again impossible, for all communication among men takes place by means of speech or of writing, and all language is composed of material signs which address themselves to our senses. Now no visible sign and no sound could reveal the infinite to one who is ignorant of it. That the circle is a symbol of the infinite I grant; but the symbol presupposes the idea and has no other aim than to recall it to memory, not to give it birth; no one, on seeing a circle, can suspect the infinite unless he already knows it. It is not, then, our fellow men who communicate to us the ideas of supra-sensible things; these ideas are in us as well as in them, and all the efforts of the teacher must be confined to calling our attention to the objects of which we bear the impress in our soul. The difficulty, besides, would only be put back, if it were granted that the scientific, moral, and social principles of the spiritual life are transmitted to us by tradition; for our fellow men have no other faculties than we, and how should they have acquired by language what we cannot acquire ourselves?

p. 110

The infinite, the absolute, the perfect are therefore not given to us indirectly by the senses or by education. What must we conclude? That they are given to us by themselves, without any intermediary; that we have a faculty which puts us in contact with supra-sensible objects, as sensibility puts us in relation with the external world; that we have an intuition of causes and of principles as we have a representation of phenomena. The consequence is inevitable and agrees perfectly with the psychological theory of reason. If it is opposed to the claims of criticism, or, to say the word, of metaphysical skepticism, it is because Kant, M. Renouvier, [p. 110] M. Mill have misconceived reason. Doubtless every clear cognition is an intuition of things, but we have two sorts of intuitions: a sensible intuition, by means of the senses and the imagination, and an intellectual intuition, according to the accepted expression, by means of reason. Only the sensualists have contested this fact, and I do no wrong to a great thinker in saying that he drew from them the strange thesis that is formulated in the “Critique of Pure Reason.” Locke is less exclusive. He admits, like Plato, that certain general truths are immediately evident by themselves, or that they are the object of an intuitive knowledge; which, in our opinion, can be understood only of an intellectual intuition, since the senses perceive nothing general; he errs only as to the origin of these truths, that is to say, as to the nature of reason. Reason, it has been said, is the eye of the mind; it is indeed the metaphysical sense which opens to us the higher world, the object of speculation, as the senses of the body open to us the lower world, the object of observation. Reason reveals to us God and all that is divine, the beautiful, the true, the good, the just, as our organs reveal to us nature. We see laws and causes, we have the intuition of the principle of identity, of the infinity of time or of space, as we have the intuition of the determinate beings that surround us. But, on the one hand, objects are drawn and painted in the imagination, where they can be grasped by every being endowed with sensibility, even by the animal; whereas, on the other hand, we must do violence to fancy and rise above the ordinary habits of thought in order to perceive objects in the purity and simplicity of their essence. Who can refuse to see that every effect has a cause, and how can we confound this general principle, applicable to an infinity of cases, with this quite special phenomenon, that the barometer has just risen and that the wind has changed? The one is a sensible intuition, the other an intellectual intuition. I have established the certain existence of intellectual intuitions, in connection with the starting point of science in psychology. These intuitions come from reason, [p. 111] OBJECT. not as the discursive faculty of judging and reasoning, but as an intuitive or receptive faculty, analogous to sensibility, although it extends to another domain of reality. Reason and the senses complete each other and show the universal character of human activity, which can unfold, thanks to the senses, in relation with nature, and thanks to reason, in relation with God. The senses give us one part of the materials that are indispensable to the life of the soul; reason gives us the second part. The data of reason are as incontestable as those of the senses, since the understanding has nothing to do with them; they are even withdrawn from every cause of alteration, since reason is not, like the senses, a material organ, subject to the vicissitudes of physical life. Only, every intuition, sensible or intellectual, is insufficient in itself and cannot by itself alone decide the existence of its object. Our sensible intuitions may be false, as in dream and in the phenomenon of complementary colors; the same is true of our intellectual intuitions. The intuition of infinite space does not dispense us from inquiring in metaphysics whether space is really without limits.

p. 112

The data of reason are ideas; those of the senses, sensations. Ideas are to sensations as reason is to the organs. Sensation results from the impression of bodies on the nerves; the idea, from the impression of divine things on the higher face of the soul. The idea is the mark of God upon his work, Descartes said, as sensation is a trace of nature. Both are independent of our will and are in consequence what they ought to be, by virtue of the general laws that preside over the communication of substances. But in taking the word idea in this precise acceptation, which assures it a considerable value in the question of the existence of principles, we must take care to distinguish it from knowledge. The idea is no more than sensation a cognition, a product of the understanding; it is, properly speaking, like sensation, an object of knowledge. Sensation is an intermediary between thought and the external world; it is in [p. 112] our organs that we grasp the bodies that modify them; it is sensation and not the bodies that is the direct object of our perceptions. The idea plays the same role in supra-sensible knowledge that sensation plays in sensible knowledge; it is an intermediary between thought and God, it is the immediate object of our intuition. Man, after all, sees everything in himself, the external world in his organs, the higher world in his reason.

Supra-sensible objects are therefore given immediately to reason, which is inseparable from the soul. By reason we are intimately united to God in thought and in feeling; we have immediate consciousness of the good, the beautiful, the true, of the infinite, of the absolute, of all that is divine in the world. This is, to speak truly, a revelation of God to human reason. De Bonald sought a primitive revelation, made to the first man and transmitted by him to society, in order to explain the problem of rational knowledge; we have not the same motive for despairing of human nature and for seeking a support in a supernatural intervention: the ordinary relation of reason with God suffices to remove the difficulties in this matter; revelation is for us a universal and permanent fact, not an exceptional and temporary one. But if man is in immediate relation with God as with himself, he does not, however, have from the beginning the consciousness of this relation. The knowledge of supra-sensible objects, in order to become exact and scientific, needs a long preparation which develops all the forces of the soul.

PDF 111

THE ORIGINS OF KNOWLEDGE

The division of knowledge according to its sources corresponds to the division of our receptive faculties: we have, on the one hand, sensible cognitions, which derive their origin from sensibility and imagination, and, on the other, non-sensible cognitions, which rest upon reason. Sensibility and reason nourish the whole life of the soul and distribute all its acts, intellectual or affective, into two groups, the one sensible or empirical, the other speculative or non-sensible. The former have a sensible intuition as their condition, the latter an intellectual intuition.

p. 114

Sensible knowledge has as its object facts, phenomena, details, everything that takes place in space or in time, all the acts of physical life or of spiritual life. It is as extensive as observation or experience, and like it comprises a double series of phenomena, the one internal or psychological, the facts of consciousness, the other external or physical, the facts of nature. If by history we understand the universal science of facts, not of laws or principles, then the whole of history—the history [p. 114] of the soul, the history of society, natural history, the history of earth and heaven, constitutes the domain of sensible knowledge. We call it sensible or experimental in order to indicate its origin: without the senses we should have no relation with the individual objects that belong to the external and social world; without imagination, which is the sense of the mind, we could not fix the states that succeed one another within us and that mark the incessant becoming of the soul. But this is not to say that sensibility suffices to give us knowledge of phenomena: all knowledge, sensible or not, is a product of active and attentive thought, that is to say, of the understanding. Only, in historical knowledge, the understanding is exercised upon the data of sensibility or upon the representations of imagination: sensibility furnishes the object or the matter of knowledge, the form comes from the understanding, which analyzes, judges, and interprets this raw matter and then concludes from the image to the object, from the sensation to the cause, thanks to the higher ideas that it borrows from reason.

p. 115

Non-sensible knowledge is as vast as the experimental knowledge to which it is opposed. If the one represents history, the other represents philosophy, the encyclopedic science of the laws, causes, and principles of the moral world and the physical world, the system of general truths that correspond to the immutable essence of things. It is not reason alone that forms this kind of knowledge: here again it supplies only the ground or matter; the form invariably proceeds from the understanding, which applies itself to the data of reason, analyzes them and combines them in order to draw cognitions from them, as it does with regard to sensations. All knowledge requires, as its condition, the functions of thought, attention, perception, and determination, and these various degrees of intellectual activity belong to the understanding. This is why error is possible in philosophical cognitions, as in experimental cognitions: error is a false combination of thought, which has its cause in the [p. 115] combinatory faculty, in the understanding. If reason alone produced our knowledge, the operations of the soul would necessarily be in conformity with reason and hence true and legitimate.

Non-sensible knowledge is twofold, like sensible knowledge. On the one hand, it may follow observation and content itself with generalizing its results: it then shows itself as abstract or common knowledge, knowledge of species and genera, which goes beyond individual things and gathers up their common properties, setting aside particular characters, but which does not yet abandon the field of experience. On the other hand, it may rise above all observation, soar in the serene regions of metaphysics, occupy itself with being as being, as Aristotle expresses it, study its universal attributes, the categories, and finally abandon itself to pure speculation upon the infinite and the absolute, the essence and the cause of all things, the divine and the ideal, what is eternally beautiful, true, and good, what can be grasped by no experience. We shall call the first kind abstract knowledge, because it is chiefly the work of the faculty of abstraction and generalization, that is to say, of the understanding; and the second kind rational knowledge, because reason must play the preponderant role in it. The one is rather a co-sensible knowledge, coordinated with observation, the other a supra-sensible knowledge, independent of all experience.

p. 116

Sensible knowledge and non-sensible knowledge combine with each other in harmonic knowledge or applied knowledge. The world, said Plato, is made in the image of the ideas. Indeed, the non-sensible is constantly realized in the sensible: every object, however limited it may be, has being, essence, unity, qualities, relations; everything has its beauty, its truth, its utility; the absolute itself still shows itself in the relative, inasmuch as the relative exists in itself and is conceived in itself, and the infinite is in the finite, inasmuch as the finite is infinitely determined and determinable to infinity by the intellect. If the infinite kept aloof from the finite, instead of [p. 116] penetrating it and marking it with its character of plenitude, it would no longer be infinite. This combination of the sensible and the non-sensible is the object of a new kind of knowledge, as extensive as the two kinds that it unites. The life of rational beings offers continual applications of it, for it would be impossible to conform to reason without manifesting, in the narrow circle of individual actions, what is universally good, beautiful, just, and true. If sensible knowledge forms history, and non-sensible knowledge philosophy, applied knowledge will be the domain of the philosophy of history, which analyzes facts from the point of view of laws. This truth is better and better understood by those scientists who are freeing themselves from sensualism, and who know how to see in the universe something other than a collection of phenomena. “We could not study the most isolated corner of the material world without finding there the mark of a divine action, just as we cannot go on contemplating the sovereign idea in a state of pure virtuality, while neglecting that infinite world of phenomena and existences which is its mobile realization and attests its eternal fecundity. Arrived at a certain height, science merges with metaphysics itself, for if the first shows us that phenomena are only ideas realized, the second shows us that the true reality of facts lies only in the absolute of the divine thought (1).”

We have, then, three kinds of knowledge, two of which are opposed to each other, in the form of the sensible and the non-sensible, of the individual and the general, and the third of which presents the synthesis of the two terms: history, philosophy, and the philosophy of history. But above these distinct kinds, it is important to remark further indeterminate knowledge, by which the object is grasped in its essence one and whole, in its undivided totality, without any designation of sensible or non-sensible elements. Indeterminate knowledge is prior to analysis and precedes, in the order of time, all our determinate knowledge.

(1) Aug. Laugel, Science et Philosophie, III, Paris, 1863.

p. 117

A remarkable example of indeterminate cognitions is offered to us by the thought I, as primitive fact of inner sense. The child is undoubtedly conscious of himself before he can affirm anything of the self, before he knows whether he is mind or body, whether he thinks or wills, whether he is finite or infinite, relative or absolute. All these particular affirmations are the result of analysis and are expressed in the form of judgment; but a judgment needs a subject, and the subject of every judgment that one passes upon oneself, by attributing to oneself a quality, were it even existence, is necessarily the self. The same holds of the knowledge of God, inasmuch as the one and whole being, the total object of reason, is above every genus and every determination. God is not only the eternal and immutable being, but also infinite life and becoming; he is not a pure spirit, withdrawn from the world, he is also nature; he is not only the first being or the highest being, but all being, beyond all comparison: God as such can be only the object of an indeterminate knowledge; he is neither a simple idea, nor a complex phenomenon, nor a fundamental proposition, nor an inevitable conclusion, he is all at once, without being anything determinate. The same holds, finally, of every other object of thought, considered in its essence one and whole. To proceed to the analysis of any thing whatever, we must first distinguish the thing itself; otherwise, what would be the object of the analysis? The attributes of a substance or of a property do not subsist by themselves alone; to what shall we attach them, if their subject does not present itself to thought? Analysis demands efforts of attention and acts of abstraction that exceed the powers of early childhood. Before knowing whether time and space are continuous and divisible, whether they are subjective forms of the mind or objective forms of matter, we must needs have some vague consciousness of them. Every reality in the world has an immutable essence and contingent manifestations, the double object of a rational and a sensible knowledge: nature, for example, is subject to eternal laws and creates in its bosom countless individualities; but these two aspects are conceived in the same

p. 118

Logic. — I. 8 [p. 118] being, and nature as such, considered in its undivided unity, is again the object of an indeterminate knowledge.

Such is human knowledge as a whole. For the present the question is of knowledge itself, and not of truth or of certainty. That is why no doubt can remain in the mind concerning the division that precedes, which is set forth in the table below. It is permissible to maintain with Kant that the only legitimate or scientific cognitions of man are contained within the limits of experience: this thesis mutilates science, no doubt, that is to say, true and certain knowledge, but not knowledge in general, as an expression of intellectual activity. But it is contrary to all reason to affirm, with the sensualists of the modern schools, that knowledge stops at phenomena. That metaphysics is a pretension, not a right of thought, I cannot at this moment dispute; but I lay it down as a fact that thought occupies itself, and has always occupied itself, with God, the universe, humanity, the laws, the causes, and the essence of things, as well as with the accidents of life. Whatever the value of these cognitions may be, they are cognitions that must be taken into account and that serve at least to measure the reach of the intellect: there is no fact of consciousness and no historical point more incontestable than the universality of our knowledge, guaranteed by the philosophical monuments of all ages and by the attestation of every mind in a condition to judge the question. It is therefore a strange illusion to imagine that the theory of human knowledge is reduced to a few considerations on sensible representations or on the observation of bodies. A somewhat more complete study of psychology would do the skeptical logicians of our day no harm.

Indeterminate knowledge. Sensible knowledge, internal and external. | Non-sensible knowl‐

edge, abstract and rational.

Applied knowledge.

p. 119

We shall concern ourselves in logic only with knowledge [p. 119] of the external sensible kind, so ill understood even now by those very persons who make it the exclusive object of their studies, with abstract knowledge, which is indispensable for the understanding of the operations of thought and of method, and with rational knowledge, which must be carefully sketched out as a preparation for metaphysics. These three kinds of knowledge stand to one another as sensibility, the understanding, and reason, which predominate in them, that is to say, as the various degrees of the application of thought. This progressive development of thought, which begins its work of analysis with sensibility, continues it by reflection, and completes it by reason, in conformity with the three stages of culture of the soul, sensible culture in childhood, reflective culture in youth, rational culture in maturity, did not escape the sagacity of Kant: the transcendental aesthetic, analytic, and dialectic follow the same order in the “Critique of Pure Reason,” but are treated there with preoccupations foreign to the pure theory of knowledge.

We shall neglect indeterminate knowledge, the existence of which it is enough for us to point out in order to fill a regrettable gap, one fruitful in consequences; applied knowledge, the developments of which are found in the philosophy of history; and internal sensible knowledge, which by itself fills experimental psychology or “the science of the soul within the limits of observation.”

CHAPTER ONE

SENSIBLE KNOWLEDGE

Logical Aesthetic.

p. 120

The subject here is external sensible knowledge, which rests upon the data of our senses and which has for its object the facts or phenomena of the external world. Considered from the point of [p. 120] view of knowledge, these facts fall into two groups: those that we know by ourselves and those that we know through others. The former are for us the object of observation; the latter the object of testimony. Testimony supplies the insufficiency of our personal powers; limited in time and in space, we cannot by our own efforts grasp all the details of the physical world, as we study by inner sense the acts of the soul, and by reason the universal laws and principles. This is why testimony ought to bear only upon external facts, subject to the senses, and always presupposes in the witness the capacity to observe. All external knowledge therefore rests in the last resort upon the deposition of the senses and is summed up in the general theory of sensible observation. The question of testimony concerns only certainty. We shall also have to inquire further on whether there does not exist a third kind of facts, which would be the object of faith.

p. 121

External observation embraces the whole descriptive part of the sciences that deal with nature and society. The rational or mathematical part of these sciences belongs to philosophical knowledge. Observation is necessarily limited in its objects: it extends to the past and the present, not to the future; it applies to what is or has been, not to what ought to be, and is expressed only in the form of a particular and assertoric judgment. Principles and causes are quite otherwise. The law of attraction, for example, inasmuch as it governs all bodies at all times and in all places, even outside our planetary system, passes beyond the limits of observation and is formulated in a general and apodictic judgment. Doubtless experience does not contradict universal gravitation, but it gives it only as a fact, applicable to the cases observed, not as a principle dominating all possible cases in infinite space. In the natural sciences, physical, chemical, physiological, and geographical, there are therefore two distinct parts: by the one, they belong to history and fall within the domain of sensible knowledge or of observation; by the other, they belong to philosophy and [p. 121] fall within rational knowledge. Political history, or the history of human societies, is a special branch of the same group. The description of past institutions, like the topographical knowledge of the earth, is transmitted to us especially by way of testimony, but can be admitted only on condition of being founded upon a regular observation of facts.

p. 122

External sensible knowledge has given birth to several contradictory doctrines. Sensualism claims that the senses alone give it to us and that we have no other knowledge than that which is furnished by sensibility. The soul is then deprived of all spontaneity, since the senses do nothing but receive the impression of objects from without, and all its faculties are sensations or transformed sensations. The mind is likened to an inert and passive matter, a “tabula rasa” on which sensible impressions leave their traces; to feel is to know, and our cognitions come to us ready-made from the external world: “Nihil est in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu.” Skeptical idealism, on the contrary, maintains that sensible knowledge has no value whatever, that the senses give us only impressions, which in no way resemble the bodies that we suppose to be their cause and which cannot serve as the basis of a legitimate affirmation, that the external world, finally, does not at all correspond to the representation that we have of it and is to be received in science only as a mere product of our own imagination: the physical world, whose objective existence common sense invariably attests, would therefore be only an illusion of the mind and would exist only in us, like the phantoms that we create in our dreams and that leave us the same conviction and the same emotions as long as sleep lasts. This strange doctrine is certainly in opposition to common consciousness and is belied by the feeling that we have of our limitation; but it is accepted by reputable authors, by Xenophanes and Parmenides, by Berkeley and Fichte, and rests upon arguments that are, without any [p. 122] doubt, more serious than those which the sensualists invoke. It errs not in its basis but in its omissions; it starts from an exact analysis of sensation, but ignores the other faculties of the soul which make up for the insufficiency of the data of our senses. Finally, it has the merit of having opened the way to the rational theory of sensible knowledge (1).

Let us examine, then, how the knowledge that we have of external objects is formed, and what the whole of its conditions is, both physiological and psychological. The result of this examination can be expressed in advance in these terms: the first condition of sensible knowledge is purely physical and resides in the sense organs, which give the sensation; but the soul then intervenes with the series of its intellectual faculties to complete the sensation and engender knowledge: imagination furnishes the representation of the object; reflection or the understanding composes the notion of it and concludes from the internal to the external, by means of the functions of thought; reason, finally, supplies the ideas or the categories that we apply to the object in order to determine it in its properties and in its relations. Let no one be astonished at this multiplicity of means which the simple knowledge of an external thing requires: it is well known that the soul is whole in each of its acts and that our faculties are neither independent of the soul nor separated from one another; when we say that imagination, reflection, and reason concur in the production of knowledge, it is understood that it is always the soul that acts; but the soul acts in various capacities, and the faculties express these manifold modes of spiritual activity. Nothing prevents us, then, from reducing the subjective conditions of sensible knowledge to the concurrence of the soul and the senses, “intellectus et sensus,” provided that we afterwards analyze the part of the soul: there we shall discover without difficulty the elements of imagination, of the understanding, and of reason.

(1) Krause, Die Lehre vom Erkennen und von der Erkenntniss. — Vorlesungen über die Grundwahrheiten der Wissenschaft. — Ahrens, Cours de psychologie, vol. II. Paris, 1838.

p. 123

The senses are part of the cerebral nervous system, which is intimately united to the soul. Their role is at once physical and spiritual; they behave as material organs, receive the action of matter, develop and decay with the body, but serve above all the interests of the spiritual life: they are destined to put the soul in contact with nature, by enabling it to understand nature, to feel it, to act upon it, and to adapt it to the requirements of man’s mission on earth; they are even the intermediaries between man and his fellows, for speech, education, and teaching are possible, under the conditions of present life, only by means of our senses. Sensualism and materialism have in this respect a juster feeling for the truth, when they extol the advantages of sensibility, than asceticism, when it disparages and despises all the sensible manifestations of human nature.

p. 124

The senses are organized in correspondence with the various physical and chemical processes of nature, manifested in the production of heat, light, sound, flavors, and odors. Oken, in the philosophy of nature, expresses this correspondence in a picturesque manner: the eye is a ray of sunlight, the ear a musical instrument, the nose an electric battery, the mouth a laboratory, the skin a crust of earth. Each sense reveals to us a special order of phenomena, which it is impossible to perceive by another: the optic nerve is affected by light, not by sound. Aristotle was therefore right: one sense the fewer, one series of cognitions the fewer. To this qualitative limitation of the senses we must further add a quantitative limitation, in the very order of their perceptions. No sense extends to the infinite in space or to the infinitely small in the decrease of the undulations of light or sound, although sight can seize bodies in the heavens at incommensurable distances and appreciate the gradation of tints with a marvelous delicacy. There are instruments that augment in enormous proportions the natural range of the senses, but the sensory [p. 124] activity has none the less necessary limits, which it is for genius to push back, not to overstep. Whatever the degree, it will always remain true to say that an impression too weak or too strong is no longer perceived by the senses. The degree of the impression results sometimes from the object, from its distance or its power of radiation, sometimes from the pathological state of the organs: there are diseases that depress, and others that heighten, sensory activity. All these circumstances must be taken into account when we consult the senses on the phenomena of nature. Their testimony is therefore valid only under reserve: they must be in a state of health and be questioned, within the limits of their strength, on facts that are within their competence. The writings of Plato and Aristotle already contain on this subject rich and precious indications, which have not been contradicted by modern science.

p. 125

The senses receive impressions and transmit them to the brain, where, according to physiology, the sensation is produced, with the concurrence of the soul, on condition of the continuity of the nervous system. The section, the ligature, the paralysis, or the numbing of the cerebral or spinal nerves does in fact abolish sensation, although the external organ remains intact. Sensation is therefore a physical phenomenon which begins at the periphery of the body and ends at the nerve center, where it affects the soul, by reason of the intimate relation that exists between the two substances in man. In the absence of any accident in the nervous system, the impression is inevitably changed into sensation. Perhaps it would even be more exact to say that the impression is the sensation itself, but that it can be perceived only if the nervous system is complete. This explanation would be more in conformity with experimental psychology; for the soul feels and perceives only the nerves as modified by objects. It would also give a better account of the fact of the localization of sensations and of the phenomenon of vision: it is conceivable that the optic nerve should receive the influence of light and colors, whereas no ray of sunlight penetrates to the brain. Be that as it may, this distinction will not affect the result of [p. 125] our inquiries; for it is in the normal state, on the hypothesis of the integrity of the nervous system, that we are going to study sensation. Whence does it come, and what does it contain? It results, we believe, from the action of external objects upon the nerves that spread out in the organs. Can objects, then, act? Doubtless; everything acts to a certain degree, every body has forces, and this datum of the dynamic theory of matter must be accepted, but nothing obliges us to think that bodies are only a combination of forces. Light, heat, and electricity act incontestably upon the nervous matter in a living body. Each nerve receives this action in a special manner, according to its own nature. It would be very difficult to say why the optic nerve has not the same properties as the auditory nerve; but whatever the cause of this diversity, the fact is certain: the one is sensitive only to waves of light and the other to waves of sound.

p. 126

Now, if sensation proceeds from an action of objects upon our nerves, it is clear that it expresses a relation between our own organs and the external world, and that it must vary accordingly with the two terms of this relation, whether according to the objects, apart from the organs, or according to the organs, apart from the objects, or finally according to the modifications that occur at once in the objects and in the organs. Thus distinct objects, like the sun and the moon, produce distinct impressions on the same organ, and the same object, for example a fire, procures different sensations, beneficial or painful, for different persons, according to the temperature of their own bodies; what is more, the same person, in relation to the same object, may experience opposite sensations in two consecutive instants, if he passes from one state to another, from hot to cold, from health to sickness. We willingly approach a blazing fire in winter, but the sensation, agreeable as it was, soon becomes intolerable. Plato had made the same observation: wine, he said, gives pleasure to him who enjoys health and is repugnant to him who is sick. Sensation appears, therefore [p. 126] quite capricious: it changes at the will of things and circumstances, and perhaps there are not two persons who receive exactly the same impression from the same object. And yet we must say that sensation is necessarily, at each instant and for each person, what it ought to be; for it always expresses the relation of the object to the organ, and this relation can be in only one manner, having regard to the two terms, at the moment when it manifests itself. Sensation, finally, according to the profound thought of Aristotle, adopted by the great physiologist Müller, sensation is the common act of the sensible and the sentient. There is no more caprice in the communication of sensations than in the action of light or of electricity; we may justly be astonished at the complications of this action upon plane, concave, or convex mirrors and at the apparent oddity of the effects of lightning; but no physicist would dare to express the slightest doubt of the necessary character of the one action and of the other in the given circumstances. When the circumstances are known, the action is foreseen, it is submitted to calculation, and nature has never failed to answer our expectation in a well-devised experiment. Now sensation is a physical phenomenon, produced by matter upon matter, and must be accomplished according to the laws of the physical world. It is therefore impossible that it should be otherwise than it is in each case. Already it is measured by means of the thermometer in the affections of the cutaneous organ. All sensations could thus be determined beforehand and fixed with certainty, if we knew exactly the degree of sensitiveness of the organ on which we operate: sensations are necessary. It is this property that has seduced severe minds and has drawn a great number of scientists into the paths of sensualism: we like to find again in the study of man the general laws that preside over the life of nature. Dr. Beneke has well studied this side of the soul in his Psychology, but he has there sacrificed, as is the fashion today, all the rest.

p. 127

Sensation is necessary, we say. Indeed, it is wholly passive and involuntary. We receive sensations [p. 127] of everything that surrounds us; we do not produce them, except in the case of hallucination, which is a derangement of the imagination, in which the sensation itself becomes imaginary. It does not depend upon us whether sensation exists or does not exist, or whether it is of one kind or another; otherwise suffering and torture would have no hold upon us. We can, indeed, open or close our eyes, turn to the right or to the left, and so put ourselves in a position to experience the impressions that please us or to avoid those that are repugnant to us: this is the influence of the mind upon the body, by means of the muscles and the nerves; but in each given position the sensation is produced without any participation of the will. Light modifies the optic nerve, heat influences the sensitive nerves, whether we will it or not, and the modifications of our nerves correspond exactly to the intensity and quality of the agents. This is why we distinguish stuffs by touch, colors by sight, sounds by hearing; we judge of objects according to the diversity of the impressions that we receive of them. The basis of all these judgments, which express our belief in the reality of the external world, is that sensation is necessary, or that it is as it ought to be. What would sensation prove with regard to bodies, if we could make it arise or change it at will? Things would then be as we wish them and not as they are, or rather there would be no longer any means of discerning between reality and our own desires. Necessity reigns only in the world of matter; in the spiritual world everything is voluntary and free. Freedom is the opposite of necessity: it is the capricious element of creation, which rejects all rule or submits to duty only voluntarily. Where necessity dominates, everything is chained and bound in an invincible manner, nothing is voluntary; where the will dominates, everything may be or not be, in one way or in another, everything is contingent, nothing is constrained or necessary. If, then, sensation is necessary, it is because the will takes no part in it.

p. 128

It is easy henceforth to judge sensation from the point of view of truth and error, a question disputed in all [p. 128] ages. Sensation is the source of most of our errors, witness the illusions of the senses, say the skeptics; sensation is knowledge itself and the principle of all science, say the sensualists. Properly speaking, sensation in itself is neither true nor false: it is a physiological phenomenon, which is doubtless as it ought to be, but which can become truth or error only through its relation to the intellect. Truth is not what is, but what is perceived or understood as it is; it is not a substance, but a relation, the exact relation between thought and its object. There is truth only for the intellect. A disease, too, is as it is, but it is not known for that reason, and so long as it remains unknown, it is neither true nor false for us. In metaphysics only is it permitted to say that all that exists is true, inasmuch as God sees everything and knows all things as they are. With regard to us, sensation as such is indifferent to truth and error.
