But it can, like any other phenomenon, become an object of the intellect, and then it will be the occasion, not the cause, either of a truth or of an error, according as it is perceived in conformity with, or contrary to, its nature.

p. 129

Sensation has a representative element for the intellect and an affective element for feeling: on the one hand, it affects the soul, in an agreeable or painful manner, according as it favors or thwarts our nervous sensibility; on the other, it calls attention and furnishes to thought the matter of a cognition. It is in this cognition that truth or error will be found; sensation is there only as an object of thought. Error, finally, is an act of the intellect, not of the senses; it denotes a vicious combination, a negative relation between thought and its object; it exists when the intellect does not grasp the thing as it is. It is therefore the understanding that deceives itself with regard to sensation, when it perceives it and sees in it something other than what is there; but the senses cannot deceive us, since they do not know, and do not know themselves; they affirm nothing, they deny nothing, they content themselves with receiving impressions [p. 129] and transmitting them to the soul. It is therefore not exact to say that sensation contains errors, even when we experience diverse and contrary modifications from one and the same object. Each sensation is as it ought to be at the moment when it takes place. But we shall infallibly fall into error if we hasten to pass a judgment upon the object, without taking account of the state of our organs. From the fact that the sensation of taste is disagreeable, we must not conclude without further examination that the dish is bad. We shall again deceive ourselves if we wish to estimate exactly the size, the distance, or the shape of objects from the impression of sight alone. I see two sticks a few paces away; I declare, on the testimony of my senses, that they are five meters off, that they are round, and that the one is twice the height of the other; I measure, and I perceive that I had put into my estimate a few centimeters too much on one side, too little on the other, and that the sticks are oval. Where is the error? It is not in my senses, which will always give me the same information in the same circumstances; it lies wholly in the judgment that I pronounced without regard to all the incidents that complicate the transmission and reflection of light. I see a tree partly plunged in water, I judge that the trunk is oblique, whereas in reality it is vertical: I have forgotten the refraction, sensation forgets nothing. The ancients thought, and children will always be of their opinion, that the moon is about as large as the sun: they judged from the apparent diameter, and misjudged the respective distance of the two heavenly bodies. The examples could be varied indefinitely, and we should always arrive at the same result: every error in sensible knowledge proceeds from the intellect, not from the senses, and finds its cause in an inexact interpretation of the sensation, either because the mind does not take into consideration the state of the organs, or because it estimates wrongly the laws under which the phenomenon is accomplished. Such is the field of the illusion of the senses: sensibility is no more responsible for it than are the instruments which, by ingenious combinations of effects, disturb the habits of sight.

p. 130

When error is imputed to the senses, sensation is confounded with perception. Sensualism has deployed all its genius in identifying these two facts, however contrary they may be, as acts of the senses and of the intellect, the one physical, passive, necessary, the other spiritual, spontaneous, and free. It understood that it might hope for the full success of its thesis, “the soul is nothing but sensibility,” if it could introduce spontaneity and reflection into the soul under cover of sensation. Indeed, if sensation is a perception, the soul, though reduced to sensibility, is then active and intelligent, and thereupon it becomes easy to explain judgment and reasoning, even reason itself. This simplicity is only a lure, and this tactic can satisfy only minds already prepossessed. Condillac begins by absorbing attention in sensation. It would be vain to tell him that we have sensations constantly, in the waking state, but that we do not always pay attention to them, that sensation can thus be conscious or not, according as it is accompanied or deprived of the concurrence of the intellect, that language itself consecrates the distinction of these two things, since it has different terms to designate each sensation in the one case and in the other, as to hear and to listen: nothing would avail; attention for him is only the most lively sensation, the one that excludes the others. If it were so, we could never reflect except upon our sensations; there would be no more meditation or contemplation, no more freedom or direction in the intellectual life, seeing that at every instant there exists a predominant sensation. The fact is that, in the absence of any serious preoccupation, the strongest or the least habitual sensation attracts attention, because it shakes the nervous system, to which the soul is intimately united; but it is one thing to provoke, another to constitute attention. Attention and sensation may converge, like the soul and the body, without being identical. Attention is a voluntary movement of thought, a function of the intellect, not of the senses, which has for its object now a sensible impression, now a rational principle. The physical is not transformed into the moral. This simple observation, which agrees [p. 131] with individual experience and with the common sense of the peoples who have recorded it in their idioms, overturns from top to bottom the sensualist doctrine and consequently materialism, since it is already established that knowledge does not come to us ready-made from without through the channel of the senses, but that it is formed within us, that it is a product of our intellect, and that its first condition in the soul is attention.

p. 132

But attention does not suffice: to know, we must grasp. Perception is the second function of the understanding and the second intellectual condition of knowledge. The sensualists confound it with attention, that is to say, with sensation. Yet it is not our senses that perceive; it is we who perceive by means of our senses. The eye is the instrument, not the cause or the agent of vision. Otherwise there would never be error in our sensible cognitions, since there is none in sensation. The mind perceives what it wills, when it wills. It chooses among sensible phenomena those that have the most attraction for it, it directs its attention to them and grasps them; it prunes away the sensations that might distract it; when it has observed enough, it closes the senses or turns them in another direction, and ceases to perceive objects in order to perceive their relations, in order to study the causes or the conditions of their appearance. All this work is done apart from sensation and may be in contradiction with sensation. To feel is therefore not to perceive or to know; for, on the one hand, we perceive what the senses do not give, laws, principles, and, on the other, we often perceive the contrary of what they give us. Someone is speaking at my side; it does not depend upon my will whether the noise strikes my ears, but it does depend upon me to listen to what is said; when I listen, I perceive, but I may deceive myself; although the auditory nerve faithfully echoes the sounds, I commit a mistake and I grasp words quite other than those that were pronounced: the sensation is exact, the perception is false; sensation is involuntary, perception is free; sensation is only a modification of the nervous matter, [p. 132] perception is an act of the mind; sensation passes unperceived if the mind is not present, and acquires value for knowledge only through perception. If the soul had only senses, far from knowing everything, it would have no knowledge at all.

p. 133

What does the mind perceive? What is the direct object of perception? It is not the external thing, the body that is found in space; it is the sensation, that is to say, the modification of the nerves or the nervous impression. Here is an important point, fruitful in consequences, which must be brought to light. Let us recall the relations of the soul in this world, which we have studied in the Psychology. The soul is in relation with the body to which it is united; but this relation is intimate, as a relation of immediate consciousness and feeling, only with one part of the body, with the nervous system of the life of relation, not at its center, in the encephalon, nor in the course of the nerves from the center to the surface, but at the periphery, where the cerebral or spinal nerves spread out in the sense organs, inasmuch as these nerves receive the action of external objects. It is a fact that we do not know by inner sense the phenomena of vegetative life, nor even the structure of the brain or the direction of the nerves that end in the organs: anatomy alone can inform us on this subject; whereas we perceive and feel immediately what takes place in the organs of the senses, when they are open, on condition of the integrity of the nervous system: anatomy is useless for seeing or hearing, for experiencing a pleasure or a pain, as for effecting the movement of the muscles by means of the same nerves. Such is the precise limit of the intimate relation of the soul with the body. All the other relations of the soul with creation are subordinate to this relation. We are, as intellect, as feeling, and as will, in communication with the world of bodies and of minds only in an indirect manner, by means of our nervous system. Bodies and rational beings reveal themselves only to our senses and can be known or felt only by [p. 133] this intermediary. We cannot see or hear spirits, but we see gestures and hear sounds which represent, as signs, the acts of the spiritual life. The relations of the soul with God alone are foreign to sensibility and are established by means of reason. Let us not forget that we have only two receptive faculties, the senses and reason, which are destined to put us in relation with the whole ensemble of things, with the world and with God, and which furnish us with all the materials of our transcendent activity.

The theory of sensible knowledge is an application of these psychological data. Just as the soul does not feel external objects, but only the pleasure or the suffering they cause it, so it does not perceive things outside, but only the sensations transmitted to it by the organs. The immediate object of perception is the sensation, nothing but the sensation, that is to say, a nervous state of the body, a modification of ourselves. Man is therefore confined to himself in sensible knowledge, and can grasp nature only through his senses and in his senses. He does not perceive things, but an impression, a shadow of things, according to the beautiful allegory of Plato. The conclusion seems strange and at first sight compromises the reality of the external world, but it is justified by the facts and confirmed even by the authority of the greatest thinkers of all periods. All philosophers agree on this point, that we do not perceive objects immediately. Reid alone holds a contrary opinion (1).

The Peripatetics, in antiquity and in the Middle Ages, supposed between the mind and objects forms or sensible species, that is to say, effluvia or images which escaped from bodies and met the soul or the sensorium in which it resides, leaving an imprint in the organs (2). They were conscious of an intermediary, but they

p. 134

Logic. — I. [p. 134] expressed it badly: the sensible species have disappeared with the entelechies, the archaei, and the occult causes; the sensation has remained. Descartes, convinced that mind and body are radically separate, replaced the sensible species by ideas, which alone have access to the soul. He hesitates about the nature of these adventitious ideas, which he is careful to distinguish from innate ideas: now they come from bodies and seem foreign to the soul, now they are formed by the mind on the occasion of something that emanates from bodies. In the first sense they are no better than the forms of Aristotle; in the second they are the product of the imagination, which accompanies sensation and represents things to us. In any case, according to the founder of modern philosophy, the soul perceives only its own impressions, and must trust to God for its belief in the existence of the external world. Malebranche merely transferred into the Creator those ideas of bodies which his master placed in us: he therefore holds that we see in God the ideas of things. Everyone agrees, he says, that we do not perceive the objects that are outside us by themselves, supposing that these objects are not intimately united to us. Spirits may perhaps discover themselves directly to our thought, when justice and order shall reign, as in heaven, through the intimate union of souls. But material things cannot be united in this way to the soul, which has no extension and is without relation to them. The soul does not go strolling in the heavens to contemplate the sun and the stars. The immediate object of our mind, when it sees the sun, is therefore not the sun, but something which is intimately united to our soul and which I call idea. In order to perceive an object, the idea of that object must be present to us, and all the ideas of bodies are found in God. — Such is the profound theory of the vision in God, born of the metaphysical conceptions of Descartes concerning the soul, the body, and ideas. The ideas of bodies take there the place of the sensible and material species, which were no longer compatible with the new psychology. Berkeley has clearly expressed the consequence: reasoning [p. 135] in the accredited hypothesis of intermediary ideas, he resolved to suppress things as useless, since we have ideas, which suffice for everything. Hume applauds. Kant imagined other intermediaries between the mind and things, namely time and space, as forms of sensibility. All these authors seem therefore to agree in admitting that the perception of the external world is indirect. But Reid is of another opinion.

(1) Th. Reid, Œuvres complètes, trans. Jouffroy, vol. III, Paris, 1828.

(2) Waddington-Kastus, de la Psychologie d’Aristote, ch. xiv. — Malebranche, Recherche de la vérité, bk. iii, 2nd part.

p. 136

If we attend, he says, to that act of our mind which we call perception, we shall find in it three things: first, some conception or notion of the object perceived; secondly, an irresistible conviction of its present existence; and, thirdly, that this belief is immediate, and not the effect of reasoning. It is indeed impossible to perceive without having some notion of that which we perceive. Sensible perception is an act of the understanding which grasps a present and determinate object, and which consequently already knows it to some degree. We are agreed on this point, but the question is to know what the object of perception is. Reid affirms that it is an external thing; we say that it is the sensation, whatever may be the cause of the sensible phenomenon. Doubtless we firmly believe in the existence of the object when the perception is distinct; if we perceive a star, we say that the star exists, and no judge will refuse the testimony of a person who has seen a crime committed, on the pretext that sight is not worthy of trust; but what is the origin of this belief? Is it primitive, or is it not rather the effect of a questionable habit, contracted from childhood? Already, in the case of the first example, astronomers know well that a star may have ceased to exist for centuries when we still believe we perceive it. The conviction is therefore not always irresistible, and the sensation, though real, does not necessarily prove the present existence of the object. Reid himself cites two exceptions to the universality of the belief which he proclaims. The first concerns hypochondriacs, who are persuaded of things that seem to contradict the evident testimony of their senses; but the general laws of the intelligence [p. 136] are not invalidated by the disorders which arise in the faculties of the sick. The second concerns the skeptics, who reject the deposition of the senses; but their doubt is theoretical rather than practical; in all the history of philosophy we never read of any skeptic that ever stepped into fire or water, or that showed in any single part of his conduct less trust in his senses than other men; which gives us reason to think that those who speak ill of the senses with so much subtlety are not convinced by their own reasonings. The reply is clever, but does not touch the theory of knowledge in the least. We shall see that there are still other exceptions, and we shall endeavor to account for them.

p. 137

Let us admit provisionally that perception is accompanied by a belief in the existence of external objects in men of sound mind, under normal conditions, and let us go to the heart of the question. Reid maintains that this conviction is immediate, or that it is not the consequence of a reasoning. The opposition which he points out between the procedures of the mind is sharply drawn, but he is mistaken in fact. He almost admits as much, for after laying down his principle he takes care to add that “this is true, however, only of persons so far advanced in understanding as to distinguish objects of mere imagination from things which have a real existence.… But whether children, from the time that they begin to use their senses, make a distinction between things which are only conceived or imagined, and things which really exist, may be doubted. Until we are able to make this distinction, we cannot properly be said to believe or to disbelieve the existence of any thing. The belief of the existence of any thing seems to suppose a notion of existence; a notion too abstract, perhaps, to enter into the mind of an infant. I speak of the power of perception in those that are adult, and of a sound mind.…” This is precisely the point we wished to reach. The conviction that there exist objects corresponding to our sensations is therefore not primitive: it is the legitimate or illegitimate result [p. 137] of the experience we have acquired since childhood. It is therefore not immediate: it is the conclusion of a series of observations which we have made on the use and range of our senses, and which, in adult age, impose themselves upon the mind and command its assent like a habit. It cannot be otherwise, since the senses give us only sensations, not cognitions, since perception is a function of the mind, and since we are not, as mind, in direct relation with the external world.

p. 138

The demonstration of the fact will result abundantly from the analysis of our senses. Let us first try to grasp the question as a whole and in its consequences. If sensation is a modification of ourselves, and if perception applies only to our impressions, it is evident that sensation and perception alone do not authorize us to affirm the existence of an external world. When I am conscious of my thoughts and picture to myself a winged horse, I am not in the least disposed to believe that an object of this kind exists; when I am conscious of my sensations, on the contrary, I involuntarily imagine that there exist bodies endowed with sensible properties. Why this difference? Are not my sensations in me as my thoughts are? And what do the acts of the self prove concerning a not-self ? How can we thus go out of ourselves and affirm something outside? By the aid of reasoning. Whether this procedure is well founded or not, I do not know, but its existence is indubitable. If the external world is not the object of an immediate perception of the soul, it can be conceived only indirectly, by means of reasoning. This solution at first sight presents difficulties, which made the common sense of Reid recoil, but they will vanish very quickly. Thus, it will be said, the affirmation of the external world is not a primitive fact of consciousness, but a conclusion of the understanding? Doubtless the mind concludes from effect to cause, from sensation to object, as soon as it has recognized the limits of its own existence and has made a distinction between the capricious images of its imagination, of which it [p. 138] is the author, and the necessary sensations which affect it independently of its will. There is but one primitive fact of thought, the consciousness of oneself: Cogito, ergo sum. The soul grasps itself without intermediary, by a direct intuition, but at first it knows nothing of nature or of its fellows. An external world exists only for a limited being, such as man or the animal, and a being can be conscious of this external world, or recognize it as such, only if it is first conscious of its own limitation: man alone has this consciousness. Why should we say that bodies are outside us, if we did not know, by our deficiencies, by our weakness, by our efforts, that our being has bounds, and that there exists in consequence something other than ourselves? We can arrive at the outside only by the prior knowledge of ourselves, and we must conclude the exterior from the limitation of our interior. This conclusion rests naturally on the phenomena of sensibility, which require a cause, and whose cause is not in us. If a new proof were needed in support of our assertion that the self recognizes itself before it is conscious of a not-self, we should find it in the singular consequence which an author has drawn from the contrary thesis: “The knowledge of the external world is therefore indispensable to the knowledge we have of ourselves, and as this latter knowledge is immediate, it follows that it is immediately and without intermediary that objects are known to us (1).” It is impossible to retail a gross error more cavalierly in order to justify an erroneous proposition. The falsity of the conclusion proves the falsity of the premises which contain it.

But then children do not grasp the world of bodies, unless they know themselves, unless they judge and reason, unless they are as learned as we are; is this not absurd? There are infinite degrees in knowledge.

(1) Léon Brothier, Ébauche d’un glossaire du langage philosophique. Paris, 1863. Verbo Connaissance.

p. 139

From his entrance into life the child has sensations, and he bears witness to them by his cries, but he knows nothing of the earth, which proves once more that to feel is not to know. The child has everything to learn in this world, but he learns quickly, thanks to his marvelous instinct: he must discover for himself, at his own expense, the use of his limbs and of his senses; he must observe in himself the sensations which affect him agreeably and those which hurt him, in order to seek the former and avoid the latter; he must find, with no other guide than his own experience, the signs and words which correspond to his thoughts, in order to enter into communication with his fellows. The child is not so ignorant as people are pleased to believe, for within the space of a year, before anyone can teach him anything, he has solved the most difficult problems of life. At his first sensation, due no doubt to the contact of the atmosphere, he announces that he is affected and that he feels himself; he affirms himself; but he has no consciousness of the change wrought in his condition, nor of the new causes which act upon his organs. When his senses are somewhat disentangled, he directs his attention outward, but is it really outward? He feels something, he perceives, that is certain, but he perceives only what passes in his organs. Why should he think that there is anything other than himself? We may say among ourselves that he sees houses, trees, animals which are not in him; but he knows nothing of it; he does not at the first stroke distinguish these external objects from the internal representations that have remained in his memory and his imagination; he does as the animals do, which perceive the external world without ever knowing that it is external, because they have no knowledge of their interior; he does as we do in our dreams, he confounds the self with the not-self. But the doubt will vanish. The child is intrigued by everything he sees and hears, he observes with the greatest attention, he is serious and will not unbend before he has had his misgivings set at rest. The period of experiments begins for him, he feels himself, he looks at himself, he gesticulates: this is mine, I feel it, I move it when I will, as I will, and I feel it doubly, in the hand and in the [p. 140] member that it touches; that is not mine, I feel it only in the hand and I cannot move it at will. Therefore I am something, but I am not everything: there is for me an inside and an outside.

Let no one be surprised that the child judges and reasons without knowing what reasoning is. Every intelligent being reasons according to its nature and its powers. The child does not make a syllogism in due form and has no need, in order to act, to analyze his operations; when he observes two things and sees some relation between them, he judges: a pleasant or painful sensation suffices as the matter of a judgment; when he perceives three things connected with one another in some manner, he reasons: the nurse, the milk, the pleasure form a natural series whose succession the child has no difficulty in grasping: the nurse brings joy, because she gives nourishment. It does not take a very considerable time to pass from the first notion to the third; the reasoning becomes instantaneous when it comprises only notions that are familiar to us. It is upon reasonings of this kind that our belief in the external world rests, on the occasion of the sensations we receive from it.

p. 141

Such is the course followed by the development of thought in the child in passing from the self to the not-self. The objection which had stopped Reid does not touch us. This course, moreover, is not only in accord with the teachings of experimental psychology; it is also indicated by physiology, whether in regard to the exercise of our senses, in childhood or in sickness, or to the illusions to which we remain exposed at every age. “Distance, size, shape, and movement of objects are appreciated solely by a labor of the intelligence. It is through it that we learn to refer the impressions which the sight of objects produces on our retina to the bodies from which the light proceeds. The child must carry out the training of his intelligence in respect of sight, as must the blind man restored by an operation.” Here is the necessity of personal experience well established in visual perceptions. It is the same [p. 141] for sound perceptions, which seem still more difficult to interpret. “Nothing shows better how much the hearing needs, in a manner, to be trained in order to develop than the observation of deaf-mutes whose hearing has been restored (examples unfortunately too rare). Such was the deaf-mute Trésel, aged ten. During the first days that followed his cure, all sounds, even noises, caused him extreme pleasure; but some time was needed before he perceived that speech was a means of communication, and even then he attached himself at first to the movements of the lips, and not to the sounds, and believed, for some days, that a child of seven months was speaking, because he saw its lips move. Nearly three months passed before he could distinguish a few words, and it was only after a very long time that he recognized the direction of sounds. A person who had hidden in the room where the child was having called him several times, he discovered only with great difficulty the place from which the voice came.” Even touch is subject to illusions and requires an apprenticeship. “If we lay our hand on a table with our eyes closed, and another person quickly passes over the tips of our fingers pieces of paper and plates of metal or glass, we readily confound these objects; but we distinguish them easily in the same case if we can run our fingers over their surface and judge of their consistency by the resistance they find there. Another experiment proves how necessary judgment is for appreciating shape. If one crosses two fingers of one hand so as to roll a ball between the edges which do not ordinarily touch each other, one thinks one holds two balls. This is because the sensation is really that of two spheres, which the judgment recomposes by habit into a single one (1).” We must therefore judge and reason in order to reach objects by means of our senses, whereas we perceive sensations directly. Pedagogy, in its turn, has seized upon this truth: the training of the senses is [p. 142] taken into serious consideration in the Kindergartens where Fröbel’s method is introduced. Surprising results would be obtained, from the standpoint of art, of science, and of all human activity, if all the senses were cultivated from an early age by regular and coordinated exercises.

We see now with what subtlety Reid evaded the difficulties of the question when, after affirming that the perception of objects is immediate, he limited this direct faculty of perceiving to adult persons of sound mind, and, he should have added, under the normal conditions of life. In that case, indeed, reasoning is superfluous to convince us of the existence of objects; the experience has long been acquired, the interpretation of sensations has become habit, and the belief in the reality of the external world is irresistibly fixed in the mind. Reid will not claim that a universal conviction, a truth of common sense, excludes reasoning, for reasoning is as much as perception a primitive and constitutive element of the soul.

(1) Dr. Gluge, Physiologie, bk. ii, ch. viii, ix, and x.

p. 143

But if the child does not know at first that the sensations he experiences relate to external things, if a prolonged exercise of the understanding is needed to explain the origin and the value of each impression; if perception itself is never applied in the end except to a modification of our sensibility, can we accept without demonstration the existence of the world of bodies? In practice, yes; in science, no. Common sense, which regulates the course of human life, is content with the fact, without seeking its cause or its possibility; it affirms a distinction between soul and body, it admits the world and society, it proclaims the existence of God and of the future life, as necessities of reason. But science, more exacting, can adopt only opinions recognized as true and certain after examination; it must raise doubts even about the beliefs of mankind. If the reality of the external world is not for us, like the facts of consciousness and the phenomena of sensibility, the object of an immediate intuition, but the conclusion of our discursive operations, it needs a demonstration, and the theory can [p. 143] demand proofs. Philosophers have understood this well. Descartes sought arguments in the veracity of God, who cannot make sport of his creatures by inspiring them with an erroneous conviction. Malebranche relied upon revelation, which speaks of heaven and earth, and obliges us to believe in them. These reasonings are not irreproachable and have perhaps value only as tendencies, or as the need of reason to seek in God, in the principle of science, the cause of all that exists. The skeptics reject them, and the idealists agree with them on this point. We must admit, in any case, that the demonstration must be adjourned, and that the cause of the skeptics gains for the moment all the ground that sensualism has lost.

p. 144

Sensualism is radically false if the senses cannot even teach us that there exists an external world. But does not idealism triumph, if we have no means of grasping directly the objects outside? What do we know of bodies and of their properties? We must hear the defenders of this cause before judging it. We have supposed until now, in order to conform to common opinion, that sensation results from the action of an object upon our organs; but we must now recognize that of these two things, the sensation and the object, only one is immediately certain: the object is drawn from the sensation by the reasoned application of the principle of causality. Whether this induction is legitimate is what the idealists ask, and the question has nothing strange or unforeseen about it; it issues naturally from the theory of indirect perception. It has long been debated in the Schools whether the secondary qualities of matter, or the sensible qualities of bodies, such as color, flavor, odor, sonority, heat and cold, are properties of our senses or properties of the objects themselves. Those who admitted an intermediary between the mind and things were disposed to deny these qualities all objective existence. Reid refutes them, but by relying upon the direct perception of the external world. “The idealist thesis, at least with regard to light, heat, and sonority [p. 144] gains new adherents today, since physicists seek to reduce the various forces of nature to unity, and consider luminous, calorific, and sonorous undulations as identical in themselves, as proceeding indistinctly from the movement of matter and as differing only in the sentient subject. Heat is reduced to light and obeys the same laws: light is heat perceived by the optic nerve; heat is light perceived by the tactile nerves. Light, in its turn, is confounded with the vibrations of bodies, transmitted by the air or by the ether, vibrations which are luminous to the eye and sonorous to the ear (1).” The same controversies were bound to arise concerning the primary qualities, which have always been regarded as the essence of bodies, such as extension, divisibility, figure, mobility, hardness and softness, especially since the conceptions of space, time, and matter had been profoundly modified by Leibniz and by Kant. The skeptical idealists, consistent with themselves, reject all the qualities of bodies, primary and secondary, or grant them at least only a subjective existence, as phenomena of sensibility. Let us hear their arguments.

Between cause and effect we always conceive some connection, a relation of analogy or similarity. Now sensation, says Berkeley, resembles only itself; to think that a sensation reproduces the qualities we attribute to things is an absurdity. What is there in common between the physical properties of that elongated body which we call a pin and the disagreeable feeling of a prick? Between the sensation of cold and the snow or the wind? Between the impression of heat and the air, the sun, or fabrics? What, then, are objects? Simply the sum of our individual and variable representations, of sensations reduced to unity, but this unity is found only in us, in consciousness. We know nothing more.

(1) Paul Janet, le Matérialisme contemporain en Allemagne. Revue des Deux- Mondes, August 15, 1863.

p. 145

Fichte arrives at the same conclusion. The consciousness we have of ourselves and of our own modifications is the necessary condition of the consciousness we have of other things. We know the existence of objects because we see or touch them, but we know that we see them only because we know it. We know it immediately. In general, we do not perceive at all what we do not perceive immediately. In every perception, therefore, I perceive only myself, only my own manner of being. The perception of objects is a consequence of the perception of my own manner of being. If I differentiate objects, it is because I grasp differences in my sensations. But then why do we speak of objects and of their qualities? Why name the red and the blue, the rough and the smooth, instead of being content to say that we are affected in a certain way? Whence comes it that we do not leave sensations where they really are, that is to say in us, but, on the contrary, transport them to an object outside us; that we make of them properties of the object, whereas they are in the end only modifications of ourselves? That is not all. To sensible qualities we suppose a prop, a support, which we conceive as extended and which we call substance. But we do not see this extension, we see only colors, and this sensation in us is like a mathematical point without length or continuity; nor do we touch it, we feel successively the rough, the smooth, and each of these sensations is as simple and indivisible as that of red. How is it, then, that instead of representing our sensations to ourselves as successive, in the order in which we really experience them, we picture them, on the contrary, in the form of simultaneous modifications, coexisting at once at several points of a surface? Will it be said that we grasp the surface of objects by means of our hand, which is itself a surface? But the question remains the same; the surface of the hand can be perceived, like any other object, only by means of our senses. We do not [p. 146] perceive extension in bodies, therefore, in any way, and yet we believe we see and feel surfaces, and behind the surface we still imagine a dimension absolutely invisible and impalpable. We go beyond our perceptions. Instead of extending our own impressions so arbitrarily over all nature, let us say plainly that there are no bodies for thought, since we cannot perceive them, or that matter has no other property than that of being perceptible. We possess no organ for grasping objects; we are not even justified in claiming that we have external senses. Each of us receives sensations, of which he is conscious, that is all; he then applies to them, according to a law of his intelligence, the principle of causality. Our impressions, we say, must have a cause, and as this cause is not in us, we conclude that it is outside us, in objects. But if we are conscious of our affections, not of objects, is it not evident that the principle of causality is employed in this case to join to a cognition which we have a cognition which we have not? And besides, how do we know that everything must have a cause, even our impressions? By the observation of our own acts, doubtless. The principle of causality does no more, then, than erect into a general law our manner of proceeding with respect to ourselves. What is its value, then, outside the self ? By what right should we impose our intellectual habits on things? We must always come back to this: in what we call the knowledge of things, it is ourselves that we know. The external world is only a creation of our thought, born of the need of the mind to objectify its representations. As an object of science, it has no existence independent of the self. But we possess another organ to which the possession of reality is promised: it is belief (1).

p. 147

Such is the idealism of Fichte. Let no one see in it a play [p. 147] of wit; it is a serious and profound work, which withstands jesting and can be only with difficulty breached by criticism. As a theory of sensation and of sensible perception, the idealist doctrine is irreproachable and contains the most exact indications that have been presented until now on this part of knowledge. The author has seen very well that sensation is only a modification of the subject, that the senses teach us nothing, neither substance, nor extension, nor cause, and that perception is reduced to grasping our own impressions, from whatever source they come. It is therefore certain henceforth that the existence of the external world can be accepted in theory only if guaranteed by a demonstration: this is what the very appearance of skeptical idealism among the ancients and among the moderns attests. The idealists declare that such a demonstration is impossible, and that common sense, which protests, has only to submit to the decisions of science. Therein lies their error. What they lack is the theory of reason, as a receptive faculty relating to supra-sensible things. Fichte avows that if the principle of causality had universal validity, the existence of the external world would be as certain as that of the self. Now cause is one of those elements which we owe to reason. Idealism thus offers us this double lesson, that sensation by itself proves nothing, and that reason alone, if it had a legitimate range, would permit us to pass from the self to the not-self. As long as the principles of reason have not acquired a transcendent validity, doubt concerning nature is the right and the duty of free thought. All the effort of philosophy must be directed toward the study of reason.

We know what sensible knowledge is in its general features. To justify our assertions and complete our sketch, let us now enter into the detail of the manifold operations of the mind by which knowledge is formed. Let us examine first the real data of each of our senses, and then see what imagination, understanding, and reason add to sensation in order to interpret it, complete it, and bring forth from it the notion of an external object.

(1) Fichte, Destination de l’homme, translated by Barchou de Penhoën, 2nd edition. Paris, 1836.

p. 148

The sense of touch is the sense most limited in relation to objects, but the most extended in relation to our body. It relates to cohesion and to heat, which, by dilatation and contraction, modifies the molecular state of bodies. The sensation of touch is a pure and simple pressure, a change wrought in the nervous papillae that are outlined beneath the epidermis. This impression has no dimension; it is the same whatever be the length, breadth, and thickness of bodies; it reveals in itself nothing external, nor anything solid existing in space. If we appreciate by touch the shape and size of objects, it is because we reflect at the same time that we feel, because we mingle with the sensation judgments founded on habit. In passing the hand over a body, with the eyes closed, we say that it is hard or soft, according to the degree of resistance we meet; we say that it is smooth or uneven, large or small, round or angular, according to the number and quality of the impressions received without break of continuity. These judgments will vary in different persons in proportion, not to their sensations, but to their capacity and to the experience acquired in the daily occupations of life.

p. 149

There is no sensation of length, but a judgment of length based on the time that elapses between the first sensation and the last; there is no sensation of shape, but a judgment of shape which depends on the manner in which the successive impressions are connected with one another when we touch an object without interrupting the contact; finally, there is no sensation of any quality whatever of bodies, because the senses do not judge: the sensation is like a geometrical point, which results doubtless from the cohesion of the nervous tissue, but which resembles no property of matter. In reality, it is not bodies, it is our own nerves that we feel, affected in one way or another. What proves this to evidence is that we can experience at the same instant, and in relation to the same object, two opposite sensations, by touching it with the two hands differently heated: if the table on which [p. 149] I lean is warmer than my right hand and colder than my left, I shall have at once a sensation of heat and of cold, and I shall be led to believe that the table is at the same time hot and cold. The table, however, has but one temperature; if I perceived it directly, I could receive from it only one impression, and my impressions would always be exactly indicated by the thermometer. Since it is otherwise, we must conclude that we perceive only the modification undergone by our tactile nerves in the presence of objects. We judge objects; we perceive immediately only ourselves. Thus the judgment ceases when the sensation becomes confused or when the nerves are altered: fingers plunged for a few minutes in hot water no longer permit us to discern the temperature of bodies. It would therefore be a profound error to imagine that we owe to the sensation of touch the notions of body, of solid, of matter, of space, of time, of externality, of causality: the fact is that since our childhood, after the first months of groping, we constantly add these notions to the sensations of touch, but we do not draw them from our senses, we borrow them from reason or from the consciousness we have of ourselves. The senses, once more, give only sensations, nothing more; knowledge comes from us.

Taste and smell serve rather the vegetative life of the organism than the life of the intellect, and appear to relate to the chemical process which presides over the composition and decomposition of bodies. The sensations they give us are again simple impressions without extension, which by themselves in no way reveal the existence of a solid. By means of these senses we perceive only the modifications which take place in our organs, in the olfactory nerve and in the glossopharyngeal nerve, as by means of touch we perceive the state of the tactile nerves. Thus the sensation changes or ceases in diseases which affect the organs of nutrition or the mucous membrane of the nose; it may even survive for some

p. 150

Logic. — I. 10 [p. 150] time after the object which produced it. Flavors and odors are therefore perceived only in us, as manners of being of our own nerves. When we speak of the sapid and odorous qualities of bodies, it is by virtue of a judgment of induction, which comes from the intelligence, not from the senses, which may be true or false and which develops with experience. Each is sole judge of his own sensations: there is no disputing about tastes and smells; but we must not hasten to pass judgment on things before being well informed as to the state of the organs.

Sight and hearing are the senses most important for science and for art. If a difference must be made between them, from the standpoint of intellectual development, preeminence belongs to hearing, on account of its relations with speech. The deaf do not speak, not because of any defect in the organs of the voice, but because, not hearing themselves, they can only with difficulty judge of the correctness of their expressions.

p. 151

The sense of hearing relates to the interior or vibratory movement of bodies, which depends on the molecular constitution or the elasticity of matter and which manifests itself either by a confused noise or by regular and musical sounds. The auditory nerve is sensitive at once to the quantitative and the qualitative differences of sounds: the former arise from the number and amplitude of the vibrations emitted and indicate the pitch and the intensity of sounds; the latter constitute the timbre and correspond to the nature of bodies. The lowest sounds for us give thirty-two vibrations a second, the highest sound gives forty-eight thousand; these extreme limits furnish the measure of the fineness of hearing. What is here the direct object of perception? Is it the body which resounds, or the nerve which is struck by the sound waves? We perceive only the nerve as it is modified, and we then judge of the kind and the distance of the body according to the diversity and the force of the sensible impressions. We know by observation what kind of sounds metals, woods, animals, and persons give out; we recognize these objects, without seeing them, by their timbre, [p. 151] by their voice, by their steps, and we estimate their distance by the intensity of the sounds; we even discern the feelings of our fellows toward us by the tone of their speech. But we are easily led into error in these various respects: we take one object for another through the effect of a skillful imitation, and dissimulation or prejudice hides from us the real dispositions of the people with whom we enter into relation. It even happens that hearing leaves us in complete ignorance of the object, for example when we hear it for the first time and cannot grasp it by the other senses. Perception in this case is evidently not addressed to the object, since we have no notion of it; it is addressed to the sensation, which is perfectly distinct. It is easy to make experiments on this point by striking metals or by touching the notes of a piano behind a person to whom these sounds are not familiar. One and the same sound, perceived by several hearers, may be referred to as many different causes. Acoustics gives occasion to analogous experiments which lead to the same conclusion. It is known that sound travels about 335 meters a second through the atmosphere, and that its velocity becomes from 4 to 16 times greater when it is propagated through liquids and solids. By applying the ear to the end of a metallic bar of sufficient length, one should therefore hear the same sound twice, since the sound waves transmitted by the iron and by the air will not arrive at the same time; moreover, if the distances are well taken and a double blow is given successively to the bar and to another metal, the two sounds will be confounded in one, or will arrive at the same time at the ear by two different ways. Nothing shows better that the proper object of perception is not external but internal: for, on the one hand, the sounding object is single, whereas the perception is double like the sensation, and, on the other hand, the object is double, whereas the sensation and the perception are single; perception therefore corresponds to the sensation, to the nervous phenomenon which is produced in us, not to the body which resounds in [p. 152] space. The same incidents occur when the two ears have not the same degree of sensitiveness, or when one is stopped while the other is left open.

The sense of sight relates to the process of light. It is the most extended, the most delicate, the richest sense, since it permits us to perceive, at incommensurable distances, stars whose light, with its velocity of 70,000 leagues a second, a million times more rapid than sound, reaches the earth only after a great number of years, and since it gives us perfectly distinct impressions of luminous bodies, such as the sun and the moon, whose intensities are at least to each other as 100,000 is to 1; it is the sense most docile to the direction of the will, the most intellectual, so to speak, and the most independent of the affections of general sensibility. Sight and hearing each have their language: the one has speech, the other writing. Hearing presides over the arts relating to time: eloquence, poetry, music; sight presides over the arts relating to space: painting, sculpture, architecture. But for science, for the observation of the animate or inanimate beings of nature, sight is more useful than hearing.

p. 153

The optic nerve is sensitive to all the quantitative and qualitative determinations of light, that is to say, to brightness, to shadows, and to the manifold degrees of chiaroscuro, on the one hand, and to colors and their infinitely varied shades, on the other. The luminous rays proceeding from an object traverse the cornea, the aqueous humor, and the crystalline lens, where they undergo a threefold refraction, and converge toward the optic axis of the eye, forming an image on the retina; this image is inverted, because the rays cross on leaving the crystalline lens to enter the vitreous body, like the pencils of light which pass through a lens to fix themselves on the daguerreotype plate. The visual angle, formed by the crossing of the rays, determines the apparent size of objects; the spread of its sides increases or diminishes according as the object approaches or recedes from the eye. Such is the very simple mechanism of vision: the eye is a reflector furnished with a dark chamber and a lens; the [p. 153] reflector is the retina, an expansion of the optic nerve; the dark chamber is formed by the sclerotic and the choroid; the lens is composed of the crystalline lens and the transparent parts of the organ of sight.

Let us now turn to perception. Objects are drawn and painted on the retina, as on a mirror, in length and in breadth, but not in depth. It is this impression that we perceive and that we must then interpret, according to the laws of optics and of perspective, by referring it to an external object endowed with the three dimensions of space, and by judging of the form, the size, and the distance of the object from the play of shadows and colors at the back of the eye. Everyone knows from experience that colors fix the contour of objects, that the bulk and the respective distances of bodies appear to diminish in proportion to their remoteness, that the most vivid colors correspond, in a homogeneous medium, to the surface that is opposed to us, and that the extent of the shadows or of the darker tints indicates the depth of objects. It is thanks to these rules of interpretation, acquired by habit, that we can without difficulty recognize the intentions of a painter who represents to us an immense scene in several planes on a smooth surface of small dimensions. What offered no difference in the intensity and the quality of the light would reveal no form to the mind. When the image shifts on the retina, we say that the object is in motion, and we are so accustomed to this process that we sometimes confound our own motion, on a boat or in a railway car, with that of objects. Distance, size, form, and motion of objects, all comes therefore, in visual perception, not from sensation, but from an operation of the intelligence.

If this is so, it is evident that perception does not directly reach an external body, for in that case judgment would be useless, but only the sensation, the modification of the optic nerve. Proofs abound in favor of this proposition.

p. 154

Why do we see objects upright, in spite of the inversion of their images? so physiologists and philosophers have asked ever since the study of optics began. I answer that the object is not perceived but inferred, that we perceive only the image that is painted on the retina, and that we form from it a representation of the object in the imagination. The external object escapes thought; we grasp only an appearance of it within us. This solution would allow the question to be evaded; but such is not my intention; I readily admit that the object exists outside us and that it conforms to its inner representation. Why, then, do we judge that objects are upright, while their images are inverted? It would not suffice to reply that the notions of up and down are relative and conventional, for the child sees or judges objects as we do, even before he is initiated into our languages and our conventions. The training of sight is wholly personal, and nevertheless gives the same results in all.

p. 155

Kepler, who was the first to study this phenomenon, sought its explanation in an operation of the mind. Since the rays that proceed from a body cross before falling on the retina, we conclude, he says, that the impulse which we feel upon the lower part of this membrane comes from above, and that the impulse which is made upon the higher part comes from below. Descartes adopted the same opinion, and remarked that we make the same reasoning when we touch an object with our hands crossed, referring to the left what the right hand touches, and conversely. There is no other possible explanation. If the image is not physically righted by virtue of some combination of light as yet unknown, reasoning is indispensable in order to connect the various points of the luminous impression with the opposite points of the object that has produced it. The interpretation is all the more natural in that it conforms to the direction of the luminous rays that traverse the crystalline lens, and that we already know from other circumstances that we must learn to see. It is the same with the judgment that we pass on the position of objects [p. 155] as with those that we pass on their form and size. But it must be added that this judgment is instinctive or unconscious, and that it shows itself from earliest childhood in a series of experiences in which the sensation of sight is compared with that of touch. It would therefore be wrong to object that the child and ordinary people do not distinguish images, do not know the theory of light or the mechanism of vision, and that no conclusion can be drawn from a fact of which one is ignorant. Ignorance of optics and of the nervous phenomena prevents one from seeing well no more than ignorance of mechanics and of the muscular phenomena prevents one from walking upright. The child does not know what he perceives, but in fact he perceives his sensations as we do, and it is from these that he must set out to find his bearings in the external world. Now one does not pass thus from the subjective to the objective, and from the effect to the cause, without the operations of thought, and one does not reason correctly in these conditions without long groping. Here Berkeley's explanation comes to complete that of Kepler. Sight and touch are independent of each other, and mutually control each other. When it has often been observed that different images correspond to different positions, which are known by touch, one learns to judge, by the manner in which the eye is affected, whether the object is upright or inverted. The mind thus passes by degrees from the image to the object, from the sign to the thing signified, by the effect of an association of ideas founded on experience, like that which exists between thoughts and words. This twofold solution does not please Reid, because according to him perception directly reaches the object. But then of what use is the image? The author extricates himself from the difficulty by invoking “the laws of nature,” a new kind of occult causes, which dispense with all investigation. A law of our constitution requires “that the object whose picture is lowest on the retina, must be seen in the highest direction from the eye; and that the object whose picture is on the right of the retina, must be seen on the left; so that if the pictures had been erect in the retina, we should have seen the object inverted [p. 156] An analogous question is that of single and double images. Why, when there are two images in the eyes, do we see the object single? The answer is again furnished by the training of sight. Anatomy teaches that the optic nerves cross each other in front of the brain, but this junction does not explain the perception; for it does not prevent there being two images for each object placed before us, and the images are distinguished or blended at our pleasure. If one wishes to make sure of this, let him close each eye in turn while fixing an object, for example the pen that runs over the paper: on closing the right eye, the image turns to the right; on closing the left eye, it turns to the left; the image that is on the left corresponds to the right eye, and the image that is on the right to the left eye; if the movements are performed slowly, without the help of the hand, the images are perfectly distinct and the object appears double; when both eyes are opened, the images draw together, then blend, and the amblyopia disappears. Perception is single when the two visual axes converge or meet upon the object; this is obtained by the imperceptible movements of the muscles of the eye, as may be recognized by moving the pen away from the organ and bringing it near. The images are then found on the identical or corresponding points of the two retinas. These points are easily found by personal experience; everyone adjusts his eyes to distances and directs their movements, whether he knows it or not, according to the conformation of his organs, the sensibility of his optic nerves, the quantity of the humors, and the degree of convexity of the cornea and of the crystalline lens. Strabismus results from the weakness or paralysis of some muscle of the eye; it is not necessarily accompanied by double vision, but it obliges one to give the eyes an abnormal position in order to obtain the corresponding points of the retinas. Myopia and presbyopia are determined by an excess or a defect of convexity of [p. 157] the eye: in the one case, the rays sent by objects too far away unite before reaching the retina; in the other, the rays sent by objects too near reach the retina before they have been able to unite. Everyone takes account of these various circumstances in order to acquire the art of seeing well. The habit of giving to the movements of the eye a convergent direction, in order to reconcile the duplicity of images with the unity of vision, is part of the training of sight (1).

(1).” This strange law is a simple operation of the understanding.

(1) Th. Reid, Œuvres complètes, vol. II, ch. vi, sect. xii.

p. 158

Single vision by means of double images, and upright vision by means of inverted images, are the result of experience, and consequently betray an intellectual activity that must complete or reform sensation. The eye gives only luminous impressions: it is we who translate them and refer them to an object, in order to know the world. We shall now see that perception does not even reach the object without a judgment of induction. The simplest proof is again drawn from amblyopia. Everyone knows what happens when one presses an eye with the finger while looking at a candle: the visual axes cease to coincide, and the image is double; we see one motionless light and another that advances or recedes according to the movement of the eye; if in the same position we press both eyes, we can see distinctly a crowd of candles, whose movement forward or backward we regulate with whatever speed we please to choose. The physical explanation is simple: it is no longer the corresponding points of the retinas that are affected by the light, the habits of vision are disturbed, the movements of the eye carry with them the mobility of the images, and we then believe we see several moving objects where there is but one at rest. What does this mean? The conclusion is prepared, and yet I still fear that it may surprise and offend. Let it be well considered: this proves that we do not see objects, that we do not see light and colors in space, that we see only the [p. 158] retina when it receives the influence of something that we take, rightly or wrongly, for light, but whose objective existence nothing so far demonstrates. The consequence is necessary in the phenomenon that occupies us: how should we see multiple what is one, how should we see in motion what is at rest, if we saw the object itself? Everything is perfectly explained, on the contrary, if it is admitted that the direct object of perception is a nervous modification; for we really do see several moving images at the back of the eyes. And what takes place in this circumstance is the emblem of the whole process of sensible perception. Never do we grasp the object immediately; but we are so convinced of its existence that we believe we see the cause in the effect; a special case is needed, outside ordinary perception and subject to all the conditions of a perfect experiment, to inspire in us a contrary conviction. There is here, at first sight, a collision between common sense and science: the one says that we see objects, the other that we see our sensations. This collision is possible if we consider that common sense pronounces only on questions of practical interest, and is not concerned with the distinctions of theory. The laws of perception in fact concern only the science of knowledge, and leave intact, as we shall see, the result to which ordinary consciousness clings. Accordingly we propose no innovation in language: it suffices to agree on the value of the terms. It is permissible to say that we see objects, provided that this definition is granted: to see is to perceive indirectly by means of the eyes. This definition presupposes others: to perceive is to grasp by the intelligence, it is a function of the understanding; the understanding cannot reach the objects of the external world without interpreting sensations, that is to say, without reflecting on them, without performing a work of judgment and reasoning, but the reflection is instantaneous, or even superabundant, when the sensation has become habitual. The same definition must apply to the words to hear, to taste, to smell, to touch; it is always [p. 159] the mind that perceives by means of sensible impressions; only the impressions vary according to the organs.

(1) Achille Comte, Traité complet d’histoire naturelle, vol. II, Appareils sensitifs externes. Paris, 1844.

p. 160

The theory of colors offers other proofs in favor of the same conclusion. It is known that the luminous impression has a certain duration, that it lasts about a third of a second before fading from the retina. If, then, impressions succeed one another with a certain rapidity, they can mingle, blend into one another, and bring about effects that relate to the sensation, not to the object, and that demonstrate once more that perception bears directly only on our own nervous modifications. When a torch is waved slowly before the eyes, the various positions of the object remain distinct, because the first impressions weaken and disappear as the others come on; but if a sufficiently rapid rotary motion is given to the torch, a circle of fire is seen. Whence comes this difference in perception? It does not come from the object, for it is the same in the two cases; it comes therefore from us, and can be explained only if the sensation alone is perceived. The experiment is still more conclusive by means of a disk on which are painted the colors of the rainbow, in the proportions indicated by Newton. Let us make this object turn about its center: if the movement is slow, the seven colors are perceived; if it is quicker, the perception becomes confused; if it is rapid enough for all the sensations to subsist together, nothing is perceived but white. Yet the object is not white, it is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. It is therefore not the object that is perceived, it is the sensation, and the sensation must be that of white light, because the seven colored rays are only the decomposition of light. Hence a series of interesting phenomena. It is generally admitted, following Brewster, that three colors are fundamental, perhaps unique: red, yellow, and blue; that three others are formed by the union of two principal colors: orange, by red and yellow, green by yellow and blue, indigo by blue and red; and that finally red, yellow, and [p. 160] blue, perfectly combined, give white. From then on the theory of complementary colors is no more than a game. Each principal color finds its complement in the one that results from the mixture of the other two: red in green, yellow in indigo, blue in orange, and conversely, since the colors thus mixed reproduce white light. Now by fixing a color for a few moments, and then closing the eyes or directing them upon a white surface, one perceives the complementary color. M. Plateau, by varying this experiment, has obtained the most ingenious combinations. But whence comes the accidental image? Assuredly not from the object, for the object is white, and the image subsists even without an object; it comes therefore from us, it is inherent in the sensory activity which, like all the faculties of the soul, feels a natural tendency to complete itself.

p. 161

The accidents and diseases of the eyes further confirm the indirect perception of objects. When the humors of the eye are tinged yellow by bile, as in jaundice, all objects appear colored with the same shade. The fact is easily explained if we see our own organs, but it would be inexplicable if we perceived what takes place outside in space. When an intermediary is admitted between the mind and the external world, we conceive that the aspect of nature changes with the state of our nerves; but when every intermediary is suppressed, how can it come about that, the subject and the object remaining the same for all, some see as yellow, during the course of their illness, what others see as red or blue; how does it happen, indeed, that some persons never perceive certain colors? Another fact: if, after turning rapidly about, one stops abruptly, objects seem to turn in the opposite direction: the movement of the body has been communicated to the cerebral mass, and after the action comes the reaction; we perceive this movement in the eye, where it is real, and we refer it by habit to objects, where it is only apparent. The same phenomenon presents itself in vertigo and in drunkenness, where the nervous system is overexcited either by the imagination [p. 161] or by spirituous drinks. Drunkenness is accompanied by confused and double images, because the will loses its influence over the muscles, and consequently also over the direction of the eyes.

To conclude these considerations on the real data of our eyes, I shall borrow from M. Ahrens some remarkable experiments made on the blind. A young man whose cataracts Dr. Cheselden couched in 1727 distinguished for a long time after his cure neither sizes, nor distances, nor figures. An object an inch across, placed before his eye, appeared to him as large as a house. He believed that objects were applied to the eyes as to the skin. He knew roundness and angles, up and down, by touch, but he did not discern them by sight. He needed a great number of experiments to make sure that painting represented solid bodies; and when he had become well convinced, by dint of looking at pictures, that what he saw were not surfaces, he put his hand to them and was greatly astonished to find only a flat plane without projection; he then asked which was the deceiver, touch or sight. He had great difficulty in recognizing his own organs; he had long before noticed their reflections in his eyes, before he conceived the thought that these organs were his own. Only slowly did he come to understand the correspondence that exists between the sensations of sight and those of touch; he imagined that a body could have only a single form, and could not understand how his cat could show itself to the eyes under so many different forms.

p. 162

We must turn to examples of this kind in order to grasp the difficulties that the interpretation of sensations presents in childhood, and to take account of the activity of the intelligence that judges sensible impressions and must seek their cause. The difficulties probably increase with age. A woman of forty-six, operated on by Dr. Wardrop in 1826, found more difficulty in finding her bearings in the external world, although she had enjoyed sight for some years. Several days passed before she could distinguish the principal colors, and several weeks before [p. 162] she noticed the images of her own limbs. At the end of the forty-second day, when she left London, she still understood so little the action of the eyes, and estimated distances so confusedly, that she stumbled at every step like little children.

Another example is offered us by the history of that mysterious young man, Kaspar Hauser, who was abandoned on the road to Nuremberg after having been shut up from his childhood to his fifteenth year in a dark dungeon, and who perished by assassination in an unheard-of manner. The most curious psychological phenomena showed themselves in him. He was still a child at the age of fifteen, and remained a long time before understanding the play of sight. When he at last perceived that his feet and his hands were his own limbs, he insisted that they be taken away from him. After having exercised his sight within the compass of a room, he could not yet apply it to greater distances. The celebrated Feuerbach, his historian, led him to the tower of the town and asked him whether the aspect of the countryside pleased him. Scarcely had he cast a glance over the fields, adorned with the splendor of spring, when he cried out: Hideous! but meeting a white wall, he added: There, not hideous! He explained himself later on this circumstance: he distinguished no particular object; it seemed to him that brushes charged with all the colors had been placed before his eyes in a horrible confusion.

All these examples agree on the principal fact, namely that at the period when one learns to see, one grasps only the images that are in the eyes, and does not yet suspect that the impressions relate to external things. It follows, therefore, from the examination that we have made of the senses in general, that man has no immediate apperception of external objects, that he perceives only the modifications of his own organs, and that, if everything were confined for him to pure sensation, sensation would never furnish him with the idea of an external world (1).

(1) H. Ahrens, Cours de psychologie, vol. II. Paris, 1838.

p. 163

Sensation must be completed by acts of the mind. What are these acts? Thus far we are in agreement with skeptical idealism: we perceive only our sensations. How, then, do we accord to our perceptions an objective validity?

The first work of the mind upon sensation consists in uniting the diverse and isolated impressions that we receive through the five modes of sensibility; the soul forms a whole of these impressions scattered through the organs, or reduces them to unity and concentrates them upon an individual object, which we represent to ourselves inwardly with the whole of its sensible qualities. Each sensation, in fact, is distinct and affects us in a wholly particular way; the color of the rose resembles in nothing its odor, the contact of its leaves and of its thorns, its taste, or the sound of its petals when they are made to burst; and yet we have within us a representation of the rose endowed with all the properties that reveal it to our senses. It is imagination that accomplishes this work of synthesis and gives us the complete image of objects, by means of the three dimensions of space which it possesses.

p. 164

Imagination is analogous to the senses, and exercises its activity in the general conditions of space, time, and motion that are common to sensible things. It is a faculty of individualization or of figuration, which draws and colors our thoughts and our feelings, clothes them with a body, and gives them the aspect of matter. The creations of the imagination extend in length, in breadth, and in depth like solids, as we make sure by evoking the memory of some plastic work. Whence come these dimensions? They do not come from touch, for the sensation of touch is only a pure and simple impression; they do not come from sight, for if the retina reflects objects or receives their imprint, it never lends them more than the two directions of the surface; and besides, the fantastic power [p. 164] of the mind is independent of the action of the eyes: a blind man represents bodies to himself without difficulty, finds his way in a city, grasps the dimensions of a house, and can even teach geometry. There is therefore an internal space, which serves as the stage for the productions and imitations of the imagination, in dreaming as in waking, and it is with the aid of this intelligible space that the soul composes the image of things.

p. 165

Imagination accompanies our sensations and represents objects to us as they strike our organs. This intervention often escapes us in our habitual dealings with nature, because we do not distinguish what is given by the senses from what comes from the imagination; convinced that we see the objects of experience just as they are outside, we do not seek to compare them with the image that we have of them, and this appearance, confounded with the reality, scarcely attracts our attention. The image exists nevertheless, now conformable, now contrary to the object, and it exists in us, as a product of the imagination, distinct from every sensible impression, even that of sight; what proves it is that it is maintained in the soul when the object has disappeared or has ceased to make an impression on our organs, and that we can recall it at will. I see, for example, a bird flying off or an animal fleeing in the fields; the sensation is fleeting, the image on the retina quickly fades, but the impression has sufficed for me to form a complete representation of the object, which subsists in the imagination as long as I wish. This internal representation is a condition of sensible knowledge. It sometimes happens that we do not succeed in picturing to ourselves the object that has acted on our senses, particularly on hearing or on smell exercised at a distance: in that case, we do not know it. So it is with all our senses when they act in isolation in the presence of new objects. I touch an object in the dark, and I do not know what it is; I put something into my mouth without noticing it, and I do not know what I have eaten. Experience comes to our aid when we have learned to know the principal [p. 165] qualities of the objects that surround us: a single sensation then suffices to recall, by way of association of ideas, the entire representation of the bodies that we touch or that we hear without seeing them: an odor, a flavor, a sound, a touch is equivalent to sight and calls up an image, but this image is not a sensation.

The activity of the imagination, which unites scattered sensations and forms the schema of objects in the sciences of observation, has been well studied by Kant. “No psychologist,” he says, “has yet seen clearly that imagination enters necessarily into perception. This is because, on the one hand, this faculty has been restricted to reproductions, and because, on the other, it has been believed that the senses not only give us impressions, but also compose them and produce images of objects. This result certainly demands, besides the receptivity of impressions, a function that synthesizes them (1).”

The absence of psychological criticism, and at times the disdain of imagination, explain many errors in the theory of knowledge. It is to imagination that we owe the notion of space, which is added to our sensations and which the sensualists attribute to the organs. Touch gives only an impression without length, but it seems to reveal extension when we feel over the surface of a body: it is that we then have a series of impressions that we link together thanks to imagination. The ancient authors rightly admitted an intermediary between the mind and external objects, but they were always mistaken about this intermediary, called now sensible species, now idea or notion: between the soul and the physical world the relation is effected by sensations. Imagination is not an intermediary, since it is already a faculty of the soul, but it accounts for the illusion: what were taken for sensible species, for appearances of bodies, for adventitious ideas, were simply the intuitions or the products

p. 166

Logic. — I. 11 [p. 166] of the imagination.
