Each time that we take cognizance of an object of nature, we have an image of it which appears to come from bodies, but which comes from the soul; in this sense one may say with Malebranche: no sensible knowledge without an idea or an image that rises before the mind; one may say with Reid: no perception without a notion or an image that accompanies the activity of the understanding. The sensible species of the Middle Ages are therefore replaced by sensations and images, and these two phenomena are now perfectly distinct: sensation is an intermediary between the mind and the external world; the image is the first manifestation of the activity of the soul exercising itself on the data of the sensory organs.

(1) Cf. E. Mauriel, le Scepticisme combattu dans ses principes, p. 84. Paris, 1857.

p. 167

The second faculty of the mind, whose intervention is required for sensible knowledge, or which forms, to speak more properly, all our knowledge, is reflection or the understanding. Reflection interprets sensation and assigns it its value. To the internal and subjective image succeeds the notion of an object that we suppose to be external. In order to pass thus from the self to the not-self, the concurrence of the functions and operations of the understanding is required. No knowledge without attention, without perception, without determination: if the soul is distracted or preoccupied, objects may affect the senses as they will, they pass unperceived and provoke no image; if the soul, though attentive, does not seize the body that modifies the organs, the object remains unknown; if the soul, finally, in seizing the sensation does not analyze it with sufficient care, it will not see the object as it is and will be the victim of some error. Thanks to these functions, the notion is acquired. But it is a question of a transcendent object, situated outside the sphere of the soul. Now no notion of an external object without judgment and without reasoning. In order to connect our nervous modifications with the objective existence of an object in space, or of a modifying cause other than the soul, experience is needed: each must train his own senses, understand the play of his organs, find a determinate cause [p. 167] for each determinate sensation, and explain to himself the phenomena outside by the phenomena that take place within us. Now this laborious experience, to which children are subject, as are adults who recover the use of sight or hearing, and even persons who enjoy the integrity of their senses, in the case of illusion, is not acquired without judgment or without reasoning. If anyone still imagines that these operations are not within the reach of children, let him be good enough to refer to the definition of the terms, and to recognize that all the acts of the mind are now conscious and now unconscious. To judge, it suffices that one perceive two things in relation to each other, for example two facts that coexist or follow each other; it is in no way necessary that one probe each term to the bottom, or know in what judgment consists. Every man judges before he is conscious of his judgments, exactly as he speaks, as he imagines, as he remembers, before distinguishing the properties of language, of imagination, or of memory. In the child, judgments are unconscious and instinctive, but they are none the less operations of the understanding. When he connects sensation with an object, he does not begin by asking himself: what is a sensation, what is an object? He is content to perceive something that is produced in his organs and something that subsists outside, and to perceive these two things, phenomenon and substance, simultaneously.

p. 168

Reasoning is no more difficult than judgment, and can be equally instantaneous. The syllogism and method, no doubt, are conquests of science that surpass the capacity of the child, but reasoning is more general than the syllogism and anterior to the rules of logic. To reason, only two judgments in relation to each other are needed, whether they be composed of the same terms or united by a middle term. Every principle contains the matter of a reasoning, as soon as it is applied to a particular case. It is already an act of reasoning to understand that every effect has a cause, and that this or that determinate effect proceeds from a cause. As soon as one inquires whence [p. 168] sensation arises, one reasons, for one combines three terms: the sensation, the effect, the cause. It is impossible to be conscious of an external world without recognizing that the impressions of the organs are bound up with the presence of certain objects. The child does not formulate his reasonings as we do, but he notices, for example, that on opening his eyes he sees a lamp, that on closing them he sees nothing more, that on opening them again he sees the same object in the same place, that he receives the same impression each time he comes back to face the lamp, and that this impression fades each time he turns his head; this suffices to make him suspect that the image of the lamp proceeds from a cause independent of his own activity, that is to say, to reason. The experiment would be decisive if the objects surrounding the child always remained in the same position and if he could touch them. But when, on waking, he no longer finds the lamp, he is at a loss: does the image come from an object, or does the object exist without one’s seeing it? Everything is called in question again, until the child is in a state to understand that the persons who move about the room can displace objects and put them back in place.

p. 169

Let us take some examples. In order to pass from sensation to the external world, one must needs say to oneself in one way or another: I experience an impression; the impression corresponds to an object; the effect has a cause; the cause is a property; the property is inherent in a being; something exists outside me. These are judgments, categorical, unassailable propositions, which denote an exact intuition of the truth, and which are founded on the consciousness of the sensation and on the application of some rational ideas to this phenomenon. It is evident that he who can neither express nor understand these judgments has no right to affirm the existence of an external object; but it is also clear that if the child, before having speech, is certain that there are outside him things that affect him, it is because he judges his sensations in their twofold relation to the self and to the not-self. All these judgments are then linked together in the form of reasoning. We say, for [p. 169] example: sensation is an effect; now no effect without a cause; sensation therefore has a cause. This cause is not in me; now what is not in me is outside; the cause of sensation is therefore external. The cause is a property; now no property without a being; the cause of sensation is therefore inherent in a being. If the cause of my impressions is external, the being on which the cause depends is so too. There exist, therefore, external objects, and these objects are doubtless endowed with all the properties that manifest themselves in sensation. Such are the reasonings that every man must have made, in one form or another, with some degree of clearsightedness, in order to convince himself of the existence of a corporeal world, subsisting in space, as distinguished from the internal representations of the imagination.

If we have lost the memory of these acts, it is because they belong to our earliest childhood, when we learned everything under the impulse of the instincts of the mind, which fade away or are transformed before psychological observation. The procedures of the child are not ours; they are more intuitive and appear surer, if one may judge by comparison with adults who recover the use of a sense. But reasoning comes back to consciousness as soon as it is necessary to explain uncommon sensations or to interpret the illusions of our senses. A noise is produced in my room while I am drowsy; I wake and listen. Is it a real sound or the echo of a dream? I hear nothing more; I remain in doubt. But the noise is renewed; this time the thing is certain: I am not asleep, I am not subject to hallucinations, the phenomenon therefore has an extraneous cause: there is something. What is it, then? A piece of furniture creaking, an animal scratching at the door, a person who has entered the apartment? I do not know… This ordinary reasoning is only the translation of this other: every phenomenon has a cause; if the cause is not in me, it is outside; what is the cause? This the senses do not teach us; but assuredly the cause does not exist without a substance.

p. 170

The activity of the imagination and of the understanding supposes, finally, reason: a new and last intervention of the mind in the formation of sensible cognitions. In uniting our sensations into a whole so as to form a single representation, in judging our diverse impressions, in concluding to the existence of external things, we constantly employ rational ideas, the ideas of whole and part, of cause and effect, of being and property, which the senses do not give, and the legitimacy of our reasonings depends even on the objective validity of these ideas.

The categories are the law of all our activity: the soul could neither think, nor love, nor will, without having an object, and this object is necessarily being or one of its determinations. The intelligence could neither imagine, nor remember, nor judge, without recourse to the universal principles of quantity, quality, relation, and modality. It is the glory of Kant to have disentangled the intimate connection that exists between judgment and the categories. Formulate any proposition whatever on the self or on the world, on a phenomenon or on God, it will always have a quantity, a quality, a relation, and a modality, so that judgment is radically impossible without the aid of the elements of reason. But it is not only judgment that depends on the categories; all the operations of thought do so at the same stroke, and more, all the acts of the spiritual life. Fix upon an act of memory or of will, and you will say: it is, it is one, it is original, it is positive, it is actual, it is caused, it is in relation with other acts; all these ideas of being and of unity, of sameness and of difference, of affirmation and of negation, of reality and of possibility, of cause and of effect, are categories borrowed from reason. It is therefore true to say that the whole life of the soul develops on the common ground of rational ideas.

p. 171

The categories are therefore also the law of the intellectual activity whose aim is the knowledge of the external world. In fact, reason raises us above our limited individuality [p. 171] and permits us to ascend to the cause or reason of things, to the world, of which we form a part, to God, principle of all existence. Reason, as M. Cousin has said, is the bridge that unites the self to the not-self: without reason, imagination and understanding would exhaust themselves in the void, incapable of grasping any reality; our images and our notions, if they were possible, would correspond to no object. To affirm an object is to perform an act of reason; for the object is the category of being, the simplest and the most universal of all. What do we say of our sensations? That they proceed from a body, that is to say, from an object or a being. What do we say of this object? That it has such and such sensible qualities, signaled by our impressions, that it acts on us, that it is the cause of the modifications of our nerves, that it exists outside us, extended in space, developing in time, and that it forms part, with all other bodies, of the whole of things or of the universe. It is evident that without these ideas of property, of action, of causality, of time, of space, of solidity, and of externality, we could pass no judgment on our sensations, nor affirm in any way whatever the objective existence of nature. Why do we not say with the idealists that bodies are internal phenomena, like the creations of our dreams? It is because we have the idea of substance, and because, endowed with the consciousness of our limitation, we must regard as external the substances that act upon us and affect us in spite of ourselves.

p. 172

The skeptics, ancient and modern, have often insisted on the importance of the rational elements in the problem of knowledge. Sextus Empiricus and Hume directed their attack above all against the ideas of cause and of substance, and, as they contested the legitimacy of these principles, they logically arrived at undermining the foundation of our knowledge and shaking our confidence in the reality of the external world. The consequence is rigorous, and the skeptics reason admirably, it must be admitted: without categories no sensible knowledge, and if knowledge escapes us, by what right could we still affirm [p. 172] that bodies exist? Why do we, in our dreams, grant an objective reality to the representations of the imagination? Because we cease to observe our acts and become unskilled in referring to them the categories of cause and substance. Carried away by the intellectual habits of waking life, in which imagination concurs with external objects in the formation of our knowledge, we no longer distinguish what comes from us and what comes from the world; we confound the subject with the object and the phenomenon with the substance. We should do the same in the waking state, we should act like true madmen, if we lost the power of applying ideas to our sensations and to the images of fancy.

p. 173

What, then, do the authors do who, after the manner of Condillac, deny reason and nevertheless imagine that they know nature? They take ideas for data of our senses. Sensation is transformed in their eyes and engenders successively the faculties of the mind, imagination, judgment, reasoning, reason. Ideas resemble sensations as principles resemble facts; yet they are the contrary elements of thought: on the one hand, the universal, the absolute, the necessary; on the other, the particular, the relative, the contingent, or, as Kant would say, the noumenon and the phenomenon. Analysis has demonstrated that sensation is a pure and simple impression, which doubtless corresponds to some quality of bodies, but which in itself gives no indication of the essence of matter. What proves it is that with all the refinements of sensibility, supported by the most delicate instruments, we have not yet succeeded in discovering this essence. Sensation is a nervous affection which may well depend on a sensible quality, on heat, on color, on sonority, if it is true that there is analogy between the effect and the cause, but which does not grasp it, for perception belongs to thought. The notions of being, substance, body, time, and space are often attached to the sense of touch. Condillac even gives this sense a singular preeminence over the others: these teach us nothing, that one is invested with the [p. 173] right to judge of external objects (1). What a very extraordinary organ, that argues like a rational soul about the continuity of matter, but forgets that a nerve ought not to permit itself to judge. Being is a universal principle that we extend, rightly or wrongly, to all the objects of thought, sensible or not, whereas the sensation of touch is an accident completely determined in all respects: can what is limited give what is general? Is the effect going to surpass the cause? Does a nervous movement engender substance? No, the sensation contains only itself, that is to say, a modification undergone by the nerves, and if to this modification we add the ideas of being, of object, of substance, it is not from sensation but from reason that we borrow these categories, and we are still left to ask whether this combination is legitimate, for perception does not even reach bodies. Touch, it is said, furnishes us with the notion of solidity, of matter, of extension. This is to forget that the sensation of touch has no dimension whatever and can at most, by repeating itself, suggest or recall the thought of a solid and the idea of space. We naturally conceive space and time as infinite: what relation is there between these ideas and sensations that are always limited? Kant formed a juster estimate of things when he considered time and space not as products of our organs but as the prior conditions of our sensible intuitions. So it is with all ideas: far from being derived from the senses, they complete the circle of sensory activity; the testimony of the senses rests on their authority and has value only through them.

We know how sensible knowledge is formed through the concurrence of the senses and the mind, with the intervention of imagination, of understanding, and of reason. From these premises some important consequences are deduced.

(1) Traité des sensations, Part Two.

p. 174

1. There is no such thing as purely sensible knowledge, that is to say, knowledge acquired by the senses alone. Knowledge does not proceed from the senses, but from thought. Only, thought must be aided by the senses when it wishes to study the phenomena of the external world. The activity of bodies is revealed to the intellect only indirectly, by the changes it works in the organs to which the soul is intimately united. Such is the part played by the senses in the whole of our knowledge. The sensualists are completely mistaken in this respect when they grant to the senses not only the first role, but the exclusive charge of acquiring all our knowledge. Locke at least had retained reflection alongside sensibility as a source of knowledge: it was a mitigated sensualism, in which sensibility supplied the matter, and reflection the form, of knowledge. Condillac wished to correct Locke, reproaching him for leaving something to the soul, and reduced all our faculties to sensibility: this is exclusive sensualism, the poorest of all doctrines, which, under pretext of simplicity, confounds reason, reflection, and imagination with the senses.

All the higher powers of the mind concur with the senses in forming the most elementary knowledge, but we must know how to disentangle their action. Reason penetrates all the manifestations of the spiritual life. Observation is impossible without elements taken from outside observation; we do not experiment without the categories of being, of unity, of relation, of substance, of cause, which the senses do not give. The sensualist maxim, long attributed to Aristotle: “Nihil est in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu,” is therefore radically false. Leibniz rightly added: “nisi ipse intellectus.” The qualification has its value, for rational ideas are inseparable from the intellect. To those authors who still maintain in our day that the senses are the sole source of external knowledge, one may reply categorically that everything comes from the senses, except knowledge.

p. 175

2. Non-sensible knowledge is prior to [p. 175] sensible knowledge, since observation is impossible without the categories that we apply to all the objects of thought. Hence the former is called a priori knowledge, and the latter a posteriori knowledge. These terms, consecrated in philosophical language, denote the priority of the speculative elements of reason over the sensible elements of experience. Several authors, however, while affirming the logical impossibility of forming any knowledge whatever without the aid of general ideas, maintain that in the order of time, from the point of view of the development of the mind, sensible observation is the first source of our knowledge. Kant, for example, asserts “that all our knowledge begins with experience, but that it is not derived from it.” From the very opening of the Critique of Pure Reason he distinguishes between the logical aspect and the chronological aspect of knowledge; he even points out an opposition between the order of time and the absolute order of things. He separates himself sharply from sensualism by saying that our knowledge does not result from experience, and he demonstrates, in fact, that all our assertions concerning the external world have as their condition the categories of the understanding and the pure intuitions of time and space, which the senses do not furnish. But he makes a concession to Locke: all knowledge begins with experience, he says, because thought needs to be excited by objects, and objects are given to us only by sensibility. Kant does not take the trouble to discuss this point: he accepts, as a legitimate result of Locke’s labors, that human knowledge requires a sensible intuition; he thus shows himself from the outset unfaithful to his project of a general critique of the mind, and misjudges the value of reason as an intuitive faculty. The consequence of these principles is that knowledge not only begins with experience, but is wholly confined within it: metaphysics no longer deserves the title of science, since we have no intuition beyond the limits of sensible observation.

p. 176

M. Cousin reproduces the same opinion in another [p. 176] form and with some reserve, relying no longer on the constitutive elements of thought, but on the stages of culture of the human mind (1). He distinguishes in knowledge the conceptions of reason and the sensible representations, and maintains that they presuppose each other reciprocally in two distinct respects. Ideas, he says, are the logical antecedent of experimental notions, and these are the chronological antecedent of the former. Thus the idea of space is the logical condition of the admission of the idea of body, for bodies are in a place and can be conceived only in space; but if we inquire into the history or the successive appearance of ideas in the mind, the idea of body precedes that of space, for in order to comprehend space we must first perceive bodies by means of sight and touch. It is the same with the ideas of finite and infinite, of succession and time, of phenomenon and substance. Idealists and sensualists, the author continues, have both grasped one side of the problem of the origin of ideas, but both are mistaken in denying the opposite side. The two doctrines must be reconciled by affirming at once the priority of reason over sensation, according to the order and logical connection of ideas, and the priority of sensation over reason, according to the order of acquisition of our knowledge.

p. 177

We are repelled by the admission of this contradiction between the life of the intellect and the principles of logic. M. Cousin, like Kant, concedes too large a share to sensualism, in declaring it conformable to thought in its historical evolution, if not in its speculative tendencies. Both have neglected to study human knowledge as a whole, and have above all forgotten indeterminate knowledge, which is the first of all and which casts a new light on the question of origin that has been raised. The primitive fact of consciousness is the thought I, as indeterminate being, in which we as yet grasp no quality, no part, and no relation of the self: before affirming [p. 177] something of the self, in the form of a judgment, we must affirm the self. The intuition I contains in germ the whole science of the self, all the sensible and supra-sensible elements that analysis must one day reveal, but nothing shows itself there at first in a distinct manner: distinctness and clearness are an effect of reflection. The vague and confused consciousness of oneself is incontestably the first knowledge of the child, and this knowledge, which does not proceed from the senses, is already non-sensible, because its object is entirely indeterminate: it is an intellectual intuition. Is the self finite or infinite, substance or phenomenon, mind or body? The child knows nothing of these properties when he begins to take possession of himself, and can acquire knowledge of his properties only if he already has consciousness of himself. All human knowledge thus issues from a primitive germ, in which the diverse forms of thought are still latent, and receives an organic development through the labor of analysis.

(1) Cours de l’histoire de la philosophie. Critique of Locke.

p. 178

Indeterminate knowledge is then succeeded by analytic knowledge, which determines or specifies the manifold sides of the self, which regards it now in its acts or in its temporal manifestations, now in its essence, in its cause, in its relations with the universe and with God, in the eternal laws of its activity. Here the stages of culture of the mind take shape and the various orders of knowledge, derived from the senses and from reason, are produced. What is the first term of this development of knowledge? It is the sensible element, observation or experience. There is no doubt that the training of the mind takes place at first under the predominance of sensibility; this is a consequence of man’s position on the earth; whether through forgetfulness or through ignorance, we do not know at birth the principle of all things, and in order to find our bearings in the world we are obliged to learn laboriously to make use of our limbs and our organs. Our first years are devoted to this labor. The child is a sensible being, whose reason is still dormant and all of whose spiritual forces, intellect, feeling, and will [p. 178] naturally take on the character of sensibility. This is the territory of sensualism, and within these limits it has its share of truth. But the sensualists forget the origins and the conclusion of the sensible culture of the soul: they fail to recognize indeterminate knowledge and rational knowledge, that is to say, the two forms of non-sensible knowledge.

We begin by grasping things in their essence, one and whole, without distinguishing between the sensible and the non-sensible; then we analyze them scientifically, passing from the sensible to the non-sensible, as determinate elements of the intellect. In other words, we proceed from indeterminate knowledge to sensible knowledge, and from this to the higher knowledge of the understanding and of reason. Sensible knowledge is therefore circumscribed, in the history of thought, between two kinds of conceptions which go beyond the reach of the senses; it is the first among our analytic or reflective cognitions, but not in the whole of our knowledge, and moreover it itself requires the categories of reason, which apply, whether or not we are conscious of it, to all the objects of thought. It is therefore not correct to say that sensible representations are the chronological antecedent of rational conceptions. The order of acquisition of our knowledge is identical with the real order of things; the laws of the intellectual life do not contradict the principles of logic.

p. 179

M. Renan makes an analogous observation with regard to language. It is popular reason, says the author, that is the creative power of language. Reflection can do nothing there; languages have come forth ready-made from the very mold of the human mind. Hence the consequence that it is not by successive juxtapositions that the various systems of languages were formed, but that, like the living beings of nature, language, from its first appearance, was endowed with all its essential parts. In effect, from the moment of its constitution the human mind was complete. The first psychological fact contains implicitly all the [p. 179] elements of the most advanced fact: learned reflection contains not one datum more than the inner phenomenon that revealed man to himself. Was it successively that man conquered his different faculties? Who would even dare to think so? Now, since language shows itself at all epochs as parallel to the human mind and as the adequate expression of its essence, we are authorized to establish a rigorous analogy between the facts relating to the development of the intellect and the facts relating to the development of language. Languages must be compared, not to the crystal that forms by agglomeration around a nucleus, but to the germ that develops by its inner force and by the necessary call of its parts. Thorough researches have obliged linguists to renounce the attempts by which the older philology sought to derive the parts of speech one from another. All these parts are primitive; all coexisted in the language of the patriarchs of each race, less distinct, no doubt, but with the principle of their individuality. The grammar of each race was made at the first stroke. There was a long way from the synthetic and obscure expression in which primitive thought was wrapped to the perfect clearness of the instrument which the modern mind has created for itself; but after all, the present exercise of thought differs still more profoundly from the thought of the first men, without our admitting on that account that any new principle has been added to the general system of the human mind. We too often imagine that simplicity, which relatively to our analytic procedures is prior to complexity, is so also in the order of time. This is a remnant of the old habits of scholasticism and of the artificial method that logicians used to carry into psychology. Far from the human mind beginning with analysis, the first act it performs is on the contrary complex, obscure, synthetic; everything is heaped together in it and indistinct. Analysis is only the slow result of its evolution (1).

p. 180

It is impossible to express better the [p. 180] organic development of thought and of language. But this parallelism supposes that there is at the beginning of our knowledge, before any analytic or reflective work, a first germ that contains in a latent state all the ulterior determinations of human knowledge. This germ is indeterminate knowledge.

3. Another consequence of the foregoing theory is that sensible knowledge is legitimate only conditionally, if rational knowledge is legitimate. Since experience is impossible without the employment of the categories, the certainty of the results of experience is subordinate to the certainty of the use of reason. We can conceive nothing without the ideas of being, of unity, of cause; this is an established fact; but have we the right to apply these ideas to transcendent objects? Is not the use we make of reason an abuse? The question is insoluble as long as we are not in possession of the principle of science. It is only in metaphysics that one can verify whether the categories have a universal and objective validity. Until then skeptical idealism is unassailable in its conclusions. Is the external world such as it appears to us, and does it even possess a real existence outside us? Common sense affirms it, but without proofs. Doubt is permissible in this situation. One might even maintain that skeptical idealism has for its mission, in the construction of science, to force man to raise his thought to God in order to find the solution of the problem of truth.

(1) E. Renan, de l’Origine du langage, III, IV, VII. Paris, 1858.

p. 181

4. Sensualism has an opposite fate. It reigns in practical life, where it feeds on all the elements that corrupt morals, but it is without value in theory. Twenty times it has been condemned, from Plato down to our own day, and if it rises again after each condemnation, it is not from a desire to bring new arguments into the debate, but from ignorance and presumption, if not from calculation. Hobbes and Condillac recruited their partisans from the ranks of those who wished to favor political or theocratic despotism, the omnipotence of the State or of the Church. The scientists and the [p. 181] physicians of our day, who are still returning to sensualism, know nothing of the state of philosophical studies and can exert some influence only on people of the world, seduced now by the apparent simplicity of the formulas, now by the attraction of maxims in harmony with their tastes. The exclusive character of the specialists, on the one hand, and the predominance of material interests, on the other, sufficiently explain the recrudescence of sensualism. Philosophical speculation has nothing to do with this movement: it has not produced it and is not touched by it. Between philosophy and sensualism the question is today what it was in the time of Socrates.

Sensualism confines itself to claiming that all our knowledge reduces to sensible notions or is only a transformation of them. The senses are therefore the sole source of human knowledge, considered in its greatest extension: everything that lies within the limits of our sensibility is given to us by our organs and only by our organs; everything that does not fall under our senses is and remains unknown. The mind possesses no other fundamental faculty than sensibility: whatever more we imagine, thought, memory, reason, will, feeling, all proceeds from sensation. And as sensibility is receptive, not spontaneous, man has only the property of receiving from without, from nature, all that he needs in order to develop. He cannot act of himself. The soul is an empty frame awaiting the action of external things, or a blank tablet on which the notions transmitted by the senses come to be engraved successively. Knowledge is the product of our impressions: to feel is to know or, as an ancient sophist said, sensation is the whole of science: οὐκ ἄλλο τί ἐστιν ἐπιστήμη ἢ αἴσθησις (1).

I defy anyone to add a new principle to this exposition of sensualism. The verification is easy to make: let one compare the doctrine of Protagoras in Plato with the writings of Hobbes, of Condillac, of Büchner, and one will find in them in

p. 182

Logic. — I. 12 [p. 182] the last analysis only the same exclusive and pretentious propositions. Certainly the sensualist system has extended itself in its applications; Hobbes presented it in its most complete and most rigorous form. But Hobbes is a bugbear whom his successors no longer dare to invoke. The modern sensualists are no longer even at the height of Epicurus. By dint of disdaining speculation they have lost the sense of logic and the elevation of thought.

Is there need to refute the principles of sensualism yet again? No, the refutation has been made. In the doctrine of sensation there is a logical point of view and a psychological point of view. Now logic, developed on the basis of observation, has shown us the absolute insufficiency of sensation for human knowledge. Psychology has led us to the same result, by pointing out the absolute insufficiency of sensibility for the explanation of the faculties and properties of the soul (1). It is useless to repeat the arguments: the sensualists will not read them, the philosophers know them. But it will be well, I think, in order to forestall any surprise and to judge the tree by its fruits, to unfold rapidly the consequences of sensualism. Plato shall serve us as guide.

(1) Plato, Théétète ou de la Science, ed. Zurich, p. 74.

p. 183

First consequence. If science reduces to sensation, says Socrates, Protagoras speaks truly in affirming that man is the measure of all things, of the existence of those that exist and of the non-existence of those that do not exist. For sensation is wholly individual, each one is judge, and sole judge, of his impressions, although our impressions may be, with respect to the same objects, contrary to those of another. Things are therefore for each what they appear to him to be. If the same wind gives cold to one and warmth to another, the first will rightly say that the wind is cold, and the second will not be wrong in maintaining that the wind is warm. Sensation always has a real object and is not susceptible of error. Objects have nothing absolute in themselves; all their properties relate [p. 183] to our senses; they are and are not, according to circumstances: all is relative, all is true. I heartily approve this view, continues Socrates. Only, I am surprised that Protagoras does not say that the pig, the dog-headed baboon, or some still stranger creature among those that have sensation, is the measure of all things. That would have been a magnificent opening, and altogether insulting to our species, by which he would have given us to understand that, while we admire him as a god for his wisdom, he does not surpass in intelligence, I will not say another man, but a tadpole. What shall we say, in fact? If the opinions that form in us by means of sensations are true for each, if no one is better able than another to discern what his fellow experiences, if each judges solely of what passes within himself, by what privilege would Protagoras be so wise as to think himself entitled to teach others, and to put a high price on his lessons? And are we only ignorant men condemned to go to his school, since each is to himself the measure of his own wisdom? Shall we not say that Protagoras meant to mock us in speaking thus?

Plato is right. Dialectic is a supremely ridiculous art, if everything is confined to sensing. Scholars have no more senses, nor more perfect senses, than the ignorant. Some animal species even surpass man in the range of sight, the fineness of hearing, or the delicacy of smell. There is certainly no essential difference between the nerves of man and those of mammals, and since sensibility constitutes science, all animals are capable of scientific culture and of intellectual labors, in proportion to the development of their nervous system. Learned and speaking animals, or “man reduced to the condition of a brute,” such is the first consequence of sensualism.

(1) La Science de l’âme dans les limites de l’observation. Brussels, 1862.

p. 184

Epicurus, Hobbes, all the sensualists, had a feeling of this necessity when they imagined, at the origin of society, savage man, wandering in the forests, without speech or laws, without moral or religious bond. The attempts of the naturalists [p. 184] such as Lamarck and Darwin, who claim that living species are transformed, and that man comes from the ape, which itself descends from a polyp, have no other cause. It is always man confounded with the animal, reason with the senses, the person with things; it is always the same contempt for the dignity that belongs to rational beings. Dr. Büchner does not know the history of sensualism, but he arrives by instinct at the same result. “The best authorities we have in physiology, he says, are at present quite agreed that the soul of animals does not differ from the human soul in quality, but only in quantity. Quite recently Charles Vogt has treated this question with the rare talent that is known to be his, and has decided it in the sense we have just indicated. Man has no absolute precedence over the animal; his intellectual superiority over the latter is only relative. Man has no intellectual faculty as a privilege; it is only the greater intensity of these faculties, and the conformity of their union with one another, that give him superiority. The natural and necessary cause of the perfection of man’s faculties is found in the more perfect development of the material organ of thought. No essential difference can be found, either in form or in chemical composition, between the brain of man and that of animals. One must have seen and frequented certain lower classes of our society to conceive that the intellectual scale, from the animal to man, is in no way interrupted. What an abyss is there between the Negro and the ape?... Language is often cited as the characteristic trait that distinguishes man from the animal. Those who make this objection certainly do not know that animals can also speak. Moreover, we have a multitude of facts and observations which demonstrate to evidence that the articulate voice of animals, as well as their gestures and their mimicry, are susceptible, to a certain degree, of development and perfecting. We know that the intellectual faculties of animals are in general susceptible of being developed and perfected like those of man.

p. 185

What admirable things do we not see performed by trained animals!... It is therefore impossible to deny the insensible transition which, through innumerable intermediate degrees, connects man with the animal, as much in intellectual as in corporeal qualities... For this reason it does not become man to put on lofty airs in regard to the organic world, and to consider himself as a being of another nature and of a higher origin (1).”

It is understood: man is a brute, and brutes are capable of observation, of morality, of language, and of perfectibility, like us. Let us await the result of their studies. The psychology of the animals, written by themselves, has perhaps already appeared, and the shrewdest of the band (pardon the expression) are seeking the means of communicating it to us. We shall then know, to within a millimeter, what the difference is between their soul and ours. Until then any comment would be superfluous.

Second consequence. If sensation is the whole of science, there is no longer any possible distinction between truth and error, since our impressions are always what they ought to be, even when they are in contradiction with those of another. Some are as true as others, although they affirm and deny one and the same quality of one and the same object. This is why Protagoras maintained that everything is true. But if everything is true, it is equally true that everything is false. The second proposition is only a variant of the first: both signify that truth and error are confounded. Now science has truth for its object, to the exclusion of error. If the two terms are identical, there is no longer any science; hence skepticism.

p. 186

Plato is right again: the sensualism of the sophists is the origin of skepticism. Everything changes in our organs and in objects; it is impossible ever to fix anything in the perpetual flux of sensible phenomena. In proportion as we express our thoughts, bodies are no longer what they [p. 186] were; white becomes black, hot becomes cold, moist becomes dry: where then is the truth of things? Moreover, sensation bears on the present instant, not on the past or the future; it applies to the individual objects of the external world, not to supra-sensible things, nor even to the relations that objects have among themselves. No principle falls under the senses, and yet science demands general truths. What would the science of nature be without knowledge of species, genera, causes, and the laws of matter? And to what sense are we indebted for these perceptions? Science is therefore impossible.

This explains to us the profound sympathy that prevails, at all epochs, between sensualism and skepticism. The one proceeds from the other. Sextus Empiricus and Hume were frankly sensualists, and it is the system of sensation that led them to doubt. Sensation, a subjective phenomenon, proves nothing with regard to objects, and the conception of an object cannot be formed without the categories of substance and of cause. But if our organs teach us nothing concerning causes and substances, what guarantees remain for the testimony of our senses? Sensualism and skepticism are the same doctrine at two stages of development; they are also the whole philosophy of the eighteenth century in France, in the state of a tendency rather than of a settled theory. Our modern sensualists have not yet attained that logical severity which one must admire in the enlightened representatives of the school. They content themselves with eliminating from science whatever touches the moral interests of man, and do not even suspect that the observation of nature could not be carried on with the elements of sensibility alone. It is ignorance that assures their security.

(1) Dr. Büchner, Force et Matière, translated by Gamper from the 7th German edition, p. 251, s. 1863.

p. 187

Third consequence. If science is confined to sensation, we can reasonably admit only the material things that present themselves to our senses: hence materialism. Every consistent sensualist is a materialist. The soul will be air, fire, blood, a secretion of the brain, or, as a modern sensualist expresses it, who sometimes avoids the proper word, the ideal product of a certain combination [p. 187] of matter endowed with forces. There exists, then, but one kind of substance in the world, bodies, as we have but one kind of faculty, the senses: souls or spirits, as distinct from matter, are a pure hypothesis, contrary to our intellectual organization. And as bodies are born and die, souls begin and end with them. The immortality of the soul is a chimera. In a word, sensualism and materialism are one and the same doctrine, regarded now from the psychological point of view of the origin of knowledge, now from the ontological point of view of the existence of objects. Epicurus, Hobbes, and the sensualists of our own day are materialists and pride themselves on it. Condillac is an exception, in his quality of abbé; but with him the soul is a datum of revelation, not of reason: this is an inconsistency which is rejected by those of his disciples who have no faith. The doctrine of Aug. Comte, which recognizes only sensible observation, is likewise materialist. It is a phrenological materialism that would not deserve a mention in a serious work, if, thanks to the absence of philosophical culture, positivism did not tend to spread among people of the world (1).

p. 188

It is curious to hear Dr. Büchner on this point. He will not have it said, with Cabanis and Vogt, that thought is a secretion of the brain, as bile is a secretion of the liver and urine a secretion of the kidneys. No, thought is immaterial, it cannot be perceived immediately by the senses (whither are we going, great heavens!); thought is a force, a function of the brain. “The brain is indeed the principle and the source, or to put it better, the sole cause of mind, of thought, but it is not for that reason the secreting organ.” Very well! Thought is not an excretion of matter, our dignity is safe. It remains only to explain how a material substance [p. 188] can be the principle, the source, and the cause of an immaterial effect, and how we have by means of our senses a knowledge, even if mediate, of what escapes the senses. But the question is perhaps indiscreet. Let us content ourselves with knowing that the soul is born, develops, and dies with the brain. Experience in this respect is decisive, according to the author. In fact, we see the soul in this life, but not beyond: therefore it exists no more. It is like a comet that vanishes as soon as one ceases to perceive it. Do not cry out; there are facts, numerous and palpable facts, which demonstrate the death of the soul, as there are certain facts, I forgot to say, which prove that animals speak, observe, and perfect themselves like us. What a fine thing experience is, when one knows how to handle it without a spirit of system, as the sensualists do! What folly to prescribe limits to experience, under pretext that there are questions which are not within its competence, and that the problem of the future life is among their number! As if we did not know a priori that the soul must die, since it is only a product of matter!

(1) Cours de philosophie positive, vol. III, lect. XLV, Paris, 1838. The author defends himself against this accusation (Discours sur l’ensemble du positivisme, 1848), but the terms of his protest prove that he was not able to give himself an account of the value of his own theories.

p. 189

Matter is immortal, but not mind, according to our author. For immortality is not the continuation of life, as the name would seem to indicate, but the continuation of existence; immortality is eternity: everything, living or dead, which persists under any form whatever, in the solid or gaseous state, is immortal; it is the more immortal the less alive it is, for, not having life, it is clear that it cannot die. Hence the author proposes an important reform in philosophy and in grammar. “The expressions mortal body and immortal soul have become banal and almost tedious. A more exact reflection would make the adjectives of these terms change places and would perhaps restore more truth to them. The body in its individual form is no doubt mortal, but not in its elements. Not only does it change in death, but also in life, without ceasing: yet it is immortal, in the higher sense, since not the least particle of it could be annihilated. On the other hand, we see vanish [p. 189] what we call soul, with the decay of the material and individual composition; and the mind exempt from prejudices sees in this phenomenon only the interruption of an effect produced by the concurrence of many molecules endowed with forces, an effect which must naturally cease with the cause. If we are not annihilated by death, says Fechner, the mode of our present existence cannot nevertheless be saved in death. We visibly become again the dust of which we are made; but while we change, the earth remains and develops without ceasing, it is an immortal being, and the stars are so with it (1).” Behold the new “immortal gods” of materialism. I take care not to protest, for “it is quite comical, says the author, that at all times the partisans who have fought with the greatest zeal for individual immortality have been, in general, those whose personal soul was perhaps not worth the trouble of so long and so minute a preservation (2).”

p. 190

Fourth consequence. If all our knowledge is enclosed within the limits of sensibility, we have no notion of God, nor any certainty of his existence: hence atheism. We know Epicurus’s respect for the gods, and Hobbes’s for religion: a fable, a means of police. If God exists, he is a great body. This is logical, and it is better than saying with Condillac that the senses raise us up to God, or with Aug. Comte that the Supreme Being is humanity. No, the senses have nothing in common with the infinite and the absolute, nor even with the conception of humanity. Beings deprived of reason do not appear to suspect the existence of God; up to now at least, despite the progress announced by some doctors, no trace of religious culture has been discovered in animals. Would they be wiser than we? Perhaps; but I should very much like to know how this idea of God, or this abstraction, if you will, ever could have entered the human mind. Man has made God [p. 190] in his own image, you will say. Granted, as for the gods of paganism, art alone can defend them; but the infinite and absolute Being is not fabricated with hands. You must deny him, and in denying him you attest that you have the idea of him. I ask whence this idea comes. You may declare that it is false, that nothing in reality corresponds to the thought of God; you will not set aside my question on the origin of this thought.

The modern sensualists do not suspect that there is any difficulty here: they seem to believe that religion and superstition are synonymous, and that the priestly castes alone are interested in affirming God. Dr. Büchner resolves in cavalier fashion the great problem that has stopped all men of genius. He begins by laying down his principle that there is no matter without forces, nor forces without matter, a principle fruitful for physics; then he adds without transition: “What is the general and philosophical consequence of this notion, as simple as it is natural? That those who speak of a creative force which would have created the world of itself or out of nothing are ignorant of the first and simplest principle of the study of nature based on philosophy and on empiricism. How could there have existed a force which did not manifest itself in matter itself, but which governed it arbitrarily and according to individual considerations? Forces existing independently could not, with any more reason, pass into formless and inert matter and so produce the world: for we have seen that forces and matter, conceived in an abstract manner, are absurd conceptions. The chapter which will treat of the immortality of matter will demonstrate to us that the world could not have been created out of nothing. A nothing is a chimera rejected by logic and by empiricism. The world or matter, with its properties which we call forces, must have existed from all eternity and will exist absolutely through all eternity; in a word, the world could not have been created (1).”

(1) Dr. Büchner, Force et Matière, p. 13, 1863.

(2) Ibid., p. 199.

p. 191

Here is a fine specimen of materialist logic, based on experience; for experience turns decidedly against [p. 191] God. A celebrated astronomer, satisfied with knowing the laws of the world, was able to treat God as a hypothesis, believing no doubt that observation did not reach the legislator of the universe and consequently permitted no conclusion, whether positive or negative, with regard to him. Dr. Büchner is less modest. With the chemical balance in his hand, he demonstrates by facts, always facts, that there is no God. Nothing can prevail against a fact, God will not withstand it. Happy age of positivism, in which humanity will at last be delivered from all preoccupation with moral interests and will be able to adore itself! What indeed can one answer to syllogisms of this kind: no force without matter; now God is a creative force; therefore God does not exist. Next: matter is eternal; now what is eternal cannot be created; therefore God does not exist. Two arguments in due form, when one alone would suffice. It is true that a captious mind might perhaps find some gaps and some gratuitous suppositions in these reasonings. If there are no forces without matter in nature, for example, the spiritualists are of the opinion that there still exist in the world, besides bodies and their properties, spiritual substances which also have their forces. In the second place, if God is a creative force, the theologians and the metaphysicians hold that he is also the infinite and absolute Being, and that consequently the major premise of the first syllogism has nothing in common with the conclusion. Finally, if matter is eternal, which is incontestable in my eyes as in the eyes of the chemists, many philosophers, and even Fathers of the Church such as Origen, maintain that the world, visible and invisible, may nevertheless have a cause, that the eternity of the elements of the universe sets aside the common hypothesis of a creation out of nothing, made in time, but not the opinion of an eternal creation, and that the idea of cause applies to everything that is finite, to minds and to bodies, whatever be their mode of existence in time or in eternity. Consequently the second syllogism is no better than the first, and we may wait for new facts to be produced against God before renouncing all conception of a moral order of the world.

(1) Dr. Büchner, Force et Matière, p. 4.

p. 192

Fifth consequence. If science is only sensation, the good is for each one what gives him pleasure; evil, what causes him pain. Nothing is good in itself, but only in relation to us. What is good for one is bad for another. And as every being acts according to its nature, man has no other end to fulfill than to seek the greatest sum of enjoyments. This is his right, his duty, his destiny. This very destiny is imposed on him, he could not free himself from it, he is not free, since he is matter, he is the slave of his senses, like the brute that attaches itself to the pursuit of pleasure. A new analogy, pointed out by Plato in the Philebus, between the animal and the man who gives himself up wholly to the impressions of the moment. Hence egoism, eudaemonism, fatalism. Epicurus and Hobbes are in perfect agreement on all these points. There are scarcely any variations in this estimate of the moral life, which has been so minutely reduced to calculation by Bentham. It is important to remark only that the idea of calculation, which transforms pleasure into interest rightly understood, is already an inconsistency in pure sensualism. In order to check the impulse of the senses and to reject a present pleasure in favor of a more considerable future pleasure, there must be in man another element than sensibility; there must be at least reflection.

p. 193

What do our modern sensualists think of this morality? I believe that they are not aware of it, that their heart protests against their maxims, that their doctrine, as philosophy, is a play of their imagination, and that they would repel it with indignation if they saw its necessary consequences clearly. Dr. Büchner protests with energy against the intentions that are attributed to his friends. “Ever since the general results of the philosophy of the natural sciences began to penetrate among the people, the greatest dangers have been apprehended for human society, in respect of the materialist tendencies of these sciences; there has even been the presumption to predict quite simply the destruction of all moral ideas, and consequently the ruin of society itself and a bellum omnium contra omnes, [p. 193] if these tendencies should come to prevail (1).” For those who know materialism through the study of philosophy or of history, these fears are not chimerical, but legitimate. There is not one moral idea, neither self-denial, nor duty, nor natural law, nor the imputability of acts, that can be reconciled with the egoistic and fatalistic principle of sensualism. There is no society capable of resisting the brutal pursuit of personal interest, if interest can ever stifle conscience and produce all its effects. The relations of men among themselves would be precisely a war of all against all, according to the just expression of Hobbes: it would be the state of nature described by that great logician. Yes, man would conduct himself like a wild beast, if he had to sacrifice everything to his material enjoyments, according to the prescriptions of the doctrine. Dr. Büchner does not understand this, and that is his excuse. But he is wrong to answer a serious criticism with foolish declamations against the social state. He is wrong above all to follow the pretended apostles of liberty in Germany who absolutely reject the liberty of man. Man is not free, and why? Because he is part of a people, whose customs depend on climate, because he is himself subject to the manifold influences of his character and of external circumstances. This has long been known, and it has never prevented a rational being, even if he denied reason, from affirming inwardly his liberty. A singular justification, in truth! You defend yourselves against the charge of attacking the moral order, and you undermine the moral order at its base. Are you then ignorant that without liberty there is no longer any responsibility, any merit, any virtue, any duty? Or do you claim that man is a machine and that it suffices for him to observe a police regulation in order to have a right to respect and to rise to the dignity of a free being?

p. 194

Sixth consequence. If man has only senses, what finally becomes of justice or right, the principle of social life? Protagoras confounded right with law, legitimacy with [p. 194] legality, and said that all laws are good for the peoples that adopt them, however contrary they may be to one another. This is the theory of accomplished facts, the justification of success, regardless of the means. Hobbes accepts it and develops it with his customary rigor, without the least hesitation. The distinction of good and evil, of just and unjust, is not the source, but the effect, of law. Everything that the law permits or commands must be held good, everything it forbids evil, even if it should order the denial of God, the exposure of children, or the massacre of a class of citizens. Murder is not culpable in itself, but becomes so by the prohibition of the law. Pure convention. In fact, go back to the origin of society, and picture to yourselves the state of nature, in which men lived like wolves. There neither good nor evil was known. Each had a right to everything, and no one spared his fellows. Justice then was the right of the stronger; in other words, right is force, as M. Proudhon still maintains, as all must claim who assimilate man to the brute. But it appears that our ancestors grew disgusted with that justice, judging no doubt that it was ruinous to all; they therefore assembled and agreed, although they had neither reason nor language: 1° that they would invent signs to understand one another; 2° that they would put an end to the state of nature; 3° that they would institute a state contrary to nature, called society; 4° that they would make a contract in due form, as soon as they should know how to write, in order to fix their reciprocal rights and duties. This was well enough imagined for savages, more savage than the most degraded populations invoked by the partisans of philosophical empiricism, since no one has yet succeeded in finding men without speech or social state. Our ancestors therefore generously renounced their claims to all things, in the hope of obtaining some security; they created good and evil, property and police, the just and the unjust; but their descendants, convinced that these claims are after all their rights, are naturally tempted to resume them. That is why there are people who say that they [p. 195] can dispose of the goods and the life of others, and who do so dispose. The rest are no better, but dare not obey the inspiration of nature, for fear of the law. Fear is the safeguard of society, the counterweight of instinct. The best society will therefore be the one in which the law inspires the keenest terror. Organize the State, give it all powers, leave to the prince the right of life and death over the citizens, over the subjects, so that no one may permit himself to speak or to act against the established order, that no one may take it into his head to have an opinion or a belief without the authorization of the prince. The ideal of society is despotism and absolutism, the only form of government that is conformable to the sensible nature of man.

The new partisans of philosophical empiricism count among them ardent democrats. Do they know these political consequences of sensualism? I doubt it. Warnings, it is true, have not been lacking to them. In an assembly of German naturalists and physicians at Göttingen, a man of science more clear-sighted than the others, Rudolf Wagner, said to them publicly: “The morality that flows from scientific materialism sums itself up in these words: let us eat and drink, tomorrow we shall be no more. All the great and noble thoughts are vain dreams, phantasmagoria, the sport of automata with two arms, running on two legs and decomposing into chemical atoms in order to combine anew.” But they pretend that these are calumnies and cry out against the hypocrisy of the virtue that takes fright at their maxims. They must be sent back to the study of Hobbes. As for Dr. Büchner, he concerns himself little with social questions in his book; he contents himself with displaying complacently the spectacle of human perversity in the state of nature, and concludes from it that there exists in us no innate idea of morality, of right, or of religion. We shall return to this problem.

(1) Dr. Büchner, Force et Matière, p. 252.

p. 196

Such is the sum of the consequences of sensualism. They are summed up in a word: there is no rational life, the life of man differs in nothing from the life of animals, from the point of view of quality: science is reduced to sensation [p. 196] good to pleasure, justice to force, God to matter. What can come of this? Disgust in all who have any moral feeling; if not, the ruin of society, a return to barbarism.

CHAPTER TWO

ABSTRACT KNOWLEDGE

Logical Analytic.

Man knows not only individual objects, perfectly determined in all respects in time and in space, accessible to the various modes of sensibility; he also grasps by the understanding general relations among the facts he observes, and can even rise by reason to notions that pass beyond all the limits of experience. The value of these non-sensible cognitions is disputed, but their existence in us is beyond all question. We know, rightly or wrongly, species, genera, classes of beings belonging to the kingdoms of nature, whereas the senses never present to us anything but individuals; and we affirm, besides, that we know something of space, of time, of nature, of humanity, of God himself, whereas observation bears only on the finite beings of the world.

p. 197

Non-sensible cognitions, which have for their object general properties, universal laws, infinite things, are more important for science than sensible cognitions, which have for their object particularities or phenomena. There is no science of phenomena, said Plato. Indeed, phenomena may well serve for the description of an object, but are useful to science only as indications of the properties of a class. The particular qualities of a horse, for example, are of interest to the [p. 197] owner, but science concerns itself only with the qualities of the horse. No science without general elements. History itself, as the encyclopedic science of facts, rests on principles which betray its relations with philosophy: political history rests on the idea of society, natural history on the idea of organization. Sensible knowledge is therefore insufficient in itself, although it forms perhaps the most extensive part of our learning, by the innumerable quantity of details that it daily furnishes us concerning everything that surrounds us; these details derive their value chiefly from the unity that thought discovers in them, by referring them to their laws and reducing them to a system, by means of the abstract notions of the understanding and the categories of reason.

Abstract knowledge and rational knowledge are both non-sensible; but they present this remarkable difference between them, that the former has its basis in observation and contents itself with generalizing its results, whereas the latter is independent of all experiment and above it. The one is properly the knowledge of the understanding, as the faculty of abstraction and generalization, that is to say, the product of analysis or of reflection exercising itself on the individual objects given by the senses and attaching itself to reproducing their common traits; the other is rather the knowledge of reason, as the higher faculty that opens to us the world of ideas, of causes and of principles, as the sense of the infinite and of the absolute. This is at bottom the distinction that is made between generalized notions and general notions. Generalized notions are induced from observation and exist in us only by virtue of the acquired knowledge of the species found on our globe: such are the notions of snow, of iron, of palm tree, of gentian, of rhinoceros, of infusorian. One or another of these notions may be lacking in many men, according to the country they inhabit and the instruction they have received, without the interests of reason being appreciably injured; all the inhabitants of the earth would have been deprived of them, if our planet had had another origin and another history, absolutely

p. 198

Logic. — I. 13 [p. 198] as we are ignorant of the mineral or organic species that may people other heavenly bodies. General notions are more extensive, because they have not the same source and admit not the same restrictions; they must illumine every rational soul that obtains a normal development, abstraction made of the times, places, and external circumstances of its career: such are the notions of mathematics and of pure philosophy. Mathematics is not a science of observation, but of reasoning, although the demonstrations may be illustrated by palpable signs and figures. Algebraic or geometrical representations are not a matter for experiment, but a simple means of rendering the demonstrations sensible: it is the aid that the imagination lends to reason, or the sensible intuition that accompanies the intellectual intuition. Hence we do not take the trouble to examine whether a theorem would retain its validity if applied to larger or smaller figures. If rational beings dwell on the different planets of our solar system, they cannot have notions of time, of space, of motion, of the properties of the triangle, of the circle, and of all that is regularly deduced from the possible combinations among the numbers or the dimensions of extension, other than ours. The same is true of the notions of the finite and the infinite, of being and cause, of true and false, of good and evil, of God and the world. General ideas are eternal, immutable, necessary, whereas generalized notions may vary with times and places, like the observation from which they come. The former are a priori, the latter a posteriori. Such is the fundamental difference between the two domains of non-sensible knowledge, between abstract or co-sensible knowledge and rational or supra-sensible knowledge.

p. 199

Abstract knowledge is the experimental knowledge of species and genera, that is to say, the study of the various classes of beings, not insofar as it can be deduced from a higher principle, as in mathematics, but [p. 199] insofar as it is drawn from observation, as in the natural sciences. It consists wholly in observing individual things, in gathering their common properties, abstracting from the characters proper to each object, and in generalizing more and more by extending the same procedure to other species and to other genera. Mathematics has nothing in common with generalization, as Mill has very well established (1). The division of the triangle, for example, from the double point of view of the angles and the sides, is not an experimental datum, but an immediate deduction from the very idea or from the definition of this figure. If a triangle is formed by the intersection of three lines, it follows that its elements may be equal or unequal, that inequality admits two cases, and that thus there are, whether one considers the angles or the sides, three possible species of triangles, neither more nor less. The first author who occupied himself with geometry must have known these combinations, and no one will ever be able to discover a new combination. It is quite otherwise in the study of nature, where it is a matter of seeking out the facts before classifying them, operations both of them laborious, and neither yet brought to completion.

p. 200

Abstraction is an act of reflection that divides what is undivided, that separates what is inseparable in itself, in order to study apart each element of a whole. Abstraction as such is a preparation for analysis, which considers objects in themselves, independently of their cause and of their relations with the totality of things, and which then decomposes them into their various parts. We know that there is no form without ground, no phenomena without substance, no properties without a being, no effect without cause, no parts without a whole; but nothing hinders us from attaching ourselves to a simple form and examining it in itself, detaching it from all matter, as we do, for example, in geometry and in [p. 200] mechanics; nothing opposes our analyzing successively the parts of a whole, the properties of a substance, as if each of these elements existed apart. These are acts of abstraction, without which we could form no determinate knowledge. Abstraction accompanies attention and perception, each time that these functions bear upon a finite object, considered as such. To grasp the infinite, one need abstract from nothing, because the infinite is all and includes even the finite. As for the finite, a distinction is indispensable, according as it is recognized or not as such. One may think of a finite being without knowing that it is finite: it is then the object of an indeterminate knowledge, which requires no act of abstraction. Such is the thought I, as the starting point of science. But if the finite being is recognized in its limit or in its determination, it can be perceived only thanks to the faculty we have of abstracting from all the rest, for the finite exists only on this footing, insofar as it is distinct from all that surrounds it. It is impossible to fix in isolation this or that determinate object, an animal, a plant, a star, without thought turning away from all the others and affirming that it is not they.

(1) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, book III, of inductions improperly so called, vol. I, p. 321. London, 1862.

p. 201

But if abstraction enters into all our determinate knowledge, all this knowledge is not called abstract: it is only analytic. In abstract knowledge abstraction rises to a higher degree and takes the name of generalization: it then embraces a whole set of individual objects, subject to observation, and reduces to unity, in a higher notion, the common qualities of these objects, to the exclusion of their particular properties. There is here a double operation that distinguishes observation properly so called from generalization: the former bears upon individual objects, minerals or organized bodies, which fall under our senses and which can be recognized in their determination only by an abstraction of thought; the latter bears upon the whole or collection of objects, upon the species which extends to all beings of the same nature, past, present, or future, which is no longer grasped [p. 201] by the senses, but formed by the understanding in consequence of a new act of abstraction.

Abstract knowledge rests on observation and generalization. It begins with the senses and goes beyond the limits of sensibility. To be legitimate, it therefore requires all the conditions inherent in sensible knowledge and, besides, the conditions proper to the procedure of generalization. Already in observation, when we rely too servilely on the testimony of the senses, we often take appearances for facts, witness the motion of the stars about the earth: the whole astronomy of antiquity and of the Middle Ages rested on a false experience, which is the very reverse of the truth. Generalization is subject to other illusions. If we neglect a few circumstances and pass with too much precipitation over the intermediate notions, we reason from one case to all cases, we invent hypotheses, and we make artificial classifications which in no way resemble the work of nature. It is important first to choose one’s ground well, not to confound heterogeneous facts with one another, for example, physical and psychical phenomena; it is important next to multiply observations and to adopt a sufficiently broad basis, the whole of the properties or of the organs, in order to construct the general division of the kingdoms of nature.

p. 202

All reservations made, let us indicate the course to be followed in order to ascend from the individual to the species and from the species to the genus. When a child sees for the first time a cat, a belfry, a pond, and hears these objects named, he does not yet know whether the names that designate them are proper or common; he is without experience and perhaps has not intelligence enough to understand that elsewhere there exist other objects of the same nature: the idea of this or that species is not innate, and the child has not yet acquired it. But if he happens to discover other objects analogous to those he knows, he does not hesitate to call them by the same name: the cat becomes a cat; the same name serves for several. How is this transformation effected? By generalization. The species is discovered, although it has not yet its scientific [p. 202] characters. Science is less prompt, but has no other procedure. To form the notion of the species, we begin by observing the greatest possible number of individuals; we divide their properties into two classes, namely the qualities common to all and the qualities proper to each, such as size, volume, color, age, health; we abstract from the proper or individual qualities, which distinguish the individuals from one another, we unite into a whole the common qualities obtained by comparison, and it is this whole that constitutes the notion of the species. From the species we then ascend to the genus, by subjecting the common properties to a new labor of revision and elimination. Indeed, among these qualities, some are proper to one species, not to all, and the others are common to all the species. We abstract from the former, the specific properties, which distinguish the species from one another; the others, the properties common to all the species, constitute the genus. These two notions of species and of genus suffice for the needs of logic; the other denominations, family, class, order, branch, and kingdom, in use in the natural sciences, are remote genera and are obtained by the same procedure. After eliminating the individual properties, then the specific properties, we eliminate in their turn the generic properties, always effecting new divisions in the whole of the common properties. We thus arrive, by successive generalizations, at notions ever more abstract, ever more extended and stripped of characters. Memory is indispensable to the accomplishment of this complicated labor of the intelligence.

p. 203

Let us take an example. I gather daisies. I observe that all these plants have common properties, drawn from the root, the leaves, the fruits, the stamens, the form and the insertion of the flowers on a common receptacle, but that they differ among themselves in the number, the size, and the more or less perfect whiteness of the corollas. I abstract from these particularities, and I obtain the species (bellis perennis). I abstract anew from the duration [p. 203] of the plant, from the division of the stem, from the form of the leaves, and I obtain the genus (bellis). I abstract again from the form of the corolla and of the seed: there then remain to me five stamens, united anthers, filiform style, sessile flowers, indehiscent fruits, common receptacle, which are the characters of the family of the composites. By the first elimination, I separate the perennial daisy from neighboring species; by the second, I separate the genus bellis from the other genera of flowers with united anthers; by the third, finally, I separate the family of the composites from the other classes of the vegetable kingdom.

p. 204

This procedure is fertile in lessons. It is plain that in ascending the scale of beings, from the individual up to the supreme genus, we arrive at notions which, on the one hand, contain a number of beings ever more considerable, and which, on the other, possess a number of properties ever smaller, and that the result is the inverse when we descend the scale of beings. It is manifest also that the quantity of properties diminishes in a proportional manner as the quantity of individuals contained in the notion increases. On this property of generalization is founded the theory of extension and comprehension, which receives so many applications in logic. The extension of a notion is the whole of the individuals or objects to which it applies; the comprehension of a notion is the whole of the properties or characters that it possesses.
