The extension of the word vertebrate, for example, is composed of all the orders of mammals, birds, reptiles, and fishes, of all the animals that possess, along with the vertebral column, a more or less marked development of the organs of the life of relation; the comprehension of the same word is composed of all the anatomical characters by which zoology recognizes a vertebrate individual among the various branches of the animal kingdom. It follows that if we compare two notions, of species and of genus, the extension will always be in inverse ratio to the comprehension, so that the more extensive will be at the same time the less comprehensive, and the more comprehensive the less extensive. The [p. 204] notion vertebrate has more extension than the notion mammal, since it comprises all mammals and, besides, birds, fishes, and reptiles; but, on the other hand, the notion of a mammal has more comprehension than the notion of a vertebrate, since the mammal possesses all the properties of vertebrate animals and, besides, the property of bringing forth living young.

Abstraction is an elimination: to form the notion of the species, we must eliminate the purely individual properties; for that of the genus, we must eliminate the purely specific properties. The genus therefore necessarily has fewer properties, less comprehension, than the species, and the species fewer properties than the individual; but, in compensation, the species extends further than the individual, and the genus further than the species. The most comprehensive and least extensive notion is that of the individual; the most extensive and least comprehensive notion is that of the supreme genus. The widest notion is therefore at the same time the simplest, and everything added to it in order to determine it restricts its sense. Being has more extension than inorganic being or organized being. To be convinced of it, it suffices to cast the eyes on a synoptic table that represents one of the kingdoms of nature: the marks accumulate, the notions grow complicated, as we approach the lower terms of the division. Hence also the method of the naturalists of adding to the name of the genus a characteristic qualification to designate the species (bellis, bellis perennis, bellis annua).

p. 205

Let us show some applications of the theory of extension and comprehension. The first relates to subordinate notions. Two notions are subordinate when they are those of genus and species: the genus is the superior notion, the species the inferior notion, and, what is most remarkable, these two notions are reciprocally contained in one another under two distinct relations. The genus envelops the species in its extension, and the species, in its turn, envelops the genus in its comprehension. The dog, for example, is included in the extension of the carnivore, for the order of carnivores extends to a multitude of animals [p. 205] which feed on insects or flesh, and dogs are of this number; but the carnivore is included in the comprehension of the dog, for the dog possesses, besides the properties of carnivores in general, the particular qualities of a flesh-eating and digitigrade carnivore. Thence are explained the rules of the subordination of notions. First, all that is affirmed of the genus must also be affirmed of each species. Indeed, what is affirmed of the genus is a quality of the genus, an element of its comprehension. Now, from the point of view of comprehension, the genus is the contained and the species the container: all that belongs to the genus must therefore belong to the species; the genus has only the qualities common to all the species. It is as if one said: all that is in the contained is also in the container. Next, what is denied of the species must also be denied of the genus; for what is denied is a quality, and the species has more comprehension than the genus. What is not a quality of the species cannot therefore be a quality of the genus. It is as if one said: all that is outside the container is also outside the contained. Such are the two rules, positive and negative, that relate to subordinate notions. But the two reciprocal propositions must be rejected. We must not say: all that is affirmed of the species must be affirmed of the genus, nor all that is denied of the genus must be denied of the species, for all that is in the container is not for that reason in the contained, and all that is outside the contained is not for that reason outside the container. The laws of the relation of containment receive an application as simple as it is complete to subordinate notions, when we recognize that it is a question of comprehension, and that in this respect it is the genus that is contained in the species.

p. 206

The same laws find their confirmation in the rules relating to subaltern judgments. Two judgments are subaltern which are composed of the same terms, and which differ from each other only in quantity, that is to say, of which one is universal and the other particular. “All men are mortal, some men are mortal.” “No angle is right, some angles are not right.” “Some [p. 206] fishes are viviparous, all fishes are viviparous.” In subaltern judgments, it is a question, as we see, of affirming or denying the same quality of a notion, taken now in its whole extension, now in a part of its extension, that is to say considered in turn as genus and as species, whether we descend from the whole to the part by deduction, or ascend from the part to the whole by generalization. We must therefore find again, in these sorts of judgments, the rules of subordinate notions. First, if the universal judgment, it is said, is true, the particular judgment is so too: what is true of the whole is true of the part. Indeed, in the universal judgment, the subject is taken as genus, and in the particular judgment, as species. Now, what can be affirmed of the genus must be so of each of its species. If the universal judgment is negative, it is easily translated into an affirmative judgment, by the transposition of the negation from the subject to the attribute, and is brought back to the same law. “No man is perfect—every man is imperfect.” It suffices therefore to apply the rule: what suits the genus must suit the species; what is in the contained is also in the container. In the second place, if the particular judgment is false, the universal judgment is so too: what is false of the part is false of the whole. Indeed, the particular judgment bears on a species, and the species envelops the genus in its comprehension. What is false of the species does not belong to it as a quality. Now we know that what is denied of the species must also be denied of the genus, that what is outside the container is likewise outside the contained. But the two reciprocals do not hold. If the universal judgment is false, the particular judgment is not false on that account, for what does not suit the genus may apply to the species, which has more comprehension. We must not therefore say: what is false of the whole is false of each part. If finally the particular judgment is true, the universal judgment is not true on that account, since the genus has not all the properties of each species. We must not therefore conclude affirmatively from the part to the whole, or judge of all by some.

p. 207

We shall see, in connection with reasoning, other applications of the same principles. This is easily conceived: reasoning decomposes into judgments, the judgment into notions, and each notion has its extension and its comprehension. Let us note only the rules relating to the conclusion of a syllogism. The conclusion is contained in the premises, as the particular judgment in a universal judgment, as the species in the genus. Consequently, we must find the same laws again. Indeed, if the premises are true, the conclusion deduced from them is so too; if the conclusion is false, the premises from which it is drawn are so too; but the reciprocals do not hold: if the premises are false, the conclusion may still be true, by virtue of other arguments. “All viviparous vertebrates are mammals; the bat is viviparous, therefore it is a mammal.” The conclusion is correct, but it would not cease to be true if I set out from false premises, saying: “birds are mammals; the bat is a bird; therefore it is a mammal.” All the parts of formal logic are therefore pervaded by the theory of the extension and comprehension of notions.

p. 208

The scientific forms of knowledge depend upon it in their turn. One of these forms consists precisely in determining the extension of a notion or of an object, the other in determining its comprehension. The first is division; the second, definition. To divide an object is to set forth its parts or its species; to define it is to set forth its properties. Definition and division give to our knowledge its highest value, and afterwards render demonstration possible. A science whose object is suitably defined and divided is almost made. But definition is exposed to some difficulties. An object may have innumerable properties which it seems impossible to unite in a simple and complete definition. The horse, for example, is at once a solid-hoofed animal, a pachyderm, a mammal, a vertebrate, an animal, an organized being, a being, and it possesses all the qualities inherent in these various classes of objects. The laws of the subordination of notions facilitate the accomplishment [p. 208] of the task and relieve the memory of useless terms. Indeed, superior notions are contained in inferior notions from the point of view of comprehension, which serves as the basis of definition. The properties of being are also the properties of organized being, vegetable or animal; the properties of the animal are included in those of the vertebrate, and so on. The mammal is a vertebrate, the vertebrate is an animal, the animal is an organized being. It is therefore superfluous to recall the qualities of the remoter genera, when we know the qualities of the proximate genus. Hence the formula of the logicians: “fiat definitio per genus proximum et differentiam ultimam.” The indication of the proximate genus sums up all the properties of the higher genera; it suffices to add to it the last difference, in order to distinguish the object to be defined from the other species enveloped in the same genus.

In the moral and political sciences, extension and comprehension are obtained by deduction as in mathematics; but in the sciences of observation, we must have recourse to generalization. A laborious and persevering analysis is needed to discover, if it is possible, all the properties and all the species of a genus, with a view to defining and dividing it. How many species Aristotle lacked! How many others still escape, in all probability, the investigations of modern scholars! No matter, we advance, guided now by induction, now by analogy; but as the collections grow richer, we are obliged to return upon the definitions and divisions consecrated by usage or by authority.

p. 209

Generalization is often confounded with induction. Mr. Mill himself, who has made so learned and so complete a study of induction, considers it, as Aristotle does, as the sole mode of generalization. All non-intuitive knowledge, he says, comes exclusively from induction, and induction is the operation by which we discover and prove general propositions; in other words, it is the procedure by virtue of which we conclude that what is true of certain individuals of a class is true of the whole class, or that what is true at some time will be true [p. 209] at all times, provided that the circumstances are similar (1). This definition is too wide and suits generalization rather than induction. Hence the author no longer succeeds in grasping the proper value of analogy. Analogy, he says, designates an inductive argument, but an incomplete one; if the argument were complete, it would be a true induction (2). Mr. Mill did not see that the theory of extension and comprehension permits introducing into the procedure of generalization a well-marked division which corresponds exactly to analogy and to induction properly so called. Generalization, in fact, has for its aim, relying on experience, to determine scientifically the notions of species and genus, from the double point of view of their extension and their comprehension. It always concludes from some cases to all possible cases; if there were nothing more in the conclusion than in the premises, there would be no generalization; it would be a simple enumeration of parts, a sum which would give no new result. But there are two ways of passing from the particular to the general, according as one starts from extension or from comprehension, according as one ends, in other words, in a definition or in a division. Experimental definitions are the product of induction; divisions, the product of analogy. The sciences of observation do not demonstrate, but show the facts that fall within their province; all their labor is concentrated on definitions and divisions, on the formation of precise and adequate notions. It is therefore important to distinguish carefully, in the procedure of generalization inherent in these sorts of sciences, what relates to extension and what concerns comprehension.

p. 210

Induction rests on extension, on the parts or species of a whole; it rises from the particular to the general, as Aristotle affirms, by concluding from some species or from the species actually known to all possible species, that is to say to the genus. The genus is only the whole [p. 210] of the qualities common to all the species. The definition of the genus is therefore found when we possess all the species that it comprises. This is why induction, reasoning from some species to all the species, furnishes, in the last analysis, a definition of the genus. Here are examples: “the fishes observed up to now are oviparous and breathe by gills; therefore all fishes have the same qualities, and fish in general may be defined as an oviparous vertebrate that breathes by gills.” “The Earth, Mars, Venus have a double motion of rotation on themselves and of revolution about a center; therefore all the planets have a double motion, and this quality must enter into the definition of the planet in general, whether subject to observation or not.”

(1) J. S. Mill, A System of Logic, book III, ch. I and II.

(2) Ibid., book III, ch. XX.

p. 211

Analogy rests on comprehension, on the consideration of the qualities of objects; it generalizes by concluding from the resemblance which a new species presents in some respects with known species, to a complete similarity in other respects not yet observed (1). The new species is then ranged under the same genus as the species to which it is comparable in certain respects; in other words, we extend the notion of the genus, we obtain a more complete division. An example will make this point understood: “The planet Mars resembles the Earth in its origin, in its physical and climatological constitution; therefore it has also, like the earth, the property of bearing living beings, which extends the signification of worlds or stars that are inhabited.” “There are in Nature organized bodies which are composed of the same elements as our own body; therefore these foreign bodies are likewise united, like ours, to a rational soul, which constitutes the human genus.” We reason again by analogy when we compare a work of art, a picture, a statue, a vase, a medal, with the works of known masters or of celebrated schools, and range it in a class determined [p. 211] by some characters more or less important, none of which, however, is recognized as decisive. It is by an application of the same method that we often decide in natural history on the rank of doubtful species, which have some traits of different genera.

We see that there exists a notable difference between analogy and induction, as fundamental forms of the procedure of generalization. Analogy is not an incomplete induction, but one of the two means offered by the experimental method for determining the abstract notions of species and genus, and this means is as legitimate as the other. A new application of the theory of extension and comprehension to the method in use in the sciences (1). It remains to know what is the value of the knowledge that we obtain by observation and generalization.

(1) Kant, Logik, Elementarlehre, § 84. — Bachmann, System der Logik, Th. II, Abschn. 2, § 236.

p. 212

Pure observation gives the sensible notions, the facts, the phenomena; generalization adds to them the abstract notions of species and genus. We know that our sensible knowledge may be legitimate, barring illusion, under the condition of the legitimacy of the rational elements on which it depends. A fact is a fact, it is said, and we must admit it, if it is ascertained, unless nothing is true. But species, the universals, as they said in another age, do not seem to be facts, and it is still doubtful whether they have an objective existence. Certainly, abstract knowledge no longer has the same guarantees as sensible knowledge; it is, as to its origin, a product of our faculty of abstraction, a creation of the understanding, and there is perhaps nothing outside that corresponds to our conceptions. The question is worth examining, although its importance should not be exaggerated. If there existed in the world neither genera nor species, scientific classifications would still be indispensable to the human mind; they would no longer be the [p. 212] system of nature, but a system of subjective notions destined to bring order into our representations.

Abstract knowledge arises naturally in us, as a spontaneous fruit of the human intelligence, and soon forms a considerable part of the notions found in the common consciousness, before any scientific culture. The knowledge that the child and the young man acquire successively of minerals, of plants and animals, of life and of social institutions, of virtues and vices, of the arts, of commerce and industry, comes from abstraction and is expressed in all languages by common nouns. Lexicons are for the most part catalogues of abstract notions. When one looks in them for the meaning of a word, “palace, college, power, ambition, sculpture,” one finds a general sense that suits all the objects of a certain category, and not the description of this or that particular object; the definition itself requires, to be understood, some force of abstraction. Many authors since Locke have seen this connection between notions and words, between intelligence and signs; some even, exaggerating the influence of signs on thought, have placed the origin of knowledge in sounds and reduced science to being only “a well-made language.” It is certain that the wealth of a language contributes to the development of individual intelligence, since it is the résumé of the efforts of preceding generations; but far from being the source of thought, it is its result. It is the sciences that make languages, and when the common language does not suffice for the needs of a particular science on the road to progress, the scholars create a special language which lends itself better to the course and the abundance of their minds. Mathematics, chemistry, botany have this advantage. Philosophy is often a dispute about words, because it must use common terms and torture them in every sense to make them express new ideas.

(1) E. Tandel, Cours de logique, § 57-64. Liège, 1844.

p. 213

It is probable that animals have no abstract notions or general notions, that is to say that they are [p. 213] deprived of all non-sensible knowledge and that their very perceptions have not the scientific character that ours possess. The abstract knowledge of species and genera is a first line of demarcation between man and the brute. The system of Locke represents perfectly this degree of human knowledge: there is in it, in fact, a double source, the materials furnished by the senses and the generalizing labor of the understanding. Locke’s only fault was to apply to rational notions what suits only abstract notions. His successors of the sensualist school fell lower: they wanted to explain abstract notions by the sole activity of the senses, as if sight or hearing had ever revealed to them the existence of a species. De Bonald puts forward in this regard a hypothesis more plausible in appearance and which tends to the same end, to lower the condition of man. He is willing to recognize in the child as in the animal the capacity necessary to form sensible notions, but he claims that abstract and general notions enter the human mind only by means of words, thanks to language established in society and created by God. It is therefore speech which not only fertilizes thought, but produces it; it is speech which is the cause of the faculty of abstracting and generalizing. And as language addresses itself to our senses, it is our senses once more which are the source of our non-sensible knowledge. Consequently, it will suffice to hear a language to understand it, and conversely the unfortunates who, for lack of a sense, remain isolated in the bosom of society will be deprived of all abstract knowledge. It is needless to say that this pseudo-sensualism, decorated with the name of traditionalism, is belied by the facts as well as by the data of psychology. Impartial observations have established that deaf-mutes from birth possess abstract notions and that they express them in their figurative language. The very signs they use designate only species, unless a special indication is added to them which can point out or characterize this or that individual, like our determinative adjectives. The most indeterminate

p. 214

Logic. — I. 14 [p. 214] genera, such as “animal, plant, thing,” are the only ones that lend themselves with difficulty to a representation by gestures. It is rather proper names than common nouns that are wanting in gestural language, a sort of sketch in which the principal features are outlined and where the details are lacking (1).

Generalization is therefore natural to the human mind. Children generalize as they observe and content themselves with applying to their conceptions the names consecrated in their language. Scholars generalize ceaselessly, and for want of words they invent them. Generalization, like all the faculties of the soul, develops and is perfected by training and by study. Science corrects abstract knowledge as observation extends. Thus it is that in natural history the ancient classifications have been successively improved and transformed. Between Aristotle and Cuvier there is an abyss, dug by the explorations of modern times. But now there reappears the question that I put a moment ago: is our abstract knowledge, acquired by the continuous labors of the scholars of all epochs, definitive? Has it a certain value, and does it correspond to real objects? People of the world do not seem to trouble themselves about this problem. They speak “of a table, of several tables and of the table,” “of their dog, of the neighbors’ dogs and of the dog,” and while grasping the difference that is found between these expressions, they do not ask whether the notion they have of the table and of the dog in general is exact, complete, nor whether there exist objects of this kind in reality.

p. 215

The value of abstract notions properly so called depends on the value of the two procedures of generalization in which they take their source. These procedures themselves rest on higher principles, without which they would be absolutely ineffective, and which nevertheless do not result from observation [p. 215] What is the good of generalizing, if there were nothing fixed, constant, regular in the life of nature, if phenomena followed phenomena without order and without connection, confounding physics with chemistry, bringing about effects of light instead of a mechanical action, if species in their turn succeeded species without generation, at random, so as to disturb ceaselessly the characters of classes, if the future were not to resemble the present and the past in the same circumstances, in a word, if there existed no law, no necessary element in the world? No more analogy, if all is confused; no more induction, if nothing lasts.

(1) P. Kersten, Essai sur l’activité du principe pensant considéré dans l’institution du langage, vol. III. Liège, 1863. — Abbé Carton, Philosophie de l’enseignement maternel. Bruges, 1862.

p. 216

Royer-Collard has perfectly expressed this truth: “The principle of induction rests on two judgments. The universe is governed by stable laws, that is the first. The universe is governed by general laws, that is the second. It follows from the first that, known at a single point of duration, the laws of nature are known in all; it follows from the second that, known in a single case, they are known in all perfectly similar cases. Thus induction gives us at once the future and analogy. Its proper character is to conclude from the particular to the general, and thereby it is diametrically opposed to deduction or pure reasoning, which always concludes from the general to the particular (1).” All authors have recognized these two conditions of the procedure of generalization: no experience, no analogy nor induction, if nature is not governed by permanent and uniform laws. Only the two judgments reduce to one, as has been remarked, since every law implies stability and generality. We must therefore say: no observation nor generalization, if the world is without laws. But what has not been recognized, and what however has been pointed out also by Royer-Collard, is that the existence of the laws of the universe is not a fact of observation and that it is in consequence a pure hypothesis in the sciences [p. 216] experimental sciences. “Who taught us this fact? Our own nature, and not experience. Experience belongs to the past and is shut up within the limits of observation. So little is it the source of the principle of induction that the latter acts with much more force at the age when experience is weakest.” The philosopher speaks truly: it is to our mind, it is to reason, that we owe the belief in the uniformity of the course of nature. This belief bears upon the future as upon the present, it embraces all events, ascertained or not, and is expressed in a universal and apodictic judgment which, as Kant assures us, passes beyond all the bounds of possible observation. Mr. Mill is therefore in error when, after declaring that the uniform course of nature is the fundamental principle or general axiom of induction, he presents it as an example of that procedure and wishes to make it the major premise of all inductive reasoning. If it were so, the conclusion of this reasoning would become a particular case contained in the premises, like the consequence of a syllogism, and generalization would no longer be generalization, but deduction (1).

Our abstract knowledge, founded on generalization, is therefore exposed to doubt even more than our sensible knowledge; it has only a hypothetical character, so long as the laws of induction and of analogy are not confirmed by metaphysics. What could we answer, in fact, to the skeptic who affirms that the world has no laws and feels no need of any? That if everything were linked and chained together without, everything would be necessitated within us also, and that if we must choose between determinism and casualism, it is better for us to reject necessity and proclaim universal contingency? It is a long way, besides, from several series of phenomena observed for some years on one corner of our globe, if observation itself deserves any credit, to an absolute law that would govern the world in infinite time and space.

(1) Royer-Collard, Fragments philosophiques, in the translation of the Œuvres de Reid.

(1) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, vol. I, Ground of induction.

p. 217

How can scientists, ordinarily so circumspect and so exclusive in the matter of speculation, thus suddenly leave the earth, renounce experience, and accept as the basis of their reasonings philosophical propositions that stand in revolt against all the habits of their minds?—It must be admitted, skepticism triumphs: observation is already open to suspicion, since it must have recourse to non-sensible elements; but even supposing it legitimate, it still gives no certain guarantee for the existence of the laws of the world. Laws and categories are objects of rational knowledge.

Induction and analogy can do nothing without reason. Are they any more valid in themselves, if we grant that all phenomena are and always will be subject to the same laws? Everything then depends on the number of facts observed and on the faithful execution of the rules of inductive reasoning. No one will dispute the astonishing progress that the sciences of observation have achieved within the last half-century. This progress was foreseen by Bacon; it is due to the experimental method, and it explains the preeminence that investigators arrogate to themselves over philosophers. But success often blinds. Do not the very variations of scientific classifications indicate the precarious character of abstract notions? Every day a new species is discovered on one continent or another. What does this mean? That the division of the genus is to be completed and the definition to be modified; for the new species, once the genus is known, necessarily differs by some properties from the other species described, and we know that the genus has for its limit the qualities common to its species. Hence one would hardly find two identical definitions in the innumerable treatises of botany or zoology that are given to the public. Yet it is on this side that the claim to exact and positive notions reigns, and it is from here that the accusation of vanity and inconstancy now brought against philosophy comes. Is there at least some hope of seeing an end to this provisional state, of arriving at last at notions that are no longer variable? Alas! can one ever be sure of having observed everything?

p. 218

When we come to know the riches of the countries and seas as yet unexplored, shall we not have to take account of the modifications and new creations that the future perhaps holds in store for us? Has the globe we inhabit definitively completed its evolution, and is the history of the faunas and floras of the earth that paleontology relates definitively closed? Very rash would be he who dared to affirm it. Finally, if man could ever know all the phenomena, all the species, all the combinations that the spectacle of nature presents on our modest sphere, generalization would have completed its task and would be transformed into a simple enumeration of parts. There would no longer be matter for induction and for analogy, if there were no longer any unknown to be disengaged, so that abstract notions would become unalterable at the very moment when they ceased to be generalized in order to be merely collective.

p. 219

In fact, induction and analogy as such, as methods of generalization, give, whatever may be said, only probable results, not certain ones. To be convinced of this, it suffices to consider their nature and their course. They go from the particular to the general, from the less to the more, from the part to the whole, and it is solely in this respect that they differ from deduction and the syllogism. Induction is inventive, that is its merit; but it is not demonstrative, that is its defect. Invention and demonstration are not companions: the one belongs to the inductive method, the other to the deductive method. Demonstration requires an argument more general than the thesis, or premises more extensive than the conclusion; invention, on the contrary, implies a conclusion that passes beyond the premises. That is precisely what happens in generalization, where we conclude from some cases to all cases. Bacon was right to deplore the sterility of the syllogism for investigation and to extol the fecundity of induction; but he ought to have added, as a corrective, that the syllogism demonstrates, whereas induction gives only hypotheses, presumptions, says Kant, probabilities greater or less in proportion to the number of [p. 219] experiments. Scientists ought to suspect as much when they recommend with such insistence the multiplication of observations.

p. 220

Let us take up again the examples of induction and analogy cited above. From the fact that the fishes observed up to now are oviparous and breathe by gills, it is concluded that these qualities are common to all possible fishes and belong to the definition of the genus. This is certainly one of the surest inductions that can be made. The conclusion has a high degree of probability, but it lacks the rigor of a demonstration. We do not yet know all the species of fishes, and so long as we do not possess the table of their common properties, every definition is premature. No matter, it will be said! If we meet with an animal that is oviparous without having gills, or that has gills without being oviparous, it is understood that it is not a fish. The thing is not so easy: in the presence of the bizarre products of New Holland, the most experienced naturalists hesitate and propose new classifications. Let us not hasten, then, to decide in what genus the species that will be discovered hereafter will come to be ranged: nature has not delivered up all her secrets to us. — In the second place, from the fact that a certain number of planets of our solar system have a double motion of rotation and of translation, it is concluded that this motion belongs to all possible planets and characterizes them. Certainly induction has rendered immense services to astronomy, since the labors of Kepler and Galileo. It is probable that its results are exact as regards the motion of the heavenly bodies. But after all, not all the planets of our system, including the microscopic planets whose number still increases every year, have been subjected to observation; otherwise there would no longer be induction, but enumeration of cases. How then can we know with certainty that all planetary bodies move exactly like our globe? There exist apparently other planets outside our system; do they obey the same law of the double motion? Since we have [p. 220] recognized double and multiple stars, it has been suspected that there are very diverse combinations in the grouping and in the revolutions of the heavenly bodies; are the same principles of mechanics always applicable to all cases in the immensity of space? It is permissible to doubt it.

p. 221

Let us pass to analogy. The planet Mars is counted among the inhabited heavenly bodies, because it has the same origin as the earth, the same constitution of solid, liquid, and gaseous elements, the same division of the year into seasons and of the zones into climates. Very well; I omit the differences resulting from temperature and from weight; the resemblances suffice to carry conviction to an unprejudiced mind. But what shall we answer to those who distrust reason, who, obliged to choose between the teachings of religion and those of science, sacrifice science to faith without hesitation? If Mars is inhabited, all the planets may or must be so, and the problem of the future destinies of man receives an unexpected solution. It is not without reason that Galileo was condemned as a heretic. If the theological system of revelation is true, the astronomical system of Copernicus is false in itself and in all its consequences. The believer will therefore invoke contrary or negative analogies to prove that Mars cannot be inhabited, and his affirmation will be as valid as that of the scientist, so long as the question of the preeminence of faith or of reason is not resolved. It is not on Mars, but on the Earth that God created man; it is not on Mars, but on the Earth that the fall and the redemption were accomplished; it is not on Mars, but on the Earth that the Christian religion and all its mysteries were instituted. Of what moment, after that, are the analogies pointed out by the astronomers? What we know of the heavenly bodies is very little beside what we do not know of them. And finally, if Mars is habitable, nothing proves that it is inhabited! To this last argument there is nothing to answer, in sound logic: analogy establishes the possibility, but not the reality, of the existence of man on the celestial globes; its conclusion must be admitted as probable by those who [p. 221] admit the legitimacy of science, but certainty must flow from other principles given by deduction.

Is there any need now to insist further on the hypothetical character of the conclusions furnished by analogy in other matters, in the discussion of works of art or of nature? Who does not know the endless disputes that arise between connoisseurs and critics over the origin of an unsigned canvas or of a vase in which styles fade or blend? Who is unaware of the divergences of nomenclature in zoology, in botany, in mineralogy, where synonymy has become an important branch of science? All these considerations agree with the very nature of the analogical or inductive procedure, which is formulated in a reasoning whose conclusion is more extensive than the premises.

Abstract or generalized notions, as such, are therefore provisional, not definitive: they are hypotheses to be verified, which have their importance and their necessity in the sciences of observation, which may become certain by the accumulation of facts, but which after all are hypotheses, true or false, and science is not made so long as it depends on hypothetical propositions. Let us now examine whether species and genera really exist, whether abstract notions, in other words, have objective validity. This is the question of nominalism and realism, which occupied men’s minds throughout the Middle Ages.

p. 222

No distinction was made then between generalized notions, drawn from observation, and general notions, given by reason: the universalia, whose mode of existence in us or in nature was discussed, included the moral ideas of goodness and justice as well as the conceptions of the understanding formed by abstraction. The realists, continuing the tradition of Plato and of the Fathers of the Church, convinced that God created all things on the model of the ideas and that these ideas in consequence subsist in the divine intelligence before the creation and are found again in the human intelligence, made in the image of God, expressed [p. 222] their doctrine in these terms: Universalia sunt ante rem; ideas are independent of phenomena, species precede individuals. The nominalists, on the contrary, following the inspiration of Aristotle, wrongly interpreted and confused with Zeno the Stoic, persuaded that all knowledge derives from the senses and that general conceptions are only abstractions of the mind, beings of reason without foundation in reality, words invented for our personal convenience, said: Universalia sunt post rem; phenomena precede ideas, individuals are anterior to species, in fact only individuals exist, species have only an imaginary existence (1). The nominalists stopped at sensible observation: they went backward as regards doctrine, but they innovated as regards method, they placed themselves in opposition to the official theology and laid the first foundation of the emancipation of thought. Applying their dialectical formula to dogmas, they maintained that the distinction of persons in God was nominal rather than real. The realists admitted the substantial existence of species; above men they saw humanity, above the parts the whole, and they were able to reduce to unity all the variety of finite things. But, deprived of the aid of experience, they proceeded without criticism and granted an objective reality to all the conceptions of the understanding.

p. 223

These long debates of the Middle Ages are at bottom the old quarrel of rationalism and sensualism. Locke approves the nominalists: “General and universal belong not to the real existence of things; but are the inventions and creatures of the understanding, made by it for its own use, and concern only signs.” M. Cousin criticizes Locke and distributes both blame and praise to nominalists and realists: there are general ideas, such as the idea of a book, which are only names, but there are others, such as the idea of space and of time, [p. 223] which correspond to an external reality; the book in itself is an abstraction, but space and time exist in themselves. Mr. Mill is more precise and answers the question directly, without confounding the abstract notions of species and genus with the general ideas of reason. Classification is without limits, he says; we can form as many classes as we wish, taking at random a general term as the principle of division: all objects, for example, are white or not white, as all animals are vertebrate or invertebrate. But one of these two kinds of classes answers more than the other to a radical distinction in things: vertebrates have an indeterminate number of common and irreducible properties, which thought cannot exhaust, whereas white bodies have no other common property than whiteness. The first notion is a species, or a genus if it contains other analogous classes endowed with a set of common qualities; the second is not a species. According to this, the term man is a species; but the terms Christian, Englishman, mathematician, hunchback are not species; for, although they embrace a great number of individuals, they confer on them no physical or moral character, beyond their qualification, that can distinguish them from other men. Species does not have the same value in logic as in natural history; in the latter the characteristic mark is unity of descent; in the former no regard is had to origin and only the common properties are considered, so that races and sexes, which are not species for scientists, might constitute species for the logician. The specific distinction, finally, is made by nature, whereas the arbitrary division of objects according to color, position, density is made by us, for our personal convenience. Species have a real existence in nature (1).

(1) H. O. Kœhler, Realismus und Nominalismus. Gotha, 1858.

p. 224

These rules are excellent and bear the stamp of good [p. 224] sense. They signify that there exist between objects, now essential distinctions, now accidental distinctions, according to the terminology of Aristotle; that the former belong to species, the latter to our fancies; and that species are thus founded in the very nature of things. The limit is useful: a nominalist of the Middle Ages, Occam, reproached his adversaries with multiplying beings without necessity. Abuse is prevented by announcing that species alone, true species, have a right to existence. Species exist; but what are they? Not beings apart from individuals, but indications of the course of nature in the production of her works. The earth has its history, and its development, if there are laws, is no more capricious from the biological point of view than from the physical or chemical. Paleontology and even teratology are not at variance with the idea of the necessary, continuous, ineluctable chain that presides over all the transformations of matter. Now as soon as the course of nature is regular, it can be understood and determined by rational beings, in its organic evolution as well as in its mechanical movements, and this is what our attempts at classification denote. We spell out the book of nature that God offers to the meditations of man. The notions of species and genus, the result of a long series of observations, have for their aim to reproduce in science what exists without, that is to say, the labor of nature, the poem of creation. Not all these notions have objective validity, because we often deceive ourselves about the intentions that we gratuitously attribute to nature; we give birth to chimerical species, for want of penetrating the essence of beings or of grasping the whole amid the profusion of details; but we may nourish the hope of one day disentangling more clearly the organization of the physical world, since we are beginning to know the organization of the mind, the elementary laws of the universe, and the structure of the heavenly bodies. We may at least hold it as certain, while reserving the question of the legitimacy of thought in general, that those of our [p. 225] abstract cognitions that are true notions of species or genus, whether complete or partial, have in the same measure as much objective validity as our individual representations. It remains only to know which are the true notions of species and genus, and it is here that I believe observation to be at once indispensable and insufficient in itself. It is already a metaphysical conception, and not a judgment of pure experience, to affirm the immutability and the necessity of the laws of the world.

(1) Kinds have a real existence in nature. Book I, ch. vii, § 4.

p. 226

The same result is reached by another course, though always relying on certain synthetic views that pass beyond the limits of observation. Every being has for its aim to realize its essence, that is to say, to manifest successively all that is possible for it. What is realized in the sphere of mind or of nature was first possible, and nothing impossible can ever be realized. If this is true in general, while taking account of the conflicts that may arise between finite beings, it is equally true that the earth, as part of the world, must realize what is possible for it at each instant and in each period of its development. This proposition applies to the possible combinations among organs for the manifestation of life, as well as to the possible combinations among inorganic elements. The earth, in a word, must exhaust her possibilities, from every point of view, and realize them, as soon as the conditions of their realization are posited. Geology confirms this principle, in establishing that the earth produced living beings as soon as she possessed the external conditions of life, by the formation and temperature of the soil, by the composition of the atmosphere and the emission of light, and that the first creation, buried in the Silurian strata of the transition epoch, disappeared as soon as the conditions of life were modified by the revolutions of the globe. Other faunas and other floras appeared, more perfect than the first, in proportion as life could maintain itself under better conditions. They belong to the secondary and tertiary [p. 226] epochs. Man was born last, because his development requires more numerous conditions. What does this mean? That the earth has always effected what was possible for her in each situation, and that even today she bears in her bosom precisely the beings that are viable. These are the species and genera that exist in our day. In fact, the present species represent the combinations at present possible among the various organs that concur in the maintenance of vegetable and animal life on the earth, and it is probable that if there exist other combinations that are not realized on our globe, it is because they are not possible or realizable in the present state of this globe. In the future as in the past, as soon as they become realizable, they will be realized. The same law is verified, for each particular system of the organism, in comparative anatomy and physiology, as Burdach, among others, has demonstrated, by laying down precisely the same principle. “Reality appears to us as an exhaustion of possibility; nature is the realization of what can be conceived; our imagination and the variety of real existence correspond to each other (1).” Now the possibilities of the earth are objective, or independent of the human mind. If the totality of terrestrial species is equivalent to the totality of possible combinations among organs on the earth, species have therefore also an objective existence, outside our thought, and from then on the problem of the knowledge of species can be attacked from another side: it is a question, given all the organs indispensable to the manifestation of life on the earth, of determining a priori the possible combinations among these organs, as in geometry we inquire, given the idea of a curved line, what are the possible forms of this kind of lines. But then we obtain in natural history, as in geometry, general notions, and it becomes easy to verify whether these notions, deduced from a higher principle [p. 227] agree or not with the generalized notions, induced from observation.

(1) Burdach, Traité de physiologie, trans. by Jourdan, vol. I, sect. III. Paris, 1837.

p. 228

The abstract notions of species and genus are capable of acquiring objective validity, because there exist species and genera in nature; they have objective validity when they are exact, and must be recognized as exact when they conform to the general notions obtained by way of deduction. Such is the result of our study thus far. Every notion of species, provided it be a notion of species, has a real value, the more important the more fundamental and complete the notion is, under the general conditions of the legitimacy of our knowledge. Do we not see now that this conclusion is in perfect harmony with the researches instituted in modern times on the natural classification of animals and plants? A natural classification implies real species, a division marked by nature, outside our thought, in a word a natural system of species and genera. It is this natural system of species, identical with the system of possibilities in the combination of organs, that natural classification claims to reproduce in botany and zoology. A natural division of the vegetable or animal kingdom supposes the fixity of species; it rests on the whole of the organs, on organography, and must have the effect of distributing beings into families, in conformity with analogy, according to the general characters of their constitution. It will then be easy, in most cases, provided one is familiar with the elements of the science, to see at first glance, from the habit of a plant or the form of an animal, in what family or in what branch it should be ranged. Such, without contradiction, are the advantages of the botanical system of Jussieu, which will remain the basis of all later labors, whatever improvements may still be brought to the science. Plants can doubtless be divided according to the number of the stamens or the form of the leaves, but these are artificial classifications, founded on a single organ and leading to absurd groupings; we obtain [p. 228] thus collections of plants, not natural families, in which should be united individuals endowed with an indeterminate number of common properties. I hold that the zoological system of Cuvier, though more criticized, has the same merit in its kind as that of Jussieu, because it has the same breadth of base. Here again it would be easy to divide animals according to size, color, blood, according to the number of limbs or the medium inhabited; but these divisions, once more, would be a caricature rather than an imitation of nature, and would resemble a catalogue of books classed according to format or a bazaar of objects of the same price or the same shade; it is on comparative anatomy that we must rely to constitute the natural families of the animal kingdom. The classification of Cuvier, moreover, considered in its main outlines, has received a striking confirmation through the substitution of the rational method for the experimental. Several attempts at division have been made from synthetic views, indicated above. The most important is that of Carus, who starts from the principle of possibility, applied to the idea of animal organization, and deduces from it, by the sole power of reasoning, the principal genera of animality. Now deduction agrees generally with the induction of Cuvier.

p. 229

Nature, says Carus, contains an infinite multiplicity of beings. To know the elements of this variety, or the existing species, we must attach ourselves to the possible forms of animal organization and see in each class of living beings the permanent realization of a possible form of the organism. The simplest form of the life of animals has its type in the egg, where the fundamental systems of the nerves and of the blood, that is to say, of animal life and of vegetative life, are not yet clearly separated. The animals that correspond to this moment of the development of life are oozoa: the infusoria, the radiata, the zoophytes. Starting from this branch, the different systems of the organization divide and become centralized in particular organs, under the predominance now of vegetative life over animal life, now of animal life over [p. 229] vegetative life. To the first degree, characterized by the predominance of the organs of the trunk over those of the head, belong the animals that reproduce the type of vegetative life; these are corpozoa, the invertebrates. But in the trunk itself a new opposition manifests itself, the contrast of the abdomen and the chest, of the systems of nutrition and generation, on the one hand, and of circulation and respiration, on the other. The animals that stop at the first degree are gastrozoa: the mollusks; those that rise to the second are thoracozoa: the articulata, the insects. Then comes the third branch of the animal kingdom, in which the life of relation, the nerves, the muscles, and the bones, in its turn prevails over the life of the internal organs destined for the elaboration of the blood; these are cephalozoa: the vertebrates. But in this higher division all the characteristic elements of the lower divisions must return, raised now to a higher power, transported into the circle of the life of relation. There are animals with a head or with vertebrae that bring back the primitive type of the egg: the fishes; others that repeat the type of the organs of the abdomen or of the chest: the reptiles and the birds; others, finally, that present a complete development of the head and that best represent the last branch: the mammals (1).

It will be seen that the agreement between the two classifications is perfect, although they are taken from two completely distinct and even opposite points of view, although the one starts from reality, the other from possibility, and the first proceeds by generalization, the second by deduction. Only the four branches of Cuvier, the four plans, the four types of animal organization, are reduced to three according to Carus, because the mollusks and the articulata, however contrasting they may be, constitute only two different degrees of the development of vegetative life. Unity, variety, harmony, such are the three

p. 230

Logic. — I. 15 [p. 230] fundamental ideas imprinted by nature in the three circles of animality. But harmony is still incomplete in the circle of the vertebrates, because it is realized there by infinitely manifold combinations, and always under the predominance of one organ or one system. Full and entire harmony is one. Hence a new possibility, the idea of a pan-harmonic organization, in which all the organs of vegetative life and of animal life arrive at a complete expansion and manifest themselves in a perfect equilibrium. This idea is realized in human nature and marks the position of man in creation, outside and above all the spheres of the animal kingdom. Here again is a difference between Carus and Cuvier and an important result of the philosophy of nature in Germany.

The modern ideas on the natural classification of living beings are a rehabilitation, almost a transfiguration, of scholastic realism. They give this doctrine an unhoped-for value and at the same time trace its limits. Generalization applies to finite beings, comparable among themselves, but does not succeed in the infinite. Each infinite is alone and unique in its kind and has no species. There is only one time that embraces all times, one space that embraces all spaces; particular periods and determinate spaces are not species, but homogeneous parts of space and of time, which contain other parts divisible without end. The continuity that some zoologists seek in the animal scale reigns here without division and absolutely prevents any distribution into species and genera. It is certainly permissible to speak of the genus nature or the genus mind, as we speak of the human genus, but these genera indicate simply a certain determination of reality, from the point of view of substance, not a set of species. Hence the terms extension and comprehension, so precise in the sciences of observation, now have only a vague signification in the domain of supra-sensible things.

(1) Carus, Anatomie comparée, trans. by Jourdan. — Ahrens, Cours de psychologie, vol. I, Paris, 1836.

p. 231

Infinite space contains all particular spaces in its extension, but it has no less comprehension [p. 231] than they, and its properties are by no means the common qualities of all the places observed. On one side are the infinite, the absolute, unity, necessity; on the other, the finite, the relative, the manifold, contingency; each determinate space has its limits, its form, its quantity, whereas infinite space is without bounds, without measure, and without number. There is no transition, no degrees that lead insensibly from a bounded place to infinite space, as if the latter were the sum or the product of any number of myriameters. Infinite space is incommensurable and is equal only to itself, that is to say, to an infinity of particular spaces, however great they may be supposed. It is the same with finite beings in the presence of infinite being, or of God.

p. 232

It is not, then, by a successive generalization that thought must ascend from the beings of the world to the cause of all that is, but by a direct intuition of the infinite. Between beings and Being, between the world and God, there is an abyss that reason alone can cross and that it must fill by an immediate vision of God. It is an abuse of abstract logic to employ the procedure of abstraction with regard to divine things. This was often done in the Middle Ages, as in the schools of Alexandria; but since generalization advances by way of the elimination of properties, instead of arriving at the notion of God as the Being of all reality, men came to conceive God as a mere form stripped of all content. God then becomes the supreme genus, whose extension is infinite and whose comprehension is nil. He is no longer real being, but abstract being, identical with nothing, according to Hegel. Divina substantia, says the School, est forma sine materia. Abstract from all matter, from all content, from all that lives or thinks in the world, endeavor to grasp the pure form, the pure idea, as Aristotle would say, and you will understand God. The Father of the world of whom Plato dreamed, the living God of St. Paul, in whom and by whom all things exist, is no longer anything but the most abstract of abstractions: such is the result of the ordinary procedure of induction transported into the infinite. It was time for Descartes to appear and arrest this current of atheism [p. 232] that was invading dialectic and undermining the foundations of all religion.

p. 233

M. l’abbé Gratry is therefore very ill inspired (for science is for him a matter of fancy) when he speaks of a new induction, of true induction, identical with the dialectical procedure of Plato, with the infinitesimal procedure of the geometers, which passes from the finite to the infinite, from the effect to the cause, and which demonstrates the existence of God with all the rigor of mathematical demonstrations (1). That there exists a procedure of transcendence is not doubtful, if by that is understood the method by which we rise from the world to God; but that this procedure is inductive and demonstrative is false and contradictory. From the finite to the infinite there is no induction, but intuition; from the relative to the absolute there is no demonstration, but hypothesis for some, immediate certainty for others, according to the state of consciousness. M. Gratry sees only induction and deduction, reasonings by transcendence and by identity, as possible movements of thought, and then calls induction everything that is not deduction or syllogism. The definition is too broad. Induction is not the whole of analysis, but forms part of it. Analysis embraces all our intuitive knowledge, obtained by the senses, by generalization, or by reason. The first constitute observation; the second, induction and analogy; the last, contemplation. Platonic dialectic is of the third kind. It is not by induction or by abstraction that Plato, on the occasion of sensible phenomena, grasps the idea or the essence, but, as he expressly declares, by a direct or immediate intuition of the divine. Malebranche explains this act of the mind by the idea of the infinite that is present to the intellect. It is in the same manner that geometers and scientists see the limit, the law, the cause in a series of terms or effects. Hence they do not give their results as demonstrated, when they are conscious of the course that they follow [p. 233] they are hypotheses to be verified, or truths self-evident in themselves that require no logical proof. Any proposition that is not deduced or demonstrated by synthesis leaves doubts remaining in the minds of those who are not sufficiently prepared to receive it. Certainty is individual. Thus Newton’s attraction, the fundamental principle of celestial mechanics, still passes for an hypothesis in the eyes of a great number of scientists who pride themselves on scientific rigor. The very principles of the infinitesimal analysis are not admitted without protest by mathematicians. It would be otherwise if intuition had the value of a demonstration. Intuition does not demonstrate, it shows, as Kepler said of his method. No one has ever protested against the theorems of geometry. The reason is that the geometrical method is something altogether different from induction. To indicate in anticipation how it applies to philosophy, I have only to refer to the Ethics of Spinoza.

CHAPTER THREE

R AT I O N A L K N O W L E D G E

Logical Dialectic.

(1) A. Gratry, Logique. 2nd ed. Paris, 1858.

p. 234

Sensible knowledge proceeds directly from observation and yields facts or phenomena that anyone can verify. Abstract knowledge, starting from known facts, goes beyond present observation, but remains within the limits of possible observation; it yields species, genera, classes, which reduce experience to a system, and which, introduced at first in a hypothetical form, await the test of deduction in order to be finally accepted by science. Abstract cognitions are of a higher order than [p. 234] sensible cognitions; their object no longer falls under the senses and can be grasped only by abstraction and generalization; but both are experimental, a posteriori cognitions, which observation supplies or brings in its train and which ask of this source their verification or their guarantee of certainty. If the rational principles on which observation and generalization rest are correct, if there exists an objective world and it is subject to constant laws, as everything leads us to believe, it will be easy to assure ourselves sooner or later of the value of our two kinds of experimental cognitions. The sphericity and the rotation of the earth, for example, long unknown, are today facts that are certain or confirmed by sufficient experiments. The identity of laws and of constitution of the human soul, in the sexes and in the races, revealed in part by the concordant studies of the philosophers of all times, is another fact that the future will not belie, although it has been contested by some critics. Doubtless all rational beings have not been observed; but the fact remains true within the bounds of observation, and one may boldly defy the contradictors to cite an exception. We therefore acquiesce in the apology that scientists make for experience, under the sole reservation, required by logic, of discussing the legitimacy of knowledge in general.

p. 235

But we still have cognitions for which every means of empirical verification is lacking, because they are by their nature independent of, and above, all possible observation. These are the supra-sensible, rational, a priori cognitions. Here we no longer agree with the scientists who believe that experience is the sole source of our knowledge. We are even in opposition to the school of Kant, which, without rejecting the rational elements of thought, nevertheless admits no legitimate or scientific knowledge beyond the limits of observation, except mathematical knowledge. We affirm, against the sensualists and against the criticists, that we have in reason a second source of knowledge, as abundant as and more important than the first, [p. 235] and that our rational cognitions are or can be as sure as our experimental cognitions. We maintain that if our a priori cognitions were radically uncertain for the sole reason that they go beyond experience, all our knowledge would be exposed to the blows of skepticism, and that the adversaries of supra-sensible knowledge themselves accept, sometimes without knowing it, the certainty of this kind of cognitions, at least in one of its applications.

p. 236

Mathematical cognitions pass for the model of exact cognitions. What, in fact, is more rigorous than algebra, geometry, mechanics? What is more universally true and certain than the theory of proportions and of equations, the measurement of regular surfaces and solids, the calculation of the motion and the equilibrium of forces? Every theorem is accompanied by a demonstration that it is impossible to resist, if one admits a few axioms as the object of an immediate certainty. Certainly it would be desirable that all our cognitions could have the same degree of self-evidence; I scarcely know what would be left to skepticism in that conjuncture; unless it abandoned the fight, it would fall back upon the facts of experience and would find in the facts a more ample matter for criticism than in the principles. We have the proof of it in the example of David Hume, whose skepticism stops before geometry. Now our mathematical cognitions are cognitions independent of all experience. Hume admits it. What need have we to observe nature in order to know that the square of a binomial is equal to the squares of the two terms increased by twice their product, and that the sum of the angles of a triangle is equal to two right angles? Observe! but we do not even find numbers or surfaces in nature, we calculate abstractions! And on these abstractions, on these pure forms, without reality in the external world, where everything is concrete, we construct universal and apodictic judgments! Everywhere, always, in all possible triangles, observed [p. 236] or not, the sum of the angles necessarily equals two right angles; such is the import of the proposition. And every being capable of reason approves and assents! We have, then, a priori cognitions, which go beyond all experience, and not only have we the power of forming such cognitions, but they are admitted as true and as certain by all who are in a condition to discuss them. What, then, does Condillac’s claim signify, of confining all human knowledge within the bounds of sensibility? Do our mathematical cognitions by chance come from the senses or from induction? Let us examine.

p. 237

The character of sensible knowledge is the perfect determination of its object. It is a matter of a phenomenon circumscribed in time and in space, which vanishes as one looks at it and which perhaps will never again present itself with all the circumstances that surround it. The character of mathematical knowledge is, on the contrary, generality. It is a matter of an object unalterable, immutable, which does not exist under the form of time, but under the form of eternity, which cannot be grasped by the senses, but by pure thought. Numbers, lines, surfaces do not change, whereas bodies are modified incessantly. Our eyes can contemplate concrete and solid things, a man, two horses, three trees of such or such a volume, but we have never seen outside us abstract numbers, bodies without thickness, directions without breadth. Mathematics concerns itself only with eternal things, inaccessible to the senses, with the pure forms of space, of time, and of motion, which are always the same. And how do we know these objects? In an entirely general manner. “All right angles are equal to one another; in every geometrical proportion the product of the extremes is equal to the product of the means.” Is it of one angle or of a few angles that we speak? No. Therefore the knowledge is not sensible, and the judgment that enunciates it is not individual or particular, but general. We speak of all right angles in all times and in all [p. 237] places. And what do we say of right angles compared with one another? Do we say that they may be equal, or that in fact the two that figure on the paper are equal? No, it is not a mere fact that is affirmed, nor a possibility that is expressed, but a necessity that is proclaimed: it is impossible that two right angles should not be equal. Therefore the knowledge is not sensible, and the judgment that enunciates it is not problematic or assertoric, but apodictic. Is there, finally, any condition or any restriction in the theorem? Does the equality of right angles depend, perhaps, on the length of the sides, or does it exist only for some species? No, the equality is absolute, without condition or division; the judgment that contains it is neither hypothetical nor disjunctive, but categorical, unconditional, absolute. Mathematical cognitions have the character of universality, of necessity, of unconditionality; mathematical cognitions, in other words, are expressed in general, apodictic, and categorical judgments. This is what distinguishes them from sensible knowledge.

p. 238

Let us see now whether these cognitions come from abstraction and generalization, as Locke maintains of rational notions in general. In every right triangle the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares formed on the other sides. I take Legendre’s figure, I transform the square of the hypotenuse into two rectangles equal to the two other squares, I recognize the exactness of the theorem. Yet the enunciation holds of all right triangles, and I have examined only one. Do I conclude from the part to the whole as in induction? No, the figure is only a sign; strictly it is false, because the line that divides the larger square has a thickness, of which I take no account in the reasoning. The demonstration does not depend on the figure, and blind geometers dispense with every external representation. Is it the same in induction? No, to define the genus one does not neglect the species; the species is not a symbol, it is the very object that one studies. In geometry, I have no need to attempt a second trial, in order to [p. 238] make sure of the result; I refrain from varying the size, the form, and the position of the right triangle; I know that the demonstration is independent of these circumstances, and that the reasoning that suits one case suits all possible cases; I do not take the trouble to verify the conclusion with a compass. Is it the same in natural history? No, there observations are multiplied, they are pursued, if possible, on a great number of specimens, one advances with prudence and endeavors to take account of the modifications that a discovery may bring into the distribution of the classes. In mathematics, finally, I pass suddenly from one example to all cases, or rather from the sign to the thing, and I state the result in an absolute manner, without fear of being contradicted by anyone or of seeing the order of nature changed: in matters of calculation, what is true on earth is true throughout the whole extent of the heavens. In the sciences of observation, on the contrary, we avoid generalizing too much, we fear miscalculations, because we know well that there are gaps in the reasoning and that the conclusion goes beyond the premises; we arrive at an hypothesis, not at a principle, we obtain a probability, not a certainty: we must make use rather of particular, problematic, and hypothetical judgments than of general, apodictic, and categorical judgments.

p. 239

Mr. Mill, who so well defends the cause of induction, does not wish it, however, to be introduced into mathematics. Geometrical propositions, he says, are really universal, and not inductive, because they contain no unknown element. When, after having demonstrated that the sum of the three angles of the triangle ABC is equal to two right angles, we conclude that this equality exists in all triangles, we do not proceed by induction; for it is not because some triangles possess this property that we affirm it of all, but because we are convinced that the demonstration for a single case is equivalent to the demonstration for all. If we choose to call this operation induction, adds the author, we must say that it is an induction by parity of reasoning. But the [p. 239] name is improper: induction implies gaps, which are not found in geometry. It is nevertheless claimed that there are cases of induction in mathematics. When one has, for example, calculated a sufficient number of terms of a series to obtain its law, one does not hesitate to set down the following terms without the help of calculation. But I greatly fear, continues Mr. Mill, that one then starts from a priori considerations, equivalent to a demonstration, on the mode of formation of the terms of the series. It is said again that Newton discovered the binomial theorem by induction, that is to say, that after having raised a binomial to a certain number of powers, he perceived the manifold relations that exist between the rank, the coefficient, and the exponents of each term of the series, on the one hand, and the index of the power and the various combinations of the terms of the binomial, on the other. The fact is not improbable, but a mathematician like Newton could not establish these relations without conceiving the a priori foundation of the law. This is another case of induction by parity of reasoning, and not a true generalization. Mr. Mill goes further and maintains that Kepler’s operation, in concluding the elliptical form of the orbit of Mars from a certain number of positions of that star, is not an induction, but a synthesis, a collection of observed or observable facts. Induction expresses the passage from known cases to unknown cases, whereas in the reasoning of the great astronomer there was nothing that was not known or that could not be known by other observations of the same nature, chosen at will (1).

p. 240

Induction, then, does not apply to mathematics, even in the cases that have seemed doubtful, because generalization ascends, not from the phenomenon to its law, but from the species to the genus, in the domain of the sciences of observation. What would it be if we took other examples where observation, and consequently induction, are manifestly impossible? Geometry cannot do without the [p. 240] theory of parallels, and yet no one has been able to assure himself by experience that lines indefinitely prolonged in the same plane never come to meet. Is it, then, on induction that the theorems of the angles formed by the section of two parallels rest? Is it induction that gives us the properties of the parabola, of the hyperbola and its asymptotes? Algebraic analysis in its turn requires the infinitely small, and yet no one has ever seen beings of this kind, a thousand times smaller than the undiscoverable atoms of physics. Is it again on induction that the infinitesimal calculus is founded? Mathematics demands negative quantities, and yet observation bears only on positive objects, dimensions, and motions. Try, then, to verify by induction that a negative quantity multiplied by itself necessarily gives a product equal to the square of the same quantity affected with the contrary sign!

But if mathematical propositions are a priori or independent of all observation, how, then, are they formed in us? That is the secret that Plato discovered, that Malebranche found again; that is the dialectical procedure that the Abbé Gratry wished to define and that he so clumsily confounded with induction. Induction is exercised only within the limits of observation and engenders only abstract cognitions, presumptions of truth that await the test of the future. Rational cognitions demand another course, which is still analytic or intuitive, but which attains at a stroke to universality and to the absolute. Such is the character of mathematical analysis, of which the infinitesimal calculus forms a part (1) and which, transported into the domain of pure philosophy, constitutes precisely the proper nature of the Platonic dialectic.

(1) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, Of Inductions Improperly So Called.

p. 241

The essential condition of dialectic, according to Plato, is the retreat of the soul into itself. The soul must free itself from the body, disengage itself from the senses, and see things in themselves [p. 241] by a pure intuition of thought. The senses give us only the variable, that which is not, that which becomes unceasingly and can never be fixed. Science must not stop at these inconstant phenomena, it wants the very essence of things, that which is, that which does not change. But all things in the world have been constructed on the model of the ideas: no object is pure being or pure unity, but each object has being and unity. We have originally in ourselves these ideas of being and of unity, but we lose the remembrance of them when the soul descends upon the earth and is united with a body. The function of the senses is to recall to us the pure ideas, on the occasion of sensible objects that bear some traces of them, which are after all the images of higher types or the shadows of the true reality. Between the world of the senses, the object of opinion, and the world of ideas, the object of science, there is no intermediary. Plato passes without transition from the one to the other and posits, as he says, a distinct idea for each multitude of like phenomena. There is nothing in this course that resembles the laborious and successive work of generalization: Plato seizes immediately the general idea, the eternal, the absolute, on occasion of the phenomena of sensation (1).

(1) G. S. Klügel, Mathematisches Wörterbuch, verbo analysis.

p. 242

It is this same transcendent movement that the thought of the mathematician follows when, on occasion of a sign or an image, it rises suddenly to a universal and apodictic proposition. The geometer does not pass gradually from one object to a few objects, then from a few objects to all objects, but from a single one to all, because the particular case is only the consequence of the general truth, and because the relation of reason or of foundation that unites them to each other is indeed composed of only two terms. Malebranche accounted for this procedure by the presence of the idea of the infinite in the human soul.
