He distinguishes first between the idea and the image and maintains rightly that the demonstration rests [p. 242] not on the image, but on the idea. “I cannot imagine a square, for example, without conceiving it at the same time. And it seems evident to me that the image of this square that I form for myself is exact and regular only in so far as it corresponds precisely to the intelligible idea that I have of the square, that is to say, of a space bounded by four lines exactly straight, entirely equal, and which, being joined at all their extremities, make their angles perfectly right. Now it is of such a square that I am sure that the diagonal is in power double each side. It is of such a square that I am sure that there is no common measure between the diagonal and the sides. In a word, it is of such a square that one can discover the properties, and demonstrate them to others. But one can know nothing in that confused and irregular image which the course of the spirits traces in the brain. The same must be said of all the other figures. Thus geometers do not draw their knowledge from the imaginations, but solely from the clear ideas of reason. These gross images may well sustain their attention, by giving, so to speak, body to their ideas; but it is the ideas, in which they find a hold, that enlighten them and convince them of the truth of their science.”

(1) Paul Janet, Études sur la dialectique dans Platon et dans Hegel, Paris, 1860.

p. 243

Geometry, then, is not a science of observation, since it concerns itself with possible combinations in space, conceived by pure reason, and not with real combinations, offered to the senses or transmitted to the imagination. Is it, then, an abstract science, founded on a process of generalization? That is impossible, since it is independent of experience and gives us, not generalized notions, but general notions. Let us nevertheless hear the objection. “You cannot get it out of your head that general ideas are only a confused assemblage of some particular ideas, or at least that you have the power of forming them from this assemblage. Let us see what is true and what is false in this thought with which you are so strongly prepossessed. You think, Ariste, of a circle one foot in diameter, then of one of two feet, of one of three, of one of four, etc., and finally you do not determine the [p. 243] size of the diameter, and you think of a circle in general. The idea of this circle in general, you will say, is therefore only the confused assemblage of the circles of which I have thought. Certainly this consequence is false; for the idea of the circle in general represents infinite circles and suits them all; and you have thought only of a finite number of circles. It is rather, then, that you have found the secret of forming the idea of the circle in general from five or six that you have seen. And that is true in one sense, and false in another. It is false in this sense, that there should be enough reality in the idea of five or six circles to form from them the idea of the circle in general. But it is true in this sense, that after having recognized that the size of circles does not change their properties, you have perhaps ceased to consider them one after another, according to their determinate size, in order to consider them in general, according to an indeterminate size. Thus you have, so to speak, formed the idea of the circle in general by spreading the idea of generality over the confused ideas of the circles that you have imagined. But I maintain to you that you could not form general ideas except because you find in the idea of the infinite enough reality to give generality to your ideas. You cannot think of an indeterminate diameter except because you see the infinite in extension, and because you can increase or diminish it to infinity. I maintain to you that you could never think of these abstract forms of genera and species, if the idea of the infinite, which is inseparable from your mind, were not joined quite naturally to the particular ideas that you perceive. You could think of such a circle, but never of the circle. You could perceive such an equality of radii, but never a general equality between indeterminate radii. The reason is that every finite and determinate idea can never represent anything infinite and indeterminate. But the mind joins without reflection to its finite ideas the idea of the generality that it finds in the infinite (1).”

Such is the dialectical procedure of geometry well explained.

(1) Malebranche, Entretiens sur la métaphysique, II, V.

p. 244

It starts from the pure ideas of reason, from the possible combinations conceived in space, and concludes with absolute self-evidence from a single object to all objects of the same genus, in the form of universal and categorical propositions, because the demonstration is not made on a determinate figure, considered as such, but on the general idea that the figure is supposed to represent. Generalization is altogether different. It starts from determinate objects, abstracts from their individual properties, compares them, and ends in a problematic generality. Nevertheless there are still authors who insist absolutely on bringing geometry and mathematics within the frame of the “natural sciences” or of the “inductive sciences.” It seems that the word has been passed round in France, in England, and in Germany, in the positivist schools, to extol experience as the sole source of science.

It is known that Kant, while committing theology, cosmology, and rational psychology to doubt, exceptionally granted to mathematical propositions an apodictic character, because they have for their basis a pure intuition of time and of space, because time and space, in other words, are not given a posteriori by the senses, but are themselves the general conditions of sensible intuition or the forms of our sensibility. One may discuss and reject the exclusively subjective role that the great critic attributes to time and space, but it is incontestable that we conceive these forms as infinite and that they are as such the object of an intellectual intuition, a priori, and not the object of experience. Hence the generality of mathematical propositions. Experience, which furnishes variable and contingent facts, cannot be the source of a necessary and universal knowledge. To wish to draw universality and necessity from an experimental datum, Kant used to say in jest, is to wish to squeeze water from a pumice stone: ex pumice aquam. Experience and necessity contradict each other (1).

(1) Kant, Kritik der praktischen Vernunft, 1788. Vorrede.

p. 245

Auguste Comte is not of this opinion; positivism is synonymous with empiricism. According to him, “geometry and mechanics must be regarded as true natural sciences, founded, like all the others, on observation.” The common error that makes geometry a purely rational science proceeds from a “remnant of the influence of the metaphysical spirit, which has so long dominated even in geometrical studies (1).” It is indeed unfortunate that metaphysicians like Descartes and Leibniz should have busied themselves with mathematics. Issuing from such a source, their discoveries are evidently suspect. Mr. Ueberweg shares in this respect Comte’s repugnance to all rational philosophy, and seeks besides to give reasons for his opinion. He acknowledges the apodictic value of mathematical propositions, but he believes it compatible with the empirical origin of the intuition of space. There is progress in certainty, according to him. The bases of geometry have at first only a relative value. But, as the principles and the consequences support one another and form a perfectly linked whole, certainty grows more and more, and even becomes absolute, if it is proved that the premises laid down alone explain the facts. “Although the fundamental propositions have in themselves a merely assertoric certainty, nevertheless the mathematical system, the product of the labor of centuries, has, as a whole, as an ensemble, an apodictic certainty which it spreads over the particular propositions.” It appears, then, that the ancients were not so convinced as we are that the straight line is the shortest way from one point to another, and that our descendants, thanks to experience, will be much surer still that the square of 2 is 4. Kant, says Mr. Ueberweg, starts from this opposition: empirical or a priori; but there is an intermediate term: rational elaboration of empirical data according to the logical laws without a priori elements of knowledge. Why did the philosopher not perceive this middle term?

p. 246

Logic. — I. 16 [p. 246] The answer is quite simple in our eyes: it is that the critique of pure reason had demonstrated that there is no knowledge without a priori elements, and that the elaboration proposed is thus a manifest absurdity. To eliminate every a priori idea from knowledge, says Kant, is to seek to demonstrate by reason that there is no reason; for rational knowledge and a priori knowledge are the same thing. Be that as it may, Mr. Ueberweg proposes to overthrow the theory of Kant, and it seems to him accordingly fitting “to substitute for the axioms of Euclid, to which habit has attached the predicate of apriority, propositions wholly different, and whose empirical origin cannot be denied. If it is proved that from these propositions all geometry can be drawn as well and even better than from the axioms of Euclid, it is shown at the same time that one can, without recourse to apriority, base geometry on principles analogous to those of the natural sciences, and rank geometry among these sciences.” Let us not discuss, but go straight to the application:

“Theorem 1. There exists a continuous and homogeneous ensemble, capable of being divided and extended to infinity, of places that a body can occupy. Definitions: We name this ensemble space; a finite part of this infinite space we name geometrical body.—It is on this homogeneity of space that the universality of geometrical propositions rests, inasmuch as what is proved for one place of this space is necessarily proved for all. Homogeneity, continuity, infinity, such are the three fundamental properties of space to be concluded from the first experience (1).” It is useless to go further. If experience gives the infinite, experience means reason, and a posteriori knowledge is nothing other than a priori knowledge. The author is in agreement with Kant, his criticism is only a quibble. It remains to be seen whether the empiricists will be of as easy composition as the apriorists.

(1) Auguste Comte, Cours de philosophie positive, vol. I, lessons ii and x. Paris, 1830.

(1) F. Ueberweg, Exposit. scientif. des principes de la géométrie, précédée d’une discussion sur le fondement de la certitude des propos. prem. de cette science; trans. by J. Delbœuf, Liège, 1860.

p. 247

Mr. Ueberweg has found an emulator. There is a double geometry, says M. Delbœuf: experimental geometry studies bodies independently of their substance, and seeks to bring a given form back to an ideal form; theoretical geometry follows the inverse course; starting from ideal, absolute principles, it creates forms without end and seeks to make them coincide with natural forms. The one is inductive, the other deductive and syllogistic. Granted, that is clear and in conformity with received notions: pure geometry is a deductive science which starts from absolute principles and which creates its forms; but a share may be allowed to experience and to induction in some applications of geometry, for example, in crystallography. These principles laid down, the author asks how one is to proceed to the building up of the science, of theoretical geometry. The question seems superfluous: since it is a matter of geometry, which is not experimental but deductive, it seems that one must proceed by deduction, and not by experience; since geometry starts from absolute principles, whereas observation bears only on complex and concrete facts, one has only to develop the principles and to draw their corollaries by the various forms of syllogistic reasoning; since, finally, geometry creates forms, whereas experience is content with the phenomena given by nature and experimentation, by combining the circumstances, merely provokes the formation of the same phenomena, it is clear that geometry is a rational science, which has nothing in common with experience. Well, all our anticipations are at fault: the method of deductive geometry is experience. Geometry combines its straight lines and its planes, as the chemist combines his simple bodies, and it watches what takes place. It is only unfortunate that the geometer does not find, like the chemist, his elements in the external world and that he must invent them. No matter, M. Delbœuf holds to his discovery; rather than sacrifice experience, he will produce a new kind of it: ordinary people make use of real experience, the geometer of ideal experience. The phrase is pretty and deserves as much success [p. 248] as “rational elaboration of empirical data without a priori elements.”

Does ideal experience at least give geometry a certain basis? That depends; subjective certainty is universal, because the abstraction that is its point of departure carries with it the universality of the results (in the abstract sciences it is quite the contrary); but objective certainty, the certainty of the truth of the science, is less, for it depends on verification, on the comparison of ideal phenomena with real phenomena, that is to say, on direct observations (1). I greatly fear that at this price geometry is no longer sure at all. If the homogeneity, the isogeneity, and the continuity of space, considered in all its parts, must be verified, which no one has ever done and no one ever will do, before proceeding to any demonstration, the geometers will do well to ask themselves whether it is not better to renounce their science. Hitherto they were dispensed from all empirical verification, because geometry passed for a science independent of experience; hitherto they cited with pride the “geometrical method” and defied the scientists to attain in their domain the same degree of rigor; but in future, thanks to the progress of thought, they must fall to the common level of empiricism and groping, what do I say? they will be the first to be devoured by skepticism, because they rest upon space without limits and because observation has not yet found any means of assuring itself whether there exists an infinitely great, whether there exist infinitely small quantities, whether there exist points, lines, and surfaces, whether extension is homogeneous and continuous everywhere and in all its combinations.

p. 249

Let us now leave the objections and conclude. If mathematical propositions are rational, general, necessary, categorical, a priori cognitions, they are philosophical cognitions; for philosophical cognitions, inasmuch as philosophy is the science of [p. 249] principles, as history is the science of facts, have precisely the same characters. Mathematics, in fact, forms part of philosophy: it belongs to the philosophy of nature. Nature may be considered in its matter and in its form. Matter, in the organic or inorganic state, is the object of the natural sciences; form, the object of the mathematical sciences. There are two opposite forms that suit all bodies: the form of coexistence, by virtue of which objects are found together in one and the same whole, and the form of succession, by virtue of which bodies are transformed and pass from one state to another: the first is space; the second, time. Time and space are combined in motion, which expresses, in fact, a change of position, or the successive translation of a body from one place to another. Time, space, and motion are homogeneous, continuous, divisible. Each part of space is like the whole of space as to its essence; each part is itself a whole, which has length, breadth, and depth, but a limited whole. A limited whole is a quantity or a magnitude, a quantum. All these propositions are independent of observation and borrowed from metaphysics. Now mathematics is the science of quantity considered in itself and in its applications to time, to space, and to motion. It develops by the sole effect of reasoning, whereas experience is indispensable in the natural sciences. Herschel has marked this difference very well. “A clever man, shut up alone and allowed unlimited time, might reason out for himself all the truths of mathematics, by proceeding from those simple notions of space and number of which he cannot divest himself without ceasing to think. But he could never tell, by any effort of reasoning, what would become of a lump of sugar if immersed in water, or what impression would be produced on his eye by mixing the colours yellow and blue (1).”

(1) J. Delbœuf, Prolegomènes philosophiques de la géométrie et solution des postulats, Liège, 1860.

(1) J. F. W. Herschel, Preliminary Discourse on the Study of Natural Philosophy, no. 66, French trans. Paris, 1834.

p. 250

We agree with Kant on the character of mathematical cognitions, but we do not admit with him that these cognitions have, as to certainty, an exceptional rank in the ensemble of the propositions of pure philosophy. Without any doubt, mathematics has a simpler object, a more exact language than metaphysics, and lends itself better to being represented in the imagination; the demonstrations in it are easier, because they are freed from every consideration relating to the moral and material interests of man and concentrated solely on the eternal forms of nature; self-evidence in consequence is more extended in it than in any other science. We contest none of these advantages, we say only that they do not make between mathematics and metaphysics such a difference that the first should be an exact science and the second an apparent science or an illusion. For, on the one hand, the first propositions of geometry, the axioms or postulates relating to space, to its characters, to its dimensions, are rather metaphysical than mathematical: they are lemmas borrowed from the general synthesis of reason, which geometry does not demonstrate and which would deprive geometry itself of the title of science if metaphysics had no certain value; and on the other hand, there are philosophical principles that are as evident as the most evident propositions of geometry. How can we deny that each thing is what it is, that of two contradictory attributes it has one and not the other, that every phenomenon supposes a cause and every property a substance, when the skeptics themselves are obliged to rely on these truths in order to defend their thesis? It is not possible, then, that there should be between mathematics and pure philosophy the whole distance from truth to appearance. What is true is that philosophy, having for its object the ensemble of principles, concerns itself with problems far more complicated and more difficult to solve than those of geometry. The question of the soul, of the universe, or of God is otherwise fruitful and raises wholly other interests than the question of the circle or of the [p. 251] square. Let us see, however, the objections in the “Critique of Pure Reason.”

Kant begins by distinguishing between analytic judgments, in which the attribute is implicitly contained in the subject and results from its decomposition, and synthetic judgments, in which the attribute is a new, transcendent datum, which is added to the subject. Then he applies this distinction to our experimental cognitions and to our rational cognitions. Judgments of experience or a posteriori judgments are synthetic, but they are limited like observation and cannot attain, even by induction, more than a comparative generality, subject to the exceptions that the future will perhaps bring. Necessity and real universality are certain marks of an a priori cognition, of a rational or philosophical cognition. Analytic judgments offer nothing difficult. But synthetic judgments may be a priori as well as a posteriori, and then it is asked how and by what right we can unite, in a universal and apodictic proposition, two ideas that are foreign to each other. Such is the problem of pure reason: “How are synthetic judgments a priori possible?”

p. 252

Here mathematics and metaphysics meet: for both sciences, says Kant, contain only synthetic a priori judgments (1). The author’s solution is well known: mathematics is possible, metaphysics is impossible as a science and must confine itself to a pure criticism. If, then, metaphysics is impossible, it is not because it goes beyond experience, nor because it contains synthetic propositions, for it shares these two characters with mathematics; it is solely because we have a pure intuition of space and of time and have no intuition of God, of the infinite, of the absolute, of principles, in a word of supra-sensible objects. Kant’s pure intuition is an intuition other than that which the senses and the imagination [p. 252] give us; it is therefore an intellectual intuition, the intuition of reason. We now see where the difficulty of philosophical cognitions lies, from Kant’s point of view. It is a matter of knowing whether we have another receptive faculty than sensibility, whether we possess other intuitions than those of the imagination; it is, in short, a matter of the nature of reason. That is a question of fact or of psychological analysis, which is easy to resolve after the labors of Krause and of Cousin, and which we have resolved in the “Science of the Soul,” in agreement with all the philosophical schools, with the exception of sensualism. The intuition of infinite time and of infinite space is of the same nature as the intuition of infinite being, and in no way implies that time and space are subjective forms of our sensibility. Kant would assuredly have perceived this if he had merely suspected that the matter of our knowledge may come from another source than the senses. The error that closed to him the path of metaphysics relates, therefore, to the theory of reason, as an intuitive faculty applying itself to supra-sensible things. This obstacle removed, metaphysics is possible. But let us not overshoot the mark. Let us occupy ourselves first with rational cognitions in general, setting aside their objective validity.

(1) Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, Einleitung.

p. 253

All rational cognitions, or cognitions independent of experience, are general, necessary, categorical, like the mathematical propositions that we have taken for example. When we say: “everything that is determinate has a cause,” we pass beyond the limits of observation, for no one has been able to observe everything that is determinate in infinite space and time; moreover, if the proposition is true, it must apply also to the spiritual world and to the physical world, as distinct or determinate genera, although observation can teach us nothing concerning the world considered as a whole. This enunciation contains neither condition, nor doubt, nor reservation: it is a categorical, apodictic, universal judgment, it is a philosophical principle, exact or not: objective truth [p. 253] is not now in question, and it is not for logic to verify the value of the principles of all the sciences. When one says, “the soul is free,” “the body is heavy,” what kind of cognitions is one formulating? That depends; for the propositions are not clearly determined and admit of a double meaning.

In experimental psychology and experimental physics, an author who proceeds methodically will mean to speak, not of all souls or all possible bodies, at whatever time and in whatever place they may exist, but only of the souls and bodies that have been subjected to observation; the judgment is then assertoric and particular: a simple fact is put forward, without prejudice to what the future holds in reserve, and a pronouncement is made on a property of some beings, those which it has been possible to observe. Knowledge in this case is empirical. In rational psychology and in mathematical physics, the same propositions would have an incomparably greater extension; freedom would be posited as an essential and necessary attribute of the soul, of all souls, in the future life as well as in the present life, and weight or gravity as a law of matter applicable to all bodies in the heavens and on the earth; the judgment would then be apodictic and universal, and the knowledge would be a priori, rational, above and apart from observation.

p. 254

Kant was therefore right: the true characters of a priori knowledge are the universality and the necessity (apodicticity) of the judgment that expresses it, and these two characters are inseparable. What is rigorously universal, what holds of a whole category of objects without exception, betrays a necessity inherent in the nature of things; and conversely, what belongs necessarily to the nature of a being is found again in all the beings of the same species. To these two marks of rational knowledge we may add unconditionality or the absolute, which manifests itself in the categorical judgment, as opposed to the hypothetical judgment. What is universal and necessary, whether in thought or in reality, is also, in the same measure, [p. 254] independent of every condition or of every relation with a contrary term. If freedom, for example, belongs only to some souls, we must ask under what condition, in what circumstances it exists; if, on the contrary, it belongs necessarily to all souls, it may well still have a higher cause, but it no longer depends on any further conditions; it is implied in our nature and exists by the mere fact that the soul exists. Rational knowledge is therefore recognized by the categorical, apodictic, and general character of the judgment that states it. M. Cousin arrives at the same result when he compares the ideas of reason with the representations of the senses and finds in the former the logical antecedent of the latter. To tell the truth, philosophy since Socrates has never varied on this capital point, as is shown by Plato’s reminiscence, the categories of Aristotle, and the theory of innate ideas of Descartes and Leibniz; only the sensualist doctrines, by suppressing all a priori knowledge, have sought to establish that there is nothing absolute, universal, or necessary in human thought. Mathematics gives a first refutation of this thesis.

p. 255

A truth that is universal, necessary, and absolute is called a principle or a law. It is in this sense that philosophy is the science of principles and is an entirely rational science, freed from empirical elements. Facts, particular, contingent, relative truths, are the object of history properly so called. The philosophy of history combines principles with phenomena, or sets forth the law of facts. For the law is the expression of what is universal, necessary, absolute in a series of variable facts. When we know that all bodies are heavy, whether they fall toward the earth or rise in the atmosphere, we know a law of nature. The phenomena are manifold and changing; the law is one and the same; bodies are in the solid, liquid, or gaseous state, but all have this in common, that they weigh: in the absence of every obstacle, all are borne toward the center of the globe with the same velocity, at equal masses and equal distances; and if they differ in composition or [p. 255] situation, they attract one another in direct proportion to their masses and in inverse proportion to the square of the distances, always in the same manner in the same circumstances, always in a way exactly determinable in determinate circumstances. The judgment “all bodies are heavy” is therefore equivalent to a law of matter. The same holds of these other judgments, “all bodies move, grow warm, combine”: so many universal and necessary properties, so many laws. Cases and accidents are innumerable, but they are reduced to unity in the laws of motion, of heat, of affinity. There is something necessary, absolute, immutable, from which no phenomenon departs: that is the law. The same relations obtain in the spiritual world; souls also have their laws, but by virtue of their freedom they can give or refuse their assent; the laws of the mind and of the heart are necessary in themselves, but must be carried out by the free will; physical necessity or fatality gives way to moral necessity, to duty.

Rational knowledge is therefore the knowledge of laws, or of the necessary relations that derive from the nature of things. The knowledge of laws, in other words, belongs to the rational part of the sciences, just as the knowledge of facts falls within the province of experience. Such is the difference between mathematical physics and experimental physics, between speculative psychology and psychology confined to observation. Pure physics is wholly discursive and requires no sensible intuition; it develops by the power of reasoning and consists in a series of theorems. Experimental physics, on the contrary, is wholly intuitive and does not require a knowledge of principles; it develops solely by observation and consists in a series of problems. In the natural sciences we often deceive ourselves on this point, and under the pretext that we begin by observing things and that facts are never in contradiction with principles, a theorem, a general and apodictic proposition, is taken for the result or the conclusion of a problem.

p. 256

The law does not result from experience. The law is universal, necessary, immutable, whereas facts have the contrary properties. Induction does not end in a certain law, but in a presumption, in a hypothesis; only, it may be that the hypothesis is true, and it is transformed into a law when it is confirmed by deduction. It is for metaphysics to demonstrate the principles of all the sciences. In the present state of our knowledge, the laws of nature, not excepting Newton’s attraction, still pass for hypotheses even in the eyes of scientists.

p. 257

Rational knowledge has for its objects either beings or properties, considered in their eternal and necessary essence. Finite beings, souls and bodies, which manifest themselves in time and in space, are given to us by a sensible intuition and are subject to internal or external observation. But above finite beings, beyond the limits of the senses and of the imagination, we conceive by pure reason beings unique in their kind, which compose the world as a whole, and above the universe we still surmise God. Of all bodies we form nature; of all minds, the spiritual world; of all rational beings, humanity. We say that these beings are unique in their kind and that each of them perhaps extends to infinity in its sphere; for the idea of humanity is not exhausted by any determinate number of men, and besides, no sufficient reason can be given for one number rather than for another. It is therefore more in accordance with reason to admit an infinity of bodies in nature, an infinity of souls in the spiritual world, an infinity of men in humanity, and then to believe that all finite beings, minds, bodies, and men, move and develop in infinite space and infinite time. We have an intellectual intuition of these three kinds of reality, but deduction alone can teach us whether this pure intuition of reason has objective validity; for sensible intuition or observation, supported by induction and by analogy, can no longer serve us in these higher regions. These questions will find their place better in the [p. 257] sequel (1). Let us first concern ourselves with the rational knowledge of properties, which will prepare the solution of the problem of the legitimacy of human thought and will serve as an introduction to the affirmation of the existence of God, as the principle of science.

The a priori knowledge of properties comprises three points. We know properties that are held to belong to all things, that are found equally in all our thoughts, and that are then the laws of intellectual activity: these are the categories. We know properties that express the moral order of the world, that are the laws of our free activity and of our social relations: these are the ideas of the good, the beautiful, the true, the just. We know, finally, properties that are regarded as the ontological attributes of God, in whom all laws are summed up: these are the ideas of the infinite, the absolute, the immutable, the necessary, the eternal. We shall examine in turn the knowledge that we possess of these three groups of predicates, and we shall show that this knowledge is independent of all observation.

p. 258

The simplest ideas are those of being, of essence, of form, of existence, of unity, of identity, of quantity, of quality, of relation, of dependence, of cause and effect, of whole and part. We find first of all that these categories are realized in us, that they are our properties, and in this sense they are really innate, as Leibniz maintained against Locke, since they are naturally imprinted in the soul, independently of the knowledge that we have of them. The mind is constituted on the model of the categories, and can discover them without leaving itself, by the sole development of immanent knowledge. Every man who questions himself in good faith recognizes that he is a being or a thing, and when he asks himself what he is, he obtains his essence: he is one, he [p. 258] is himself, he is all that he is, he is his essence, one and whole, one and identical. The body is posited in space, under the form of extension in length, breadth, and depth; the soul is folded back upon itself under the form of concentration, and manifests this character in the inner sense. In so far as its essence is posited, the self exists; its proper existence constitutes its substantiality, and if there exist outside us other substances, which form an external world, we are limited, dependent, subject to foreign conditions, enveloped in all sorts of relations. Not only does the soul know that it exists, but it is conscious of its activity and of its life; it sees that it changes in passing successively from one thought to another, although its essence and its properties remain immutable; it appraises its activity from the point of view of quality and of quantity; it is spontaneous, it is a force that unfolds, it is a cause that develops through a continuous series of phenomena (1).

(1) Krause, Die Lehre vom Erkennen: Nichtsinnliche Behauptungen über die Natur, die Vernunft und die Menschheit. Göttingen, 1836.

p. 259

These same categories, which preside over our spiritual constitution, not only as forms of the understanding, in Kant’s sense, but as attributes of our essence, then accompany thought throughout the whole course of its acts and serve to determine all the transcendent objects of the intellect. They then become the regulative principles of knowledge. For we can conceive nothing except by the application of the categories. Every object of thought presents itself necessarily to the mind as substance or as property, spiritual or physical, finite or infinite, and as soon as we wish to judge it, we give it a quality and a quantity, a relation and a modality. Try to understand a plant, a star, an angel, nature, motion, otherwise than as things whose essence is one, identical, positive, which exist in us or outside us, which sustain relations with themselves or with external beings; you will not succeed. We think, and can think, only by the aid [p. 259] of the categories. Whether this is a right or an abuse of reason, I shall not say at this moment, but it is assuredly an effect of our spiritual organization. Thought is a manifestation of our essence; by the very fact that this essence is organized according to the categories, we can think only with the categories, and every other mode of knowing must appear impossible to us. If there is some defect here, it is original and irreparable. But on the other hand, if there really exists a system of properties common to all things, the categories must also apply to the self, and then our manner of thinking is perfectly legitimate, or in conformity with the universal constitution. There lies the question on which the value of human thought depends. We must postpone its solution, and merely point out the difference that exists in the certainty of the categories according as they are referred to the self or to the not-self. In the domain of the self, where consciousness is sovereign, everyone can immediately affirm his properties, and if he goes no further, he escapes the objections of skepticism. But in the external world and in pure speculation, where consciousness ceases to make itself heard, before affirming anything with authority we must know whether the categories have an objective and transcendent bearing.

(1) Cf. Psychologie, on the Fundamental Properties of the Soul.

p. 260

All reservation concerning truth aside, the categories are the object of a universal, necessary, absolute knowledge. Rightly or wrongly, we apply them to everything that is, without regard to experience, and we express them by categorical, apodictic, and universal judgments, like theorems: every being has an essence; every essence is one and identical with itself; every thing is distinct from all that is not itself; every property presupposes a substance; every substance is active; every part is in the whole; everything that happens in the world has a cause. These are indeed a priori propositions. Is it observation that teaches us that every being has an essence? No, for we are speaking not merely of some beings, those whose nature has been recognized, but of all the objects of thought, finite or infinite, not excepting God: the universality [p. 260] of things lies outside experience. Nor do we speak of conditions, giving it to be understood, for example, that beings have an essence if it please God; we state in an absolute manner the relation that we see between the subject and the attribute. Finally, we do not say that beings may, but that they must have an essence. Observation does not permit such judgments to be made. No doubt none of these propositions is contrary to observation, but none either is confirmed by it in its generality. Verification is possible only in particular cases. We have never found a property that was independent of all substance, we have never witnessed a phenomenon that had not a known or presumed cause, but that does not suffice to affirm categorically that every substance, even the infinite substance, has attributes, and that every change that occurs in heaven or on earth proceeds necessarily from a cause. The skeptics and the dogmatists who give their confidence only to observation would not tolerate such an extension of the data of experience. They would readily accept a certain subjective necessity, born of custom, imposed by our intellectual habits, but they would take care not to transform the conveniences of thought into laws of reality.

p. 261

The categories have their source not in observation but in reason. They are not contrary, but anterior and superior to experience. They are therefore independent of sensibility, as we have already recognized against the sensualists. In effect, our sensible perceptions demand supra-sensible conditions. If sensualism were the expression of the truth, our organs ought to give us the ideas of being, of substance, of cause, whereas they give only phenomena, nervous modifications, and we ourselves must add to our impressions the categories of cause, of property, of relation, in order to interpret them and draw some advantage from them. Far from depending on observation, rational ideas are therefore the prior and necessary condition without which no observation is possible. Plato already [p. 261] had pointed out this matter in the Theaetetus. As each sense, he says, has a special order of perceptions, and as it is impossible to feel through one organ what is felt through another, we must admit that the things common to all our sensations are perceived by no organ of the body. Now the first idea that we have concerning two sensations, for example, a sound and a color, is that both of them are; then that each is identical with itself and different from the other, that taken together they are two, and that each taken apart is one. These ideas of being and non-being, of identity and difference, of unity and of the other numbers are acquired neither by sight, nor by hearing, nor by any other sense, since they are common to all objects; they are among those things that the soul knows immediately by itself without the aid of the body (1). Such is Plato’s intellectual intuition; from it the ideas come.

The categories do not result from observation. Aristotle may have inscribed them on his table while meditating on various subjects, but the application that he made of them to metaphysics proves clearly enough that he did not intend to restrict them to the facts of experience. Might they perhaps come from induction? No; they have not the abstract character of the generic notions of the understanding, but the ideal character of the general elements of reason. Would they, finally, be a chimerical invention, a creation of the human mind, analogous to the divinities of fable, to the entelechies and the monads of the Schools? No more so; the mind can do without gods, but not without being, unity, cause; myths are often a diversion of the imagination, the categories are a necessity of reason: it is in this capacity that they are laws of thought. No being creates the laws of its activity, for it would have to act without laws, which seems impossible, in order to give itself laws, which is contrary to the very idea of law. Besides, how could one invent unity without thinking of it, without

p. 262

Logic. — I. 17 [p. 262] knowing it in some fashion, and what need is there to invent it if we already have it? So many hypotheses, so many errors or circles.

(1) αὐτὴ δὶ αὑτῆς ἡ ψυχὴ τα κοινά μοι φαίνεται περὶ πάντων ἐπισκοπεῖν. Theaetetus, 185. Ed. Turici.

p. 263

Let us now conclude. If the categories do not come from us, as products of the understanding, they are given to us by our receptive or intuitive faculties; and if they are not given to us by the senses, they are given to us by reason, for there remains no other alternative. This reasoning contains a double dilemma, which cannot be escaped: what in our knowledge is not our own work comes from without, and what comes from without has its source either in sensibility or in reason. The first argument contains the distinction between the form and the matter of knowledge; the second, the distinction between sensible intuition and intellectual intuition, between the image and the idea. The opposition of matter and form is admitted by all; but the opposition between the intuition of the imagination and that of reason is attacked, on the one hand, by the sensualists, who see in the categories only objects of our senses, and on the other, by the criticists, who take them for pure forms of the understanding. The error of sensualism no longer needs to be pointed out; the error of Kant is that of a great mind, who, seeing that thought did not succeed in grasping the objects of reason, reversed the conditions of the problem, shut the ideas up within us, and created subjectivism. The hypothesis is only half false: the ideas, in effect, are in us, they are also the forms of our understanding, since they are met with in all our judgments; far more, they are the characters of our essence; but are they only in us? We say that they are in us because they are in all things. Otherwise, why do you apply them to the data of experience, and why do you believe in the reality of the phenomena of nature? To be logical, you would have to transfer appearances also into the self and deny, like Fichte, everything that goes beyond the sphere of the subject. Such is the consequence of subjectivism, and the doctrine itself is the consequence of another hypothesis, belied by psychology, namely [p. 263] that we have only one receptive faculty, or that the matter of knowledge can be given to us only by sensibility. If Kant had recognized the value of reason, he would not have imagined those strange paradoxes, that time and space exist only in us, that the categories and the ideas are only forms of the mind; he would have preserved for the principles their objective bearing, and would have been content to seek their origin in reason.

p. 264

The categories are the first elements of reason. In this capacity they are innate. They do not come from without through the channel of the senses, like impressions; they are not engendered in time by reflection, like abstract notions; they are literally innate, born and abiding in the soul, by the sole fact that we possess reason. They illumine the mind like a revelation from on high and preside over its intellectual activity. They guide thought in the distinction of things, letting it see here beings, there properties, now unity, now multiplicity, pointing out to it differences and analogies and preventing it from straying too far in the profusion of details. They impose themselves on the will and command our assent. No doubt the child is not conscious of the categories, and far from being able to define them, he would not even understand the definition that one might wish to give; wholly absorbed in the work of analysis that the use of his limbs, the interpretation of his senses, and the study of language demand, he does not disentangle his faculties and does not know their content; nevertheless he judges, he is moved, he acts, and he does not fail to apply the categories to the objects that captivate his attention. He is conscious of his unity before he knows whether he is mind or body; he has the feeling of his identity when he remembers his name or his acts; he glimpses causality when he grasps the play of his organs and affirms an external world; he suspects, finally, all the categories when he begins to speak, for language corresponds to reason and reflects all its ideas. It is one thing to possess the categories in the folds of the intellect, another to know them. The child does not think of his thought, [p. 264] but he thinks; he does not discern reason, but he makes use of it. To know the categories, one must give attention to them and perceive them. This the child does not seem to do unless he is invited to. But as soon as his attention is called to a category, he knows it, to the measure of his powers. Ask him whether it is not true that an apple is an apple and that a pear is not an orange; he will be astonished and will scarcely understand that anyone could doubt these principles; far from contesting the laws of identity and of contradiction, he will take the arguments of the skeptics for mere jesting. Is it education or nature that has trained this mind? If you hesitate, repeat the experiment on the child of a skeptic: he will think like everybody else. Take another case. Does the child know the principle of causality from his birth? No; before knowing it, he applies it, and applies it every time he asks you why? Make him reflect on his question, give him the words he lacks, and he will be a metaphysician without knowing it. In this sense the ideas are innate, but it is the virtual innateness of Leibniz: the ideas are not in us as ready-made cognitions or as formulated propositions, but as principles, laws, data of reason; all knowledge, immanent or transcendent, requires the functions of the understanding and proceeds from intellectual activity. To maintain that knowledge itself is innate, one would have to go back up the course of the ages beyond the present life, and resume the hypothesis of Plato and of Origen on the preexistence of souls. Rational cognitions, independent of the accidents of earth, would then be reminiscences of an earlier life.

p. 265

The most important of the categories, the root of all the others, is that of being, the object of ontology. Metaphysics can define God only by being. To determine being in itself, in its content and in its relations, is the whole of science. All the laws of thought derive from the universal and necessary idea of being, as Rosmini recognized, under these two principal forms: “What is, is; what is cannot not be.” It is evident that a [p. 265] idea which thus lies at the bottom of all our thoughts, which we affirm in all our acts, which regulates the movement of the intellect to whatever object, sensible or not, it may be applied, is anterior and superior to experience. Observation reaches beings, it will be said; granted, but it does not reach them all, and could grasp none of them if the idea of being did not already occupy thought. The senses do not give us beings or substances, but phenomena. This is what the exclusive apologists of the experimental method persist in not recognizing, in spite of all the warnings of Plato and Aristotle, of Descartes and Leibniz, of Kant, of Reid, and of Cousin; they take observation in the raw state, with all its elements, with the participation of the senses and of reason, of images and of ideas; then, when observation so furnished pronounces on external objects and sees in them beings that have an essence, they imagine that the categories of being and of essence are derived from experience. They do not perceive that observation is a form of knowledge, that knowledge is a complex whole which is worth the trouble of decomposing into its parts, and that analysis establishes beyond reply that no knowledge, even experimental, is possible without a priori principles. The categories which they seek outside by observation are already in the mind, as the condition of observation. The ideas of cause and of quantity give rise to the same misunderstandings. Scientists note that bodies act and react as cause, and that the conclusion of a theorem can often be verified by observation; nothing more is needed: the law of causality comes to us through the senses, mathematics is an experimental science, metaphysics will soon be one. From the moment that a principle conforms to experience, it comes from experience! This is to turn in a circle and to proclaim a priori that there exist only a posteriori cognitions. Let them observe knowledge at least, and they will be convinced that space, time, and numbers, the general conditions of our sensible intuitions, are conceived only by rational beings, and that if the idea of cause rested only in the external world, [p. 266] we should never suspect its existence, seeing that without it it would be impossible for us to affirm the external world.

Each category is the object of a knowledge and even of a rational science, independent of experience but not contrary to experience. To the science of being, of essence, of quantity, we may add the science of form, the science of quality, the science of relations, the science of unity and of harmony, the science of direction and of containment, the science of causality, and so on. All these sciences, scarcely glimpsed as yet, rest upon metaphysical principles that go beyond observation. Let us take as an example the idea of causality, so important for the theory of knowledge.

p. 267

Causality expresses a certain relation between two things, of which one is called cause and the other effect. There exist among facts not merely relations of coexistence and succession, as Mr. Mill supposes; beings sustain all sorts of relations, internal and external relations, relations of subordination, of containment, of possession, of inherence, of juxtaposition, of conditionality, of action, of foundation, of cause, of origin, of end and means. Relation is a universal category, which M. Renouvier places at the head of his list, and whose simplest elements are marked in all languages by the inflections of nouns or by prepositions. Among all these relations, which is it that designates the causal connection? Let us take as an example man, considered as an organized whole, of which the mind and the body form part. The mind is with the body; there we have coexistence and juxtaposition; but if there existed no other relations between the two sides of human nature, if there were not between them union, reciprocal action, mutual influence and dependence, man would be only the sum of two fractions and would have no other unity than that of a mineral; when two things are together in such a way that they are indispensable to one another, like the various functions of an organism, they are bound together by the relation of conditionality. Conditionality is [p. 267] therefore the coordinate and bilateral dependence of the parts of one and the same whole, in so far as these parts, considered in their reciprocal relations, are necessary to one another or cannot act one without the others. Such is the position of the soul with regard to the body according to observation in the present life; such also is the position of the animal kingdom with regard to the vegetable kingdom on earth. This is why we say that the mind finds in the body, in the nervous system, in sensibility, some of the conditions of its development on the globe. But we must beware of transforming this conditional relation into a relation of causality, as the materialists do. Causality is another sort of dependence, a unilateral and subordinative dependence between the whole and the parts. The mind and the body, as parts of one and the same whole, stand in relation to man in relations of subordination, of containment, and of reason or foundation. Here we no longer have two opposed terms, in the form of coordination, which serve one another reciprocally as end and means; we have two unequal terms, one superior, the other inferior, the whole and the part, and the relations in this case present themselves under two different aspects: the whole is not to the part as the part is to the whole. The part is subordinate to the whole, contained and founded in the whole, but the whole is not contained or founded in the part. The category of reason or foundation (ratio, principium) indicates the relation of two things of which one is inherent in the essence, or contained in the essence, of the other. Properties belong to the essence and constitute it; parts are in the essence and manifest it. The properties and the parts of human nature are alike founded in the idea of humanity: to understand the unity and the perfectibility of man, to find the reason of the constitution of the human mind and of the human body, we must go back to the scientific notion of human nature; the mind and the body form part of our essence; it is the essence of man, as a being of harmony in creation, that alone can explain the similarities and the differences presented by our spiritual organization and [p. 268] physical, compared with that of animals. The two terms of this relation are called Principle and Consequence. The syllogism and demonstration are an application of this category: the conclusion of every deductive reasoning must be founded in the premises.

p. 269

The category of causality is a determination of the idea of reason. It supposes, first, between the effect and the cause, the same relations of subordination and of containment as exist between the part and the whole. This is why we say, on the one hand, that the effect is under the cause and in the cause, and on the other, that the cause is superior to the effect, that it is more than the effect, and that it can produce an indefinite series of phenomena. Causes must not be multiplied without necessity; one and the same cause suffices for all effects of the same nature. We recognize, for example, that the mind is the cause of its acts of thought, that the body is the cause of the acts of organic life, that the earth, as a center of attraction, is the cause of the fall of bodies within the limits of its action. In these various cases we see, on the one hand, a whole, the mind, the body, the earth, and on the other, a series of intellectual, physiological, and physical facts; we understand that all our acts of thought are in the soul and form part of the soul, but that the soul is not merely this or that particular thought, that it manifests itself in the whole course of our thoughts, and that there thus exist between the cause and each of its effects relations of containment and of subordination. Sometimes it seems that the effect issues from the sphere of the cause, for example in the knowledge that we have of space, of nature, of God, or in the works of art that we realize outside ourselves. But the cause must not be confounded with the object of knowledge, nor with the matter of art. All our cognitions, from the subjective point of view, are in us, in thought, in the soul, and are in effect only the acts of a limited being, capable of error; but the objects of our transcendent cognitions are not in us; perhaps there is in this phenomenon a double cause, but in any case what comes from us is in us and subsists in consciousness. In the same way [p. 269] the aesthetic form is in us, in the imagination of the artist, and if the form itself passes into the marble or onto the canvas, account must be taken of the concurrence of matter, which is capable of taking all forms. In general, a being produces only what is possible for it, what is in its power, and all its possible states are contained in its essence. In this sense the effect is always in the cause, unless it be found that a fact is complex and is contained as possible in the relation of two substances. Starting from the principle of containment, we can penetrate further into the analysis of the causal connection. All that is in the effect is also in the cause; all that is outside the cause is outside the effect; but the two reciprocal propositions do not hold; for the cause is more extensive than the effect; it must explain the whole effect, if the effect is entirely within its domain, but it can furnish no explanation of the facts that go beyond its essence and its relations. All the phenomena of consciousness borrow their clearness from the nature of the mind, and there is nothing in them that is not found in our properties; but the nature of the soul can throw no light on the phenomena of the external world.

p. 270

But causality does not express merely relations of containment and of subordination; it designates in addition, and this is what distinguishes it, a relation of determination; it is the relation of the determining to the determined, the relation that is marked by the preposition by. The cause is that by which another thing is. The effect is always something determinate, limited in time or in space; it has this or that quality, this or that form; all these determinations have their reason in the being that has produced them by its activity. If the effect is physical and necessary, it is because the cause is a body whose action is necessary; if the effect is spiritual and arbitrary, it is because the cause is a soul whose action is free; if the effect is weak or powerful, transient or lasting, it is because the cause manifests itself under the same characters. Hence the axiom: such a cause, such an effect; such an effect, such a cause; everything that is determined is determined according to the essence of its cause; in other words, the cause and the effect are alike [p. 270] and proportional; they have the same form and the same essence under different magnitudes. All the determinations of the effect must therefore be explained by the cause. This is why the cause may also be defined as the determining or sufficient reason, the reason by virtue of which the effect is such as it is and not otherwise. For the cause is a species of reason and has all the characters of this category, but it is reason in so far as, by its activity, it brings about something determinate that is made in its image. Whatever is cause is at the same time reason, but whatever is reason is not cause. For a relation of reason to exist between two things, it suffices that the one be contained in the essence of the other; for a relation of causality to exist between them, it is further necessary that the one be effected by the other in conformity with its essence. In this sense a simple property, like space or motion, is the reason of all the combinations with which geometry or mechanics is concerned; but a being alone, a spiritual or material substance, can be a cause. The idea of cause, so important in the experimental sciences, is foreign to mathematical studies (1). When it is said that our cognitions have their cause in thought, an improper expression is used, it is given to be understood that thought is a being that acts, whereas it is only a property; we must say that our cognitions are effects of the soul, considered as thought, or modifications of the soul, in so far as it is an intelligent substance.

p. 271

Causality therefore designates a threefold relation: containment, subordination, determination, and consequently similarity. In this relation we must examine the terms and the connection. The cause is a being that effects something according to its essence. The effect is sometimes a phenomenon, sometimes a substance, which are determined by the agent. The effect may in its turn become a cause with respect to new phenomena, but not with respect to its own cause. Between the cause and the effect the relation is unilateral and not circular. Ignorance may engender misery and [p. 271] misery engender crime, but crime does not create the ignorance from which it proceeds. The causal connection is not a mere conjunction, a fortuitous meeting, but a connection, a necessary bond. I do not mean by this that the effect is always necessitated, which would do away with every free cause, but that it is such as it is, necessitated or free, by virtue of its cause. Between a free cause and free acts there exists a morally necessary connection, in the sense that the soul, as free, can act only freely; between a corporeal cause and corporeal phenomena, the connection is physically necessary. This relation may be stated in the consecrated formulas: “Data causa, datur effectus; sublata causa, tollitur effectus.” If the cause exists, the effect exists, in an open or latent manner, and the effect will be realized as soon as it finds the conditions of its realization in external circumstances, as physicists, chemists, and geologists know; moreover, if the cause is material, the effect can be foreseen and calculated with entire certainty. When the cause ceases or diminishes, the effect ceases or is gradually weakened, as the course of diseases bears witness. No effects without a cause, or rather no phenomena without a cause. Chance makes no exception to this rule. The accidents of life, the contingent events that make happiness and misfortune, are not facts without a cause, but facts that result from the concurrence of several causes, beyond our foresight. That a distant relative should bequeath us his property is often a natural thing which might have been expected; but if he had children and had shown ill-disposed intentions toward us, the same fact becomes chance; yet it is not without a cause that the children die, that feelings change, and that we are still alive to gather the inheritance. That a ship should perish and a single passenger escape the wreck, that lightning should strike us in the midst of a crowd, are unforeseen events, but not facts without a cause.

(1) Herschel, Discours sur l’étude de la philosophie naturelle, Part II, ch. i.

p. 272

Aristotle distinguished four kinds of causes: the material cause, the formal cause, the efficient cause, and the final cause. The first two are not causes, but the [p. 272] constitutive elements of beings; the last indicates the end, the aim, the destination of things. The efficient cause alone deserves the name: it is the determining or sufficient reason of which we have spoken and of which Leibniz made such broad applications. To the efficient cause the Schools oppose the deficient cause, which is rather the suppression of a counter-cause or of an obstacle, for example the omission of a remedy or the absence of a sentinel. A negation as such can never cause a positive effect, but can only favor the action of another cause by leaving it free scope. Instrumental causes are of the same kind, pure instruments that need no other name. Occasional causes, brought into honor by the Cartesian doctrine, are still only a verbal satisfaction given to common sense. God alone is the real cause of all that happens in the world, Malebranche thought, but men like to believe that they are causes: occasional causes, granted; real causes, no. The mind cannot act upon matter, nor matter upon the mind; it is God who moves our limbs, on the occasion of our will. Occasional causes are therefore occasions for the exercise of another causality.

p. 273

Of all this series of causes, multiplied at pleasure or inspired by the difficulties of science, there remains only the efficient cause. But nothing prevents us from distinguishing in causality as many forms as there are kinds of beings: there are moral causes and physical causes, first causes and second causes, free causes and necessitated causes. The denial of a first cause in the chain of causes is a captious reasoning that Aristotle described as progress to infinity, because it leaves no rest to the thought that pursues the cause of the world. A more important distinction is that of isolated causes and concomitant causes. Two causes may act against each other or with each other: in the first case there is opposition, and within certain limits a neutralization of causes; in the second case there is concurrence, or concomitant causes. The concurrence of causes presents as many varieties as there are [p. 273] kinds of substances. In the chemical combination of two bodies, as in the parallelogram of forces, there is a concurrence of physical causes. In the education and in the affinities of souls, from which friendship and love are born, there is a concurrence of moral causes. In the movements of the life of relation, there is a concurrence of a moral force and a physical force. If Malebranche and Leibniz had recognized the possibility of this concurrence, founded on the intimate relation that exists between the soul and the cerebral nerves, they would have avoided the hypotheses of occasional causes and of preestablished harmony. Metaphysics, finally, can establish the concurrence of an infinite cause and a finite cause in inspiration, in the discovery of the true, in the realization of the good, in the providential government of the world.

p. 274

Let us now see to what the idea of cause is applied. Whether the fact be legitimate or not, we must confess that man raises the question of cause with regard to everything that is finite, substance or phenomenon, things eternal or temporal, without even respecting the limits of experience. It is doubtless in relation to the self that we are first conscious of causality. Each of us possesses the intuition of himself and the intuition of his acts; between the self and its acts each likewise sees a bond, and affirms that this bond is the relation of cause to effect. Hume alone denies the power of the soul over itself and over the body, because he declares it inexplicable; but, explicable or not, this power is attested by all who have the feeling of their will and of their responsibility; it is a property which experimental psychology points out and which it ought to admit even if we knew neither its circumstances, nor its conditions, nor its reason. Why are we causes, or what is the cause of our causality? Metaphysics will answer, but let us not forget that a fact loses nothing of its reality because its cause is unknown. Where, then, is the cause of our acts? It is in us, in the self, whether in the soul, if the act is purely spiritual, or in the body, if the act is physical, or in man, if the act is at once spiritual and physical, like speech. The child does not know these distinctions [p. 274] and is content to affirm the self as the cause of its acts. Between these two terms, indeed, are found all the relations that constitute causality. But thought does not stop at this first answer; when it knows that the self is the cause of its modifications, it asks what is the cause of the self itself. Just now we were dealing with phenomena, and we found their cause in a substance; the question now is whether this substance in its turn has not a cause.

Let us observe in this connection that cause always indicates a relation of containment and subordination, and that, consequently, to inquire into the cause of a thing is to inquire into the whole of which it is a part, or into the higher essence in which it is contained and by which it is determined. Thought rises and extends itself more and more in the search for causes; it goes from the phenomenon to the substance, and from the finite to the infinite: this is the dialectical procedure of reason. I return to my question: what is the cause of the self? Could it perhaps be the self itself? No; the self is not contained in the self, nor subordinate to the self; it is the self and nothing more; between our acts and ourselves there exists a relation of dependence and inclusion, but nothing of the kind exists between the self and its essence. The self is nothing without its essence; how, then, being nothing, could it have effected its essence and created its properties? Fénelon says very well: “Did I make myself? No, for to make, one must be; nothingness makes nothing. Therefore, to make myself, I would have had to be before being, which is a manifest contradiction (1).” But the proposition is general, if the principle of causality is exact. We must therefore say: no being is the cause of itself, although it has often been said: “Deus causa sui.” God is nothing without the divine essence, and it is not as nothing that he can acquire divinity. If God were the cause of himself, he would also be the effect of himself, which is absurd.

p. 275

To find the cause of the self, we must rise above [p. 275] the self. If the self is body, it will have its cause in nature; if it is mind, it will find its cause in the spiritual world; if it is the being that unites a mind and a body, its cause will be humanity. Man, indeed, as body, is part of the world of bodies; he is subject to all the laws of nature, and his material constitution is wholly determined by the elements, by the volume, by the motion of the earth; as mind, he is part of the realm of minds, of universal reason, and must seek there the explanation of his intellectual properties and of the laws which he freely obeys; as man, finally, he is a member of the human race, he is subordinate to his species, he is determined in his attributes and in his limits, in conformity with the whole that he represents. The idea of causality seems therefore to apply exactly, according to its scientific characteristics, to the search for the sufficient reason of the self; and yet we have already passed beyond the limits of experience. We speak of humanity, of nature, of mind, that is to say, of things that are unique in their kind and perhaps infinite, whereas observation permits us to perceive only a small portion of the universe. The globe and the solar system, to which our body belongs, are part of a vaster whole, of the whole of nature, and it is this nature, which escapes our senses, that we conceive as the cause of the general properties of bodies. In the same way terrestrial humanity, if our hypotheses are verified, is a ring detached from a more extensive whole, from the universal humanity that occupies all the habitable globes of space; it is there that we place the cause of man, although no sensible intuition can attain this object.

(1) Fénelon, Traité de l’existence et des attributs de Dieu, Part II, ch. ii.

p. 276

We have not reached the end of our investigations. The bodily and spiritual constitution of man is bound up with the system of the moral world and of the physical world, and these two worlds appear to us as infinite in their kind, or as containing in their essence an infinity of finite beings, minds or bodies. Can dialectic mount higher, and apply the principle of causality still further to infinite kinds? The cause of man resides in [p. 276] the world; but where is the cause of the world? We have said that the effect is contained in the cause; consequently, the question of cause may be raised with regard to everything that is finite or determinate, but only with regard to the finite; for the finite alone is contained in something else; the infinite contains all, but is contained in nothing. If the idea of cause cannot be adapted scientifically to the infinite, what are we to think of the cause of the world, supposing the world infinite in each of its kinds, as mind, as nature, and as humanity? There is a difficulty here, which will be resolved later by the distinction between relative infinites and the absolute infinite. Let us remark only that the world is nothing but the collection of finite beings, distributed in species and genera, united in nature, in mind, and in humanity, and that every kind as such is a determination of reality, a part of the whole, even though it should extend to the infinite or comprise an infinity of individual things. In this sense each kind in the world is still limited or finite, since it is determinate; it is a particular face of the essence, and must also as such have its cause. One being alone is outside the series of causes, the one that is absolutely infinite, above every kind, the one that we call God. We may ask the cause of the universe without wronging the scientific theory of causality; but we cannot ask without contradiction what is the cause of God, once we have conceived the thought of pure and simple Being, of the essence one and whole, which is all and comprehends all. It is to misunderstand God as sole and unique Being to raise in his regard the question of cause, by saying: why God? God would no longer be God if he had a cause above him. God is therefore without cause; he is himself the ultimate cause of all that is in the world. Consequently, we must no longer say: everything has a cause; but we shall say: everything has a cause, except God; or rather: everything that is determinate has a cause. Likewise, we must not say: God is the cause of everything; but we shall say: God is the cause of everything, except himself; or rather: God is the cause of everything that is determinate.

p. 277

An objection presents itself. Causality implies a certain similarity between the cause and the effect: what resemblance, then, is there between the infinite and the finite, between God and the nature which he has created, between nature and bodies, between God, humanity, and the self? We can only indicate the answer, leaving it to be justified in metaphysics; and instead of relying on the analogy of the categories, which are common to Being and to beings, we shall hold only to the finite and the infinite, which often appear contrary. The finite is like the infinite, because it too is infinite after its own manner, in potency, if not in reality: every part of space, of time, of matter, is continuous and divisible to infinity like its whole, and consequently embraces an infinity of parts, which are infinitely small; likewise every rational mind possesses the idea of the infinite and can develop in infinite time by realizing successively an infinity of possible acts or states. Humanity, like its author, is unique and infinite, but in its own kind; it is the being of harmony of the world within the limits of creation, as God is the being of infinite and absolute harmony; the self, which has its cause in humanity, is also unique, as an individuality representative of its kind.

Between the absolute infinite and individuals there is the relative infinite, which serves as a link between them and maintains the similarity, in the plan of the world, between the first cause and the last effects. The finite is to the relative infinite as the relative infinite is to God. Everything is linked together in the universe, and contrasts do not efface resemblances. Let us not, then, set aside divine causality on the pretext that there is no proportionality between the cause and the effect: a world infinite in time and in space corresponds to the majesty of the supreme cause, and the infinite series of bodies, of minds, and of men corresponds to the relative infinity of the physical world, of the spiritual world, and of humanity.

It would be superfluous to insist on the importance of the principle of causality for philosophy and for science in general. Most of our reasonings rest on its authority. Man is in some sort reduced to himself in

p. 278

Logic. — I. 18 [p. 278] knowledge, and must seize in himself, in his organs or in his reason, either the image or the idea of external or supra-sensible objects. In this situation it is only thanks to the law of causality that he can issue from the sphere of the self and gain a foothold in the world. If our sensations have a cause, we have reason to believe that a material universe exists. If our ideas have a cause, we have the hope of reaching God: for then the idea of cause, as a determinate element of reason, will likewise have its cause, and the ideas of the infinite and the absolute, as distinct from our own nature, will raise us up to the infinite and absolute Being. But if the principle of causality is a vain illusion of the mind, we are condemned to withdraw into ourselves, we have no longer the right to affirm any transcendent reality, God and the world cease to exist for reason. What do I say? The self itself escapes us and is reduced to a pure phenomenology, for it is by the consciousness of our causality that we take the direction of our activity, that we seek to realize an end, and that we perceive some order, some connection in the series of our acts. Set aside all cause, and there is nothing left but incoherence and confusion in the succession of phenomena within us and in nature; all science becomes impossible. The skeptics, ancient and modern, have had a feeling of this truth. When men have wished to shake the foundations of science, it is almost always the idea of causality that they have attacked. The destiny of philosophy is particularly bound up with the notion of cause.

p. 279

In antiquity, after the decline of the schools of Plato and Aristotle, Aenesidemus and Sextus Empiricus opened the struggle against the principle of causality. Taking the standpoint of materialism, Sextus declares that the causal connection can be effected only by the contact of bodies, and that this contact is impossible, since it is not the bodies but their limits that touch. This thought is ingenious, and might very well be adapted to the material world, where continuity in fact reigns between the most distant bodies, thanks to the ether; but surely nothing prevents the contact of bodies [p. 279] themselves, for surfaces are nothing without the bodies whose limit they mark. The cause, adds Sextus, cannot be distinguished from the effect, for a thing produces only what is in its nature, and if it produces what is already in its nature, it brings nothing new, it has no effect.
