Xenophanes had long before alleged this argument against the creation of the world, but Aristotle had set it aside by distinguishing between potency and act. The effect exists in potency in the cause before being realized, but it is not confounded with its cause; two things of the same nature, like a substance and its phenomena, are not identical for that reason. The same observation applies to the relation of succession which is ordinarily supposed between the cause and the effect, and which Sextus rejects on this ground, that if the cause were prior to the effect there would be a cause without an effect, and that if the effect were posterior to the cause there would be an effect without a cause: the effect and the cause are therefore contemporaneous, and consequently indistinct. There is here a serious difficulty on which authors are not yet agreed.

p. 280

We admit that to cause is to produce, to act, and that activity manifests itself in time, at this or that moment, in all the cases which observation reveals to us: then, indeed, there is a relation of succession between the cause and its effects taken separately, but it does not follow that the cause is without effect or the effect without cause, for what does not exist in act may still exist in potency, in the state of the possible. But has all activity necessarily a beginning in time? Are there not eternal causes as well as temporal causes? To decide the question without appealing to metaphysics would be to prejudge the theory of creation. Let us remark only that, according to the definition of the cause, relations of containment, of subordination, and of determination are as easily conceived between eternal things as between temporal phenomena. When it is said: matter is eternal, therefore it is without cause, therefore there is no creation, one reasons as a materialist, not as a logician; for the only conclusion that logic permits us to deduce from the premise is that [p. 280] matter is without cause in time, or that creation is not temporal. It is fitting, then, to make every reservation with regard to eternity. But, eternal causes once admitted, Sextus is right in maintaining that the cause is not necessarily prior to the effect, or that the effect and the cause may be simultaneous.

Finally, says the skeptic, the cause and the effect are constantly intermingled; the cause does not act in isolation, by virtue of its own proper energy, but concurs with the effect to produce the most heterogeneous combinations, witness the sun, which now burns, warms, lights, now hardens, softens, liquefies. The physics of the ancients had nothing to answer to such objections; but the modern theory of caloric makes us understand these diverse effects of one and the same cause by the diverse reactions of bodies that belong to multiple species or are found in distinct states. Sextus confounds the action of an isolated cause, either with the conditions, or with the concurrence of several causes. To all these difficulties he naturally added the impossibility of comprehending the supreme cause. If God is infinite, he is immobile and inanimate; if he is bounded, he is too small; if he is corporeal, he is without soul or reason, and if he is incorporeal, he is insensible. There are others besides Sextus Empiricus who hesitate before these problems, and who have not, like him, the excuse of the age.

p. 281

David Hume is a sensualist like his forebear; which is to say that he accepts as legitimate only the data of experience, except the mathematical truths, which consist in relations of ideas. Matters of fact, he says, can be known only by observation, and all the reasonings that we form with regard to them have for their basis the relation of cause to effect. Let us examine this relation carefully. It comes from the senses, no doubt, like all our knowledge. Well, no: it does not come from the senses, it does not result from experience. Causality expresses a necessary connection between two things of which one is the infallible sequel of the other. Now, however much we may consult internal or external observation, and scrutinize the action of consciousness [p. 281] and of the senses, we find facts that succeed one another, but we perceive between them no necessary bond, no connection. One ball strikes another ball, and this moves; the senses teach us nothing more; never do they point out, in the operations of objects, that mysterious power which makes causes of them. The empire of the soul over itself and over the body furnishes us with no more information concerning causality, and would itself stand much in need of explanation. If causality flows neither from bodies nor from souls, might it have its source in God, sole and immediate cause of all that happens in the world? This hypothesis leads us beyond the reach of our faculties. If we do not know how bodies act upon one another, how our soul produces ideas and determines movements in our limbs, we must, all the more, be ignorant how the sovereign intelligence operates upon beings. All that we know in this regard is that we know nothing.

p. 282

This result, moreover, was easy to foresee: causality is a necessary bond; but experience presents us with nothing absolute; it deposes in regard to determinate objects, observed at precise epochs; by what right would one carry it over to other times and other objects? In inductions of this kind there is not a shadow of necessity. All our reasonings concerning matters of fact are founded on the supposition that the future will resemble the past; as soon as there is the least suspicion that nature may change its course, the past ceases to be a rule for the future, experience loses its use and can give birth to no conclusion. It is impossible that observation should prove this resemblance of the future to the past, since it could employ no proof which does not presuppose it. Such is the real value of experience: it contains nothing necessary or absolute; how, then, could it make known to us the principle of causality? And yet experience is the source of our knowledge. What does this mean? “As we can have no idea of any thing which never appeared to our outward sense or inward sentiment, the necessary conclusion seems [p. 282] to be that we have no idea of connexion or power at all, and that these words are absolutely without any meaning, when employed either in philosophical reasonings or common life.” Causality is therefore a prejudice. There is but one way of avoiding this conclusion, and that is to make of the causal bond a simple relation of succession founded on custom or on similarity. Hence these two experimental definitions: the cause is an object so followed by another object that the presence of the first always makes us think of the second; — the cause is an object so followed by another object that all objects similar to the first are followed by objects similar to the second.

Hume has laid bare the impotence of sensualism by reducing experience to its just value. Kant does no more than translate this thought into scientific language when he declares that judgments of experience can be neither apodictic nor universal. But apart from this service, Hume has a singular logic. Here is his reasoning: the principle of causality indicates a necessary connection between the cause and the effect; now experience discovers no necessity in the succession of facts; therefore the principle of causality does not exist. Another would have concluded thus: therefore we have cognitions independent of experience; but Hume had already decided that we know nothing beyond the limits of observation, except mathematics; he had therefore to adapt the conclusion to the preconceived opinion in order to remain consistent with himself; he had to save sensualism in spite of its skeptical consequences, at the cost of contradicting himself on another point, by rejecting a principle which the author himself regards as evident and which he seeks everywhere, in the soul and in nature.

p. 283

The idea of cause is no longer attacked in our day. Only, the sensualists and the criticists wish to limit its application to the domain of experience. The latter accept it as necessary and avow that we pursue its realization even into metaphysics, but they regard this search as a usurpation of reason. The former [p. 283] deny it all necessity, take seriously the makeshift of Hume, and boldly confound causality with the habitual succession of phenomena. Succession, indeed, is a fact of observation, but it by no means corresponds to causality. First, we conceive eternal causes and effects, which coexist and do not follow one another. Next, in relation to time, causality supposes something quite other than a simple relation of priority. There exists between the cause and the effect an essential relation which is precisely the wherefore of the succession, and which escapes observation, as Hume has demonstrated. From the fact that two events follow one another, like fire and smoke, experience does not permit us to conclude that they must follow one another everywhere and always. Moreover, two things may succeed one another, even habitually, like day and night, health and sickness, war and peace, eating and drinking, without having any direct connection between them. To reason thus is to commit a paralogism: post hoc, ergo propter hoc.

p. 284

It is with causality as with the other categories. It is not contrary to experience, but prior and superior to it. Strictly speaking, experience is possible only through it, but once established, experience confirms the principle of causality as far as it can reach. It is from this point of view that Mr. Mill writes in the remarkable chapters which he devotes to causation. Mr. Mill has not taken sufficient account of the observations of Hume. The law of causality, he says, according to which whatever begins has a cause, is the root of the whole theory of induction; it concerns physical causes, not efficient or productive causes; it confines itself to establishing an invariable succession between certain phenomena, and does not pretend to pass beyond the limits of experience. Certain facts are always followed by other facts: such is the law; the invariable antecedent is the cause, and the invariable consequent the effect. So far all goes well; experience is possible; but, pressed by objections, the author soon leaves his own domain. The cause, he says, is not precisely the antecedent which is or has been followed by the same phenomenon in all our previous experiences, but the antecedent which must [p. 284] be followed by it, as long as the present order of the world lasts. Here the thesis changes: a principle is substituted for a fact, and an apodictic judgment for an assertoric judgment. The author understands well that without this substitution causality vanishes into succession. The cause therefore involves the idea of necessity, that is to say, of unconditionalness: it is the invariable antecedent which is necessarily or absolutely followed by some phenomenon. The cause and the effect are phenomena that form pairs without exception or condition. Elsewhere causality appears as a universal law, which applies to the whole present state of the world, the effect of the antecedent state, the cause of the future state, although observation can teach us nothing of these states; and the author regrets only that psychologists make an exception in favor of free will: he still takes the motives that solicit the will for determining causes, instead of considering them as conditions of voluntary activity, according to the science of the soul. This error, moreover, is explicable: the cause itself is sometimes defined as “the sum total of the conditions, positive and negative taken together (1).”

These defects in the logic of Mr. Mill are purely theoretical; but the practical sense of the author reveals itself admirably in what he calls the canons of induction. These canons are methodical rules for the search for causes within the limits of experience. The experimental methods are four in number, and each of them is summed up in a canonical formula (2).

Method of Agreement: If several instances of the same phenomenon have only one circumstance in common, this circumstance is the cause or the effect of the phenomenon in question. Take the phenomenon: the production of a soap. This phenomenon appears every time an alkali combines with a fatty matter. It may therefore be maintained that this combination is the cause of the production of soap.

(1) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, book III, ch. v: Of the Law of Universal Causation.

(2) Ibid., ch. VIII, Of the Four Methods of Experimental Inquiry.

p. 285

Method of Difference: If a case in which the phenomenon in question occurs and a case in which it does not occur have all their circumstances in common save one, this last circumstance is the cause or the effect of the phenomenon, in whole or in part. Take the phenomenon: the death of a person. It is observed that the person is found, at two consecutive moments, in a set of identical circumstances, save one, a wound in the heart. It may therefore be asserted that this wound is the cause of the death.

Method of Residues: If from a phenomenon we subtract the part that is the effect of certain antecedents, the residue of the phenomenon is the effect of the remaining antecedents. To this procedure we owe great discoveries in chemistry and in astronomy. Whenever the description of a phenomenon presents some deficiency, by virtue of known causes, it is probable that there exists an antecedent which had passed unnoticed and which is the cause of the deficiency observed. The discovery of the precession of the equinoxes, for example, has its source in an imperfect explanation of the return of the seasons by the return of the sun to the same positions in the sky.

Method of Concomitant Variations: If a phenomenon varies in any manner whatever every time that another phenomenon varies in a certain manner, the first is a cause or a direct or indirect effect of the second. Thus the oscillations of the pendulum vary according as one approaches or recedes from a mountain. The neighborhood of the mountain is the cause of the deviations of the pendulum, as the method of differences teaches; but the oscillations themselves, whose direction changes with the position of our globe, have for their cause the attraction of the earth. In the same way the movement of the tides, which corresponds exactly to the movement of the moon, has for its cause the influence of that body (1).

p. 286

These rules are ingenious, to be sure; but they are not so new as M. Taine supposes: they are the expression of procedures in use in chemistry, in physics [p. 286] in astronomy, that is to say, in the experimental sciences which are chiefly concerned with the search for causes. Herschel had broadly sketched the practical applications of the principle of causality (1); Mill has reduced them to a system and has presented the theory of them. Are they really the canons of induction? It is permissible to doubt it. No doubt the knowledge of the law of a phenomenon extends the significance of the phenomenon and brings it under a general class; but, the law once found, there remains no unknown to be disengaged, as in ordinary induction, and the certainty is often as complete after a single trial as in mathematics. When we know, for example, by the method of concomitant variations, that mercury rises in the barometric tube because of the weight of the air, conviction is formed as soon as the phenomenon is understood, and we conceive no disturbance in the order of nature, nor any discovery of analogous or contrary facts, that could modify it. Thought, in pursuing causes in the world, does not rise from the individual to the species, nor from the species to the genus, as in the abstract sciences, but from the fact to the law; it does not proceed by successive generalization, but by intuition, as we seize the infinite on the occasion of the finite or a geometrical truth on the occasion of an image. This is a new case of the dialectical procedure of reason, where the extension and the comprehension of subordinate notions have no longer any value. If we still arrive at times at a definition, as by the use of inductive reasoning, it is only a genetic and not a theoretical definition, explaining a phenomenon by its origin instead of setting forth its properties. Such are the ordinary definitions of the tides as movements of the great waters produced by lunar attraction, or of eclipses as a subtraction of light caused by the interposition of an opaque body.

(1) H. Taine, Le Positivisme anglais, étude sur Stuart Mill, VII. Paris, 1864.

p. 287

But if the principle of causality is verified in experience, it does not depend on it. The canons of Mr. Mill, far from creating it, presuppose it. Their aim is not to search [p. 287] whether a general law of causality exists in the world, but, this law being given, to apply it to the various orders of phenomena, in order to learn what is the cause of each of them. It is a question of application and not of principle. Causality is none the less an a priori category, which preexists observation, which everyone understands without being taught and adapts as best he can to all the phenomena of which he wishes to give himself an account, to his sensations, to his acts, to his essence, to everything that he grasps within the limits of experience and even beyond. Inductive logic therefore makes use of it, as dialectic does, in the form of apodictic and universal judgments. Everything that is determinate has a cause; every effect is proportioned to its cause; everything that is in the effect is in the cause. “The principle of causality,” says Royer-Collard, “is expressed thus: Whatever begins to exist has a cause. This principle is necessary and universal; it suffers no exception at any moment of duration, at any point of space; the contrary appears to us not only impossible, but absurd.” It is not a prejudice, as Hume maintained, nor a generalized notion, as Locke claimed, but a truth evident in itself. Experience does not teach what is necessarily. Leibniz, in one of his Letters, makes the same observation: “Si Lockius discrimen inter veritates necessarias et eas quæ nobis sola inductione utcumque innotescunt, satis considerasset, animadvertisset necessarias non posse comprobari nisi ex principiis mente insitis, cum sensus quidem doceant quid fiat, sed non quid necessario fiat.” [If Locke had sufficiently considered the distinction between necessary truths and those which become known to us in some fashion by induction alone, he would have observed that necessary truths cannot be proved except from principles inborn in the mind, since the senses indeed teach what happens, but not what happens necessarily.] Causality is a law of our nature. It is in the feeling of our own activity that it is first revealed. But consciousness shows us only the fact, not the necessity. The fact is the occasion and not the principle of this necessary conception; it does not contain it, it suggests it (1).

(1) Herschel, Discours sur l’étude de la philosophie natur., Part II, ch. vi.

p. 288

Cause, substance, unity, identity, quantity are categories of reason which we know directly [p. 288] in themselves, without the aid of the senses, and the sciences that deal with them are independent of experience. The moral and political sciences, a new dismemberment of philosophy, share the same fate, although the current of materialism and positivism seeks to draw them into the movement of the experimental sciences. Their object is the ideas of the good, the just, the beautiful, the true, of God, and they comprise ethics, law, aesthetics, logic, religion. To be sure, the history of manners, of laws, of the arts, of the sciences, and of cults is an empirical study: the facts of social and religious life are subject to observation, and moral statistics are a collection of documents obtained by the testimony of the senses. But besides facts there are principles; besides actions, duty; besides human laws, right; besides opinions and schools, truth and beauty; besides beliefs, God. When one knows the history of manners or the facts of the moral life in ancient and modern times, there remains to be studied moral philosophy, or the principles that must direct the human will; after positive law and positive religions, natural law and natural religion. In a word, each of the sciences that have for their object the good, the just, the beautiful, the true, the perfect, comprises two parts, the one historical, which gives the facts or phenomena, the other philosophical, which sets forth the principles or absolute laws. Now of these two parts, the one is purely experimental, the other purely rational or a priori, in conformity with the opposition of history and philosophy throughout their whole extent. The pretension of the materialists and positivists is to efface this difference, to reduce the science of human life, in its individual, social, or religious manifestations, to the comparative knowledge of facts, of positive institutions, setting principles aside, which amounts to suppressing philosophy. Nowhere is this thesis less justified, and nowhere does it turn more directly against the intention of most of its defenders, than in the domain of the moral and political sciences.

(1) Royer-Collard, Fragments théoriques, VI; Œuvres de Reid, vol. IV.

p. 289

The ideas of the good, the beautiful, the true, the just, which preside [p. 289] over these sciences, are neither a result of sensible observation, nor a product of induction or analogy, nor an arbitrary creation of the human mind, but data of reason, which each of us bears originally within himself, which he regards as the necessary laws of his activity, and which he applies constantly, according to his lights, to all the facts of individual and social life (1). This is what we have to establish.

p. 290

These ideas, first, are universal. They enlighten every man coming into this world and seem to suit all times and all places. What child, what savage in a state of health, cannot say: this is true, that is false; this is good, that is bad? The notions of the beautiful and the true will be more or less incomplete, I grant, and the judgments of approval or blame will vary according to the culture of the conscience; but good and evil, the just and the unjust will be recognized everywhere, now under one form, now under another, and can be rendered in all languages. Otherwise human nature would cease to be the same, and it could be said that there exist men without conscience, without heart, and without reason. If the good and the beautiful are lacking to no intelligence, can we better understand that they should be absent from certain epochs or exiled from certain points of space, than that on other globes, where rational beings live, there should be neither good nor evil, neither truth nor error, as there is perhaps no mercury nor coal, no ferns nor orchids, no whales nor lions? No, the ideas of reason are not particular and variable, but immutable and universal. The ancients attributed to them the same characters as the moderns: “una lex et sempiterna et immortalis.” [one law, both everlasting and immortal] They are, moreover, necessary and not contingent; they impose themselves on the conscience, in spite of our freedom, they are imperative and become the source of duty, as the moral necessity of human life. He who has recognized the truth owes it obedience, unless he revolts against himself; he who sees a [p. 290] good to do or a wrong to repair cannot hesitate, if he wishes to spare himself regrets or remorse. Justice is like a master who commands and binds the will; only this bond is of another nature than the blind attraction that chains the movements of matter: duty is not fatality, because it addresses itself to the free will and can be fulfilled only freely; that is precisely what makes the imperative.

(1) V. Cousin, Cours de philosophie sur le fondement des idées absolues du vrai, du beau et du bien.

p. 291

Rational ideas, finally, are absolute and demand to be recognized in themselves and realized for themselves, in an absolute manner. They are diverse faces of absolute reality, or attributes of God, if the metaphysics of all ages is not deceptive: it is God who is truth one and whole, inasmuch as he has the consciousness of all that is; it is God who is the good one and whole, inasmuch as he realizes all that is conformable to his essence; it is God who is justice one and whole, inasmuch as he grants to all beings in the world the conditions necessary to the accomplishment of their destiny. This is why the good, the beautiful, and the true must be seized immediately by an intellectual intuition, as Plato wished; they shine by their own light and illumine reason independently of every condition of sensibility and training. The beautiful strikes the mind, not because it is useful or agreeable, but because it is beautiful; it may be useless, like the coloring of flowers or of birds, it may be frightening or overwhelming to the senses, like a storm or a desert, without ceasing to be beautiful. The feeling of the good is like the feeling of the beautiful, immediate and pure of all selfish consideration. This is why, finally, the true and the beautiful, the good and the just must be sought and realized for themselves: “honesta expetenda per se, et turpia per se fugienda sunt.” [honorable things are to be sought for their own sake, and base things to be shunned for their own sake] Certain classes of truths appear foreign to the interests of man; others seem contrary to the habits of thought and to the stability of traditional institutions; no matter, we must examine everything and test everything; our nature demands it and God wills it. Duty also is at times in opposition with our conveniences and our personal [p. 291] advantages; no matter, conscience speaks, we must obey. Our destiny is not to enjoy, but to do good, and in case of conflict between the good and pleasure, it is not the good that must be sacrificed to pleasure, but pleasure to the good. Otherwise there is no more merit, no more dignity, no more beauty in human life. Do what you ought, come what may: this is the sincere voice of conscience and the source of moral heroism. The most profound science is in accord on this capital point with the common opinion of men and of peoples. The good, says Kant, imposes itself on rational beings as a categorical imperative, and not as a counsel or a conditional command, like pleasure and the interests of life. What does this mean? That we must do good for the sake of the good, purely and simply, in an absolute manner, without consulting our inclinations, without regard to the possible consequences of our acts, without even thinking of the penalties and rewards that may overtake us in this life or in the other. To accomplish the good for the sake of the good, to practice justice for the sake of justice, to seek truth for the sake of truth, is the form of the absolute in the activity of creatures; to abandon this line of conduct is to accommodate oneself to circumstances and to fall into the corruption of casuistry. Every human conscience, questioned at the right moment, brands trickery and admires devotion.

p. 292

The ideas of the good, the beautiful, the true, the just are therefore really different in their characters from individual notions and abstract conceptions: they are absolute, necessary, universal. Hence they are prior and superior to observation. I grant that we may find in experience generous actions, excellent laws, works full of merit; but let us not forget that in these acts there are two things: a sensible phenomenon which is produced in time and in space and which is given by the senses; an immutable and eternal principle which is given to us by reason. The phenomenon is the object of a sensible intuition, the idea is the object of an intellectual intuition. In a good action we must distinguish, first, the action, and then that which makes the action good or [p. 292] conformable to the good. Now there is nothing in the action that reveals to the senses that it is good or bad, that it is or is not as it ought to be. In fact, its morality resides in the intention of the agent, which escapes external observation, and its legitimacy consists in its relation to an absolute principle, which reason alone can grasp. A being deprived of reason may, like us, perceive an act, but never will it suspect that this act is good or bad. This is why the authors who, following the example of Hutcheson, insist with too much complacency on the sensible part of our organization, have been obliged to invent for the good and the bad, for the beautiful and the ugly, a special sense which animals do not possess. This sense, unknown to the physiologists, is reason. To admit that observation bears within certain limits on good and evil, on the just and the unjust, we must therefore suppose that sensible knowledge is already constituted by the concurrence of reason; for, strictly speaking, these ideas are primitive data which, considered in themselves, apart from the phenomena in which they are mingled, are above all experience. The good, the beautiful, the true, in their purity and in their fullness, are God himself, who is in no respect an object of observation.

As universal and necessary, the ideas of the good and the beautiful, of the true and the just are assuredly the object of judgments that pass beyond all the bounds of a possible experimentation. The moral and political sciences are of the same family as the mathematical sciences, and their principles or theorems are enunciated in categorical, apodictic, and universal propositions. Everything that is conformable to the divine essence is conformable to reason and to the general order of the world; everything that is rational is good, is beautiful, is true, is just; everything that is true is beautiful, everything that is just is good, everything that is unjust is false. Metaphysics alone can justify these propositions; but, setting aside their objective validity, they are cognitions which reign in all epochs of philosophical development and which singularly confound the modern mania for reducing everything to experience.

p. 293

It is not only by their generality, but also by their use, that moral, political, and aesthetic principles are independent of observation. Far from being drawn from experience, they serve precisely as a check upon empiricism. What would be the matter for observation here? The facts of rational life, the productions of the human mind in the past and in the present, that is to say customs and manners, laws and social institutions, the arts and letters. It is evident that if we had of good and evil only an experimental knowledge, this knowledge would never rise above the present state of manners and could in no case be contrary to it. Facts and laws would be the inviolable rule of conscience in the moral world, as in the physical world thought lets itself be guided by the phenomena that it subjects to analysis. Is this the real situation of the soul in the presence of the works of the human will? No, it is the inverse relation that is true. Conscience is not crushed by facts, stifled by customs, oppressed by traditions; it dominates them, it summons them before the inner tribunal, it judges and condemns them, it annuls or reforms them, it replaces them by new facts and by opposite institutions. What is Socrates? The insurrection of conscience against the moral and religious state of Greece. What are Plato and Zeno? The reign of wisdom and virtue substituted for the reign of violence, the end of the Hellenic spirit and the beginning of a new era. What are Descartes and Bacon? The sovereignty of reason succeeding the old authorities that enslaved the free action of the intellect. There is no epoch of history in which these protests do not break out against contemporary society; there is certainly no man in his right mind who has not groaned and suffered over the weaknesses, the vices, the ignorance, or the corruption of his fellow citizens.

Conscience therefore bears within itself a criterium for the appraisal of the phenomena of moral and social life; so far from borrowing from manners the idea of the good, from the civil laws the idea of the just, from the arts the idea of the beautiful, from letters

p. 294

Logic. — I. 19 [p. 294] the idea of the true, it criticizes manners by means of the idea of the good, it provokes a social improvement by relying on the idea of right, it transforms, finally, the whole life of rational beings by comparing what it is with what it ought to be. It is thus that progress comes to light and that the future is prepared by the invisible work of conscience, because this work is independent of all experience. Observation has for its object what is or has been; the moral sciences, on the contrary, have for their object what ought to be. It is always the difference between the a posteriori and the a priori elements of knowledge, between history and philosophy. Now to know what the life of man ought to be, as rational, what society ought to be, as conformed to the absolute principle of right, it is certainly not experience but reason that must be followed. We seek perfection, whereas experience offers us only imperfect things.

p. 295

We can now glimpse that there exists, beside the physical world, subject to the laws of motion or of efficient causes, as Leibniz said, another world, subject to the laws of final causes or of the good. The former is essentially invariable, and all the bodies in it gravitate perpetually toward their center in orbits that are always uniform. The latter is essentially variable, if not in its principles, at least in its phenomena and in its internal combinations, because it is formed gradually by the action of free causes that gravitate toward God. This moral world, whose genesis history offers us in one of its manifestations, in its earthly life, is the antithesis of the physical world: it is the world of souls, of intelligent and free beings, governed by reason. The ideas of the good and the just, of the true and the beautiful are its fundamental laws, and the same ideas, determined by the understanding with the aid of the imagination, become an ideal, a type of absolute perfection, which is the aim or the end of rational activity. The good, in fact, inasmuch as it imposes itself upon conscience as an imperative, possesses the characters of necessity and generality that make it easily [p. 295] recognized as law: what must be met with in all our actions, what is common to all the phenomena of moral life, is the good. Here is the law, a natural, universal, immutable law, which, combined with the freedom of the agents charged with carrying it out, engenders duty. But the good rests upon good will and is realized only progressively in life, as the soul cultivates itself in its various directions and rises to the feeling of divine things: here is perfectibility in the moral world, in place of the inertia that dominates in matter, and the last term of this progress, in which we abstract from all the imperfections inherent in finite things, is the ideal, the beacon of reason. There is an ideal only in the realm of freedom: it is in individual life, in the family, in society, in the cultivation of the arts and sciences, that we must unceasingly distinguish between the real state and the ideal state, between the positive and the absolute, between what is and what ought to be; in nature pure reality reigns, the brute fact, the positive, from which the ideal is absent; it is there, but there only, that everything is as it ought to be.

p. 296

The error of positivism is to confound these two aspects of the world. Whence it follows that there is no longer an ideal for man: “the ideal is not, it is made; it is less the goal toward which humanity tends than the changing result of the efforts of all peoples.” Here is thought abandoned to its own uncertainties, without rule and without direction. Individual feeling is once more the measure of all things (1). The mission of art will therefore be the imitation of nature and the reproduction of the hideous rather than of the beautiful, because beautiful nature resembles the ideal too much: here is realism. The mission of society will be to turn constantly in the same circle of traditional institutions, for all is well as it is, and innovation has no longer any reason to be; it is not even understood that improvements could have occurred in the past. What, then, will become of natural right and natural religion, the fairest conquests of philosophy [p. 296] modern, the most brilliant signs of a limitless progress in the domain of the moral and political sciences? The question is idle: natural right means ideal right, absolute right, rational right, right conformed in every point to the nature of man, apart from every consideration of time, place, and culture. It is the vague feeling of the rights of man and of the citizen that has aroused the most decisive social movement of our epoch; but positivism does not know this order of facts and has no place for reason, for the absolute, for the ideal in its catalogue of the faculties of the soul. Natural right is therefore suppressed; positive right suffices. Natural religion will doubtless follow the same path and yield its place to positive religions. Error! Positive religions are still too lofty, for they concern themselves with God, with the infinite and the absolute, with the supreme ideal of reason: they belong, according to Comte, to the primitive phase of the development of thought, which, passing through metaphysics, ends in positivism. Now positivism does not know the infinite and the absolute, which are not observable facts. It proposes, in consequence, to replace God by humanity, and urges man to worship himself.

(1) E. Caro, l'Idée de Dieu et ses nouveaux critiques, ch. i. Paris, 1864.

p. 297

Between natural right, which is absolute and immutable, and positive legislations, which are variable and contingent, there is room for an intermediate science, charged with applying the principles to the facts, according to times, places, and relations, or with setting forth the ways and means by which present society may advance gradually along the paths of ideal society, without groping or violence. This science is Politics, often confused with the whole body of the social sciences: owing to its double basis, the one philosophical, the other historical, it proceeds now a priori, by deduction, now a posteriori, seeking the most favorable occasion for the application of a truth that has reached the state of maturity (1). The statesman has a [p. 297] twofold problem to solve: he must know, first, what reforms are to be introduced in order that institutions may approach the ideal conditions of human nature; he must know, next, when and how they are to be carried out, having regard to all the historical circumstances of national life. Experience does not teach what is good or bad in society, but it alone can indicate the most opportune moment for executing what is recognized as good. In a word, the question of legitimacy in every social debate belongs to pure reason, but the question of opportuneness belongs wholly to experience.

Let us now listen to an author who does not conceal from himself the force of the objections. Can politics be anything other than an empirical science, which, observing the character of nations, their manners, their origin, their climate, shows the variations that social forms must undergo by reason of these diverse data? Is not the attempt to discover an absolute principle in these matters a chimera? No people resembles another people, no epoch another epoch: everything in institutions and in laws must therefore be variable and relative. See what evils the illusion of an absolute truth in politics has produced. Peoples have forgotten their traditions, they have set out in pursuit of a perfect society; they have wished to remake their institutions a priori on this imaginary model, and ever since, society has drifted at random without finding anywhere to cast anchor. Finally, consider the science itself. The greatest publicists in the world are not dreamers, theorists like Plato or Rousseau, but observers like Aristotle and Montesquieu.

(1) H. Ahrens, Cours de droit naturel, Introd., ch. i, § 2. 5th ed. Brussels, 1860.

p. 298

Experience, answers M. Janet, is doubtless indispensable; an a priori politics is insufficient and incomplete; even if we knew what is best, we should still have to consult the aptitudes of peoples, their manners, and the means at our disposal for doing good. What appears just in itself may be unjust in a given case. No political form should be rejected. But I maintain that there is something [p. 298] just in itself; that the State is not a mere mechanism, that it is composed of moral persons, that it is itself a moral person, having a moral end, duties and rights, and that, if it is permitted to attain this destiny in various ways, it is not permitted to ignore it entirely. I will add that the efforts the modern peoples have made to improve their condition are more worthy of esteem than of aversion, though I have no indulgence for the excesses that have accompanied these undertakings. Modern society is better constituted than the society of the Middle Ages; the most necessary interests and rights have never been better guaranteed than today. Finally, as to the argument drawn from the publicists, I hold to the very examples that are set against me. Aristotle is an empirical politician: hence he justified slavery. As slavery was a universal fact in his time, he thought this fact was conformable to right, and he sought to give the reason for it. “But if it suffices that a fact be a fact in order to be legitimate, I ask why we have a horror of cannibals. For to feed on human flesh is also a fact; and the cannibals themselves give of this fact a reason that is not contemptible: it is that this flesh is very good.” Montesquieu, in his turn, had the genius of observation, but this adversary of slavery, of torture, of intolerance, of barbarity in punishments, of despotism, did not lack an ideal (1).

p. 299

The moral and political sciences, inasmuch as they are ideal, are therefore independent of observation. It is clear from this that they are not a product of generalization or of the inductive method either, a question learnedly discussed by M. Blanc Saint-Bonnet, starting from the attributes of freedom and perfectibility that characterize rational beings. Induction is sure, says this author, in an order in which the fundamental property of objects is inertia, or the impossibility of giving themselves any [p. 299] modification. Since in this order nothing can happen without the concurrence of an external force, all facts lead infallibly to their law. But in the moral world, where the fundamental property of beings is will, the faculty of modifying oneself in conformity with or in opposition to the law, we must begin by distinguishing the facts produced by obedience to the law from the contrary facts produced by a guilty will. Of these two classes of actions, which must be chosen in order to induce the law from it? If we do not know the law beforehand, how are we to know the facts that conform to it; and if we cannot distinguish the facts conformable to the law from those contrary to it, how are we to ascend from facts to laws in the moral world (1)?

(1) P. Janet, Histoire de la philosophie morale et politique, Introduction. Paris, 1858.

p. 300

There, in fact, is the question. In the physical world, all facts reveal and proclaim their law, whereas in the moral world many facts conceal and obscure the law of free beings. In the physical world, all facts are good: to arrive at the law it suffices to observe what is; in the moral world, on the contrary, facts are doubtful, and to obtain the law we must know what ought to be. Now one of two things: either those who conclude to a moral law by induction begin by dividing moral facts into two kinds, the good and the bad, accepting the one, repudiating the other, and finding the law in the analysis of the former; or else they ignore this distinction, they admit all facts, just and unjust, and rely on this basis to discover the law. In the first case, they beg the question, they already know the law they are seeking, for acts can pass for good or bad only in relation to the law that they fulfill or infringe; in the second case, they regard all facts as legitimate, as perfect, as being the result of necessary causes, and consequently deny that there is in the moral world any other force [p. 300] than the necessity that reigns in nature. Empiricists or positivists cannot escape this alternative: they either turn in a circle or must admit the fatalistic theory of accomplished facts. By what right would they condemn slavery, the Inquisition, the St. Bartholomew massacre, conquest, the oppression of nationalities, in a word, the vices, the crimes, the abuses of force? These are constant facts in the life of men and of peoples, just as much as virtue and the practice of justice; and empiricism, without consciousness of the law, ignores the moral quality of acts and must confine itself to inducing the law from the whole body of facts. It will therefore seek a law that can explain and justify at once violence and right, persecution and charity, despotism and political liberty, as the opposite motions of bodies, from above downward and from below upward, are accounted for by the same formula. Here is the confusion of the physical world and the moral world in all its rigor. It suffices to understand it to be revolted by the consequences it brings with it.

(1) Blanc Saint-Bonnet, de l'Unité spirituelle ou de la Société et de son but au delà du temps, Prolégomènes, ch. v. Paris, 1841.

p. 301

Hence the theory of accomplished facts willingly assumes some disguise that makes it less repellent. Without much concern to remain in agreement with itself, it chooses in its turn a criterium for the appraisal of acts and the judgment of history, and this criterium is success. All is well as it is, but the best thing is to succeed. Actions are therefore no longer indifferent, they have an appearance of morality, but this morality is wholly external and consists in victory. The good is what shines, right is might, as the sophists say. Whence it follows that crime and virtue are once more identified in their end and become equally meritorious, provided they triumph. Applied to the great movements of civilization, this theory will seem conformable to the law of progress, since on the whole good prevails over evil. It will salute all powers as they rise and pursue them with insults when they leave the stage of the world. Athens, Rome, the barbarians, the papacy, the Reformation, the Revolution, the dictatorship will in turn be an object of admiration and of contempt. But [p. 301] if we carry this same fatalistic spirit into the detail of historical facts, we shall have to glorify all the scandals, all the turpitudes, all the infamies that have succeeded, and to present a Cesare Borgia as the type of the hero. The clearest result of the experimental method introduced into the domain of the moral and political sciences is Machiavellianism (1).

p. 302

There are, moreover, many other impossibilities that condemn this application of experience. Whereas the phenomena of nature are always the same in the same circumstances and can be foreseen with certainty, the facts of individual and social life, engendered by freedom, vary according to times, climates, situations, and stages of culture. How, then, are we to ascend from the facts to the law, when the facts, inspired now by interest or passion, now by the feeling of duty, do not at all resemble one another? How shall the moral or social law be, by the effect of induction, necessary, when observation finds that it is not always executed; universal, when we see everywhere privileges and derogations; immutable, when manners and laws are not merely diverse but contrary? Will it be the same law that authorizes theft at Sparta and commands respect for the goods of others at Rome; that permits polygamy in the East and forbids it in the West; that gives the father of a family the right of life and death over his children at one time, and obliges him at another to feed them, to maintain them, and to bring them up? Will it be the same law that proclaims the Supreme Being and the immortal gods, that puts the Church in the State and the State in the Church? It would be childish to dwell longer on these contradictions. Let us remark only that it is from the introduction of experience into the rational sciences that there flows moral skepticism, which contests the existence of the natural law, on the pretext that the facts belie it. The universality of approval, says Montaigne, is the only likely sign by which one can argue any natural laws; for what nature would have truly [p. 302] ordained for us, we should doubtless follow by common consent, and not only every nation but every particular man would feel the force and violence done to him by anyone who wished to push him contrary to this law. Let them show me one of that condition, just to see! Montaigne forgets that the laws of the moral order, being addressed to free beings, have only a moral necessity, which imposes itself on conscience and prescribes on pain of remorse, without subjugating the will, and that these laws therefore do not cease to be immutable, universal, absolute in themselves and for reason because they are not everywhere and always respected. Every man knows and feels that he ought to obey the law, that he ought to do what he believes good and just: here is the permanent law; but each also knows that he can do the contrary of what he ought: here is freedom. Between law and freedom, between duty and power, conflict is possible in an imperfect being, but the aim of life is to put an end to this conflict by the free fulfillment of the law. Conscience is perfectible, like the will. Every man knows the distinction of good and evil, but he does not know everything that is good or everything that is bad: as to the fundamental precepts of the law, there is agreement, there is universal approval, within the limits of experience, in the sense that all rational beings, at all times and in all places, agree, not in doing the same acts, but in judging them in the same manner; divergence of opinions and feelings breaks out only with regard to the secondary or remote precepts of the law: it is a question of training and of science. Is there any country on earth, cries Rousseau, where it is a crime to keep one’s faith, to be merciful, beneficent, generous, where the good man is despised and the perfidious honored? Many just men, doubtless, have been persecuted and branded, but it was never on account of their justice that they were condemned.

(1) Blanc Saint-Bonnet, de l'Unité spirituelle, Prolégomènes, ch. vi.

p. 303

The perfectibility of the soul is no less opposed than freedom to the use of the procedure of generalization in the search for the laws of rational life. If by virtue of free will our acts are contingent, by virtue of perfectibility [p. 303] they must vary unceasingly in time. The past, therefore, cannot serve as a rule for the future. The facts subject to observation belong to history and are necessarily less perfect than the future facts to which the law must apply. In other words, the induction in question would bear on the present and the past, whereas the law that issues from it would govern our future activity. Now the past is worth less than the future, if man is perfectible. How, then, could an inferior culture be the measure of a superior culture, and how could contemporaries suspect that elevation of moral, religious, and social life which escapes all observation, if they did not bear within themselves the ideal of human perfection? The principle is therefore false; the consequences are no less so. For if the moral laws are drawn from the past, it is the manners and customs of our ancestors, and not the innate principles of reason, that we must follow, it is traditions that must be preserved at any price, it is antiquity that is the type of modern civilization. I am far from contesting the utility of traditions and of history. It does not suffice to know the principles, we must inquire into the facts. Politics, as the science of the application of right to the life of nations, must take account of the character and antecedents of the people, that is to say adapt reforms to manners, in order that society may follow a regular and continuous evolution. But, after all, history by itself is as insufficient as pure philosophy; it teaches the opinions and feelings that formerly reigned, not those that ought henceforth to prevail; and if progress is not a chimera, far from finding in the past what ought to be in the future, we meet with there, most often, only what ought no longer to be. Humanity would never have advanced a single step if each generation had docilely conformed to the customs of the preceding generation. These customs are apparently respectable, but are they legitimate? Those who know how to appreciate the difference between barbarism and civilization, or only between the old law and the new law, according to the Sermon on the Mount, will have no difficulty in answering. “Humanity [p. 304] is not a thing that turns, but a thing that marches on; otherwise one would draw up the theory of humanity as one has drawn up the theory of comets, and one would say in advance, to within a second, the duration, the revolutions, and the end of empires (1).”

p. 305

Applied to the study of right and of society, the experimental method has given birth to the historical school of Hugo and Savigny, which rejects every absolute principle of justice and holds that institutions develop spontaneously, instinctively, without the intervention of the legislator, by virtue of the plastic force inherent in organized bodies. This is the abolition of codes of law, the work of individual wills guided by preconceived ideas, and the restoration or the perpetual maintenance of the customary regime of our fathers. This school has rendered great services to the history of law and has furnished precious information on the course of human societies; but it fails to recognize the characters of freedom and perfectibility that distinguish a moral organism from a physical organism, and forgets the distance that separates ancient times, when peoples were ignorant of their rights and their destiny, from modern times, when nations gradually acquire consciousness of themselves. The notion of right cannot be drawn from experience or from history, says M. Ahrens very justly, because this experience is contradictory. There is no matter of civil or political law that is regulated in an identical manner even among civilized nations. The form of government, the organization of property, family law, everything varies. It is impossible to draw from these contrary data a universal principle; and if one wished to make a choice among them, one would already have to know the general ideas by which the just and the unjust are discerned. Moreover, the life of peoples has not at present reached its highest degree of culture; as new needs come to manifest themselves, the juridical institutions will have to be modified or completed. But for the social body, the existence of this state of perfect [p. 305] development cannot be demonstrated by experience, for want of comparison with future and more advanced societies. To know what ought to be, to know the ideal of man and of humanity, we must study human nature. This problem is not historical but philosophical (1).

(1) Blanc Saint-Bonnet, de l'Unité spirituelle. Prolégom., ch. v.

p. 306

The historical school makes no claim to be progressive. Called forth by the French Revolution, which in its evil days remade society a priori and changed manners and beliefs by dint of decrees, it reacted against these innovations and condemned the good along with the bad. It is perfectly in its role in recommending the experimental method in the science of right and of the State. But what are we to say of those other sensualist, materialist, positivist doctrines which, resorting to the same procedure, believe that they serve the cause of freedom and of civilization? Seeing the fury with which they combat free will, while flattering the liberal party, one would be tempted to think that they wish to mislead public opinion. But no, blindness suffices. One may be blind to the point of imagining that civil and political liberty has nothing in common with moral freedom. Why do they not at least study the history of materialism? They would learn from Hobbes that if man has only senses and knows only how to observe facts, he is, like the animal, the plaything of his sensations and can yield only to fear or to violence: despotism is the logical consequence of materialism; it is a seditious opinion, it has been said, to grant every man the innate knowledge of good and evil; for with this instrument each is judge of the laws and can rise up against the State. That innate ideas, the source of the rational method, should be denounced as factious by those who dread the light, is understandable; for they render the mind independent of the milieu in which it lives and allow it freely to criticize established customs, manners, and institutions. Has not Descartes, the restorer of this theory, delivered human reason from all the authorities [p. 306] outside itself that weighed upon it in the Middle Ages? Free thought in modern times comes from this, and the bitter enemies of progress have not been mistaken about it. In ancient times it comes from Socrates, whose method of delivering minds rests on the same rational data. It is true that Socrates and Descartes, in setting aside the domination of the political and moral opinions of their time, did not think of withdrawing man from God. Is that by chance a reason for servitude of the mind? Contemporary sophists have dared to say so. But metaphysics demonstrates that the freedom of the creature has need of a superior cause, and the history of Christianity proves in its turn that it is the religious feeling, the intimate union of the soul with God, that overthrew the whole political system of antiquity, in which the citizen belonged to the State, and consecrated inner freedom, the first source of civil liberty. Let us not be ungrateful to a doctrine that is after all one of the principal causes of the civilization of the peoples of the West. Materialism and positivism disdain reason and pursue it in all its applications. But without reason there is no freedom, because freedom demands discernment, develops in proportion to intelligence, and calls for a counterpoise to sensible influences. Speculation is the honor of thought; devotion is the glory of the heart; heroism is the victory of the will; the ideal is the aureole of the imagination; religion is the crowning of reason: all these great things, which positivism ignores, belong to the absolute and constitute the supreme dignity of man. It is permissible to think that they interest humanity at least as much as the petty calculations of morality and politics in which materialists take their complacent pleasure.

(1) H. Ahrens, Cours de droit naturel ou de philosophie du droit. Introd. On the Historical School. 5th ed. Brussels, 1860.

p. 307

The ideas of the good, the beautiful, the true, the just are absolute, necessary, universal, independent of observation, prior and superior to every inductive procedure. The moral and political sciences, founded on these principles, are therefore rational a priori sciences. The contrary doctrines, which would introduce into the moral order of the world the methods in use in the physical order, lead [p. 307] to consequences as absurd as they are revolting. This is established. There remains, however, a hypothesis to be discussed. Are not the general ideas that preside over the life of rational beings, like abstract notions, arbitrary creations of the understanding, effects of training or of social conventions? This is the theory of the state of nature.

We know the relations of this theory with sensualism. All that can be alleged in its favor is that the writers who invented it in the seventeenth century found themselves confronted with artificial customs and institutions and wished to appeal against them to the feeling of nature. But they were mistaken in the application of this thought. Instead of interrogating human nature, which society cannot alter, they placed man outside society and sought to define what he was in himself before he was corrupted by contact with his fellows. They forgot that it is precisely of the nature of man to live in society: first fault. Next, they saw in man only the animal, they stripped him of reason and of all the attributes of rational life: no language, no notion of right, of duty, of religion. Here is the primitive man of Hobbes and of Rousseau. How, then, did this creature, more imperfect than the brute, for the latter has instinct for a guide, come to form the notions of good and evil, of the just and the unjust? A matter of convention. On leaving the state of nature, men made a contract, the social contract, to stipulate the rights they reserved to themselves and those they consented to abandon to the community. This contract had the force of law. Now everything it prohibited became bad and unjust, for no other reason than the prohibition, and everything it permitted or prescribed passed for good and just.

p. 308

There is only one thing to object to in this hypothesis: that it explains nothing, neither morality nor right, and that it is no more conformable to history than to philosophy. No traveler has yet found men without language, without moral ties, living isolated in the woods like the [p. 308] beasts. The invention of good and evil would be the invention of conscience, and conscience is not invented without conscience. Before agreeing upon good and evil, men must have felt that the state of nature was bad and that the social state would be better. In order to make a contract about their rights and duties, they must have believed that they had the right to bind themselves and their descendants, and that pacts oblige. But even admitting that a contract were possible without begging the question, it would still have to account for the essential characters of the ideas of the good and the just. Now the contrary is true. The good and the just are no longer laws that regulate the action of the will, but products of the will of our fathers; they are no longer innate ideas that are met with in every reason, but notions acquired like those of prefect or lord; they are no longer principles superior to the data of experience, but maxims that adapt themselves rigorously to it and take from us every faculty of checking institutions, every means of distinguishing between law and right; they are no longer, finally, universal, necessary, absolute cognitions, but variable, particular, and contingent cognitions, which came into being at a certain moment, under such and such a form, and may disappear when future generations shall judge it good that there should be no more good and shall find it unjust that there should still be justice.

p. 309

The mathematical and moral sciences are independent of observation. The same holds a fortiori of pure philosophy, of metaphysics, which is the rational science par excellence. Metaphysics, in fact, concerns itself with the absolute, the infinite, the immutable, the necessary, the eternal, with those properties that are generally regarded as the attributes of God. Now no series of empirical phenomena could give us or inspire in us the knowledge of these divine properties, if we did not originally possess it within us. Observation, far from grasping any quality of this kind, grasps precisely the contrary qualities, the relative, the finite, the variable, the contingent, [p. 309] the temporal. And it is clear that by extending the finite or the relative as far as one likes, one will never arrive at the infinite or the absolute, but at a sum of finite and relative things. A multitude of kilometers or of centuries does not make the infinite in space or in time; a crowd of circumstances does not constitute the absolute, and changes that accumulate do not compose immutability. No addition or multiplication of one quality can furnish the contrary quality. It would take an infinity of particular quantities to equal the infinite; but then there is no longer any need to seek the infinite, we already have it; and it is not observation that presents us with quantities to infinity. The knowledge we have of the infinite and of the absolute therefore does not result from experience. If we had no other source of knowledge than the senses, we should be entirely deprived of these supra-sensible notions; for the senses cannot reach them, and we could not acquire them by drawing them from our sensations. Nothing demonstrates better the receptive character of reason as a source of knowledge.

Let us dwell especially on the absolute and the infinite. The sensualists, incapable of explaining the presence of these ideas in the soul, have decided to banish them from philosophical language. They do violence to reason and to history, which attest their existence among all civilized peoples, but they are consistent with themselves. They point out that the infinite and the absolute or unconditioned are negative terms, and claim that we also have of them only a negative knowledge, that is to say, that we know them only by way of abstraction, by successively eliminating all bounds and all conditions, or, to put it better, that we do not know them at all. They then confound the infinite with the indefinite, which they derive from experience, and pass over the absolute in silence, affirming that all is relative. Other authors, without going so far, maintain that the absolute and the infinite are objects of conception, not of knowledge, that we can indeed say what they are not, not what they are, that we must finally content ourselves with giving a negative definition of them, saying that the infinite

p. 310

Logic. — I. 20 [p. 310] is what is without bounds, that the absolute is what exists without conditions, and that this is a radical difference between the domain of reason and that of the understanding (1). Yet another writer, while granting that God is the infinite and absolute Being, declares that these are not genuine attributes, but mere characters that belong to a property and that, apart from this application, represent nothing and are only abstractions (2).

p. 311

Such are the most serious objections that can be made against the knowledge of the infinite and the absolute. If they are well founded, I admit without hesitation that metaphysics is impossible; but it must also be acknowledged that, if they are chimerical, there remains no insurmountable obstacle to the science of God. It is to the notions of the infinite and the absolute, in fact, that the greatest difficulties of metaphysics relate. What remains inaccessible to thought, once reason can grasp with certainty the infinite and absolute essence? Now all these objections rest on a vice of method or on a psychological error. The sensualists deny reason as a distinct faculty of the soul: with them the negation of rational knowledge is only the consequence of a lacuna in their psychology. M. Vacherot confounds reason with the understanding, as the faculty of abstraction and analysis, and maintains with Kant that empirical intuitions are the sole matter of thought: the pretension to construct a metaphysics on the data of experience is then the conclusion of a false theory of reason. A thorough study of the science of the soul and of knowledge can alone do justice to these opinions. That external or internal experience awakens the ideas of reason is a thesis that can be defended with regard to mathematical notions and moral conceptions, for the figures of geometry, the works of nature, the actions of man, offer at least some resemblance [p. 311] with the ideal combinations of space, with the absolute principles of the beautiful and the good; but that the finite should engender the infinite and the relative the absolute can be conceived only if the infinite and the absolute do in fact proceed from the contrary terms. The psychological method, developed on the basis of Krause’s categories, leads us to a result diametrically opposed, and this is one of the least noticed and most important points for the edification of metaphysics as a science.

Psychology teaches that the self is a being, that being is essence, and that essence is one. This determination of the self can give rise to no dispute if by being we understand a thing, any object whatever; by essence, what the being is, or the whole of its properties; and if by unity we signify that the essence of the self is purely and simply the essence of the self and nothing else. Now how is this unity of essence of the self manifested? By two new and coordinate attributes: inasmuch as it is one, the self is itself what it is and it is all that it is; in other words, its essence is its own, it is proper to it, from the point of view of quality, and its essence is whole, or is wholly its own, from the point of view of quantity. Each of us, interrogating consciousness about his essence, can say: it is I who am my essence, between this essence and myself there is identity, I am not this or that, I am myself, I am my essence. But I am not merely a part of my essence, I am all that this essence can contain, I am my faculties, my forces, my tendencies, my acts, I am my essence one and whole, whatever discoveries analysis may reserve for future psychologists.

Proper essence and whole essence, selfhood and wholeness, express in equal measure the pure and simple unity of essence. It is not only to the self that we apply these qualities; we attribute them, rightly or wrongly, to all the objects of thought, within and beyond the limits of observation, so that it would be impossible for us to form any cognition whatever without their aid.

(1) E. Vacherot, La Métaphysique et la Science, conversation IX. Paris, 1858.

(2) L. A. Gruyer, Observations sur le Dieu-Monde de M. Vacherot et de M. Tiberghien, p. 35. Paris, 1860.

p. 312

Indeed, every object, substance or accident, can and must be considered as such, such as it is, according to its proper essence, on the one hand; and on the other, it can and must be considered in its entirety, as a whole, according to its whole essence. Every object presents itself to thought as distinct from every other, in its originality or its individuality, without being confounded even with its like; and every object, however minute, is still a whole that contains a certain number of qualities, parts, phenomena, or relations. If it forms part of a larger whole, it will be this part and not another, and if it is itself the whole, it will still have this peculiarity of being the whole. Thought itself has its proper essence, since it differs from feeling and from will, and its whole essence, since it develops and organizes itself in science. What is proper to thought is precisely to grasp what is proper in all things, as what is proper to feeling is to attach itself to things in their entirety in a concrete manner.

p. 313

God is determined in the same way as the self, which is made in his image. He is being, he is essence, he is being alone and unique, or the unity of being and of essence. The difference between God and the self subsists, despite the similitude. The self is this or that being, God is being itself; the self is this or that essence, God is essence itself; and this essence is one, because it is purely and simply the divine essence. Outside of being and essence there is nothing; all the possible objects of thought are summed up in one and the same term: being or God; what is not God is in God, under God, through God: “ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia.” [of him, and through him, and in him, are all things] What now are the attributes of the divine essence? The same as those of the self, taking account of the difference that exists between beings and being: the self is itself its essence and it is all its essence, God is himself essence and he is all essence. On the one hand, the essence one and whole is the very essence of God and of no other, since there is no other beside Being; and on the other hand, the divine essence is all essence, all that is. These qualities both derive from the pure and simple unity of essence: inasmuch as God [p. 313] is alone and unique, he is all, and he is all of himself. If he is all that is, if he is the whole essence, he is what is called infinite; and if he is of himself all that he is, if the whole essence is his own essence, he is what is named absolute. The infinite and the absolute are but the translation of whole essence and proper essence, applied to the unity of essence. Whatever is alone and unique is without limits and without conditions: it is without limits, because there is nothing outside it that could restrict its essence; it is without conditions and without relation, because nothing exists outside it on which it could depend; in other words, that which is alone and unique is infinite and absolute, because it is one, whether in its own genus or above all genus. Thus we say of God that he is infinite, since he is all essence, or the whole essence, without any restriction, and that he is absolute, since he is of himself what he is, or is independent of everything other than himself.

The metaphysicians and theologians who have sought to explain the nature of God call him the infinite and absolute Being, and consider these attributes as characteristic and parallel; but they follow no methodical procedure; they have no other guide than the intuition of reason. We now recognize that they are not mistaken, and that the results of the method on this point agree with the inspiration of consciousness. God is indeed the infinite and absolute Being, and these qualities, which manifest the unity of essence, are only other expressions of the whole essence and of the proper essence. But there is this difference between the proper and the absolute, between the whole and the infinite, that these terms, as elements of language, are some positive, the others negative. The particles in and ab, which enter into infinite and into absolute or unconditioned, announce a negation: infinite means, from this point of view, non-finite or endless, and absolute signifies freed from all relation, or without condition. The terms selfhood and wholeness, the proper and the whole, are on the contrary positive. Now words also have their own propriety as signs of our thoughts, and this propriety requires that positive attributes be designated by positive terms.

p. 314

The negative construction of the terms infinite and absolute is often invoked as a symbol of rational knowledge, but in reality it proves nothing regarding the notions we have of the absolute and the infinite. These terms, in fact, are an analytic work of popular reason, and we have agreed that in analysis the sensible element, the finite, the relative, precedes the rational element, the infinite, the absolute; but we also know that before any act of decomposition thought possesses indeterminate cognitions, and that sensible perceptions themselves logically imply a priori ideas. Let us therefore leave words aside and go to the heart of things. Is it true, as M. Vacherot asserts, that the infinite can be defined only by the finite and the absolute by the relative? No: the infinite is defined by the whole (totum, omne) and the absolute by the proper or the same (proprium, ipse, a se, per se). Infinite essence is the whole essence, infinite science is omniscience; the absolute being is the being that exists of itself, absolute truth is pure truth, which shines by its own light and is self-evident. Negative determinations can doubtless be added to these propositions, but by way of explanation, not of definition. M. Gruyer appears to be more exact when he says that the absolute and the infinite are rather the characters of an attribute than properties of God. Metaphysics in fact affirms that wisdom, power, and love are infinite and absolute in God, finite and relative in us. But the author forgets that these characters can belong to the attributes of a being only if they belong to its essence, and as such they are themselves fundamental attributes of God.

p. 315

What, then, remains of the distinction made by M. Vacherot between conception and knowledge? Nothing. The pretext for this terminology is that the objects of the understanding are determined positively and those of reason negatively. This pretext is ruined, and there is no other motive that can establish a difference between the acts of these two faculties from the point of view of certainty. The conceptions of reason, like the perceptions of the senses, are cognitions, on the same footing as all the products of thought, [p. 315] and the former may be as legitimate as the latter. But here is the consequence that the adversaries of philosophy draw from such propositions: the infinite and the absolute are not objects of knowledge, and it is therefore chimerical to concern oneself with them; let us abandon these vain speculations to theology, for there is no science of God. If there is no science of God, then, I say, faith alone, blind faith, is competent in religious questions, and modern philosophy since Descartes is a silly insurrection against the authority of revelation. Let us therefore submit without a murmur and restore as soon as possible the moral condition of the Middle Ages, when philosophy was the vassal of theology. Such are the pretensions accredited by progressive minds, who venture into metaphysics without sufficient study of psychology and of the science of knowledge!

p. 316

Other authors almost invert the thesis of M. Vacherot and maintain that we can indeed know the infinite and the absolute, but that we do not comprehend them, that God is incomprehensible. By comprehending they then mean enclosing within the bounds of a representation or of an image. In this sense they are not wrong: the infinite and the absolute are not objects of sensible intuitions for the imagination, but of intellectual intuitions for reason. Imagination is a faculty of determination, which cannot represent the infinite to itself without destroying it. But if certain objects are inaccessible to fancy, they are not so to reason. Reason has not the limits of imagination, and comprehends what sensibility does not reach. It is time to put an end to these verbal disputes, which favor only sophistry. Taking the word knowledge in its most general acceptation, as expressing any relation whatever between thought and its object, we may consider the terms to comprehend, to conceive, to perceive, as synonymous with to know.
