Everything that is perceived by means of sense, everything that is conceived with the aid of reason, everything that is comprehended by the understanding or by reflection, is known in some manner. But knowledge may be [p. 316] true or false, certain or hypothetical, complete or partial. There lies the whole question. We know an object by the mere fact that it is present to consciousness; but our knowledge does not necessarily correspond to the essence of the object, and even when we have of it an exact and adequate notion, we are still exposed to doubt. If knowledge is certain, it is true, but it may be true without being certain.

p. 317

Full and complete knowledge, I shall readily agree, is not the lot of man. We are perfectible, not perfect, and perfectibility shows itself in all the operations of the mind, in science as in art. Human knowledge is always in the way of progress but is never completed, and if truth is infinite, it is rigorously certain that we need infinite time to exhaust it. Observation does not belie this principle. The sciences extend and divide more and more; truth, immutable in itself, grows for us in proportion as we see more things and see them better. What was formerly the object of a single science has become the object of a great number of particular sciences, thanks to analysis, and it is impossible to set limits to this specialization of intellectual labor. The nomenclature of the sciences is not settled and could not be so for all the future. New groups are formed when new horizons open to the intellect. Not only do objects multiply, but the relations between objects arise ceaselessly more numerous and more complicated. Between things there exist relations without end, and these relations in their turn sustain relations among themselves. Who can flatter himself that he knows everything? Who would even dare to assert that he knows a single object in all its properties, in all its manifestations, in all its relations? Have the theory of numbers, the division of curved lines, the determinations of our own nature no more secrets for us? Yes, each object is determinable to infinity in science and cannot be exhausted at any given time by a finite being. We shall never know the soul and matter as God [p. 317] knows them: we have not omniscience. Our knowledge therefore has limits; we must resign ourselves to it, for it is a necessary consequence of our limitation.

But if our knowledge is imperfect, whether its object be the finite or the infinite, it is none the less knowledge. Here we are concerned only with knowledge itself, setting aside its objective validity. Do we know the infinite and the absolute? Yes, for we name them, and whoever would deny it would already be in contradiction with himself, since he must know what he denies. Do we know the infinite and the absolute completely? No: each of these terms is inexhaustible for a bounded intellect. The infinite contains an infinity of combinations or aspects, of which only a few present themselves to our thought. Do we at least know the infinite and the absolute in an exact and certain manner from the points of view that present themselves to our thought? This is the question of the legitimacy of our rational cognitions, which will be discussed later.

Nothing is simpler or more evident than these degrees of knowledge. Why then do philosophers and theologians, M. Vacherot and M. Simon as well as M. Gratry, take so much trouble to prove now that we conceive the infinite without knowing it, now that we know it without comprehending it? It is because they have, I regret to say, only a confused notion of intellect and of knowledge. In the midst of these contrary affirmations, I am glad to meet at least one author who understands the matter.

p. 318

“I know perfectly well,” says M. Fabre, “that I perceive the infinite, since I distinguish the infinite from the finite, the perfect from the imperfect, and I also know very well that I could not distinguish them if I did not perceive them. Indeed, two objects that are not perceived can be neither compared nor distinguished. When I compare and distinguish them, it is clear that I perceive them. Now I compare the infinite with the finite, and I do not confound the infinite with what is not itself. I know that it is not colored, heavy or light, round or square, and I affirm besides many properties of it; I see, for [p. 318] example, that it is unique and that nothing can be added to its being or to its perfections. The idea of the infinite is therefore incontestably present to the human intellect.

“Let no one object to us, then, that we do not conceive the infinite, since it is, on the contrary, certain that we have the idea of this being, and that we perceive this idea with the same self-evidence as any other idea. If, however, by this word to conceive it is meant that we do not imagine the infinite, we shall avow that in this sense it is true that we do not conceive it. We shall add further that one is equally right if one gives this word the sense of to comprehend (to encompass), and if one supposes that the infinite cannot be perceived without exhausting its idea, without knowing it as far as it is intelligible. For if it is true that to have the idea of an infinite being is to have the idea of a being whose perfections have no limits, it is equally certain that, in order for us to perceive it, it is not necessary that we comprehend it, that we enclose its infinity within our intellect, or that we know all its perfections in an adequate manner, since we do not know even all of them in finite beings, of which we nevertheless certainly have the idea. In order for our intellect to grasp the infinite, it suffices, indeed, that it perceive it as a being whose limit it will not only never attain, but whose essence it positively knows to consist in having no limit. Now this is what our intellect can perceive at will when it attentively contemplates the infinite.

p. 319

“Condillac therefore advances an absurdity when he imagines that he can ‘demonstrate that we have not the idea of the infinite….’ The mere statement of his thesis overthrows all the demonstration that he could give of it, since, by saying, ‘I have not the idea of the infinite,’ he proves at the same time, and in spite of himself, that he has this idea. For either he knows then what he says or he does not know it. In the first case, he has the idea of the infinite, since it is quite evident that, in order to demonstrate the truth or falsity of a proposition, one must at least perceive its terms. He has, then, the idea of the infinite. In the [p. 319] second case, he would not know what he says, he would be uttering words at random, and consequently would arrive at no demonstration (1).”

The same dilemma and the same remarks apply to the absolute. In short, these objects are inexhaustible for us, but not incomprehensible. Mathematics offers many objects of this kind, which no one thinks of denying on the pretext that they refuse all representation. The square root of two, for example, is incommensurable; it is none the less an element of calculation, and expresses exactly the diagonal of a square whose side is one. We can therefore know by one means what we do not know by another; we can grasp by an intellectual intuition what imagination does not give as a sensible intuition.

Let us now determine the knowledge that we have of the absolute and the infinite.

p. 320

A learned professor of the University of Edinburgh, Mr. Hamilton, has made the most complete criticism of the absolute. More recent authors, sensualists, positivists, criticists, or men of letters, who side with his opinion, scarcely take the trouble to discuss the question. It is an axiom for M. Renouvier and for Auguste Comte that everything is relative, as Protagoras and Gorgias taught. Hamilton divides into four classes the opinions put forward on the absolute: the absolute can be conceived but not known, according to Kant; it can be known but not conceived, according to Schelling; it can be known and conceived, according to M. Cousin; it can be neither known nor conceived, according to the author. Needless to observe how false such a division is, both in itself and in its applications, founded as it is on the arbitrary distinction between conception and knowledge. Kant does not exclude knowledge, nor Schelling conception, of the absolute; the critic merely claims that this knowledge is not scientific, because it passes beyond the bounds of experience. And why can the absolute [p. 320] be neither known nor conceived? Here it is: there are three things: the unconditionally unlimited, or the infinite; the unconditionally limited, or the absolute; and the conditionally limited, which comprises finite beings. Whence does the author know all this? Does he set out categories of substances or of properties, or does he merely show the possible combinations between the limited and the unlimited, the conditioned and the unconditioned? In the first case, how does he know that these categories exist, if he can neither conceive nor know them? In the second case, why does he give only three combinations instead of four, and why should not even the unlimited be united with the limited? There is some mystery beneath this. The mystery increases still further when we see the author declare that the terms absolute, infinite, and unconditioned must be carefully distinguished, and then refuse the reader every element of distinction. How are we to distinguish what cannot be known? How, above all, are we to recognize a difference that has never been made between the absolute and the unconditioned? This omission renders the criticism almost unintelligible. We see only that the unconditioned applies now to what is limited, now to what has no limits, and that the absolute exists only in the domain of finite things. Certainly it is not there that one ordinarily looks for it; but when one does not conceive the absolute, how can one discover it? Let us listen to the author; at bottom, perhaps, he is no more exclusive than another. The absolute and the infinite, he says, cannot positively be construed to the mind; they can be conceived only by a thinking away from, or abstraction of, those very conditions under which thought itself is realized; consequently, the notion of the unconditioned is only negative (it exists, then), negative of the conceivable itself (I greatly fear that it exists no longer). The conditioned is the only possible object of knowledge and of positive thought; thought necessarily supposes conditions; to think is to condition (it is as if one said: thought supposes a cause, therefore to think is to cause). Nothing should astonish us more than to see it doubted that thought is only of the conditioned (unless the law of conditional limitation, inherent in [p. 321] human thought, is also manifested in our conception of the unconditioned). Consciousness is only possible under the antithesis of a subject and object of thought, known only in correlation, and mutually limiting each other (here at least is a serious argument, but it is a manifest error, already refuted in psychology and in logic: the proposition advanced applies only to the analytic knowledge of a finite object, considered as such). Furthermore, all that we know of the subject or of the object reduces to modifications and phenomena: philosophy is impossible if it goes beyond the conditioned (it is impossible, on the contrary, if it wishes to stop at phenomena, abstracting from all substance). Hence we shall be taught the salutary lesson that the capacity of thought is not to be constituted into the measure of existence (a theological prejudice unknown to the sophists). “And by a wonderful revelation, we are thus, in the very consciousness of our inability to conceive aught above the relative and finite, inspired with a belief in the existence of something unconditioned beyond the sphere of all comprehensible reality (1).” That is it: the absolute is an object of faith, not of thought; we must believe in its existence, without hope of knowing it. The soul is divided into two parts that have nothing in common between them: the one believing and blind, which will admit anything you please, even the absolute, according to the chance of birth; the other intelligent and critical, which will reject the absolute and accept only facts. Here is the stumbling block of the adversaries of the absolute: if logical, they are atheists, they maintain that there exist only phenomena without causes and without laws; if inconsistent, they fall into credulity regarding the very absolute that they exclude from thought.

(1) Abbé Jules Fabre, Cours de philosophie, vol. I, Psychologie, bk. iv. Paris, 1863.

p. 322

The thesis of the absolute has nothing to fear from these attacks. The absolute is everywhere, in the infinite and in the finite. Whatever [p. 322] is in certain respects alone and unique is absolute, because as such it suffices to itself; it exists in itself, without relation, without dependence, without condition. The absolute is independence, it is the absence of all relation with anything else. Whatever is considered as alone and unique, without relation to a contrary, is considered as absolute within the limits of creation. What is not alone, what is engaged in a relation or considered in relation to something else, is relative or conditioned. The relative is the negation of the absolute, of that which exists in itself or is conceived as such; the relative appears only where there is a plurality of beings, where relations exist, that is to say, in the world. But no thing is exclusively relative, because every relation supposes at least two terms, and these terms have a proper essence and exist in themselves as well as they have relations and a relative existence. Now, insofar as they have a proper essence and existence, or are considered as such, in themselves, finite beings are marked with the character of the absolute within the bounds of their nature. It is in this sense that the word absolute is commonly taken in all the domains of science and of reality. What does absolute power signify? It is power pure and simple, power without counterpoise, restricted by no foreign element, by no public liberty. What is absolute obedience? It is obedience itself, obedience that is only that, troubled by no contrary, by no velleity of insubordination. Absolute silence, absolute rest, the absolute void, express the thing considered in itself, in its proper essence, without any mixture with noise, with motion, with the full, which are the negation of its essence. An absolute right is an essential right, which depends on no ulterior condition, and which cannot, under any pretext, be contested or diminished. An absolute proposition is a categorical judgment which affirms that the attribute belongs to the subject without restriction. The absolute future is simply the future without comparison between several events that are to happen. The absolute figure of the population is the [p. 323] number of inhabitants itself, without regard to the extent of the country. This is enough to show that the word absolute has a very precise meaning and constitutes an indispensable term of language for designating a thing considered in itself, in its own essence (positive definition), that is to say, without comparison or relation with the contrary idea (negative explanation). The absolute is therefore in everything that has a proper essence or that is considered as having one.

(1) William Hamilton, Fragments de philosophie, trans. L. Peisse, I, Paris, 1840.

p. 324

If it is in the very essence of finite beings, it is also in their activity, insofar as activity is proper or spontaneous. Every being that acts of itself, that is the proper cause or the first cause of its acts, acts absolutely. This activity rises to its highest power in the proper determination of spiritual substances, or in the will and moral freedom of rational beings. The rational activity of man bears essentially the mark of the absolute. The moral law, for example, imposes itself on conscience as a categorical imperative, in the form of an absolute command: do good; no hesitation, no accommodation, no capitulation between duty and interest or passion; honor speaks, it is enough, we must obey without a murmur. Thus man can and must do good for the sake of the good itself, accomplish justice with no other consideration than justice, love the beautiful for the sole reason that it is beautiful, and spread the truth even to the detriment of his own position, that is to say, realize something absolute or divine in an absolute manner, as God himself realizes his essence. The ideal freedom of rational creatures consists precisely in this absolute pursuit of the good for the good, which lets the will direct itself toward its end without turning it aside by the self-interested solicitations of the enjoyments or advantages of earthly life. He who possesses this freedom, were it only for an instant, is a hero, capable of sacrificing his goods to the good, honors to honor, and life to duty. The cause of the absolute is therefore the cause of freedom and of heroism, and consequently the cause of moral progress and of the sublime in human activity. And yet such is still the blindness of men that, among the adversaries of [p. 324] the absolute, we must cite in the first rank passionate lovers of freedom and of progress (1).

p. 325

There are, according to what precedes, three degrees in the application of the absolute. That is infinitely absolute which is alone in every respect: such is the one and whole being, which is not comprised in the series of beings, but itself comprises the whole series in its essence. God has no second, since he is all that is; he is therefore without any sort of relation to anything outside or above him, he is absolute in a complete and unique manner, he is the absolute whole. That is absolute in its genus, or partially absolute, which is unique in its genus, as space, time, nature, humanity. There is only one space; whence it follows that space is the whole reality of this order, without being all that is, and that it is also without relation to a second of the same order. Space as such is infinite and absolute; but it is not the whole infinite, nor the whole absolute, it has these qualities only in its own sphere. The absolute of space does no wrong to the absolute of time, of nature, or of humanity, because they apply to different genera, which exclude one another. Space can never be confounded with time, nor consequently limit any of its properties. Finally, that is absolute in certain respects, absolute within the limits of individual existence, which, though finite, is considered as alone, outside every relation with other beings. It is in this measure that limited beings, individuals, have part in the absolute and thus bear witness to their likeness to God. A finite being is not isolated, it has its like, it lives with other creatures, and necessarily sustains with what is outside it relations of conditionality, just as it depends on a higher cause. But finite beings are still alone and unique in some manner, insofar as they represent their species in an altogether singular fashion, that is to say, insofar as they are individuals. All the individuals of one and the same species differ among themselves, even by the qualities that [p. 325] are common to them; if all have activity and sensibility, for example, each has its own proper activity and its original mode of feeling. By virtue of this principle of originality, each thing, though finite and enveloped in the bonds of a species or a family, can therefore be considered as such, in itself, in its own essence, abstracting from all relation, and in this respect it is absolute. Conditionality does not concern essence itself, as pure essence, but as determinate essence. Thus the self has consciousness and feeling of itself before knowing that it is a limited and relative being; before affirming something of the self, in the form of a judgment, we affirm the self as an indeterminate object of thought. Hence other important consequences relating to the moral life. It is because each being has a proper essence that it also has a proper value; it is because it can be considered as such that it must also be treated as such. The relative value of things is their utility; the absolute value is dignity. Every thing has its dignity within the limits of its essence. Man must have regard to the dignity of the works of nature and respect it as far as the care of his own destination permits. He must treat the animal as such, as a being endowed with sensibility; he must love his fellow men as such, as rational and perfectible beings; he must adore God as such, as the infinite being, endowed with absolute perfections.

Let us pass to the infinite and the finite.

Locke occupies himself at length with infinity in his Essay, and seeks to show that the idea we have of it, however remote it may appear from any object of the senses or any operation of the mind, none the less derives its origin from sensation and reflection, in a word from experience. Whoever has the idea of a determinate length, a foot for example, says he, finds that he can repeat this idea as often as he wishes without ever arriving at the end of his additions. He has no reason to stop, and though he advances ceaselessly, he is never a point nearer the term of his inquiries than when he began them. The power he has of enlarging without

(1) A. Pezzani, Principes supér. de la morale, bk. I, Réfutation du scepticisme. Paris, 1859.

p. 326

Logic. — I. 21 [p. 326] end his idea of space by new additions is therefore always the same: it is from this that he draws his idea of an infinite space, or, if he operates on time, of an infinite duration. The infinite and the finite are only modes of quantity, and apply only to things that are susceptible of division. Time and space are really and actually infinite; matter in its turn is divisible to infinity; but we have no positive idea of this infinity; we conceive the infinite only as the negation of limits, by the addition, multiplication, or successive progression of finite quantities: our idea of the infinite is a fugitive idea, which increases without ceasing and cannot be fixed anywhere. Every positive idea of a certain space is commensurable; but we have no positive and distinct notion of what always remains beyond. The idea of an infinite space, necessarily composed of an infinity of parts, can have no other infinity than that of numbers capable of being multiplied without end; it would be absurd to claim that we have a positive idea of an actually infinite number. The addition of finite things could produce the idea of the infinite only by the power we find in ourselves of increasing the sum without ceasing, without approaching in the least the end of such a progression. Those who say that the idea of the infinite is positive maintain that the end is something negative, but that the negation of this negation is positive. A frivolous argument, says Locke, for the end is as positive as the beginning. The idea of so much is clear and positive; the idea of something greater is still distinct, but comparative; the idea of a quantity that so far surpasses all magnitude that it cannot be comprehended is purely negative. The infinite is precisely that which is always greater. To those who imagine they have a positive idea of infinite space or infinite time, we need only ask whether they could add anything to this idea or not, which shows without difficulty how little foundation this pretended idea has (1).

(1) Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding, bk. II, ch. XVII.

p. 327

Locke’s criticism is valuable. It teaches, on the one hand, how we must acquire the rational ideas when reason ceases to be a source of cognitions, and on the other, how one necessarily falls into falsehood and contradiction when one compares ideas thus turned aside from their origin with the real ideas that he who denies them still possesses. Locke is not an exclusive sensualist. He contests, or rather does not suspect, reason as an intuitive faculty, and confounds it with reasoning, but he admits the understanding, which is exercised on the data of the senses. All our knowledge therefore proceeds from sensation or experience. How then are we to explain the presence in us of the ideas of the infinite and the absolute? They will have to be drawn from the senses by means of reflection, through the gradual extension of the sensible elements, by constantly eliminating limits and conditions; and we shall then imagine that the idea of the infinite is the power we have of repeating the finite without end. Locke knows very well that the infinite contains an infinity of parts, and that it is not enough to multiply a number a million times to attain the infinite; no, this operation must be continued without end, to infinity, for the finite to equal the infinite. Locke therefore has, like ourselves, the distinct idea of the infinite, and reasons exactly on this idea. How could he not have it, when he recognizes the actual infinity of time, of space, of God, the divisibility of matter to infinity, and the faculty possessed by the mind of adding the finite to the finite without end? But logic prevails; without reason we cannot have the positive idea of the infinite, and consequently the infinite can arise in the mind only progressively, as the negation of the positive realities offered to our senses. The number 7 is positive; the same number followed by as many zeros as one pleases is positive still; but the infinite is negative, because we do not know how many times the number 7 is contained in it. Thus every number has a positive value, but the infinite, being greater than every assignable number, is negative and is worth less than unity: a quantity becomes negative when, instead of being multiplied by a billion, it is multiplied by billions to infinity. Strange [p. 328] arithmetic! Locke might answer: the idea is negative, but the thing is positive. In fact, if the infinite were negative in itself, the infinite being would be a pure negation, and such is not the author’s thought. But then the idea of the infinite is false, since it is contrary to the object that it represents, and yet, according to him, it is the negative idea of the infinite that is the only true one.

To refute Locke’s assertions, we need only set forth the notions of the finite, the infinite, and the indefinite, which the author almost always confounds with the infinite.

The finite and the infinite can be characterized in two words: the one is posited alone, without a second; the other is posited beside other things, and presents itself under the form of opposition or antithesis. Finite beings are necessarily multiple and opposed to one another, living with one another in one and the same whole; each has its limits, that is to say, its initial point, if it is viewed from without inward, and its final point, if it is considered from within outward; each has its particular form, each is a determinate whole, susceptible of increase and diminution, whether in its existence or in its activity, and a whole of this kind is a quantity. When we have a determinate whole, for example the terrestrial globe, we can appraise it in its content or in its outer envelope: the envelope is the limit, which manifests itself as beginning and as end; the content or the ground is the quantity or magnitude. Every quantity is therefore enclosed within limits, and if quantity is represented by a figure, we may say with Locke that every number is limited, or that there is no infinite number. The infinite, in fact, is not susceptible of addition or of subtraction; the infinite is not a quantity, but surpasses all quantity; the infinite is not a number, but is innumerable. But then it is not exact to say that the finite and the infinite are modes of quantity: the infinite is the indeterminate whole, quantity is a determinate or finite whole. This is the first error of Locke, one that was bound to vitiate his whole analysis of the infinite as a mode of quantity.

p. 329

Every finite being has a content, parts, acts or [p. 329] phenomena, but this content has limits, since the finite is not alone. The limit is therefore the line of demarcation between the interior and the exterior. For every finite being, to whatever kingdom it belongs, there exists an external world; but man alone, having consciousness of his limitation, has consciousness of what exists outside. Thus it is that the not-self is opposed to the self; but then the self and the not-self limit each other reciprocally: a determinate self alone supposes a not-self, and a not-self is opposed only to the determinate self. If the self were infinite, there would be no not-self for it. The categories of the inside and the outside are therefore inseparable from all that is finite. The same is true of affirmation and negation. Every finite being is positive insofar as it is posited, or is something; but as it is not all, as there exist other beings outside it, it is equally affected with negation: it lacks something, it is deprived of all the reality that surpasses its own. This lacuna, this defect, this imperfection constitutes the negative character, or, if one will, the nothingness of creatures. In this respect the idea of the finite, conformable to its object, is essentially, but not exclusively, negative. The nothingness of the world is only a relative nothingness; if creatures are not all, they are something; the positive and the negative are combined in the finite. But it remains true to say that the finite, as such, can be conceived only by a process of elimination that sets aside all the rest. This is Locke’s second error. This philosopher is completely mistaken about the relative value of the ideas of the finite and the infinite. It is not the end that is a negation for the finite; it is the ulterior reality that it lacks, and that begins where it itself ends. Affirmation is reality; negation is nothingness; the more reality a being has, the more positive it is; if it is the whole of reality, it is wholly positive, if it has no reality, it is wholly negative. The finite is positive within its limits, in the reality that it possesses, but it is negative beyond its limits, in respect of the reality that it does not possess.

The finite is an object of observation, not that the senses give us the general idea of the finite, but they put us in relation with finite elements, never with any others.

p. 330

The infinite is an object of contemplation, a datum of reason, which the senses and the imagination do not reach. To the finite applies sensible intuition, to the infinite intellectual intuition. Between the two terms there is no middle. The indefinite, which is often brought near to the infinite, whether in the infinitely great or in the infinitely small, is only an evasion of the imagination, which wishes to content itself with a word and save appearances. The indefinite is nothing other than the finite: it is a magnitude that the mind extends more and more, whose limits it ceaselessly pushes back, and which thus becomes incommensurable while remaining a limited quantity. The indefinite is acquired by the procedure that Locke employs to obtain the infinite, by repeating or multiplying the finite until we lose sight of its bounds, and can no longer measure it by the relation of our ordinary units. Modern astronomy and geology offer us remarkable examples of it. There are stars whose light, with its velocity of seventy thousand leagues a second, travels through space for centuries before it reaches the earth! How many meters does this distance contain? A century of travel gives something like unity followed by eighteen zeros. Here is an immense magnitude that is represented to the mind only confusedly, and which is called indefinite. But it is by no means infinite, for we can increase it as much as we wish by adding ceaselessly new series of zeros. The indefinite therefore always preserves its primitive nature of finite quantity, and a rigorous mind will never confound what has no bound whatever with that whose bounds are lost in the depths of time or space.

p. 331

Imagination, we have said, is powerless to grasp the infinite, but it labors, it swells in the presence of the infinite, and the product of its efforts is then the indefinite, the mirage of the infinite. Hence this twofold consequence, that the indefinite can in no way be substituted for the infinite in science, and that its image can be explained in us only by the idea of the infinite. Why have we the power of putting back ever and ever further the limits of a magnitude, [p. 331] of heaping up quantities upon quantities without end, and so of going beyond the reach of our senses? Because we have the idea of the infinite as the basis and support of fancy. If the infinite were not present to thought, there would necessarily be a limit to our faculty of representation, and the series of numbers would stop for us at a last number, greater than all the others, beyond which it would be impossible for us to conceive anything. We should then say: there is a beginning and an end to all things; time and space can be figured by lines fixed between two points, whose magnitude is like unity followed by a hundred zeros. Beyond the two points where space begins and ends, there is no more space, there is absolute nothingness. Now if it were so, and Locke himself rejects such a hypothesis, should we still have the faculty of forming numbers indefinitely increasing or decreasing? No; by the efforts we should make to repeat the finite ceaselessly, we should soon arrive at the last possible limit of our representations, and there we should have to stop. Thought would not go beyond its means. Hence the indefinite would disappear along with the infinite. Consequently, we have the right to say that the idea of the infinite is the very condition of the notion of the indefinite, and that if the former did not exist a priori in reason, the latter would never have appeared in the human mind (1).

p. 332

The idea of the infinite, indeed, exists primitively in reason, for it cannot be an invention of the human mind, nor an abstraction from sensible elements. A finite being, on the one hand, is incapable of creating the infinite as it forges chimeras, if it is true that the effect is always contained within the limits of the cause. And on the other hand, the abstraction of sensible elements, or the successive elimination of limits, gives birth to the indefinite, not to the infinite. By gradually removing the bounds of a period or of a place, we extend the quantity of time or of space, we obtain the incommensurable, but the incommensurable is as far removed from [p. 332] the infinite as unity is. Locke makes of the infinite an abstract notion, derived from experience. Yet there is nothing in common between the idea of the infinite and the notions of species and genus due to the process of generalization. From the individual to the species, and from the species to the genus, there is gradation: extension increases, comprehension diminishes; from the finite to the infinite, there is no gradation at all, there is contradiction. There is no transition between the finite and the infinite, as if thought could be led insensibly from the first term to the second. He who did not have the idea of the infinite a priori would never succeed in drawing it from the consideration of finite things. To arrive at the infinite by way of elimination, it is not from a certain number of bounds but from all bounds that we must abstract; but to abstract from all bounds, we must already have the idea of the infinite. The same thought can be rendered in another way, in a positive form, since to push back the limit is to add to the quantity. To pass from the finite to the infinite, it is not a certain number of times that a finite quantity, commensurable or not, must be repeated; it must be repeated without end, to infinity, an infinity of times, but then we already have the infinite.

M. Taine believes he has made a great discovery in substituting the process of abstraction or subtraction for the process of addition proposed by Locke to engender the notion of the infinite. It is plain that the two methods are identical and equally impotent: the one operates on positive quantities which it adds, the other on negative quantities or limits which it removes; but to remove negations is equivalent to making an addition. It is always the same confusion between generalization, which yields the abstract notions of species and genus, and dialectic, which rests on the immediate intuition of the infinite and the absolute (1).

(1) Javary, de la Certitude, bk. II, ch. I. Paris, 1847.

p. 333

If the infinite is not a product of the human mind, it is given to us, as we said in speaking of the objects of knowledge. Given by the senses? No, the senses do not go [p. 333] so far; the infinite is not within the reach of observation. Given by our fellow men? No, our fellow men communicate with us only by means of language, and language again addresses itself to our senses; no word contains the infinite, and besides, our parents or our teachers have no other faculties than we. Therefore the infinite is given to us by itself: as bodies offer themselves to us in our senses, the infinite offers itself to us in reason. To recognize the soundness of this conclusion, so important for the very existence of the infinite, it suffices to observe that the soul has two objective or intuitive faculties, which furnish it with the matter of its knowledge, sensibility for the physical world, reason for the moral world. The infinite, in fact, is the object of an intuitive, not a discursive, knowledge. It is even, together with the absolute and with God, the only object that can be reached only by intuition, because it is impossible to deduce it from a higher principle by means of reasoning or demonstration. Demonstration is excellently suited to our mathematical and moral knowledge, when the relation between two truths is not evident in itself and we need a middle term to discover it. But what point of comparison is there for the infinite? There is nothing beside or above the infinite; it has no other relations than those it sustains with the finite elements that lie in its essence; and what intermediary could be imagined between the finite and the infinite? It is not, then, reasoning that will reveal the infinite to him who is ignorant of it. The infinite shows itself, but does not demonstrate itself. That we know it in some manner is not doubtful, even for Locke and for M. Taine; language, if need be, would suffice to prove it. But how do we know it? By a direct view, by an immediate intuition of reason. Locke admits without hesitation that we know the principles of identity and of contradiction by intuition. That, however, is an intellectual intuition. The intuition of the infinite is of the same kind. We see that the infinite is greater than any given quantity, and that it contains an infinity of finite terms, absolutely as we see that a thing [p. 334] is what it is and is not its contrary. Everything that is evident in itself, without comparison, is an object of intuition, whether sensible or rational.

What does intuition give us regarding the infinite? Explained negatively, the infinite expresses the absence of all limit, of all restriction, of all number, of all sensible form. To understand that space has no beginning or end in length, in breadth, or in depth, that it has none of the qualities we attribute to bodies and which fall under our senses, such as color, savor, odor, hardness, sonority, that it has none of the properties of geometrical figures, that it is neither a circle nor any polygon whatever, and that it can at most be compared to a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere, is already, as Malebranche remarks, to have a notion of infinite space. But this negative determination is not enough. As the limit marks the separation between the inside and the outside and excludes everything that lies beyond the object it circumscribes, if the infinite is without limits, it clearly follows that it excludes nothing, not even the finite, that there is no outside for it, that it is consequently the fullness of reality, that it contains everything in its essence, or better still that it is all. A finite being is only a part of things; the infinite is the whole of which even the finite is a part and whose fullness it accomplishes. The finite is determined in its species, it is such or such and can be confused with another; the infinite is itself, it is alone and is confused with nothing.

(1) H. Taine, les Philosophes français au dix-neuvième siècle, ch. VII. Paris, 1857.

p. 335

The infinite has only this peculiarity, of being indeterminate, or of rejecting all the restrictive determinations that befit finite things. The distinction that shines forth everywhere in the world between the inside and the outside no longer exists for it: it is the universal container and is contained in nothing. Every creature is at once effect and cause, at once conditioned and absolute: the infinite is without cause and without condition, it completes and perfects everything and is completed by nothing. Affirmation and negation, perfection and defect, mingle ceaselessly in limited existences: the infinite has no [p. 335] gaps and is affected by no negation. All that is positive belongs to the infinite, all that is negative to the finite. Let us picture to ourselves, in fact, a series of spheres in space. Infinite space possesses all the positive of extension, since it is the sole and unique reality of this kind and no length is lacking to it; each sphere, on the other hand, is at once positive and negative: positive in what it is, in the space it encloses; negative in what it is not, in the space it excludes. All the privation of extension therefore belongs to the limited spheres, but how? Is not each sphere positive, and then how is there negation on the one hand, and how, on the other, is infinite space the whole affirmation of extension? It is because infinite space is also each sphere, each particular space, its limit included; but it is not merely the first sphere, it is also the second and the others to infinity; and thus, while containing in its essence a series of limited spheres, with all their limits, it has no limits itself. The limits, which mark separations and negations in space, belong to the particular spheres considered as such, inasmuch as the first is not the second, the second excludes the third, and so on; but the restrictions that are in space do not in any way affect the whole of space, since the whole of space is as much the outside as the inside of each globe. Negation therefore remains inherent in the finite, inasmuch as the finite stops short in its extension; as to its content, the finite is positive and returns into the infinite. This example may serve to explain a fundamental problem of metaphysics, the relation of Being to beings; only we have had to abstract from every principle of individuality and of liberty in speaking of space.

p. 336

The infinite is therefore the negation of all negation, the full and entire affirmation of essence, the all. It is an essentially and exclusively positive property, which it is fitting to designate by the term totality, or rather wholeness. The infinite is the totality of essence, essence one and whole, all reality. To say that a being is infinite is to say that it is alone and that consequently it is all. But here arises [p. 336] a distinction. A being may be alone and unique in its genus without being all that is: it is thus that we conceive space, time, humanity, nature; or else the being may be alone and unique without comparison, in an absolute manner, above every genus: it is thus that we understand God. Hence two orders of infinites: the relative infinite and the absolute infinite. That which is all in its genus is relatively infinite, just as it is partially absolute; that which is all without any restriction is absolutely infinite as it is infinitely absolute. The infinite and the absolute correspond to each other as parallel properties, inherent in the unity of essence: to pure and simple unity, the complete infinite and the complete absolute; to the unity of a genus, the determinate absolute and infinite, enclosed within the limits and conditions of a genus. Whoever says genus says a precise difference, a sharp distinction in reality. If the genus is unique, it will be infinite, but its infinity will not go beyond its own essence, which is not the whole essence. Time and space are infinite in their genus, that is to say, there is only a single time, which embraces all possible times, or in which all beings, past, present, and future, live in the same time, and there is only a single space, which comprises all spaces and in which all bodies move, observed or not. Space is doubtless not all that is, since, besides space, outside of space, we still apprehend spirits and God; but it is all the reality of this order, it possesses the fullness of the properties that constitute the essence of this genus. Likewise, infinite time is all time, but nothing but time. Time and space are homogeneous and continuous; they divide to infinity into similar parts. Nature and humanity, which we suppose equally infinite in their genus, do not lend themselves to such a division, but they manifest their essence in individualities that represent them, in bodies and in rational beings. How then are humanity and nature infinite? On the condition that the individual beings of their genus, men and stars, are without number or that there is an infinity of them. Any number of suns, scattered [p. 337] in space, would not render the world infinite; an infinity of them is required. Is an infinity of bodies more difficult to conceive than an infinity of circles or of spheres in infinite space? I do not think so. Doubtless stars may form or be extinguished in space, but what does it matter? The sum of matter does not change. If there were a million suns, one fewer would be an appreciable diminution; but if there is an infinity of them, the loss is rigorously null.

Relative infinites coexist without wronging one another. Would space be greater if time were less, or would time gain in length what space would lose in depth? Absurd hypotheses: time and space develop in different directions, as forms of succession and of coexistence, and nothing assuredly prevents their both being infinite, as almost all authors admit. From this point the question formerly controverted is resolved: whether several infinites exist and whether they can be conceived. There are as many relative infinites as there are unique genera in creation, but there is only a single absolute infinite. Distinct genera coordinate themselves and may extend to the infinite, but what is absolutely infinite is absolutely all, and the absolute whole is unique or is not at all. God is infinite in all respects and under all relations; but if he shared reality with another, he would be no more than a genus and would have only a relative infinity. Two absolute infinites contradict each other, destroy each other; they could not be two without falling into relation and without mutually limiting each other. A relative infinite is still finite from a certain point of view, since it stops at a genus, at a determination of reality; the absolute infinite alone is entirely or infinitely infinite, as Malebranche expresses it. A relative infinite may still have a cause, a condition, an outside, not as infinite, but as relative, since it is not all; the absolute infinite is above all these determinations: it is no longer a genus of reality, engaged in the series of beings, it is all being, it excludes nothing and is affected by no negation. Such is the most important notion for the scientific knowledge of God.

p. 338

If God is absolutely infinite, the scholastic distinctions between the intensive infinite and the extensive infinite, between the spiritual infinite and the material infinite, cannot be applied to the divine essence. For God is not such or such a being, but being pure and simple; he is not such or such an infinite, but the whole of the infinite; he is not infinite in some manner, but in all manners. It must not therefore be said that God is a pure spirit, opposed to nature, for spirit is a determinate genus which excludes matter, whereas God is above every genus and excludes nothing. Malebranche and Fénelon already, nourished on the Cartesian doctrine, rejected this ordinary definition and affirmed that God is he who is, the whole of being. Nor must it be said that the world subsists outside the divine essence, for there is no outside for him who is all. God on the one side and the world on the other would be two terms that would limit each other mutually by the mere fact that they are two: the world would begin where God ends. If God is infinite, he contains all; not only does he contain all in his essence, but he is also himself all that is real and positive in creatures, in the same way that space is every determinate space and that the self is also all that is contained in its nature. It must not be said, finally, that God embraces the universe only potentially, not in reality, by his intellect and his will, not by his essence; for reality in the infinite is adequate to potency, and intellect and will cannot be separated from the divine essence. The catechism of the Council of Trent is broader and more exact on this point than the ordinary theologians: it affirms purely and simply that God is present in all things by his essence as well as by his moral attributes.

p. 339

The relations between God and the world are only an application of the relations which intuition ascertains between the infinite and the finite. A rather common error, or rather a prejudice which deprives thought of every means of scientific knowledge, is to consider the finite and the infinite as coordinate objects. When a thinker affirms that he does not understand the infinite, it is because, yielding to the analytic habits of the understanding, [p. 339] he puts the infinite beside the finite. He does not perceive that the infinite is destroyed by opposing it to some other reality. Finite beings are opposed to one another, but the infinite is posited alone, without another, and is infinite only on this condition. The finite is therefore not coordinate with, but subordinate to, the infinite. Their relations are those of the whole to the part, since the infinite designates the totality of essence and the finite possesses only a determinate essence. The infinite is all, even the finite. The finite is not outside the infinite, but in the infinite. The finite is not with the infinite, as two objects that are the condition of one another, but by the infinite. Relations of containment, of subordination, and of causality, such are the bonds that exist between the part and the whole, between the finite and the infinite. Hence also the singular similarity which finite beings present to the infinite being. Each being, having its reason in being, bears the imprint of its origin: it is its essence, as God is the essence; it is one, as God is unique; it is itself what it is, as God is himself what is; it is all its essence, as God is all essence. Yes, the finite being is still a whole, as the infinite is the whole, and if it is a whole, it must be infinite in its own way, as it is already absolute within the limits of its nature.

p. 340

What is there, then, that is infinite in the finite? The finite is potentially infinite and infinitely determinable in science. If it is part of a continuous whole such as space or time, it will be divisible like time, like space, whose properties it has, and since division will always give as quotient, however far it is prolonged, some portion of time or of space, this portion will be divisible in its turn, and so on without end. Hence this incontestable proposition: every part of a continuous whole, however small it may be, is divisible to infinity. I do not claim that we can perform this division or give an experimental demonstration of it; I maintain on the contrary that observation never has the infinite for its object, and it is evident indeed that we should need an infinite time to complete the division of time. But if observation does not confirm our proposition, neither does it invalidate it, in this sense [p. 340] that we can pursue the division of a century or of a second as far as we like, without ever approaching the end. Now, if any part whatever of time or of space is divisible to infinity, it must contain an infinity of parts; for if it contained only a determinate number of parts, division continued indefinitely would soon exhaust this number and would have to stop, contrary to the law of divisibility to infinity. Here is the infinite laid bare in a finite quantity, in a line, in a minute. A line considered in its content is as vast as the world, for it contains parts to infinity as the universe embraces an infinity of beings; a line still possesses in its own way the fullness of essence! This is not all: if there is an infinity of parts in a finite quantity, these parts must be infinitely small; for if they had any magnitude whatever, were it but a millionth of a millionth of a second, since there is an infinity of millions in the infinite, an infinity of these parts would be worth not a finite quantum, but infinite time. Here again is the infinite, but the infinite in smallness, the infinitely small, the basis of the infinitesimal calculus, in any part whatever of a continuous whole or in a number that will represent this part. The infinitely small is to the indefinitely small as the infinite is to the indefinite. The infinitely small is to the finite as the finite is to the infinite: an infinity of infinitely small quantities form a finite quantity, as an infinity of finite quantities form an infinite whole. But just as a finite quantity can vanish before the infinite, so any number whatever of infinitely small quantities is null before unity. All finite quantities, small or great, are equal to one another, equally null, in comparison with the infinite, but they differ when compared with one another; likewise all infinitely small quantities are of no magnitude, in relation to a whole number, but they vary when they are in the presence of one another (1).

(1) Théorie de l'infini, ch. II. Brussels, 1846. — Abbé Gratry, Logique, bk. IV, ch. VI, 2nd ed. Paris, 1858.

p. 341

If the finite, instead of being a simple form, a portion of space or of time, a number, is a spiritual or material substance, has it still some relation to the infinite? Yes, a finite substance is an individual object, and everything that is individual is infinitely determined, or determined in every respect, under all relations, from all points of view. In an individual being, to whatever kingdom it may belong, nothing remains indeterminate, neither matter, nor form, nor mass, nor action, nor relations with other substances. It is this infinite determination which constitutes individuality and makes it possible to distinguish from one another objects of the same species.

From this point a difference appears between the two orders of created substances. The infinite is the whole or the entire essence; the absolute is the proper essence or autonomy. Now anthropology teaches that mind and body are precisely opposed to each other according to these two manifestations of essence; for in matter the idea of wholeness, of connection, of continuity, of the linking of everything with everything predominates, whereas in the soul the idea of proper activity, of independence, of will and of abstraction predominates: on the one side, everything is continuous and necessary; on the other, everything is spontaneous and free. Consequently, it is in the domain of nature, in physical individualities, that we shall chiefly have to find again the character of the infinite. In fact, matter is divisible to infinity, like space, from which it is inseparable. Plants and animals are marvels of organization in which details abound, in which relations multiply and combine ceaselessly, to the last limits of microscopic observation. The heavens, on the other hand, almost make us witness the spectacle of the infinitely great. In nature everything is connected, everything holds together from one thing to the next and without end, under the double form of succession and of coexistence: each phenomenon has its cause in another phenomenon which precedes it and becomes in its turn the cause of the one that is to follow: whence an uninterrupted series of facts which is prolonged to infinity in the past and in the future by its origins and by its consequences. So, too, in space

p. 342

Logic. — I. 22 [p. 342] each molecule acts upon everything that surrounds it, each star upon all the others, without our being able to fix a limit where attraction would cease to exercise its influence, if it were not balanced by contrary attractions. In spirit, the reverse takes place. There everything is voluntary and arbitrary, free and often incoherent. The substance of the soul is not divided. Its activity lacks linkage, but we can fill this gap, concentrate our forces, cooperate with our fellow men, and take as the aim of our efforts that profound organization which harmonizes everything in nature. Is this to say that the infinite and continuity are foreign to the spiritual life? No, the course of our thoughts is continuous, in the sense that it is impossible for us not to think, but the direction of the intellect has less sequence than the movement of matter. The soul nevertheless has its fullness like the body, but in its own way: it realizes in time the possible states that are contained in its essence, and if it is permitted to judge from the fact that our faculties are not at all exhausted as our activity increases, there exists in us an infinity of these possible states. Here is the infinite in the soul, the potential infinite, as the condition of our unlimited perfectibility, as the guarantee of our immortality. Add that we have the idea of the infinite, which is something of God, according to Bossuet: est Deus in nobis.

p. 343

We can now account for the illusion of M. Taine, who draws the infinite from the finite by the elimination of limits. The finite has the same essence as the infinite, plus the negative element of determination, of exclusion, or of imperfection. Remove all determination, there remains the indeterminate essence, which is in fact infinite; cut off all negation, you have pure and simple affirmation, or the infinite, the all. The infinite is drawn from the finite because it is there. But it is there only potentially, as the cause is in the effect, as God is in man. It is not the finite that must make us understand the infinite, but the infinite the finite. Of these two elements, the one is positive, the other negative; the first is the whole, the second the part. Now every negation supposes an affirmation to which it is opposed and is itself only a contrary affirmation. A negation [p. 343] pure, which would imply nothing positive, does not exist and cannot be conceived, whereas affirmation subsists and is conceived in itself. Thus the not-self necessarily has a relation to the self, whose limit it marks; but the self is understood without its contrary. The notion of the finite therefore cannot be formed independently of the notion of the infinite, since the finite is in the infinite and by the infinite. Doubtless thought can have finite things for its object without knowing the infinite, but it cannot apprehend them as finite unless it apprehends at the same time the infinite as a point of comparison. The animal perceives finite elements; man alone perceives them as such, man alone knows the finite, because he knows the infinite. The part is nothing without the whole in which it is grounded. To determine a particular object well, we must begin by embracing the whole ensemble of things, as Malebranche observes, then prune away the surplus and concentrate attention on the object under consideration. The object is then conceived in its cause and in its relations as it exists in reality.

PDF 342

T H E L AW S O F K N O W L E D G E

Is knowledge subject to laws? What are these laws, and what is their value? These questions are still disputed and deserve a rigorous examination, for they are of a nature to cast some light upon the theory of knowledge. Sensualism and positivism, with the pretension of confining the whole of science within the limits of phenomena, are absolutely ignorant of the laws of thought, and the excommunication they pronounce upon the a priori elements of human knowledge proceeds, for the most part, from this oversight.

CHAPTER ONE

THE NOTION AND DIVISION OF THE

L AW S O F T H O U G H T

Laws are neither substances nor active causes, but relations. They are the expression of the necessary relations that exist between things, according to Montesquieu.

p. 346

Only, these relations are sometimes founded in the very nature of beings, without any intervention of our will, and sometimes established by man, to serve as a rule and a curb for the free activity of rational beings in social life. Hence divine or natural laws, indicating the relations that necessarily exist between things, and human or civil laws, indicating the relations that ought to exist in society or that are recognized as necessary for the accomplishment of our destiny. In both cases there is a series of phenomena, which are always different, and relations, which remain always the same. The phenomena are, for example, in the domain of the natural laws of the physical or moral order, the mechanical, chemical, and physiological facts that result from the activity of matter, or the voluntary and free acts that proceed from individual minds. In the domain of the civil laws, they are the actions and the juridical obligations of men united in society. These facts and acts change ceaselessly according to time, place, antecedents, relations, and influences of every kind that act upon bodies or upon souls. Each fact is completely determined in all respects, and, in this sense, is never rigorously identical with another fact of the same species. But everything is not different in a series of similar facts. The relations are constant, as in a mathematical proportion or progression. All facts resemble one another in that they have a beginning, an end, a cause, a condition, an aim; and although the causes and conditions may vary for two successive facts, the relations between each fact and its cause or its condition are invariable. All bodies gravitate toward their center, by virtue of attraction; the phenomena of gravitation may change to infinity according to circumstances; but they are always determined by the masses and the distances. In the same way, all acts of the will gravitate toward the good, which is their center or the aim of their movement; moral phenomena likewise differ to infinity, according to the culture of the heart and of the mind; some have [p. 347] for their object the good of the individual, others the good of all; but, in sum, it is always the good as each one conceives and feels it that attracts the will. There is therefore something permanent in this double series of phenomena; there is a common element that remains fixed amid all the changes brought about in time. This invariable element is the law of the phenomena. Natural law is therefore not foreign to facts, outside of them or above them; it is the very expression of the facts, insofar as they have a common element or necessary and constant relations.

p. 348

M. Renouvier arrives at an analogous conception. Law consists “in the common relations of phenomena constantly reproduced.” But the author, in order to remain consistent with himself, is obliged to sacrifice this notion to the general principle of criticism, according to which we know only phenomena. Law is therefore a composite phenomenon, and the permanence it presupposes is only apparent, because phenomena admit of no other. On this view there are only appearances of laws (1). Mr. Mill, who insists so much upon laws, confounds them with causes. But, starting from experience like M. Renouvier, he arrives logically at the same consequences, at the denial of laws as universal and necessary, at the doctrine of chance, at casuism. The domain of experience, in fact, is limited in time and in space; this is admitted. Observation bears upon the earth and upon the stars of our planetary system, not upon the entire universe; it embraces a few periods of time, not the future. If, then, the laws of the world have no other guarantee than experience, they might well be themselves only local and passing phenomena. “I am convinced,” says the author, “that any one accustomed to abstraction and analysis, who will fairly exert his faculties for the purpose, will, when his imagination has once learned to entertain the notion, find no difficulty in conceiving that in some one, for instance, of the many firmaments into which sidereal astronomy now divides the universe, [p. 348] events may succeed one another at random, without any fixed law; nor can any thing in our experience, or in our mental nature, constitute a sufficient, or indeed any, reason for believing that this is nowhere the case.” In practice we may rely upon the law of cause and effect, which has never been belied by experience; but “in distant parts of the stellar regions, where the phenomena may be entirely unlike those with which we are acquainted, it would be folly to affirm confidently that this general law prevails, any more than those special ones which we have found to hold universally on our own planet.” In short, the regular succession of phenomena must not be accepted as a law of the universe, but as a law of that portion of the universe which lies within the limits of observation, and only provisionally (1).

Mr. Mill has still more confused notions of the laws of spiritual life. He sees no other cause of the acts of the mind than the acts themselves. The laws of thought are therefore for him the laws according to which “the phenomena of consciousness are engendered one by another.” This is to confound the logical question of the necessities of knowledge with the psychological question of the association of ideas (2).

(1) Ch. Renouvier, Essais de critique générale, I, § XVIII.

p. 349

Laws are the necessary relations that exist between things, of whatever nature these relations may be and whatever may be the cause of the facts that they unite. Causality is one of these relations, but is not the only one. There are necessary relations between quantities, without one number being the cause of another number. Are there in this sense laws for knowledge? In other words, can we find some invariable element that affects all the phenomena of thought? The question thus put is easy to resolve. Let us [p. 349] first note the diversity of intellectual states; we shall see afterward where their unity lies.

Every thought differs from every other thought in energy, in vivacity, in brilliance, in elevation, in direction, in correctness, from the double point of view of subject and object. This diversity is further increased by individual dispositions and by stages of culture. One has more memory than judgment, another more judgment than memory. This man has more aptitude for observation, that one for speculation. In the first there develops the sensible memory of facts, names, times, or places; in the second the ideal memory of principles, laws, or causes. Now the imagination is more schematic or more creative; now it lends itself better to imitation than to production, and is distinguished by a turn more poetic than scientific. One readily grasps analogies, another differences. Here all the intellectual faculties are more disengaged from one another or more independent of the emotions of the heart; there they are better linked to one another or more closely united to the affections. All these shades, and many others, are to be remarked in the characters of minds, and give to each individual intellect and to each of its states an altogether original physiognomy. Every man, within the limits of observation, has a thought that is his own, and each manifestation of this thought again has its own essence, which distinguishes it from all other manifestations, whether of the same thought or of the thought of all other men. Each phenomenon is unique of its kind.

(1) J. Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, bk. III, ch. xxi. — H. Taine, Le positivisme anglais, Exposition, X.

(2) Ibid., bk. VI, ch. iv, “Of the Laws of Mind.”

p. 350

This variety, or this perpetual flux of phenomena, does not, however, destroy the unity of thought, as Herbart supposes. All intellectual phenomena have common characters and are subject to a common direction; all have a subject and an object; all have an essence that is one, identical, simple, like the essence of the soul itself; all have relations with the coordinate states of feeling and will and with the earlier or later states of the intellect. Finally, in all the states of thought [p. 350] there is something voluntary and something involuntary. Let us dwell on these two points.

It depends on us to think of one object or another, with this or that degree of attention, in each determinate portion of time. It depends on us, in other words, to bring from possibility to reality a phenomenon chosen at will from among all the phenomena that are at present within our reach, and this power belongs to us at every instant without any break of continuity. We are therefore masters of the whole course of our thoughts; we can prolong as long as we please a series of thoughts that occupies us at the moment; we can also interrupt it when we wish, begin a new series, and resume the first at the point that suits us, without ever meeting any obstacle in our preceding activity. Each intellectual state that is realized in life finds its cause directly, not in an earlier state, as Mr. Mill believes, but in the initiative of the mind or in the will, as consciousness attests. Our thoughts therefore do not form an ineluctable chain that develops in us in spite of us, but a series of terms that are united or disunited by ourselves, among which there is no other sequence than the one we choose to put there. Such is the domain of the freedom of thought, which essentially distinguishes mind from matter.

p. 351

But it does not depend on us to think or not to think, to think with or without an object, to think in one manner or in another; it does not depend on us to change the conditions, the mode of development, the aim, or the scientific characters of thought. We always think, whether we will or not. Thought is a property of the soul, and the will creates no property, but directs their manifestations in life. The soul is a thinking substance, whose nature is not the product, but the rule, of our activity. We are not as we will to be, but we will as we are. To think is a necessity for man, and to will is another necessity; for the existence of the will is no more voluntary than that of thought. Not only must we think and [p. 351] think at every instant in a continuous manner, but we must think according to the very nature of our intellect and not otherwise. One does not think without thinking of something, that is to say, without an object. And as knowledge in its widest acceptation expresses every relation between thought and its object, one cannot either think without knowing to some degree. Every intellectual state is therefore a state of true or false knowledge. No rational being is deprived of knowledge, whatever he may will. If he applied himself to know nothing, he would at least know his will. There is more: thought must develop in life as the faculty of knowing, and this mode of development is again independent of our caprices. The activity of the intellect is attached on earth to the activity of the body and especially of the brain, and its stages or degrees of culture are no more arbitrary than the ages of physical life. Just as childhood necessarily precedes youth, and youth maturity, so sensibility is exercised in a preponderant manner before the understanding, and the understanding before reason, in the evolution of the intellect. The conditions, the aim, and the scientific procedures of knowledge are no less necessary. Whoever wishes to know must pay attention, must grasp, must determine the object of thought; there is no other means of acquiring cognitions, and these cognitions cannot be formulated in any other way than in the form of notions, judgments, and reasonings. Whoever desires to arrive at truth and certainty must constrain himself to pursue the proper essence of things and to have recourse to analysis and synthesis in order to assure himself of the result of his researches. In a word, the whole of logic, which characterizes the organic movement of thought, is withdrawn from the empire of the will.

p. 352

Now what is common to all intellectual states is a law of thought; for an element common to all the terms of a series of phenomena marks necessary relations between these terms, according to the definition of law. If no thought can be realized in time without an intervention [p. 352] of the will, freedom itself is a law of the intellect; and indeed we cannot make consciousness cease to be free; even those who abdicate their autonomy in favor of an external authority remain in possession of their thought, and can resume its direction whenever they wish. Everything that is involuntary, or everything that is above the will, in the intellectual states of the soul is consequently a law of thought or of knowledge. The laws of thought are natural or divine laws, which are established for the activity of minds, which derive from the very nature of things, without any participation of our will. Science, logic, and truth are the organism of the laws of knowledge.

The laws of knowledge can be divided into two groups, according to the very notion of knowledge. There are subjective laws, which concern the development and the conditions of thought, abstraction made of objects: such are the functions of the understanding and the stages of culture of the intellect. There are next objective laws, which regard the manifestations of thought in its relations with things: such are the categories of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, which include, among others, the principles of identity, of contradiction, and of sufficient reason, indicated by authors as the fundamental rules of logical operations.

The laws that preside over the various stages of culture may be called laws of the intellectual life: they indicate how thought, in the course of ages, rises little by little from sensibility to the understanding, and from the understanding to reason, where it attains its complete development and is in a position to know everything that is accessible to the human mind in its earthly condition.

p. 353

The functions, or the various moments of the internal activity of the intellect, are rather the laws of thought as a faculty of knowing: they indicate how thought, fully developed, proceeds to the knowledge of facts or of principles, what are the general and permanent [p. 353] conditions of the formation of all knowledge, and finally what are the ways and means at the disposal of the mind for the determination of the objects it wishes to examine thoroughly.

The categories are, strictly speaking, the laws of knowledge: they indicate how things are, or what is the order of their properties, and consequently how they must be studied in order to know them as they are. Metaphysics demonstrates that the laws of knowledge are identical with the laws of reality, and that consequently thought, in obeying its laws, can know things not only as they appear to us but as they are. This proposition, however, is not yet recognized with certainty at the point we have reached; for it depends itself on the question of the legitimacy of our knowledge. In order to avoid all hypothesis, we must therefore confine ourselves to saying that the laws of knowledge simply express how, by virtue of our spiritual constitution, we know and ought to know things. They are still the laws of our reason, saving the proof to be given later that they are also the laws of existence.

p. 354

It is evident, in any case, that from the laws of thought and of knowledge the philosophical method clearly emerges. These two questions are connected, and it is because the philosophers of France and of England have paid so little attention to the laws of thought that they still understand methodology so poorly. The lacunae and the deplorable errors of the materialists of all countries, as apostles of experience, have no other cause. Method is the march of thought toward its goal, toward science, in conformity with the laws of its activity. The movement of thought that aspires to certainty is not arbitrary, but regulated, since certainty is the port at which one must arrive, avoiding the reefs. Method is a set of rules or prescriptions, said Descartes; it is in fact a gradual and regular evolution, it is the most direct and surest way that leads to science. By thinking at random, by yielding to the current of inspiration, one may arrive at some [p. 354] truth; but most often one goes astray, and never is one assured of having reached the end or of possessing complete elements that withstand criticism. Science is not improvised. We must proceed with method in the search for truth. Now to proceed with method is to follow exactly the laws of thought and of knowledge. The functions of thought consist in reflecting, grasping, and determining, and there are only two ways of determining an object; it may be observed in itself by intuition, or it may be referred to its principle by deduction. Hence analysis and synthesis, which are combined in construction. Whoever has grasped these laws sees at the same time how exclusive are the authors who absolutely reject one or the other of the instruments of the mind, and who imagine, for example, that experience is the sole and only method of science. But it is not enough to analyze and to deduce; these two inverse directions, ascending and descending, require a basis; a certain order must be observed in analysis and in synthesis, in order to obtain a sufficient determination and to be able afterward to compare the results of the two methods. This order resides in the system of the categories. The categories are the fundamental properties of things. If, then, method is to be applied to reality or to be regulated by the objects of science, as has been repeated since Aristotle, the table of the categories, or of the laws of knowledge, is the first necessity of method.

CHAPTER TWO

T H E L AW S O F T H O U G H T

p. 355

Let us first follow the development of thought in life.
