Life is the property of a being that realizes its essence in time by a continuous series of states or phenomena [p. 355] Insofar as the soul manifests itself as intellect, it has an intellectual life, and it is the laws of this life that we must first study.

We recall the formula of the chronological antecedents and the logical antecedents of knowledge laid down by M. Cousin, after the proposition of Kant: all knowledge begins with experience, but does not derive from it. We saw, as a result of the theory of sensible knowledge, that this law is inexact, insofar as it alleges a contradiction between life and the logical requirements of thought; for it takes no account of the indeterminate knowledge that is found at the beginning of all intellectual activity. But the law in question applies perfectly to our analytic or determinate cognitions. In the order of time, sensibility develops before reason, in the sense that we are conscious of the sensible elements of thought before being conscious of its rational elements. When the sensualists seize upon this fact and see in it a proof of the truth of their doctrine, they not only forget, like M. Cousin, the starting point of science, but they entirely confound a question of time with a question of logic, or they apply to the nature of ideas what is true only of their appearance in the mind, as the eclectic school expresses it.

p. 356

The stages of culture of the soul are three in number, and correspond fairly well to childhood, youth, and maturity in physical life. They embrace the whole activity of the soul considered as thought, as feeling, and as will; but since thought exercises the greatest influence on the direction of life, they are clearly characterized by the three phases that mark the application of the intellect to knowledge, by sensibility, the understanding, and reason, the faculties preponderant in sensible knowledge, in abstract knowledge, and in rational knowledge. The soul is one; it is therefore not a question of the exclusive action of the senses or of the understanding, but of the simple predominance of one faculty over the others. At the first stage [p. 356] of culture sensibility predominates; at the second, the understanding joins itself to the senses and generalizes the impressions they deliver to us; at the third, reason joins itself to the understanding and the senses, and completes the circle of spiritual activity in its double relation with principles and facts. To the training given by nature succeeds social training; to social training, personal training. The mind realizes itself more and more in the whole of its forces, like the body, and without ever coming to suffice entirely for itself, it becomes at least the regulator of external influences and the arbiter of its destiny.

p. 357

The predominance of sensibility in childhood is sufficiently explained by the position of the mind upon the earth and by the role of the senses in the whole of our relations. The soul arrives in this world as a stranger, and finds itself associated for its whole life with a body that it does not know and that must become the instrument of its activity. It is therefore a necessity for it to begin by making acquaintance with the body to which it is united, to learn to use its limbs and to interpret the impressions of its organs. The senses are the necessary intermediary of all our relations with nature and with our fellow men. It is right, it is indispensable, that our attention should be directed first to them, since it is in the bosom of nature that we must live, and since our fellow men must be our initiators on this globe. That is why our first determinate cognitions are sensible cognitions. We reflect upon the objects that surround us, we distinguish the thoughts and feelings that arise in us, we observe the gestures and the sounds that express them, we study the language that is to put us in communication with other minds and to extend indefinitely the circle of our knowledge. The child notes what passes within him and what passes without, he sees a double series of phenomena, internal and external, and begins to decipher our conventional languages as soon as he has grasped the correspondence that exists between the terms of these two series. All phenomena are the object of sensible or empirical cognitions. Experience [p. 357] reigns at the beginning of life. Each must train his senses, and make use of them to find his bearings in the external world.

When thought develops in relation with sensibility, the other faculties follow the same impulse. Sensibility is one of the currents that feed all the forces of the soul. Sensible cognitions bring with them sensible feelings and give only sensible motives to the voluntary and moral activity of man. At this stage of culture absolute principles make no impression on the mind, but one feels keenly the feelings of pleasure and pain, of hope and fear, concerning the things that interest the sensible nature. The will is not yet free, for it lacks the counterpoise of rational motives, drawn from the consideration of general interests and of the moral order of the world. The mind lives in bondage to the senses. And as pleasure is a purely subjective element, which can be appreciated only by the individual, the child, disposed to refer everything to himself and ignorant of the proprieties and obligations of the family, manifests as yet only the qualities of an egoist. He is exactly in the condition of the animal, with this difference, that the animal never passes beyond the sphere of sensible representations, whereas the child begins where the lower beings stop and must go beyond.

Thought disengages itself little by little from external influences, in proportion as the mind makes itself master of the bodily forces and appropriates them to its own ends. Already the understanding intervenes in the formation of sensible cognitions, by the aid of its functions and its operations, but at first it is crushed by the multiplicity of phenomena. Now attention is more sustained, perception more vivid, determination more complete; abstraction and generalization extend more and more, and the understanding, then dominating phenomena, becomes the mark of a new stage of culture. The proper office of this faculty is to combine, to calculate, to classify, to reduce the variety of things to unity, by ranging individuals in a species,

p. 358

Logic. — I. 23 [p. 358] species in a genus, genera in a wider order or branch. The comparative study of facts leads to abstract knowledge, which is already non-sensible and which prepares purely rational knowledge. But reason is not yet fully awakened; principles remain obscure and uncertain to consciousness; the mind has a vague presentiment of the infinite, of the absolute, of God, of the laws of the moral order, as objects of faith rather than of reason. Deprived of the support of reason, reflection is exercised only on the data of sensibility, as in the system of Locke. Science, however, begins and progresses by analysis, in the form of induction and analogy, on the basis of observation. The mind may advance very far in this way without recourse to a general synthesis of human knowledge, and may even persuade itself that this synthesis is inaccessible to thought.

p. 359

The life of the heart is regulated by the life of the intellect. Pleasure and pain retain the supremacy they had acquired in the whole of the affections, but they are subjected to a rule that prevents them from degenerating into excess, and at the same time other, higher feelings come to light; the family and the fatherland excite generous emotions; beauty, justice, and heroism sometimes provoke enthusiasm; but these feelings are not yet recognized in their truth and do not strike deep roots in the soul. Hence fluctuations and contradictions that now debase and now glorify human nature. In sum, feeling remains passionate and personal under the exclusive direction of the understanding; it is less naive, but more skillful than in childhood; it is a refined sensualism, the sensualism of Bentham, which makes of the art of living a calculation in which one weighs all the consequences of each act in pleasures and pains, in profits and losses, in which happiness, as the aim of reason, is sought in the maximum of possible satisfactions of sensibility. The will, tossed between contrary influences, readily conforms to the proprieties of fortune and position, to the customs and to the [p. 359] prejudices received in society. Equally incapable of an absolute devotion to the divine law and of an unreflecting surrender to the caprices of sensibility, it obeys the utilitarian maxim of enlightened self-interest, and sacrifices now enjoyment to duty, now duty to enjoyment. Duty, in this moral situation, presents itself as a hard necessity imposed upon conscience by a foreign authority; but, from whatever source it comes, it is often understood as according with the true interests of human nature, whether in this life or in the other. The accomplishment of the good is itself a delightful pleasure that the Epicurean does not disdain. The will exercises itself and receives its training in this struggle of reason against the senses; when it has sufficiently practiced the good from interest, it finally gains strength enough to do the good for the sake of the good itself, against the interest of sensibility.

At the third stage of culture reason predominates. But this predominance is not a want of balance in the development of the spiritual forces, for it is itself in conformity with the hierarchical order of the faculties of the soul. Reason is the organ of the divine, which must preside over all the manifestations of a rational being; it is the authority invoked as the sign of truth in all the conflicts of intellectual and moral life; the subordination of our acts to the laws of reason is therefore legitimate, necessary, and in conformity with the nature of man. Reason, moreover, suppresses neither the senses nor the understanding; it recognizes their rights and is content to subject them to its empire; when it reigns over the mind and over the heart, it does not hinder, it completes the circle of their activity and connects them with their source. This third stage of culture is the highest to which rational beings can rise, in whatever place and at whatever time they live. It comprises in itself infinite shades and can develop without end, but it cannot be surpassed by any other state within the limits of creation.

p. 360

It opens with the formation of rational knowledge and above all of the knowledge of God as infinite and absolute Being, cause of all things, principle of science, ideal [p. 360] of reason. The mind has not completed its development as long as it stops at the conception of individual objects, of species, of genera enclosed within the limits of the world, and possesses only a vague notion of a Supreme Being, as the basis of its religious convictions. Everything remains confused, incoherent, and uncertain for thought; the unity of things and the connection of the various parts of reality escape us, if we have not a precise and scientific notion of God. This results, evidently, from the lacunae of all the experimental doctrines, which are incapable of rising to a general synthesis or even to the idea of law. The finite calls for the infinite, as the effect for the cause, and the part for the whole. Thanks to these simple elements of thought, the notion of God is susceptible of a rigorous determination in science, provided that one proceeds with method and knows how to disengage oneself from the procedures of sensualism. When the thought of God enlightens the mind, everything is explained: the world is bound to God, beings are bound to one another in the world, all the objects of the intellect group themselves in a system, science has recognized its principle, and, with science, the whole rational life has found its law. Practice completes theory; God is not only the true, he is also the good, the beautiful, the just, the object of all activity, the ideal perfection that we must seek to imitate in all things.

p. 361

From the notion of God rightly understood flows the organization of all our knowledge, distributed according to its kinds and brought back to its principle. Truth and certainty are won. The same order is then established in our affections. No feeling conformable to nature is stifled by the religious feeling developed in its fullness, in conformity with reason; but the disorderly movements of the heart are quieted in the presence of the infinite; to passion succeed calm, serenity, confidence in God. The will, by the same stroke, freed from the oppression of the senses, goes henceforth to its goal without hindrance. Its goal is the good. It does the good purely and simply, without any consideration foreign to the good; in other words, it [p. 361] does the good in an absolute manner, without condition or compromise, as a necessity of the moral life, as God wills and does it. Do the good, that is everything, it is the law, it is duty, it is freedom. Add nothing to the formula, do not do the good for enjoyment or for interest, in the hope of being rewarded in this life or in the other, do the good because it is good, and egoism is vanquished by devotion, duty is accomplished, the law is respected, the will is free, with that heroic freedom which knows how to cut its way through obstacles, and which is stronger than all the powers of the world.

Such are the three stages of culture of the intellect. Hence this law of intellectual life: the soul develops first by the senses, then by the understanding, finally by reason, without its being possible to invert this order. Under the preponderant influence of sensible impressions, it is at the lowest rung of the ladder; under the influence of abstract notions formed by reflection, it perfects itself, rises, and ceaselessly extends the circle of its activity; under the influence of the absolute principles of reason, it attains its full maturity. The life of the soul in its earthly condition reproduces the succession of ages that marks the life of the body, and the one is no less than the other independent of our will. No intermediary can be suppressed, no term can change places with another. Sensibility is the basis of our activity, reason is its crown. It would be as chimerical to wish to prevent the advent of reason as to wish to tear out the senses in order to restore freedom to the mind.

p. 362

Man, in this respect, differs essentially from the animal. Animals stop at the first stage of culture, without ever passing it. They have a sensitive soul, according to the forceful expression of Aristotle. The child begins where the animal ends, but he has a higher destiny, for he is endowed with a rational soul. Reason already shows itself in sensible cognitions, although the child is not conscious of it. In every man there appear at least gleams of the higher culture of the understanding and of reason, [p. 362] even in those who fail to recognize reason as a distinct faculty, and who confound it either with sensibility, or with reasoning, or with abstraction. One may be mistaken about the origin of a principle and see in it a transformation or a generalization of the data of experience; but this error of psychology does not interrupt the laws of the development of the soul. One does not cease to belong to rational beings by denying reason. Yet we must also take into account the nature of the mind in the analysis of its laws. We have said how the mind is cultivated and in what order its various stages of culture necessarily follow one another; but the mind does not always attain its complete development in this world. The activity of the soul bears other characters than the activity of matter. An organized body, meeting with no contrary influence, passes inevitably through the course of its ages. But the mind has at its disposal a free will which permits it to slow down or to hasten its movements, and which makes it responsible for the accomplishment of its mission. That is why the stages of culture of the soul do not always coincide with the ages of the body. The maturity of the intellect may precede or follow at a distance the maturity of the organism; it may even be wanting in the whole of the present life, as observation shows in individuals, in social classes, and in peoples. The culture of sensibility in our time is still preponderant in the lower strata of our most civilized societies, and reigns without a rival among savages. The culture of the understanding distinguishes today the majority of the members belonging to the upper regions of society, among the civilized nations of Europe and America. Rational culture, as a permanent state of life, shows itself only as an exception, in the period in which we are. But if we may judge of humanity from the individual, and of the future from the past, there is no doubt that the exception will become the rule. That is the profoundest significance of progress (1).

(1) Krause, Psychische Anthropologie, S. 133, 157, 201 ff.

p. 363

To the first stage of culture corresponds, in the history of philosophy, sensualism, as the exclusive system of sensation. It is a doctrine of the past, whose restoration in our time can be explained only by a complete ignorance of the destinies of philosophy and of the faculties of the human mind. To the second stage of this culture correspond the abstract systems, which add to sensibility a power of combination and generalization. These are doctrines of transition, whose model is found in Locke’s Essay concerning Human Understanding. To the last stage of culture, finally, corresponds rationalism, as a harmonic system founded on the whole of the faculties of the mind and laying down the absolute principles of rational life. This is the doctrine of the future, glimpsed by Plato, by Descartes, by Leibniz, by Spinoza, by Kant, by Cousin, from various points of view, and developed in its basis and in its principal moral, social, and religious applications by Krause.

We know the laws of the development of thought in life. What now are the laws of its activity in the formation of sensible or rational knowledge?

p. 364

The laws of thought are summed up in the functions of the understanding, that is to say, in the various moments of the subjective activity of the intellect, abstraction made of its objects. Here again we have three successive stages that manifest the movement of thought, when it applies itself to know either an object or a relation, either a fact or a principle. Thought first stretches toward the object, then it grasps it, finally it determines it in the whole of its properties, its parts, and its relations. The succession is regular and independent of our will. Attention, perception, and determination always follow one another in the same order, whatever the object, and can present themselves in only one way. The will intervenes only to hasten the evolution of the intellect or to let it ripen at each phase of its activity. We have here, then, all the elements of a law. Bossuet had already remarked that “every [p. 364] operation of the mind, in order to be well performed, must be performed attentively, so that attention is a quality common to all three (1).” The same observation applies to perception and to determination. In order to understand, judge, and conclude, an act of attention is not enough; the terms and their relation must be grasped, and it is important to determine them from every point of view, if one wishes to avoid error.

The scientific determination of the objects of thought is accomplished in two ways, neither more nor less, because we have two ways of knowing things, either in themselves, by way of intuition, or in their principle or their cause, by way of deduction. Hence the two methodical procedures of analysis and synthesis. Method is therefore founded on the laws of thought and fulfills them. There are only two paths for the intellect to follow in the search for truth, because there are only two modes of knowledge, intuition and deduction. This is what Descartes had glimpsed. On the one hand, one may derive a thing from its principle, without seeing it in itself, without knowing whether it has a name. Thus the vibratory motion is deduced from the elasticity of bodies. The laws of acoustics are intelligible even to those who have never heard a sound. On the other hand, one may study things as they appear to us, in their own essence, without ascending to their principle, without even knowing whether they are connected with some higher truth. Thus sounds are observed in experimental physics.

p. 365

To proceed by intuition, to determine things in themselves, is to perform an act of analysis. To proceed by deduction, to determine things in their principle, is to perform an act of synthesis. These are the two laws that guide the march of thought in the determination of its objects. Both must be recognized, for both derive from the nature of the human mind. Analysis is observation, it is the intuitive knowledge that embraces all that we know a posteriori; synthesis is the deductive knowledge that [p. 365] envelops what we know a priori. The positivists are therefore in error when they reduce to experience all our means of knowing. It is next necessary to legitimate the two organs of science in all their applications. Intuition bears not only on the phenomena of life, but also on universal laws and principles. The positivists err again when they grant to man only sensible intuitions, to the exclusion of the intellectual intuitions of reason. The skeptical conclusions of their doctrine concerning God, the future life, and the principles of rational life have no other motive than this narrow conception of the problem of method and of knowledge.

Analysis and synthesis are independent of each other and may be employed separately by a limited intellect. But they must unite, complete each other, and be applied to each other. This application constitutes construction, as the third part of method. Analysis, viewed as a whole, is an elevation of the self to God; synthesis starts from God and returns to the self. The one develops in an ascending series of notions that tend toward the absolute principle of science, as toward the center of gravitation of the mind; the other develops in a descending series of notions that radiate from the center toward the circumference. It is then a matter of comparing the terms of these two series, of seeing whether they correspond to one another, and finally of confronting the results of synthesis with those of analysis. Without this precaution one would often obtain only arbitrary deductions that would glide past reality, that would be only plays of wit, of which the system of Hegel offers a striking image. The aim of construction is to prevent these mistakes and to secure the foundations of knowledge. When there is perfect concordance between analysis and synthesis, truth obtains all the guarantees it demands in order to become certainty; for this concordance signifies that we know things in themselves such as they ought to be by virtue of their principle.

(1) Bossuet, la Logique, bk. i, ch. v.

p. 366

Geometry presents us with a remarkable example of [p. 366] methodical construction. This science owes its age-old perfection to the regular combination of analysis and synthesis. General truths are deduced, then compared with the sensible intuitions that figures give, and from this comparison is born the exact definition of each geometrical element. Infinite space has three dimensions and contains all the possible combinations between these dimensions. Hence limited spaces within infinite space. Hence also limits that have only a single dimension. Let us stop at this last deduction. I take a sheet of paper and draw a line. I observe this object attentively, I recognize that it is limited, and, abstracting from its thickness, I see in it only a single dimension. I now compare the image with the deduced object and find that they are identical. I then obtain by construction a definition of the line: it is that interior limit of space which has only one dimension. I determine the line anew by deduction and intuition. I know that everything that exists has an essence and a form, whence I conclude that the line also must have a form and a ground. I return to the line I have drawn and discover that it has a length and a certain direction. Comparing the two points of view, I affirm that they coincide, that the length of the line is its essence and that its direction is the form of this essence. Hence a new and more complete definition of the line: it is a simple dimension, that is to say, a length with a determinate direction. I proceed further in order to arrive at a division of this object. I apply to length the idea of quantity and to direction the idea of quality, in the form of identity and difference. Everything that is limited is susceptible of increase and decrease, therefore the line also: the length can therefore grow or diminish, the line can be divided into parts, and as each part is still a line, it is in its turn divisible, the line is therefore divisible without end into similar parts. I now return to the line that is on the paper, I see that in fact I can divide it into a certain number of parts, but I recognize at the same time that observation has limits and that I cannot carry out [p. 367] a division to infinity. I take up again the form or the direction of the line. The direction will be either always the same or always other, variable, changing. I draw a straight line and a curved line, I observe their properties, and, applying the deduced proposition to the result of the intuition, I find once more that the agreement is perfect. What, then, is a straight line? It is the line whose form is homogeneous, whose direction is identical, the line that goes to its goal without ever swerving either to the right or to the left. And what is a curved line? The line whose direction is always different, or whose form varies incessantly. These are the two kinds of lines given by construction (1).

Geometry, then, is not an experimental science, as some positivists assert. Experience, in the ordinary sense of the word, insofar as it has for its object real things subject to the senses, plays no part in it. But analysis shows itself in it in one of its applications, in its relations with the schemata of the imagination, which have only an abstract existence, like numbers. It is this application that is confounded with experience, in order afterward to confound experience with the whole of method. This is sheer ignorance of the laws of thought. Geometry is essentially deductive, a priori, like metaphysics, and sensible intuitions are manifested in it only as signs or symbols of general truths. The same system of construction is applicable to all the philosophical sciences.

CHAPTER THREE

T H E L AW S O F K N O W L E D G E

p. 368

Analysis, synthesis, and construction are the various procedures of the mind, as subject of knowledge, for the determination of things. But if from the subject we pass to the object, what shall we find in things by the use of [p. 368] these methods? We must find in them what is in them, neither more nor less, for the aim of thought is to know all that is, as it is. Now what things are we call their essence or their nature. Determination therefore has for its object the essence or the nature of beings. But beings make themselves known only by their properties; if the essences differ, the properties differ; if the properties are the same, the essences are the same. To determine the essence of things is therefore to determine the whole of their properties. But beings have a multitude of properties, whether they are considered in themselves or in their relations. What order must be followed in the determination of things, in the analysis or the deduction of their properties? This is the question of the categories.

(1) Krause, Encyclopædie der philosophischen Wissenschaften.

p. 369

The categories are an instrument of methodical and universal determination. Whatever their objective validity may be, it is certain that we know nothing except by the use of the categories. What shall we say of God? That he is Being, essence, one; that he is himself essence and is the whole essence; that he is posited, that he exists, that he is substance. What shall we say of the mind and the body of man? That they are beings which have an essence, that each has its proper essence and its whole essence, that both are posited and exist in themselves as substances. What shall we say of a grain of sand? That it is a being, that it has an essence, that this essence is one, that it is its own essence and its whole essence, that it is posited, that like every body it has a substantial existence. To whatever object thought is applied, it is always the same elements that it affirms. Kant made the categories the forms of the understanding. In this character they would already be the sinew of our judgments and our reasonings. But is not this point of view too narrow? Are not the categories found also in notions, and consequently in all the operations of thought? Without any doubt, for we never see anything but beings or properties, that is to say, manifestations of essence. But are the categories only subjective forms which exist in us without existing [p. 369] outside us? This is the very ground of subjectivism, which sets up a barrier between thought and reality. It was well to raise the hypothesis in order to check rash affirmations, but the difficulty can be resolved only in what follows. All that we maintain at this moment is that being, essence, unity, selfhood, seem to belong to things as much as to the mind, and that if they are not constitutive principles of things, in harmony with the regulative principles of thought, they are at least laws of knowledge in general, according to the distinction that must be drawn between knowledge and truth. The forms of thought are assuredly common and necessary elements of all our knowledge, since we have only thought with which to know.

Hence the utility of a table of categories, as the organism of the laws of knowledge or as a logical topic. If there exists an exact table of the simplest and most fundamental attributes that the mind can discover in things, we shall determine the objects of thought in the most profound and most complete manner by considering them in turn from the point of view of each category. And as method is the course of thought according to determinate laws, to proceed methodically to the scientific determination of things will be to follow the order of the categories. The rigor admired in the works of Kant comes from the use of the categories, however imperfect they were, as rules of method. There is, besides, no fear that uniformity of plan in the determination of the most different objects of thought will bring confusion into the mind; for proper essence, the principle of originality, is also a category, which is united with all the others and diversifies them in each of their applications. Kant did not confound the moral sciences with the natural sciences in analyzing right and matter according to the constant formulas of quantity, quality, relation, and modality. His point of view merely was neither extended enough nor lofty enough.

p. 370

The first, or rather the only, law of knowledge is [p. 370] the category of being. It is impossible to think without thinking of something, whether substance or property, that is to say, without conceiving being in itself or in one of its determinations. Being is therefore permanently at the foundation of all human thought, whether one knows it or not, and if it were not also in the objects of thought, nothing would be, except the self: a consequence of subjectivism accepted by Fichte. The self itself would both be and not be: it would be as subject, it would not be as object for the thought of another. Let us not dwell on these puerilities of idealism, but say simply that being is, since it is necessarily, in one form or another, the object of thought, every time we think of something, every time we think. Being and thing are identical. “Every idea, whatever it may be, containing that of being, or rather being only a modification of it, it follows that the idea of being, prior to all the others, is also the most general to which it is possible for the mind to rise (1).” Rosmini made this category the basis of his treatise on the origin of ideas. He affirms in turn that it is universal, that it is indispensable to thought, that it is the primitive element of all knowledge. An author has contested these assertions, but he takes the idea of being for an abstract notion of relations or of qualities, whereas being expresses all that is, possibility as well as reality, substance and all that is detached from it by abstraction (2). M. Renouvier, who reduces everything to phenomena, also begins with the affirmation of being, that is to say, with a notion far higher than the one which, according to him, can alone occupy thought. “What are the objects of analysis and of synthesis? What do we consider, whether separately or together? Sensations, notions, volitions, affections; or again bodies, minerals, plants, animals, men, peoples, stars, worlds. I mean that we [p. 371] consider things. Things! Here is a word of sovereign utility in philosophy. Novices disdain it, and yet it is inevitable. It is the first of syntheses, the most complete and the clearest, as well as the vaguest, and while it says everything, it encumbers the mind with no system (1).”

The idea of being is the fundamental law of knowledge. If, then, metaphysics teaches us in what follows that God himself is being, pure and simple being, one and whole being, we shall be able to conclude with entire certainty that it is God who is the law or the principle of thought, that it is God whom we affirm, with or without consciousness, in all our affirmations, even when we deny God, and that science agrees on this point with the religious feeling. If God were not, nothing would be, not even thought. Certainly there is some difficulty in passing from being to beings, but these difficulties, even if they were inextricable, ought not to make us renounce self-evidence. Now it is evident that the category of being is the first law of knowledge, and that by virtue of this law God can be conceived only as being without restriction, and consequently as the very law, and the whole law, of intelligence. We now understand Spinoza, when he says that the perfect method is that which directs the mind under the law of the perfect being (2).

(1) Lamennais, Esquisse d’une philos., 1st part, bk. I, ch. v. Paris, 1840.

(2) Buchez, Traité complet de philos., vol. II, Appendix. Paris, 1839.

p. 372

The other laws of knowledge must be deduced from the category of being and can be only partial determinations of it, applicable to the particular forms of thought. To discover the whole of the special laws of knowledge, a matter still unexplored in logic, we must consider being successively in itself, in the unity of its essence, then in its interior or in its content, and finally in its relations with what it contains. From the first point of view, being is alone and unique, it is in unity all that it is and nothing else; from the second, it manifests [p. 372] itself inwardly under the character of plurality and of the opposition of parts or species; from the third, it presents itself in union or in harmony with all that is contained in its essence. These three aspects of being are designated by the names of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, and express the whole essence of things. There is no fourth term in this order of considerations. When an object has been studied as whole, as an ensemble of parts, and as the relation of the whole to the parts and of the parts to one another, the essence of the object has been exhausted. Hence this new formula of the law of being, developed in its general elements: All things must be thought and known according to thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. When this law is faithfully observed in all its prescriptions, knowledge is organic or complete, for organization has no other conditions; when, on the contrary, the law is followed only in part, knowledge is incomplete or defective. If the thesis is lacking, the object is not known in itself, it cannot be defined; if the antithesis fails, its parts or its manifestations are not known, it cannot be divided; if, finally, the synthesis leaves something to be desired, the relations of the parts to the whole are not understood, they cannot be connected with the essence of the object, and consequently cannot be demonstrated. To proceed methodically is once more to fulfill the law of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis; it is, in other terms, to determine things as they are, as beings, as they really are.

(1) Renouvier, Essais de critique générale, I, § 11.

(2) Spinoza, de la Réforme de l’entendement.

p. 373

Anthropology develops regularly according to this law: the thesis is man; the antithesis is mind and body, as the opposed objects of psychology and of somatology; the synthesis is the union of mind and body with each other and with man. Metaphysics must set forth the notion of God according to the same plan: the thesis is God; the antithesis which is contained in God is that of the physical world and the spiritual world; the synthesis is the union of the two faces of the world with each other and with God. Each science can determine its object in the same manner, by making it known first in general, in its ensemble [p. 373] or in its undivided unity; then in decomposing it into its parts or examining it from every point of view; and finally in combining these manifold manifestations with one another and with the whole. Only, in the present state of the sciences, there are often gaps to be pointed out, whether the general part is forgotten and abandoned to philosophy, or the combinations are made only at random and without order. Finally, every object of thought lends itself to the application of the same law. If we wish to study light, for example, we shall ask what it is in itself, whether it is substance or property and what sort of property; we shall inquire what its content is, or what the fundamental colors are; and finally we shall analyze the colors in their relations with one another and with light. If we wish to construct the theory of the line, we shall give its comprehension, as length and as direction; we shall pass to its extension, as straight and as curved; we shall see, finally, whether these two species, however opposed they may be, cannot also be united, as in the sections of the circle. The idea of relation, which M. Renouvier erects into the supreme law of thought, does not present itself, and can never present itself, except in the third place in the methodical knowledge of things.

With the principles of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, still so ill understood by authors and by Hegel himself, are now connected the special laws of knowledge, notably the principles of identity, of contradiction, and of sufficient reason, the only ones that have been subjected to serious examination and that are admitted almost without dispute in logic. The first is a particular case of the law of the thesis; the second, of the antithesis; the third, of the synthesis. We are about to recognize their value and their place in the whole of the laws of thought.

The law of the thesis comprises all the categories that relate to being considered in itself, among others the general ideas of essence, of form, and of existence, of unity, of identity, and of totality. It may be expressed thus: Every thing must be thought and determined according to its

p. 374

Logic. — I. 24 [p. 374] essence and its form, in the unity of all that belongs to it as its own. It is the law of unity that we apply when we refer to one and the same object the various impressions that we receive of it through our five senses, or when we reduce to a system the series of our cognitions. Identity is another moment of the thesis; but it is neither the first nor the only one. The idea of identity is that of selfhood or of the same, apart from every consideration of time. As a principle of knowledge, principium identitatis, it does not mean that things remain the same, without change or alteration, but simply that they are what they are, neither more nor less, that they are equal to themselves, that they have a proper essence and that they are that essence, not another. Each thing is what it is and must be known as such: idem est sibimetipsi idem, a = a, such is the general formula. This law applies to all objects of thought and may assume as many forms as there are objects: God is God, I am myself, the true is true. Hence the judgments of identity, which are wrongly disdained. They are absolutely incontestable and say in a single word almost all that can be said of an object. The judgment “man is man” is sometimes worth a long discourse. All scientific research would be illusory if we did not begin by admitting the legitimacy of the principle of identity. What is the use of demonstrating the truth of a proposition, if we doubt that the true is rather true than false? The skeptics think no differently in this respect from the dogmatists. In contesting the possibility of science, it is certainty that they contest, not the hypothesis. But if the law of identity is unassailable, it must not be made, as by Fichte and Schelling, the absolute and complete principle of science. Identity is an essential property, but it is not the whole essence. It is therefore a grave error to enclose all psychology in the axiom “the self is the self,” or all metaphysics in the proposition “God is absolute identity.”

p. 375

The law of identity is often confounded with other principles. It is almost the fashion in logic to regard it as the basis of the theory of syllogisms. There is, however, [p. 375] a distinction to be made. Syllogisms by equivalence, in which the terms have the same extension and can be substituted for one another, do indeed rest on the principle of identity: two notions equal to one and the same third are equal to each other. But syllogisms by subordination, in which the terms are to one another as species and genus, are founded on another principle, on the law of containment: whatever is in the contained is also in the container. The error committed by most authors on this subject is to be explained only by ignorance of the most elementary laws of knowledge. The principle of identity prevails above all in mathematics, as equality of quantities or of relations, as equation or proportion. Applied to distinct things that are compared with each other, it does not suppress the distinction, but affirms that the unity of essence subsists in the difference. Two series of numbers may be the same from the point of view of quantity without being the same in all respects, without losing their characteristic properties. The same is true in the philosophical applications of the principle of identity. Two men are equal as rational beings and unequal as individuals. Two species of one and the same genus, like animal and plant, however opposed they may be, are identical in their genus, inasmuch as both possess the common properties of organized beings. All beings are identical as beings, if we abstract from the qualities that differentiate them in their species.

The law of the antithesis comprises all the categories of contraries, determination and exclusion, affirmation and negation, being and non-being. It may be expressed in general in this form: Every thing must be thought and known in the multiplicity of the elements that it contains and in the reciprocal opposition of all its parts. To this law are related, among others, the principles of determination, of contradiction, of originality, of analogy, and of parallelism.

p. 376

The principle of determination, principium determinationis per omnia prædicata, requires that the object of thought be [p. 376] examined on all its sides and in all its content, so that nothing obscure may remain in it and all vagueness may disappear from the intellect. Every being is what it is and is only that, but in what it is it can be determined to infinity, in a positive or negative manner, by the application of all the properties or the combination of all the categories. The Great Art of Raymond Lull had no other aim than to facilitate this determination, by means of tables, from a certain number of points of view. The idea was just, but badly executed and arbitrarily restricted. Thought obeys this law instinctively in probing the objects of science, but must fulfill it knowingly, according to the order of the categories. Everything that is finite is determined in all respects, in all its properties, as far as observation reaches; even the infinite is still determined, in the sense that it excludes all limit and all negation. The science of God is possible only on this condition, that thought can determine everything, even the indeterminate.

p. 377

The law of contradiction, principium contradictionis, relates to the contrary elements contained in a whole, that is to say, to the determinate members of an opposition, insofar as these members are limited or affected by negation. The terms of an antithesis are, for example, the straight line and the curved line, and not the line and the curved line, or the line and the straight line; mind and body, and not man and body; the male and the female, “vir et mulier” and not “homo et mulier”; thought and feeling, knowledge and emotion, science and felicity, and not mind and thought; the physical world and the spiritual world, and not God and nature; all these terms are posited over against their contraries and thereby opposed to each other in the form of affirmation and negation; but none of them is opposed to the higher whole which contains both members of the antithesis at once. It is to contraries as such, and only to contraries, that the principle of contradiction applies, as the law of the antithesis. Of two opposed or coordinate terms, each is what it is, but neither is its contrary; each is identical with itself, but is the contrary of the other; the first, far [p. 377] from being the second, is not what the second is, and is what the second is not; which does not prevent both from still having common properties and being united in the same genus; it is not in their common qualities that they are contrary, but in the opposed characters that affect these qualities. The straight line and the curved line both have a direction, but this direction is determined in two ways which exclude each other. The principle of contradiction, founded on this inner opposition in the essence of a being, is expressed thus: no thing is its contrary; a being is not what it is not; one and the same object cannot have two contradictory attributes of which the one would be the negation of the other; it must either be or not be, one of the two; yes or no, no middle; to be or not to be; a is not non-a, a is not b; principium exclusi tertii. Within these limits, applied to contraries considered as such, the principle of contradiction is as certain and as indispensable as the principle of identity, of which it is the complement. The true and the false are the contradictory elements of knowledge; it would be perfectly useless to engage in the search for truth if we could suppose that the true is the false, or that one and the same proposition is at once true and false in the same respect. The child instinctively rejects this confusion and can cultivate his intelligence only at that price; logic demonstrates that the law which he obeys without being conscious of it is conformable to reason.

p. 378

The species of one and the same genus exclude each other, the parts of one and the same whole repel each other. There would be contradiction in conceiving an animal that should be at once vertebrate and invertebrate, an angle that should be at the same time acute and obtuse, a will that should be at once free and determined by external causes. But we must take good care not to apply the principle of contradiction in the same sense to the whole considered in its relations with its parts, to the genus regarded in its relations with its species; for here there is no longer antithesis and coordination, but subordination and synthesis. The principle of contradiction does not govern this case, or, if you will, it governs it in a positive manner, leaving the [p. 378] contradiction subsisting, whereas it adapts itself in a negative manner to species compared with one another. It is therefore inexact to say in an indeterminate way that nothing contradictory exists in the world. Every being, on the contrary, is, and contains in itself, contrasting parts or contradictory elements, each of which can be at once affirmed and denied without injury to truth. Man, for example, is mind and is not mind; the triangle is equilateral and is not equilateral; matter changes and does not change; each thing is and is not each of its inner manifestations, since it is the second as well as the first, and is not the one insofar as it is the other. It is because the contradiction in this respect is real or positive that we cannot attribute one of the parts to the whole in the form of a universal judgment, that is to say, without restriction, and say, for example: every angle is right, man is only mind.

The principle of contradiction can therefore be applied negatively, in its ordinary form, only to parts considered in their reciprocal relations, because the parts as such are completely determined or are the negation of one another. Even this application is made under the reservation of the identity that subsists between the parts as members of one and the same whole and of the synthesis that remains possible between them. The laws of thought complete one another, but do not destroy one another. Contradiction does not efface the unity of essence, and unity does not wrong variety. That is why it is not enough to enunciate this general formula: one and the same object cannot be and not be at the same time; we must make it precise, as Aristotle did, and add that the object is considered in the same respect. Then, indeed, the object is determined and finds itself in contradictory opposition with every other determinate point of view.

p. 379

These distinctions are necessary, for there is no logical principle of which so much abuse has been made as of the law of contradiction. The abuse is easy when we do not grasp the whole of the laws of knowledge, and antitheses, besides, have a charm for the imagination. Hegel raises his whole system upon [p. 379] the principle of contradiction, and he attributes to this same principle all the errors of the old logic. What does this mean? He accepts the positive formula and rejects the negative formula of the principle. Contradiction is therefore the universal law of things, everything is contradictory, and truth consists, not in affirming or denying one and the same attribute of a given subject, but in affirming and denying at once the same attribute of the same subject. This is a renewed theory of the sophists, refuted by Plato and by Aristotle, as annihilating all reality and permitting thought to pronounce neither for nor against any proposition. Is snow white or black? Both. Am I? Yes and no. Unhappily this theory has made many minds giddy. People love to imitate the rhythm of the Hegelian dialectic, and think themselves profound thinkers when they dare to belie common sense and to proceed in all things by contradictory affirmations. Contradiction thus becomes, without rule or measure, the sign of truth: every truth needs to be completed by its contrary. “The beautiful is the ugly, God is evil, right is might.” Caprice of imagination, exercise in rhetoric.

p. 380

Hegel set the example of this aberration by not respecting the limits of the principle of contradiction, as the law of the antithesis. His method confines itself to affirming a thesis, denying it, and then uniting the affirmation and the negation in a third term: principium tertii intervenientis. Contradiction therefore exists between the thesis and the antithesis, and not between the two members of the antithesis, which are both contained in the thesis. Therein lies the whole error. Contradiction is indeed a general law founded in the nature of things, but it is neither the first nor the only law. It must be seen where it is and not where it is not. There is something above contradiction; it is the thesis, it is the whole or the one and entire essence of the object under consideration. It is not, then, to the thesis that a contradictory proposition must be opposed, but in the thesis that we must look for two determinations or two parts which exclude each other reciprocally and which can at once be affirmed and denied [p. 380] of the whole or of the higher genus. If the thesis, for example, is the organism, the antithesis will be, in natural history, the vegetable organism and the animal organism; vegetation will be diametrically opposed to animality, but not to organization; we may say of the organism that it is and is not vegetable, but we shall not say the same of the animal. Hegel took no account of these prescriptions; he understood, the first in our day to do so, that the principle of contradiction has also a positive value, but he made a false application of it.

p. 381

The first thesis in his system is being, and the first antithesis non-being or nothingness, which are united in becoming. The being of which he speaks is pure being, absolute being. But absolute being is opposed to nothing, for beside it there is no pure non-being or absolute nothingness, a thing inconceivable and which, if it were, would devour being itself. Outside of being there is nothing; we must not say: there is the nothing, for the nothing is neither a being nor a quality, it is nothing, not even the second term of an antithesis whose other term would be being. Being is the one and entire thesis, the thesis without antithesis, because it is impossible for us to grasp above being something that would embrace at once being and its contrary, pure being and pure non-being. This something would already be being. It is therefore in being itself that we must find two determinate terms which are contradictorily opposed, which are posited the one over against the other, as contraries or coordinates, which are consequently both affected by negation. This negation is called non-being, nothingness, but if we wish to keep this name for it, it is a relative nothingness, a privation of some reality and not of all reality. This is the only nothingness that exists in the world, and this nothingness is not opposed to being as its contrary, but to determinate beings, as determinate, which are contained in being: the first of these determinations is not the second, the second is not the first, each is what it is, nothing more, to the exclusion of its contrary; but nothing is therefore denied of being itself, which is not determinate, which is neither first nor second, which is above [p. 381] both, and contains them in its essence with all their properties, stripped of their restrictions. It is therefore not permissible to say that being and nothingness are identical, unless one takes pleasure in speculating on abstractions and in propounding charades. It is assuredly not being as such that is identical with non-being as such; it is therefore abstract being which, inasmuch as it is only an abstraction, is equivalent to nothingness. But then any terms whatever may be put through the same evolutions, for example pleasure and chance. Pleasure is not chance, the one is certain, the other uncertain, they are therefore contraries; yet pleasure and chance are two names of things, they are therefore identical, and moreover they are united in happiness, which is an accidental pleasure. In short, Hegel’s system is a skillful construction of fancy which is made in defiance of reason and which misconceives all the laws of knowledge (1).

p. 382

The law of the antithesis contains still other principles. Identity and contradiction combined apply to the individual things comprised in the species. Each individuality is identical with itself and excludes all other individualities of the same genus; in other terms, each is alone what it is, to the exclusion of its fellows. Thus men differ from one another although members of one and the same species, and each, by reason of his infinite determination, is a unique exemplar of humanity, as experience attests as far as it can extend. The same is true of animals and plants in each genus. The same law is verified in objects of the same sort which are completely determined: for example, in the leaves of a tree, in the hairs of the head, in grains of sand, in drops of water, in the acts of life, in the physical or chemical phenomena of matter. Microscopic observation has [p. 382] never found at fault this principle, that everything is the same as itself and other than everything else, that everything differs from everything, down to the least details of reality. This is what Leibniz called principium identitatis indiscernibilium, and what it would be better to name “the principle of originality.”

(1) A. Véra, Logique de Hegel. — P. Janet, Études sur la dialectique dans Platon et dans Hegel. — E. Vacherot, la Métaphysique et la Science. — A. Gratry, Logique.

p. 383

But originality does not exclude similarity, principium analogiæ seu congruentiæ. The individualities that reveal themselves as distinct in the same species have nevertheless all the common properties of their species, and consequently of their genus and of their order. A straight line and a curved line, although opposed to each other, resemble each other as lines, that is to say, as lengths endowed with a certain direction. It is true that the direction varies according to the proper essence of the object, but the lines are still similar in that each has its own proper essence. The similarity would be complete if the two objects had the same proper essence, as is the case with two straight lines or two curves of the same species. In the widest acceptation of the word, we may say that everything is analogous to everything, since in all things subject to thought we find essence, form, existence, unity, identity, relation, in a word all the categories of being. Hence the law of universal analogy, so fruitful in applications in the sciences. But in a narrower sense, similarity attaches to things that are identical down to their very proper essence, like two circles or two equilateral triangles. When analogy manifests itself between the two members of an antithesis, it becomes parallelism, or contrasting similarity. Thus mind and body develop in parallel in life as homologous organisms, in which each determination of the one corresponds to a determination of the other: thought to the brain, feeling to the heart, will to movement, imagination to the senses, reason to instinct. The same is true of the vegetative activity and the sensorial activity of the body, of feeling and intelligence in the soul, of man and woman in humanity. The two sexes are entirely opposed and entirely equal in all respects, and consequently [p. 383] constituted with a view to each other and destined to complete each other mutually. In the same way the elements of language and the elements of the mind correspond member to member, thought is molded in speech, and sounds become signs of intellectual acts. Convinced of this profound connection, Leibniz said that there is between contraries a harmony pre-established by God. Such is the law of parallelism, which completes knowledge in the order of the antithesis and shows that extremes meet in the organism of the world as in the circle of life.

The law of the synthesis comprises the categories of the relations which bind the parts to one another and to the whole, such as condition, containment, reason or foundation, causality. It may be expressed in general in this form: Every thing must be known in the union of all with all; it must be connected with the whole of which it is a part, if it is determinate, and itself developed in all the relations of its parts.

p. 384

The law of relation deserves the importance that several authors accord it, but must be understood also in its relations with the other laws of thought, on pain of being falsified in its applications. It requires that the object be developed in the whole of its internal and external relations, as the condition of a perfect knowledge; but it does not say, as is often imagined, that the object can be known only in relation to another, by way of comparison. The law of relation does not overthrow the other laws according to which the object is first known as it is in itself; it completes them; the synthesis can come only after the thesis and the antithesis. Every relation supposes at least two terms, depends on them, and exists only through them: if the terms are unknown, their relation is unknown too, but knowledge of the terms does not yet give knowledge of their relation. It is therefore things, beings, that must first fix the attention; comparison begins only later. This is why the notion is prior to judgment; the one is the intuition of an object, the other [p. 384] the intuition of a relation. To erect relation into the exclusive principle of knowledge is to prejudge the question of the legitimacy of thought, or rather it is to declare in advance and without examination that the question is insoluble. Science needs a starting point and a principle; the one is the self, the other is God. Now what term of comparison is there for the first thought that appears in consciousness, and what term of comparison for the one and entire thought which crowns the whole development of the intellect? The law of relation must therefore be kept within its just limits: if external relations between two objects are in question, it has value only for finite things, which alone have relations of this kind; it does not apply, then, to God, to the sole and unique Being outside of whom there is nothing; moreover, it has value for finite things only when they are known as such, when we take account of their limits, for only then do we see that limitation implies the distinction between the interior and the exterior, and that external relations are possible; neither does it apply, then, to the primitive fact of consciousness, in which thought grasps the self without yet knowing that the self is limited. The idea of relation does not enter into indeterminate knowledge. Fichte was therefore mistaken in affirming that the self can be known only in opposition to a not-self. M. Renouvier and M. Vacherot have committed the same error, and they have concluded from it that there is no infinite self, since the self supposes a not-self and is then not infinite (1). Hence the denial of the divine personality, a denial very logical from the point of view of these authors; but the point of view is false and arises from a vicious application of the law of relation, as I have already observed in psychology (2).

p. 385

Let us pass to the internal relations of the parts contained in being or in the object of thought. These parts, as organs [p. 385] of one and the same whole, are necessary to one another and cannot be the one without the other. Hence the law of conditionality, which applies to the determinate members of an antithesis: these members exist with one another and for one another, and are to each other as end and as means. Therefore they must be recognized in their reciprocal dependence and explained each by its contrary, by means of contrast, as correlative terms. Hence also the law of reciprocity, principium influxus seu commercii mutui, according to which everything that is united in a whole acts and reacts on the other and is mutually modified. Thus mind and body, essentially united in man, are both changed by this union, so that in uniting they contract properties which they would not have in isolation: the mind takes part in the life of nature, and the body in the life of the mind. The chemical process already offers a remarkable example of this community of action in substances which unite with one another: when an acid and a metal combine, the first acts on the second and the second on the first.

(1) Essais de critique génér., vol. I, § 40; vol. II, § 25. — La Métaphysique et la Science, II, 14th conversation.

(2) La Science de l’âme, starting point of science.

p. 386

Conditionality and community of action concern the correlation of the parts with one another. If we now consider the relations of the parts with the whole, we obtain the laws of subordination. The general form of these laws is found in the principle of containment, which was brought into evidence by Euler and applied geometrically to the logical forms of thought, especially to the syllogism. The parts are in the whole and the whole is also each of its parts. All the imaginable parts of space are in space, and space is itself all these parts with all the extent that they embrace. In the same way mind and body are in man, as constituent parts of human nature, and man is also mind and body with all their determinations and the whole series of their phenomena. It is therefore permissible to say that man is an intelligence or that man is matter, provided that we determine the propositions and give it to be understood that man is not merely matter and that he is not either a pure [p. 386] intelligence. In examining the relations of these terms, of which one expresses the whole and the other a part, we see that all that is in the part is also in the whole, since the whole is itself each of its parts, but that all that is in the whole is not for that reason in the part, since no part is equal to the whole. These relations, and those which precede, may be represented by two intersecting circles, A and B, contained both in the circle C. This latter is the whole, the former the parts. The circle C is also each of the circles A and B, but neither of these two circles is equal to the great circle which contains them in itself. Hence the formulas of the principle of containment, the one positive, the other negative: Whatever is in the contained is also in the container; whatever is not in the container is not in the contained either. But the two converses do not hold. Whatever is in the container is not for that reason in the contained, and whatever is outside the contained is not for that reason outside the container. These formulas apply to all the relations of subordination, to the relations of species to genus, of the world to God, of effect to cause, of consequence to principle, of phenomenon to law. Deduction, which proceeds from the general to the particular, is founded upon them. Logic cannot dispense with them in the explanation of the organic forms of thought, which are called notions, judgments, and reasonings.

p. 387

The principles of reason and of cause imply the principle of containment. Whatever is in the effect or in the consequence is also in the cause or in the reason; what is not in the cause or in the reason is not in the effect or in the consequence either. But the two converses do not hold, for the cause and the reason exceed each of their particular manifestations: all that is in the cause is not in the effect, and all that is outside the effect is not outside the cause. These principles are fundamental laws of knowledge and satisfy the need of thought to know the origin and the end of things. The mind from childhood is not content with the fact, it asks the wherefore of it. This is indeed, according to the remark [p. 387] of Aristotle, the character of philosophical thought: “Rerum cognoscere causas.” The synthetic method, which deduces beings from their principles, has no other foundation than the idea of reason or of principle. Where, then, is the reason of things? It can be found only in being itself. Indeed, from all that precedes, being is one with its properties and its parts; all the determinations of being are united to being and united among themselves in the essence of being. Now this property which expresses the essential relation of two things, of which one is to the other or in the other, is called reason, foundation, principle par excellence, principium rationis determinantis. Thus omniscience has its reason, in metaphysics, in the infinite essence of God, and imperfect knowledge, mingled with errors and uncertainties, is founded in the limited essence of man. By virtue of this principle, everything that is determinate has its cause or its determining reason. When facts or phenomena produced by the activity of a being are in question, the determining reason takes the name of cause. Authors, however, do not agree on the difference that exists between cause and reason; most of them confound them, and the distinction matters little at the moment. For thought the law is the same, whatever name is given to it: in seeking the cause or the foundation of everything that happens and of everything that exists in a state of determination, it is always the higher essence that we wish to reach, the essence in which substances, with their qualities and their phenomena, are determined in one manner rather than another. It goes without saying that the reason must suffice for the explanation of the fact in all its circumstances. This is why, since Leibniz, the term sufficient reason is often substituted for that of determining reason. But this substitution itself lacks reason, for every law suffices for its use, and there is no ground to fear that the application of the principle of determining reason leads to determinism, that is to say, to the negation of all freedom in the world. A free act does not become necessitated because it has a determining reason, but it would be necessitated if this reason were [p. 388] found in the series of prior acts and not in the free determination of the mind.

Such is the whole of the laws of knowledge, recognized in their organic relations and connected with the fundamental idea of being. The laws of thought are linked with the categories; both are indispensable to the solution of the problem of the legitimacy of our cognitions (1).

(1) Krause, Encyclopädie der philosophischen Wissenschaften.

PDF 386

THE LEGITIMACY OF KNOWLEDGE

We have studied knowledge in itself, in its origins and in its laws; we know what it is, into what species it is divided, and by what principles it is formed. It remains to examine whether it is legitimate, whether it attains its object, whether thought has an objective validity. This is the question of truth and certainty, or the question of science. Are our cognitions always exact? Evidently not, since error is possible for us. Can they be exact, and furthermore can we have firm assurance of that exactness? In other words, if by truth we understand the equation between thought and its object, and by certainty the consciousness of this adequate relation, can our cognitions ever be true and certain? Such is the point in dispute between dogmatism and skepticism. For the one, the human mind is capable of truth and certainty, under conditions to be determined in science; for the other, it is, whatever it may do, condemned to error and doubt. Truth, say the skeptics, is an illusion of which we are the dupes, and the

p. 390

Logic. — I. 25. [p. 390] certainty a dream that charms the intellect. The senses deceive us, reason leads us astray, the senses contradict reason, and reason the senses. Between thought and reality there is an abyss, and this abyss can never be bridged, since we have but one means of knowing, which is to think, and it is impossible for us to decide by thought whether thought is not constituted in antagonism with things. Science is a circle without beginning and without outlet. Objects are appearances, essence escapes us, every affirmation is rash. Everyone may think what he pleases, but the best course is to say nothing. This is absolute doubt. Other writers, such as Kant, under the name of criticism, sacrifice a part to save the rest. They abandon to the enemy the rational cognitions, which lack the guarantee of sensible intuitions, and wish to save experimental knowledge. Criticism is only a dismemberment of skepticism; in refuting the latter in all its pretensions we refute the former at the same time.

p. 391

Let us define the object of the debate still more precisely, disregarding the vain outcries against the weakness of the mind. A legitimate cognition is a true and certain cognition, a scientific cognition. To ask whether our cognitions are legitimate is therefore to ask whether we know that things are in themselves such as we know them; that is to say, whether we are assured that the object is given, whether to the senses or to reason, such as it is, and that we comprehend it through the understanding such as it is. Skepticism in all its extent results, and can result, only from the possibility of a disagreement between the subject and the object of thought, whether this disagreement be imputed to the subject or to the object. Can we certify that these two terms agree in knowledge? There lies the whole question. In other words, true knowledge applies to the proper essence of things, which is independent of our thought: how are we to know whether this essence is in itself, beyond the limits of our intellect, such as we conceive it or such as it appears to us in intuition? Has not the mind its own forms, which disfigure the [p. 391] objects? Have the categories that it employs as instruments of all knowledge an objective validity? and if they are only anticipations, provisional notions, do they not render hypothetical all the results that can be obtained in science? How is certainty to be reached by relying on uncertain elements?

Such is the state of the question. It is always, as we see, in one form or another, a matter of the harmony between thought and reality. This point established, all the rest follows. If we know the object as it is, we know the essence of things, for by essence we understand simply what things are, and we are thenceforth in a position to judge of the difference that may exist between the object as it is and the object as it appears to us in our intuitions. Moreover, if we know the object as it is, since we know nothing except by the aid of the categories and the forms of thought, every hypothesis of error or illusion arising from that source likewise falls to the ground.

p. 392

But can we know things as they are? Yes, by proceeding methodically. The philosophical method is composed of analysis and synthesis. By analysis we ascertain how things appear to us or are given to us in intuition; by synthesis we ascertain how they must be by virtue of their principles. If things appear to us in observation as they must be for reason, the question of certainty is decided. Truth is secured against every serious doubt by the reciprocal independence of the two procedures, intuition and deduction, which serve knowledge and which check one another. Analysis sees, observes, contemplates the object in itself, abstraction made of its cause or its reason for being; synthesis demonstrates the object as the consequence of a higher truth with no other guide than reasoning: what is left to object if the demonstration agrees with the observation? That they are still only thoughts? Ah! no doubt, we know nothing without thinking; the dogmatist has this in common with the [p. 392] skeptic; but it is not the fact of thought that is in question, it is its legitimacy, and this legitimacy is established as soon as thought conforms to the nature of things. But demonstration presupposes a principle. Is there an absolute principle, and can we know it in an exact and certain manner? This is the first condition of science, and it is the most difficult point. It is evident that if the human mind were without effort in possession of the absolute principle of knowledge, science in general would raise no more dispute than the particular sciences that rest on certain principles, such as mathematics. We are therefore reduced to seeking the principle, and we do not know whether we shall find it; we know only that the legitimacy of our knowledge depends on the success of this search. No principle, no science.

In the meantime we must find our bearings in the world, run through the various orders of things, gather facts by way of observation, increase the sum of our knowledge, and develop all our powers, in order to rise gradually to the notion of the principle. But where are we to begin in this work of analysis? With the external world, with our fellow men, or with ourselves? Knowledge of the external world and of our fellow men is transcendent and cannot be acquired without the intermediary of our senses. If we engaged upon this path, the skeptics would at once remind us that the subject and the object of knowledge are opposed and heterogeneous, and that perhaps neither bodies nor minds exist. Let us begin, then, with ourselves; there at least knowledge is immanent, there every intermediary between subject and object disappears, there we shall perhaps find a truth that stands above the opposition of these two terms and that consequently resists all the objections of skepticism. This truth will be the starting point, the second condition of science. If a starting point exists, science has a certain beginning; if not, science is impossible and even inaccessible.

p. 393

A starting point and a principle, linked together by method: such are the fundamental conditions of [p. 393] scientific knowledge. By the one, science begins; by the other, it is completed. The first is the subjective basis of the development of thought; the second is its objective basis. The latter supports synthesis; the former, analysis. To demonstrate that these two conditions are fulfilled is to demonstrate the legitimacy of knowledge. The starting point belongs to our immanent knowledge, the principle to our transcendent knowledge. Let us examine the question from these two points of view.

CHAPTER ONE

IMMANENT KNOWLEDGE

p. 394

The starting point of science must be immediate, certain, universal. Psychology proves that there is a truth that unites these three conditions, that this truth is single and unique, and that it consists in the thought I. It is not a question of the existence of the self, nor of the identity of the self, according to the formulas of Descartes and of Fichte; for existence and identity are properties which would have to be defined and could be contested; that is not the primitive fact of consciousness; before affirming its existence and its identity, the child affirms itself, and it can recognize its existence and its identity only by referring them to the self in the form of a judgment, after already having the intuition of itself. It is a question purely and simply of the self, without designation, but also without exclusion of any of its qualities. This is the first example of a notion that implies neither judgment nor reasoning.
