The thought I is prior to every particular thought relating to the properties, the parts, the acts, the relations of the self. Nothing can be affirmed of the self without first affirming the self. A fortiori, the thought I is prior to every thought relating to the not-self, to all knowledge of the world or of God. For the not-self [p. 394] as a negative term exists only in relation to the self, to which it is opposed and which it limits, and can enter consciousness only if the self already has consciousness of its limitation, that is, of one of its properties. There is therefore one thought, and only one, that necessarily precedes the others, immanent or transcendent: the thought I. This thought is immediate, since it is not derived from another by way of consequence; it is universal, since it exists for all rational beings, not excepting the skeptics, and could not be denied without contradiction; it is certain, since the self is not yet determined in it either as mind or as body, either as subject or as object, and since it is thus truly above the opposition that exists between the two terms of knowledge. On this ground it is the starting point of science (1).

p. 395

Let us remark in passing that this starting point is an intuition, an indeterminate intuition that has the whole self for its object, before all analysis, and consequently an intellectual intuition. Sensible intuitions relate only to determinate objects considered as such. The existence of intellectual intuitions is therefore established at one stroke, at the very beginning of science. This intellectual intuition contains in unity all the sensible intuitions that apply to the various determinations of the self, as thought, as feeling, and as will. The whole science of the self is only the development of the intuition I, and this development appears inexhaustible. This is why the thought I, which serves as the starting point of the entire science, is at the same time the particular principle of psychology; for we call principle that which is the reason of another thing, that which contains it in its essence. We do not say that the intuition I is the absolute principle of the entire science, for it does not envelop our transcendent thoughts; we say only that it is the principle of all our thoughts relating to the self, or of our immanent knowledge. Fichte confounded these two orders of thoughts, [p. 395] and taking the intuition I for the principle of the whole of science, he concluded logically that the self is everything and that the not-self is only another face of the self. Subjective idealism is the consequence of this mistake.

Immanent knowledge is confined strictly within the sphere of the self, and presents this interesting peculiarity, that the subject and the object of thought are the same, or that the object does not go beyond the limits of the subject. Its aim is to determine the self in all that it is and in all that it contains, by means of inner sense or internal observation.

What is the self? A being whose essence is one, simple, identical, which is posited with other beings and then recognizes itself as a finite and relative thing, which exists in itself and for itself as an individual and personal substance, which is at once spontaneous and subject to external conditions, which develops in life a continuous series of acts or phenomena of which it is the cause, which is distinguished from this point of view as faculty, activity, force, and tendency, as thought, feeling, and will. The development of these propositions embraces nearly the whole framework of psychology: none of them goes beyond the immediate data of consciousness, none is foreign to the intuition I, which is our starting point. It is always one and the same thought which, indeterminate at its origin, determines itself more and more and without end under the effort of analysis. Such is the whole body of our immanent knowledge.

(1) Krause, System der Philosophie, 1828.

p. 396

It is time to ask whether this knowledge is legitimate. Does it fulfill the conditions of science? Has it a starting point and a principle? Yes; therefore it is legitimate, provided we proceed methodically. The certainty of the intuition I carries with it the certainty of the particular intuitions that are founded on it. It is a criterium with regard to these determinate affirmations. Everyone can say: As truly as I am conscious of myself, I am conscious of my identity, of my causality, of my emotions, of my cognitions. The one is no more evident than the other, and the [p. 396] contradiction is impossible in most cases. To one who should say: I doubt whether I have inner sense, whether I will, whether I am a cause, one may answer: Your doubts testify against yourself; one does not doubt without thinking, one does not think without willing, one does not will without being a cause. Everything is linked together in psychology, thanks to the unity of our essence. Hence skepticism in general respects the facts of consciousness, which are grasped directly by thought, unlike the phenomena of the external world, which thought discovers only through the prism of the senses. The mind has the property of referring to itself, of questioning itself, of answering itself, of judging itself; it is the mind that observes, and it is itself that it observes; what source of error could there be in knowledge when the subject and the object are the same thing? One does not lie to oneself when one seeks the truth sincerely. Psychology is therefore possible as a science, at least within the limits of individual observation.

p. 397

Immanent knowledge, in fact, concerns only the individual self. An author has objected that rational beings endowed with consciousness are perhaps wholly different from one another. This is improbable, if they can understand one another in a common language; but what does it matter? Immanent knowledge does not concern itself with all selves and does not even know whether they exist. Each person possesses in himself the starting point of science and must ascertain for himself what he discovers there. It is for others to see whether they find in themselves what I fix in myself. The science of the self is not the science of humanity, a transcendent object of the intellect, but the science of a determinate being which for me is myself. This is how experimental psychology is distinguished from general or rational psychology. Metaphysics may be able to say whether the properties of the individual self are the properties of all rational beings, the properties of the human race, but we have not got that far. It is important to recognize these limits of immanent knowledge well. It follows that when we apply to the self certain properties called categories, such as being, essence, [p. 397] unity, identity, causality, it is not as categories that we employ them, but as simple attributes of the self. We do not grant these elements a universal validity, since we do not leave the field of the self; we give them no other objective validity than that which results from their application to the self. We affirm that the self is a being or an object, that the self exists, that the self is substance, according to the sense attached to these words; we affirm nothing more. Are there other beings, other causes, other substances outside of and above the self ? The solution of this question goes beyond the sphere of immanent knowledge.

If the object of science is individual, the certainty that it admits of is individual also. I am certain of the testimony of my consciousness, but no one is obliged to give credence to truths that I alone can grasp. Hence I ought always to express myself in the form of an individual judgment in order to characterize properly the situation of the self in immanent knowledge: I think, I am. I am a witness who testifies to what he has seen in his inmost self. Since it is a question only of myself, I must refrain from generalizing. If I speak of the essence and the properties of the self, it is well understood that I do not go beyond the bounds of psychological observation: I do not know whether the self must have an essence, or whether it will always have one; I state a simple fact, namely that the self has an essence or properties. Certainly, in examining myself attentively, I find in myself many general and apodictic propositions, such as these: every being has an essence, every phenomenon has a cause, every property presupposes a substance; I content myself with pointing out these propositions, for I am sure that they exist, but I do not wish to pronounce on their validity. Under these conditions certainty is complete.

p. 398

Does this mean that psychology is safe from error? Error is possible in every matter, but it can be avoided once the basis of science is laid down. In immanent knowledge we must conform to the rules of observation, record the facts, nothing but the facts, without [p. 398] party spirit, guarding against hypotheses and preconceived opinions, whether philosophical or religious; we must also watch for abuses of language and define with care the terms we use, without diverting them, if possible, from their established meaning; we must, finally, and this says everything, proceed methodically from the known to the unknown, preserving for the facts their natural order and connection. Questions are often obscure only because they do not present themselves in their proper place. Such, for example, is the thesis of moral freedom. Put to a theologian who is convinced that God knows infallibly from all eternity the series of events that will unfold in the world, or to a physicist who has persuaded himself that everything is necessarily determined in relation to everything else, the problem of free will will offer insurmountable difficulties. But begin by ridding yourself of every system concerning God and nature, place yourself on the ground of experimental psychology, and ask yourself whether the mind determines itself to act, whether it depends on it to perform one act rather than another, and you will surely arrive at the truth.

p. 399

Kant's objections to pure psychology rest on this capital error, that we have no intellectual intuition of the self, considered in its essence as an object of thought, but only a sensible intuition of the acts of the self as subject of knowledge. Our intuitions bear only upon phenomena; we do not know things in themselves. Now, to conclude from acts to essence, from subject to object, from the individual self to all rational beings, is a threefold paralogism. We might content ourselves with replying that this criticism is addressed to pure or rational psychology, which does not belong to immanent knowledge. But that would be an evasion, because the author often absorbs experimental psychology into rational psychology, under the pretext that the essence of things is in no way revealed to observation. Restoring to this word its received meaning, we claim for experimental psychology everything that relates to essence, that is, to the properties of the soul [p. 399] posited as facts. We are then obliged to examine the arguments of our adversary and to rebut them so far as they concern us.

The sole foundation of pure psychology, says Kant, is the empty representation of the self, which is not even a concept, but a simple act of consciousness inseparable from every concept. This self that thinks is only the subject of thought, an unknown of which I can know nothing except through the thoughts that are its attributes, and which I can judge only by its own intuition, turning in a circle. It must seem strange that the condition under which I think, and which is only a property of my subject, should be extended by me to everything that thinks, and that upon a purely empirical proposition we should arrogate to ourselves the right of founding an apodictic and universal judgment, in this form: everything that thinks has the same properties that I discover in myself by my own consciousness. The cause of this is that we are obliged to attribute a priori to all things the properties which are the very condition under which we conceive them. Now it is clear that I cannot represent to myself a thinking being by way of external observation, but only by my own consciousness. In order to affirm that thinking beings exist, I must therefore transmit my own consciousness to foreign things. Such are the illusions and hypotheses that serve as the basis of pure psychology (1).

p. 400

In these terms Kant clearly pointed out the rashness of psychological analysis as it was practiced before him in the schools of Descartes and of Leibniz; but his reproaches cannot touch us, and in some points are themselves lacking in accuracy. It is true that the intuition I is the foundation of psychology, but this intuition is not empty, since it contains the whole science of the self and the whole system of our knowledge as acts of the self. It is true that this intuition is not a concept, that is, the notion of what is common to all selves, but [p. 400] an indeterminate notion, forgotten in the logical classifications. It was the earlier dogmatism that concluded hastily from the self, given by consciousness, to all thinking beings, and criticism in this respect provoked the reform of Krause. It is true that the self is the subject of thought, but it is also its object, and can be known as such in its essence and in its properties; to know that it thinks is already to indicate its essence. The self is therefore not an unknown, of which nothing can be said, but a thing eminently intelligible and determinable without end. Even if the essence of the self were not manifested directly to thought, it would not be a paralogism to conclude in its case from phenomena to properties, from properties to essence, and from subject to object; for the self is also each of its determinations, each of its attributes and of its acts, and no one is ignorant that the subject and the object are one and the same being in one's own consciousness. The fact of inner sense is unassailable, whatever its cause may be, and this fact signifies that the self that knows is identical with the self that is known, when one knows oneself. It is true again that we know our own self only by the aid of our own thought; but there is in this only the exclusion of one chance of error, and not a circle. According to the notion of knowledge, nothing prevents the self, as well as the not-self, from becoming the object of thought. This possibility is realized for beings endowed with personality. Besides, in the primitive fact of consciousness the self is not yet determined as subject or as object, and it was again Kant's objections that led philosophers to seek a truth that should escape the conflict of these two terms. It is true, finally, that we attribute to all things, to our fellow men as to ourselves, the general properties that are the laws of knowledge; but this transcendent application of the categories is an abuse of reason only in those who regard it as legitimate in itself without further examination. We are forewarned; we shall know how to avoid error. By all these observations the philosopher of Königsberg ruined the earlier dogmatism, [p. 401] but he did not in the least overthrow the foundations of all scientific psychology.

Kant next sets forth that psychology is contained in four propositions, which determine the soul according to the categories of relation, quality, quantity, and modality: the soul is substance; it is simple; it is one; it is in relation with possible objects in space. From these are deduced the concepts of immateriality, incorruptibility, personality, and immortality, the fundamental points of pure psychology. There is no need to point out how insufficient and arbitrary this determination of the soul is. It is the defect of the system of categories.

In criticizing the four formulas that sum up the science of the soul, the author acknowledges that the self is conscious of itself as the simple and identical subject of thought. This proposition, he says, is analytic; but it must not be transformed into a synthetic judgment in this form: the self is an identical and simple substance. From the fact that the soul is the invariable subject of its acts, does it follow that it subsists in itself as substance? To constitute this notion, other data are needed than the fact of thought. An object is known as substance only by an intellectual intuition, and we have none. We must not, therefore, confuse the logical explanation of thought with the metaphysical determination of an object. There would be only one way of vanquishing criticism, which would be to demonstrate a priori that all thinking beings are simple substances. By this demonstration thought would pass beyond the world of sensibility and soar in the region of noumena.

(1) Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft: von den Paralogismen der rein. Vernunft.

p. 402

These objections apply once more to those who arbitrarily exceed the limits of psychological observation, by concluding from one object to all objects. Metaphysics alone can legitimate general and necessary propositions; we agree with criticism on this point. The argument therefore does not hurt us. For those, indeed, who confine themselves strictly to the analysis of the individual self, the proposition “the soul is substance” is not synthetic but analytic. It does not signify for us [p. 402] that there exist in the totality of things substances and accidents and that the soul is included in the first category, but only that the self possesses among other properties that of existing in itself, or of being what is called substance. The attribute therefore results from the decomposition of the subject; it is a fact of consciousness, nothing more. We still do not know whether there are other substances, although we have the notion of them. No doubt the affirmation of substance presupposes other data than the phenomenon of thought; for a phenomenon is not a substance, and the soul, while existing according to the axiom cogito, ergo sum, might be an accident; but these other data are not lacking: the self is conscious of its being, of its essence, of its properties as well as of its acts; the self is not merely a thought, it is above all a thinking thing.

Immanent knowledge, rigorously circumscribed within its domain, thus withstands the attacks of criticism. It is legitimate as soon as it fulfills the conditions of science. Hence a whole body of certain truths, which doubt can no longer shake. Thought is no longer in contradiction with all reality, for it is at least in agreement with itself. Skepticism is no longer absolute; it has hold now only upon the not-self, upon transcendent knowledge. It remains to examine whether it can be dislodged from that post.

CHAPTER TWO

TRANSCENDENT KNOWLEDGE

p. 403

Doubt is logically possible only with regard to objects that are outside the self and above the self. There, in fact, the testimony of consciousness no longer suffices; the intervention of the senses and of reason is required. There the subject and the object of knowledge are foreign to each other, perhaps even [p. 403] incompatible and contradictory. Do the senses and reason transmit their objects to us faithfully? We are often the dupes of some illusion of optics or acoustics; is this not the permanent condition of the human mind? Does the understanding grasp external things as they are in themselves? How are we to know it, since we cannot go out of ourselves and verify in the fact the exactness of our conceptions? Are there even bodies, or is the physical world not a phantasmagoria of the imagination, like the phenomenon of dreams, as the idealists maintain? Have we fellow men, or is the self isolated and absolute, as Fichte holds? Who is right, those who affirm or those who deny the existence of God? Everything is open to dispute, except the self. Whether there be a God or not, whether there be a world or not, whether the senses and reason lead us into error or not, each of us can say with certainty: I am. But is that all that we know? Perhaps. If we try to go further, we shall need the categories that we apply to all the objects of thought; but if the categories are legitimate in reference to the self, what guarantee have we still of their validity in a transcendent world?

We do not conceal from ourselves the difficulties of the undertaking; we rather exaggerate them. It is because we have the hope of overcoming them. By what singular anomaly, in fact, could science begin and yet be unable to end? We know ourselves, we are conscious of our limitation, we have organs that put us in relation with the outside; by what trick of nature should we be forbidden to know anything of this world in which we live and of the very author of our existence? We have a starting point; why should science not also have a principle? A principle: therein lies perhaps the whole difficulty. If we knew the principle of science, it is probable that all obstacles would disappear in the light of this higher truth. The principle is precisely the reason of things, and it is in the reason of things that their explanation must be sought.

p. 404

The principle of knowledge is the ultimate reason of knowledge; it is there that we must find the solution of the doubts that embarrass the theory of knowledge. If the principle of knowledge were at the same time the principle of reality, would not science be constituted in its unity, from the point of view of both subject and object, and would there not thenceforth be harmony between intelligence and reality, between the laws of the mind and the laws of things?

The passage from immanent to transcendent knowledge is found in reason. In opening to us the absolute and divine world, reason gives us principles and laws that exceed the narrow sphere of our individuality and permit us to gain a footing in the not-self. It is thanks to the principles of cause and condition, of whole and part, of inner and outer, that we affirm the existence of a totality of things which envelops us on every side, which subsists independently of us, beside us, above us, and in which we find the means and the reason of our own existence. The self then posits itself over against the not-self, and acquires through this opposition an ever more vivid feeling of its limitation, of its dependence, of its relations of every kind with the outside. Then begins the development of transcendent knowledge according to the laws of intellectual life, under the successive predominance of sensibility, of the understanding, and of reason. By means of the senses we ascertain phenomena, individual things, minerals, plants, animals; by means of language we enter into communication with our fellow men and profit by their experience to increase indefinitely the sum of our knowledge; by means of the understanding we combine and generalize the impressions of the senses, we classify beings into species and genera; by means of reason, finally, we rise above the self, above the world, up to God. Hence our sensible cognitions, our abstract cognitions, our rational cognitions, which embrace all the transcendent objects of thought.

p. 405

Are these cognitions legitimate? This is what we must examine. It is well understood that the question is to be decided in general and not in its details. The point is to establish, for example, the legitimacy of sensible knowledge in principle, but not in all its applications to all the particular objects of experience. Logic cannot go beyond this. Besides, when the problem is solved in its general conditions, all the sciences can avail themselves of the solution. If observation is secured in its rights against the skeptical hypotheses drawn from the weakness of thought, from the impenetrability of things, from the impossibility of ascertaining the relation between the subject and the object of knowledge, the experimental sciences no longer have to make the demonstration over again, one after another, but only to justify that they keep within the bounds of exact observation. The same is true of speculation in relation to the mathematical, philosophical, and moral sciences. Scientists ought to be conscious of this truth and to remain within the limits of their science, without encroaching on logic. It is no more for a physicist to criticize speculation than for a geometer to contest the value of observation. Let each keep to his own house.

What course must we follow in our inquiry? Let us remember that sensible cognitions require the concurrence of the understanding and of reason, that abstract cognitions are only the generalization of the data of sensibility, and that rational cognitions, finally, are independent of all experience. The course is therefore traced by the nature of things: rational cognitions are implied as a condition in all the others; it is with them that we must begin. The categories are attached, rightly or wrongly, to all the objects of thought, sensible or supra-sensible; we already know that they are legitimate when applied to the self; are they still so in their transcendent use? have they an objective and universal validity? This is the preliminary question. Moreover, it is rational knowledge that has for its object the study of the principle of science, and without a principle we can do nothing.

Logic. — I. 26

p. 406

Let us begin, then, with rational knowledge. For if rational knowledge is illegitimate, the others are so likewise; and if it is legitimate, the legitimacy of the others will be proved without difficulty by way of consequence. Supra-sensible objects are the most difficult to reach in theory, and raise doubts that do not exist for the objects of experience, as Kant's critique demonstrates. Now the certainty of the objects of reason carries with it the certainty of the principle of science, the certainty of the transcendent use of the categories, the certainty of the agreement of thought with its object in the order of speculation. What, then, remains to be done in favor of sensible and abstract knowledge, when certainty is secured on these various points? Simply to establish that thought agrees with its object in the order of observation also, which is admitted in advance by the skeptics of Kant's school.

Let us now go straight to the point. We have a starting point; have we a principle? It is a matter of the principle of the entire science, of all human science, and not of the principle of this or that domain of science. Mathematics, it is said, has for its principle the universal idea of quantity; the moral and political sciences, the absolute ideas of the good, of right, of the true, of the beautiful; but these sciences, however vast they may be, are not the whole of science, and their principles are not the sole object of thought. I ask whether there exists a higher principle that embraces at once the principles of all the sciences and brings them together in unity in the organism of science, one and entire.

p. 407

The principle of a science contains in itself all the developments of that science; it is the common reason of all the truths that belong to its domain, it links them together by the bonds of demonstration, it makes of the science a single whole, or reduces it to unity. Thus all the propositions relating to geometry find their reason in one and the same principle, in the idea of space. Before approaching the search for the principle of the entire science, let us see what its characters must be. Since science implies the distinction between the subject and the object of knowledge, [p. 407] the principle of the entire science must also contain the whole of science, from the double point of view of the subject and the object. It must therefore first of all envelop all our thoughts, in such a way that it is impossible for us to put forward any proposition whatever that would not be founded in the principle, even when we contest its existence: all thoughts united in one, or developing one and the same theme, this is the subjective unity of science. It must next envelop all the objects of the intellect, all the species of beings, all the kinds of reality, all the orders of things with which the particular sciences are concerned, and the very principles of those sciences: all beings united in being, this is the objective unity of science. It must therefore be at once the principle of knowledge for thought and the principle of existence for reality, and these two must be but one, that is, the principle of things must also be the principle of knowledge. On this ground science is one, and the principle is the expression of this unity. The principle of the entire science is therefore that which contains everything in thought and in reality. But if it contains everything, it also is in unity everything that is; it is itself the whole; for the whole is also each of its parts or of its inner determinations, without being bounded by this part or shut up within its limits, without being anything determinate. Finally, if the principle of science is everything and contains everything that is determinate, it is necessarily one; for it is impossible to conceive two principles each of which should be everything.

p. 408

If science has a principle, this principle must therefore be, by virtue of the definition, a unique thing, or rather the unique being who is everything and contains in his essence all that is limited, who thus renders possible an explanation of all our knowledge and of all its objects. But does this principle exist? There is the question. If it exists, knowledge is legitimate; if not, not. Let us remark only, before going further, that all peoples, in all times, have believed in its existence; for all speak of a being who is one, who is all reality, who is the cause of all that is determinate; this being is called God. The characters of the principle of [p. 408] the entire science are precisely the characters that have everywhere and always been attributed to the divinity. The question of the principle of science is therefore transformed into another, that of the existence of God.

The principle of science is God. But have we certainty of the existence of God? Certainty presupposes knowledge: one can be certain only of what one knows. To resolve the question, and even to understand it, we must therefore possess the notions of certainty, of existence, and of God. Otherwise we do not know what we are talking about. The conviction that one has regarding the existence of God depends on the notion that one forms of him. If one regards God as a finite being situated beyond the world, one must deny his existence. This is how a modern writer decides the question. “By God I understand a being existing outside the universe, author, preserver, and regulator of this universe. Now, God being thus understood, and he cannot be understood otherwise, I say that theism is always anthropomorphism. God is personal or he is not. Now a personal God is someone, and someone is necessarily a man.” The author is right to deny God as he defines him, but he defines him like a child and understands nothing of the question. The secret of his atheism is sensualism. Let him resume the study of the soul and of knowledge. “What is certain is that thoughts proceed from sensations. The soul is sensibility, that is, the sensitizable substance. Now the sensitizable substance needs, in order to be sensitized, a sensitizing thing, which is the body (1).”

p. 409

By certainty I understand the consciousness that we have of truth: a thing is certain when one knows that it is true, when one has recognized it as such in consciousness, after mature examination. A proposition that should repel examination, that should be above the faculties of the human mind, might be true, but would not be evident or [p. 409] certain. Dogmas, inasmuch as they are inaccessible to reason, are not an object of certainty. A supernatural certainty is a contradiction in terms. Certainty results from our efforts to grasp the truth; it is the reward of the spontaneous labor of the intellect; it presupposes free examination as a preliminary condition. Certainty is acquired most often by way of demonstration, but is not to be confounded with it. Demonstration is a means of arriving at certainty, but not the only one. If certainty were no more extensive than demonstration, science would be impossible, for demonstration can no more be applied to the principle than to the starting point of science. The axioms of geometry are evident without demonstration. We must therefore begin by distinguishing between demonstration and certainty: to ask whether the existence of God is certain is not to ask whether God can be demonstrated, but whether we have the consciousness of his existence.

(1) P. Poulin, Qu’est-ce que l’homme? Qu’est-ce que Dieu? 1st part, ch. II. Brussels, 1863.

p. 410

By existence I understand the property of things, inasmuch as they are posited. It is a combination of essence and of position or form. A thing exists when its essence is posited, when it is positive. But essence may be posited in various ways, either in us or outside us, either alone or with other things. That whose essence is posited only in us, in our imagination, has only an imaginary existence. Such are the creations of Fable. That whose essence is posited outside us exists outside us, and has an objective existence in the world. Such are animals and plants. That which exists with something else is called finite and has only a limited existence. The finite is therefore that which stands in opposition to an ensemble of objects. The finite is not the whole essence, but a part of the essence; it is not the whole of being, but a determinate being. It necessarily supposes other beings, and excludes them. It is therefore positive in itself, and negative in relation to all that it is not. The idea of negation is inseparable from that of limitation. The same is true of the idea of exteriority. Since the finite being exists with others, it is encompassed on [p. 410] every side, and for it there is an outer world. That which is posited as alone and unique, without antithesis, that which is the whole essence, to which nothing is exterior, that which is in no respect negative, is called infinite. The infinite therefore denies negation and exteriority. The infinite is all; nothing is opposed or exterior to it. From which it follows that the infinite cannot logically exist in the imagination alone; otherwise it would be only a term opposed to nature; it would no longer be all that is, it would no longer be infinite. Only infinite existence befits the infinite, and infinite existence is necessarily subjective and objective at once. It envelops within itself the world of the imagination as well as the exterior world, whereas finite existence, by the very fact that it is finite, can be circumscribed within one or the other of these worlds. There is no likelihood that sphinxes, fairies, or demons exist outside our mind; these things can be thought without our acknowledging in them an objective reality; but this distinction between what exists in us and outside us cannot be applied to the infinite without contradiction.

p. 411

By God I understand being, all being, the whole of being, without restriction or limitation, infinite and absolute being. I do not say, therefore, that God is a being, a spirit or a body, for a being is something determinate, which is opposed to other beings; I do not even say that God is the highest being, the most perfect, he who is above all the others; for such a being would still be determinate, it would be only a particular term in the series of essences, it would be the first or the last being, the first or the last link in the chain of beings. God is not a species, nor a genus of reality; he is being itself, the whole of being, all reality, the all. God is in unity all that is. It is in this sense that he is infinite; for the infinite, in its double negation, designates the totality of essence, or the whole essence. And since he is all being, God is also alone and unique; he has no second; there exists no being outside God that is opposed to God. Nothing is exterior or superior to infinite being. God therefore depends on nothing, since he is not with another; he is of himself all that he is, he possesses in [p. 411] himself all the conditions of his existence; his essence and all his qualities are proper to him. It is in this sense that he is unconditioned or absolute; for the absolute excludes all condition and all dependence.

Such is the notion that we ought to form of God according to the natural development of the mind. This notion is prepared by the analysis of rational knowledge and of the laws of thought. It supposes that we are in possession of the ideas of being, of essence, of unity, of the infinite, of the absolute, and can present itself distinctly to consciousness only at the higher degree of intellectual culture, when the insufficiency of the elements given by sensible observation, and of the various kinds of realities furnished by abstraction, has been recognized. Let no one say, then, that the notion of God is a prejudice of education or an arbitrary product of the understanding, for it penetrates necessarily into the mind that rises from the finite to the infinite and from the parts of the world to the whole. It lies, moreover, at the bottom of all philosophical speculation, whether in the East, or in Greece since Plato and Aristotle, or in Christendom. It is true that in the Middle Ages, under the influence of a narrow spiritualism, in consequence of a too gross conception of nature, the theologians placed the world outside God, for fear of compromising the purity of the divine essence by its contact with matter. But they none the less continued to affirm the infinity of God; only they put themselves in contradiction with themselves, since God is really infinite only if he is all being, if he consequently contains the world also in his essence. This error was bound to disappear with the progress of philosophy and of the sciences. Descartes restored to the infinite all its value, and his disciples have not failed to draw out the consequences.

Here are some testimonies that will not be suspected:

p. 412

“The divine substance is everywhere, not only in the universe, but infinitely beyond it; for God is not enclosed in his work, but his work is in him and subsists in his substance, which preserves it by its almighty efficacy. It is in him that we are; it is in [p. 412] him that we have motion and life, as the Apostle says. In ipso enim vivimus, movemur et sumus… Yes, God is everywhere, or rather everything is in God… Minds are in the divine reason, and bodies in his immensity… The one and the other participate in the divine being. God, who gives them reality, possesses it; for he possesses all the perfections of creatures, without their limitations… Thus God is everywhere, not only by his operation, but also by his substance; for what would the operation of God be, distinguished and separated from his substance?… His true name is He who is, that is to say, being without restriction, all being, infinite and universal being (1).”

“God is truly in himself all that there is of the real and the positive in minds, all that there is of the real and the positive in bodies, all that there is of the real and the positive in the essences of all the other possible creatures of which I have no distinct idea. He has all the being of body, without being limited to body; all the being of mind without being limited to mind, and likewise of the other possible essences. He is so entirely all being, that he has all the being of each of his creatures, but cutting off the limit that restricts it. Take away all limits, take away every difference that confines being within species, and you remain in the universality of being, and consequently in the infinite perfection of being by itself.

“It follows that, infinite being not being able to be confined within any species, God is no more mind than body, nor body than mind; properly speaking, he is neither the one nor the other: for he who says these two sorts of substances says a precise difference of being, and consequently a limit that can never befit universal being (2).”

p. 413

“God contains all, without being able to be contained anywhere, and the universe, which presents no bounds to my frightened imagination, is reduced, before the eyes of its author, to the [p. 413] dimensions of an atom, to the simplicity of a monad. God is all. Before him the creature, that deceitful nothing, vanishes and leaves no trace of its lie.” I borrow here the words of the most religious of our sages.

“And this is not a merely affectionate feeling, a language of the passions, a metaphor; it is a just and literal expression, it is a great physical truth, stated without emphasis. God is nothing, or, in the most natural and truest sense, he is all, he produces all, he contains all, he acts in all and everywhere. At every instant he gives being to all that receives it, with all that accompanies being. He is the first mover of every action, the life of every thought. Time and space are only modes in him, or rather relations, which coexist necessarily with creatures, born imperfect, changing, but perfectible. Finally, what says all, what surpasses all, God is in us, est Deus in nobis, he is nearer to us than we are to ourselves (1).”

(1) Father Malebranche, Entretiens sur la métaphysique, VIII. — Recherche de la vérité, bk. III, part II, ch. IX.

(2) Fénelon, Traité de l’existence et des attributs de Dieu, 2nd part, ch. V.

p. 414

I could multiply the citations, but without profit to my thesis. I must confine myself to saying that I understand by God infinite and absolute being, one and whole being, all being, and leave it to the sagacity of the reader to decide whether this notion is conformable or contrary to the philosophical tradition. In these terms the question of the existence of God can be resolved. But if God is regarded as a determinate being, relegated outside the world, upon the throne of his deserted immensity, as M. Cousin expressed it, the question is radically insoluble. God is then no longer a necessary object of thought, but a product of the imagination and perhaps a prejudice. A determinate being supposes others; one will admit as many gods as one pleases. A god who shows all the weaknesses of man, anger, jealousy, vengeance, is a fine ideal of absolute royalty, but cannot impose himself upon reason. God is not a phantom of the imagination. Ordinary atheism has no other cause in [p. 414] modern times than this narrow conception of the Divinity which prevailed in the Middle Ages. The progress of enlightenment, the culture of the intellect and of the heart that succeed barbarism, were bound to bring about a transformation in religious beliefs. But this transformation has not been accomplished in a regular manner and has not always confined itself within its just limits. Ardent minds have not known how to distinguish between the image and the reality. They believed that the denial of a particular worship entailed the denial of God, and that in rejecting predestination to hell they must also reject the future life and the sanction of the moral order. This is an error. The notion of God must not be abolished, but enlarged. Atheism is only an excess begotten by another excess. Let us reestablish the notion of God in its fullness and in its purity, and atheism will become impossible.

But can we comprehend God? The objection has already been set aside in connection with the infinite and the absolute. It is hardly necessary to mention it again, since the discussion is engaged upon the existence of God and we grasp its terms. For my part, to comprehend is to know, but to know is not to exhaust the object of thought. We know God by reason, not by the imagination, as we know space and time, without being able to complete the determination of these objects. Our knowledge has imperfections and limits, inherent in the nature of a limited being, but it is none the less knowledge. The science of God progresses in us like the science of man and of the world; we shall never know God as God knows himself, for we should ourselves have to possess omniscience in order to fathom this one attribute. But knowledge can exist, and can even be true, without being complete. He who knows some parts of a science knows some truths, and no one can boast of having traversed the whole field of discoveries in any order of research whatever.

(1) De Nélis, Bishop of Antwerp, 1736–1798. L’Aveugle de la Montagne, dialogue VI.

p. 415

Let us not confound, moreover, knowledge with truth or with certainty. Knowledge expresses simply a relation between thought and its object, whether this relation be scientific or not. Opinion is already knowledge [p. 415] however vague it may be. In this sense the question of the incomprehensibility of God is not doubtful, for we already have a notion of God. It suffices that God present himself to thought for him to be known. I do not thereby affirm that he is always known as he is in himself. Thought is carried toward the proper essence of things, but may fail to grasp it. But God is not only the object of our individual thought; he is also the object of the thought of the human race or of universal reason. Our own consciousness is in agreement with common sense. In fact, all peoples have a religion, and consequently maintain relations of intelligence with God. Every language possesses a term corresponding to the term God, which attests that the thing it represents is an object of thought. God is therefore not an unknown thing. On what ground, finally, would the incomprehensibility of God rest? Is it on the notion of knowledge? But this notion does not imply that the object be finite rather than infinite. Is it on the relations that one apprehends between the finite and the infinite, as subject and as object of thought? A begging of the question. To maintain that God is incomprehensible, one must already know God. What, indeed, is said? That man is finite, that God is infinite, and that the finite could not embrace the infinite. It is therefore understood that God is infinite, and it is affirmed that he is not understood. This is a pure contradiction. Every man who declares that he does not know God must know him, if he knows what he is saying.

But is the knowledge we have of God legitimate or scientific? In other terms, is it true and certain? That is precisely what is in question.

Two ways have been followed in solving the question of the existence of God: the way of revelation and that of reason.

p. 416

The word revelation is one that is abused; it is the lazy argument, ignava ratio, the argument of minds that do not take the trouble to reflect and are content with a word to decide everything. The same is true of the omnipotence of God, which suffices for theologians to remove all the difficulties [p. 416] of metaphysics. Since reason emancipated itself from faith, the domain of historical revelation has been more and more circumscribed. It may be laid down today as a principle that revelation is useless for everything that can be determined by reason; it is invoked only for want of a scientific argument; the theologians themselves would gladly dispense with it, if they could justify all the points of their doctrine in an intelligible manner; it is restricted to what is called the supernatural order, whose magnificences are exalted, but whose value for real life can hardly be established. Certainly, I have no right to say that there is no object for revelation; but I shall say, with Leibniz, that revelation cannot take the place of any of our means of knowing, nor contradict any proposition recognized as certain. “To wish to proscribe reason in order to make room for revelation would be to tear out one’s eyes in order to see the satellites of Jupiter better through a telescope.” — “This is why revelation cannot go against the clear evidence of reason, because, even when the revelation is immediate and original, we must know with evidence that we deceive not ourselves in ascribing it to God, and that we understand it right; and this evidence can never be greater than that of our intuitive knowledge, and consequently no proposition can be received for divine revelation when it is contradictory to this immediate knowledge; otherwise there would be left no difference in the world between truth and falsehood, no measures of credible and incredible. And it is not conceivable that anything should come from God, the bountiful Author of our being, which, if received for true, must overturn the foundations of our knowledge and render all our faculties useless. And those who have revelation only mediately, whether by tradition from mouth to mouth, or in writing, have still more need of reason to make sure of it (1).” Revelation, in a word, must be subordinated to reason.

(1) Leibniz, Nouv. Essais sur l’entend. humain, bk. IV, ch. XVIII and XIX.

p. 417

Indeed, we are in the presence of several revealed systems. Every people of the East has its own. Buddha, Zoroaster, Hermes, Moses, Mohammed, the evangelists are all held to be revealers in the eyes of their fellow citizens and their proselytes. I do not speak of impostors or of diseased minds, who pretend that they are favored with an extraordinary communication from the divinity. Now all these revealed systems, which are to explain God, the world, and humanity, contradict one another on many points. It is in vain, then, that each affirms that it alone is in possession of the truth; the principle of contradiction and common sense refuse to admit them all. But which is to be adopted, and on what basis shall a choice be made? To appeal to faith is impossible, for that is to settle the question by the question. Has not every system its believers? They would therefore all be equally true and respectable, and it would have to be maintained that God has dictated contradictory solutions on the fundamental interests of man, that there is no difference between affirmation and negation, between truth and error, that everything is true or false, as one pleases. But if it is not faith, it is then reason that must decide the superiority of one revelation over another. The true religion is that which is conformable to reason, and whatever, in a revealed system, is contrary to reason is false.

p. 418

Revelation is therefore insufficient. But even were it incontestable in our eyes, it could never be consulted on the question of the existence of God; for those who deny God equally deny revelation, and would thus be unable to recognize the principle of science. Revelation is possible only if God is, but it is not a necessary consequence of the existence of God. Doubtless, if there is a revelation, there is a God; but how is the existence of revelation to be established without first establishing the existence of the Supreme Being? Revelation is less evident than God, and one must not demonstrate an uncertain thing by another still more uncertain. These logical observations are, moreover, confirmed by history. The Greeks had [p. 418] no sacred book, no revealed doctrine; and yet they admitted the existence of God, and their philosophers treated of the ontological and moral attributes of God in a more scientific manner than the Orientals; they even left their works as models to the Fathers of the Church and to the doctors of the Middle Ages.

Revelation is therefore useless and impossible to follow for the question that occupies us. Traditionalism must abandon this position, which it regarded as impregnable and from which it poured insult upon human reason. The matter is no longer doubtful. M. de Bonald is condemned and reason is avenged by a theologian who has returned to worthier views. We gladly record his judgment, and we beg the philosophers who are behind the times to take account of it. “The knowledge of the existence of God, of the first moral duties, of the immortality of the soul, forms the proper domain of reason, in the order of natural, religious, and moral truth. Man, by his own nature, by his own essence, by the necessity of ideas and of their consequences, is therefore in possession of the elements of the intellectual, religious, and moral life. There are therefore in reality religious and moral truths, natural, essential to reason and to conscience (1).”

These propositions deliver to reason the knowledge of the fundamental problems of the moral and religious order. It suffices for us to point out their importance and to remark that they are in conformity with the decisions of the Roman authority. Some years ago the Archbishop of Paris published four propositions, formulated and approved in the bosom of the Congregation of the Index. The second is thus worded: Ratiocinatio Dei existentiam, animæ spiritualitatem, hominis libertatem cum certitudine probare potest [Reasoning can prove with certainty the existence of God, the spirituality of the soul, the freedom of man].

p. 419

It is therefore by reason alone that the existence of God must be established. Indeed, all questions of principle fall within the province of reason. For centuries reason has seized [p. 419] upon this problem, and has grown strong in seeking to solve it. Three procedures have been followed: the demonstrative procedure, the hypothetical procedure, and the analytic procedure (1).

The demonstrative procedure itself comprises various orders of proofs: the ontological proof concludes from the thought that we have of the infinite, necessary, all-perfect Being to the reality of this being; the cosmological proof concludes from the existence of the world to the existence of God, as cause; the teleological proof starts from the order, the beauty, the proportion, the correspondence of ends and means that shine forth everywhere in nature, and so rises to the recognition of a supremely intelligent being; the moral proof, finally, establishes the necessity of an accord between virtue and felicity, and, seeing this relation often disturbed in the present life, invokes a supremely just being to give in the future life full satisfaction to the moral order.

(1) Philosophie et religion, by Maret, Dean of the Faculty of Theology, Vicar- General of Paris. 1856. Lectures 17, 23.

p. 420

We shall not pause upon the exposition of these various proofs; we shall make only some general observations. The demonstrative procedure has its advantages and its defects. It has the merit of accustoming reason to metaphysical speculations, of elucidating some fundamental ideas, of fathoming some of the attributes of God. It is an excellent gymnastic for the mind and a real profit for science. The very development of the demonstrative procedure proves that thought has grown in its struggle with supersensible things, and has more and more clarified the notion of God. Indeed, the principal properties of Being have been successively subjected to analysis. In the ontological proof, opened by St. Anselm and continued by the whole Cartesian school, God appears to us as the infinite and all-perfect Being, who exists necessarily, by the mere fact that we have the thought of him, because this thought, unlike all our other notions, can proceed only from the infinite Being himself. In the cosmological proof, expounded by Leibniz, God is conceived as the first and immediate [p. 420] cause of all the successive states of the world, as the Supreme Being who is outside and above the series of effects, and who alone can satisfy the needs of reason in its search for causes. In the teleological proof, which speaks to the heart and agrees so well with the marvelous discoveries of the natural sciences, God is the infinitely wise and beneficent Providence, who created the universal order and disposed everything in harmony with everything. Finally, in the moral proof of Kant, God puts on a new character: He is the last end of man, he is the absolute justice that sanctions all our acts, he is the lawgiver of the moral order. All these proofs support and complete one another mutually; they are conformable to the beliefs of the human race; they serve to determine in a scientific manner, and render accessible to every cultivated reason, the essential truths of religion.

(1) H. Ahrens, Cours de psychologie. Paris, 1836. — Bouchitté, Histoire des preuves de l’existence de Dieu. Paris, 1841.

p. 421

But if they can contribute to the solution of the problem, they have not solved it. One must be singularly deluded to believe that God is demonstrated as a proposition of geometry is demonstrated. Here lies the radical vice of the demonstrative procedure. The matter is quite simple, and yet modern authors, in special works, have not succeeded in grasping it (1). Indeed, demonstration has limits. It supposes a thesis, an argument, and a relation of containment or subordination between the thesis and the argument. The argument must contain the thesis, as the premises of a syllogism contain the conclusion. From which it follows naturally that demonstration is a deductive and not an inductive reasoning, that it can be applied to everything that is enclosed within a higher principle, that is to say, to everything that is finite, but that it cannot befit the infinite, which is all and contains all. The finite has its reason in the infinite, but not the infinite in the finite. The finite is subordinated to the infinite and flows from it; but the infinite is subordinated to nothing. God, then, is not demonstrated, because there exists nothing above or outside the infinite Being, [p. 421] since he is himself the higher principle on which all the others depend and which must serve to demonstrate them. The notion of God is unique, in the sense that it embraces all the others; the others can therefore be derived from it, but not reciprocally. God is conceived as the one and whole Being, without cause, without principle, and demonstration has for its aim only to attach a thing to its principle. To demonstrate God is therefore a formal contradiction; those who attempt this operation have not yet an exact notion of God. A demonstration of God would be the negation of God, because God is precisely the one thing that is not demonstrated.

It is therefore evident that in all the proofs of the existence of God arguments are employed whose certainty depends on the very thesis that is to be demonstrated. Such are the objective existence of the world and the universal validity of the principle of causality. God alone, it is said, can be the cause of the world and the cause of the thought of infinite perfection that is in us. But who proves to us that everything has a cause? It is only in God himself that this principle can be recognized in its absolute certainty; for the cause is not superior, but subordinate to God. The idea of cause is therefore not yet cleared up in its just relations with the idea of God. That is taken for an argument which can only be a consequence of the thesis; the rash ventures of reason are confounded with the reality of things.

To this common error are added particular errors. In the ontological proof, the conclusion goes beyond the premises; for the premises bear only on the thought of God, and the conclusion bears on his existence. This reasoning proves only one thing, that it is logically impossible for us to think God without thinking him as existing. Reduced to these proportions, it is unassailable, but is no longer a demonstration. In the other proofs, drawn either from the world in general, or from the moral or physical world, one arrives likewise at a conclusion more extensive than the premises; for the world is not adequate to God. A series of finite effects does not give an infinite cause, but can only suggest this notion to us, in virtue of the laws of our

(1) A. Gratry, De la connaissance de Dieu. Paris, 1854.

p. 422

Logic. — I. 27 [p. 422] intellect. Experience, in its turn, or the observation of the marvels of nature, cannot contain God, nor reveal an infinitely wise providence. Nature is beautiful and harmonious, doubtless; but the little that we know of it on our globe is not exempt from disorders. This is why Kant reduced to nothing these pretended proofs of the existence of God and overthrew at the same stroke the dogmatic metaphysics of the Schools; and he himself avows that his own proof has not the value of an apodictic demonstration.

The insufficiency of the demonstrative procedure gave birth, after Kant, to the hypothetical procedure: since God is not proved, said the successors of this philosopher, it suffices to affirm him; since he cannot be obtained as a consequence of reasoning, he must be posited as a principle; since he repels the discursive and laborious march of demonstration, reason must grasp him by an immediate or direct intuition. Kant, it is true, denied to the human mind the possibility of an intellectual intuition, disengaged from every sensible element; but he allowed himself to be led astray by Locke and by Hume. It is one of those sensualist prejudices of which he could not divest himself, in spite of his project of a universal critique. There exist for man two kinds of intuitions: the one sensible, inherent in the senses and in the imagination, the other intellectual, inherent in reason. Without intellectual intuition we should have no knowledge of God, and metaphysics would be impossible. It is therefore with God that philosophy must begin, not by demonstrating him, but by showing him, by revealing him to reason, as nature is revealed to our senses, by manifesting him to the mind and to the heart, as the supreme hypothesis that explains everything and that must itself be justified by the whole of the consequences it brings with it, that is to say, by the entire system of science.

p. 423

The hypothetical procedure is a reaction against the demonstrative procedure. This reaction is legitimate in itself, but exaggerated and defective in some points. It is true that demonstration does not reach God, since he is the [p. 423] first principle; it is true also that God must be grasped by an immediate intuition of reason, since there are no degrees between the world and God, between the finite and the infinite, and no sum of experiences could engender or equal the absolute; but it does not follow from this that the philosophical work must begin with God. The mind needs a preparation in order to conceive being in its purity and in its truth; this is a necessity of human nature, at least in its earthly condition. Indeed, the first development of the mind is effected through sensibility. The child must learn above all to interpret his sensations. During this period the higher ideas of reason appear as if lost to his consciousness; he employs them without knowing it; his attention is not yet awakened to divine things. Then he rises successively above variable and contingent phenomena, to laws, to causes, to what is immutable and necessary, and at last takes possession of the infinite and absolute being, of which he had only a confused feeling. It is this course, indicated by nature, that must be followed and developed in science. If one begins with God, before the powers of the mind are sufficiently exercised, one will stop at a vague, arbitrary notion, mingled with errors; one will expose oneself to falsifying the whole system of philosophy, because one will have posited, as the base of the edifice, an illegitimate hypothesis. The slightest imperfection in the principle will express itself in a series of consequences that revolt common sense. This is what the example of Schelling and of Hegel, who follow the track of Spinoza, teaches us among others. Criticism and observation are therefore indispensable as preliminaries for the regular development of the notion of God. This notion is not the initial point, but the end of philosophical training.

p. 424

The earlier procedures are imperfect and full of dangers, notwithstanding the qualities that distinguish them. Neither the one nor the other can establish with certainty the existence of God, nor dispel the objections of skepticism on the gravest question of science. The first is a vicious circle, and [p. 424] the second a hypothesis. Science would be lost if it remained shut up in this blind alley. Serious minds, who know how to appraise the state of things and to profit by acquired experience, were therefore bound to direct their attention to this difficult problem. Thence arose the analytic or dialectical procedure, inaugurated by Krause and rightly designated as the most important result of modern philosophy.

The analytic procedure takes account of the portion of truth that is met with in the other procedures and guards itself against their errors. It is a methodical combination, not an amalgam, of these methods, in the sense that, being complete in itself, it gathers up their partial truths, without any set purpose of practicing eclecticism, and links them one to another, stripping them of what they had of exclusiveness, without falling into any extreme: this is the sign of a superior system. Like the demonstrative procedure, it requires that the thought of God be elucidated in the mind before one pronounces upon its objective validity, and demands even a more extensive and more regular preparation than that which is offered us by the various proofs of the existence of God; but it makes no claim to demonstrate what is indemonstrable. Like the hypothetical procedure, it wills that the intellect conceive God by an immediate or direct intuition; but it does not confound the starting point with the principle, and the notion of God, maturely elaborated and discussed in consciousness, thus escapes the character of a hypothesis.

p. 425

It is seen that the analytic procedure is composed of two distinct parts, the one preparatory, the other final, which correspond to the earlier methods. The first is a successive elevation to God. Its aim is to sound the mind, to awaken its energies, to strengthen its speculative activity, and to lead it progressively, step by step, face to face with the infinite and absolute being. It consists in resting upon a first truth recognized by each as certain, in his consciousness, in analyzing the mind in its properties, in its faculties, in its relations with the whole of the beings that form the world, in developing above all the theory of the [p. 425] knowledge, carefully distinguishing the rational elements that form part of it, in grouping and uniting the notions according to the fundamental objects of thought, humanity, spirit, nature, and in thus rising gradually to the highest and fullest notion, to the notion of God, which contains all the others. This psychological and progressive course, sustained by the powers of the self, should bring every mind capable of intellectual labor to be thoroughly penetrated by the thought of God, and should consequently free it from the need of an external support in its relations with God. But the course is long; it extends from the origin to the principle of science, and constitutes the whole analytic or subjective basis of the system of philosophy.

The second part of the procedure is simpler. When the mind is in the presence of God and has grasped the relations of this supreme notion with the other fundamental notions, which belong to the series of our cognitions, with the world and the self, with being, essence, and existence, with the infinite, the absolute, and the cause, it is only a matter of seeing with evidence that God is above all demonstration, that neither his existence nor his non-existence can be proved without making a circle, that we can and must content ourselves with a rational intuition. Indeed, from the notion of the world to the notion of God there is no transition for thought, since God is not a particular term of the series of beings, but the whole of being, the all. One must rise suddenly above the world, beyond all that is finite, to find God. Intuition alone can therefore show us the infinite and absolute being. But this intuition, provoked by the needs of reason, suffices and satisfies all the requirements of logic. After having developed the thought of God, we can no longer conceive him except as existing, on pain of renouncing all mental operation or of being in contradiction with the laws of our own intelligence.

It remains for us to sketch rapidly this analytic procedure for acquiring certainty of the existence of God.

p. 426

Self-consciousness offers us a first truth, immediately and universally certain. Everyone can doubt everything, except himself. But the intuition I is insufficient: we cannot concentrate upon it all our thoughts or all our feelings. The child, who at first sees only himself, soon comes to be convinced of the existence of other realities. If, then, the self is the starting point, it could not be the principle of science. For the notion of the principle must contain all the other notions; the principle must suffice to itself and explain all the rest. Such is the thought God, but such is not the thought I. The self recognizes itself, on the contrary, as a limited being, and at the same time that it is conscious of its limitation, it is conscious of an exterior world or of an ensemble of things that subsist outside itself.

Hence two kinds of knowledge, which have for their object the self and the not-self. Our immanent cognitions do not go out of the sphere of the self and find the guarantee of their validity in the certainty of self-consciousness. We can, without difficulty, recognize the self as a being whose essence is one, which modifies itself in time and which is the cause of its modifications. Doubt is not permitted in this respect, provided that the terms are defined and that one is content to apply them to the self. But our transcendent cognitions are more uncertain. Can we grasp exterior things as they are in themselves? We know all that is by means of the categories of essence, of unity, of identity, of causality. Have we the right to attribute to these ideas an objective validity and to apply them to all things? These questions cannot be resolved by experience and oblige us to ascend higher.

p. 427

Let us consider to this end our transcendent cognitions, first in themselves, then in their object, by raising the idea of cause. Causality expresses between two things a relation of determination: the effect is determined by the cause. This relation supposes two others, containment and subordination: the effect is in the cause and under [p. 427] the cause. Indeed, observation establishes that a being never effects as cause anything but what is in its nature, what is in its power, what is possible for it. A spirit cannot produce physical effects, nor a body spiritual effects, nor a finite being what passes every limit. To depart from this rule is to fail the test of experience, it is to revive miracles and occult causes, which science must drive out. It follows from this that the idea of cause can be applied to everything that is contained in something else, consequently to everything that is finite. This application, at least, is a need of reason, to which the child himself is subject. Before our eyes the idea of cause is constantly verified, but does it remain legitimate beyond observation? This is what it is impossible for us to affirm at this moment. Be that as it may, there are two cases to be distinguished: the one concerns the acts that take place in time; the other, the properties or the very essence of beings. The cause of an act is found in the being that produced it; but if the cause of this being itself is asked, one must rise higher and seek a superior essence that contains it. No being is the cause of itself, of its own essence; for the essence is not contained in the being, but is adequate to the being. The idea of cause does not befit this relation of the being to its essence. But why do we raise the idea of cause in regard to everything that is finite, substance or phenomenon? It is because the finite does not suffice to itself, because it is only a part of reality, and because the notion of the part is correlative to that of the whole, in which it finds its complement. In seeking the cause, it is the whole that we seek, and we wish to know the whole, because the part cannot satisfy us. But the whole itself, the infinite, has no longer a cause, since it is contained in no other thing; he who is all suffices to himself and supposes nothing else.

p. 428

The cause itself has its cause, for it is only a particular property, and this cause of the cause is doubtless God. The cause is not above the infinite Being, but founded in him. It can indeed serve us as an instrument for rising to the notion of God, but not as a logical [p. 428] argument to establish his existence. The idea of cause does not contain the idea of God; it is contained in it and must find its justification there. Until the existence of God is certain, the category of causality, like all the others, is only a hypothesis; this hypothesis is conformable, it is true, to the constitution of the human mind, but it needs to be verified. Thus the principle of cause is for us only a means that permits us to develop the thought of God, and not a premise that is to decide his existence. Writers have failed to recognize the relation of these two ideas. This is why all the proofs of the existence of God are circles: they grant to the idea of cause a universal and absolute validity, whereas this validity must be derived, as a consequence, from the very existence of God.

p. 429

Let us apply this idea to our cognitions. First, our cognitions have a cause, since they are a particular property of the self considered in its relations with an object. Our immanent cognitions have their cause in ourselves, for they are enclosed entire, as subject and as object, in the self. But where is the cause of our transcendent cognitions, which express a relation between the self and the not-self? This cause is not solely in us, nor solely outside us. The self may well be the cause of its thoughts and of their direction, but not of their object. The not-self may be the cause of the object of our thoughts, but not of our thoughts themselves. Moreover, the union between the self and the not-self, which constitutes transcendent knowledge, passes beyond at once the sphere of the self and of the not-self. The self is not the cause of its relations with a foreign thing, nor the not-self the cause of its relations with our thought. We must therefore seek the cause of our transcendent cognitions above the self and the not-self, in a superior essence that contains both the one and the other and explains their union. This superior essence, which envelops the whole of the self and the not-self, which is the reason of all our thoughts and of all their objects, is the principle of science. Science is thus reduced to unity. All that we think and all that we can think of, it is to [p. 429] that is, everything that is, reduces to one and the same cause. The principle of reality is identical with the principle of knowledge.

This principle is one, infinite, absolute, since it is everything and must account for everything determinate that it contains, and consequently also for the thought that we have of the infinite and of the absolute. In fact, we conceive the infinite, whether this conception be true or false. Where is the cause of so remarkable a phenomenon? It is not entirely in us, since we are finite, and nothing finite can produce or contain the infinite; nor is it entirely outside us, since it is our thought that has to be explained; finally, it is in no finite or determinate thing, since the infinite as such excludes determination, and the cause must comprehend at least the whole of the effect. The transcendent notion of the infinite can therefore come only from an infinite being, who is and contains at once the self and the not-self. This being is called God. By this I do not yet affirm the existence of God; I say only that we are obliged to conceive of him, by a just application of the idea of cause, which is a law of our thought, and that we necessarily conceive of him as the one, infinite, absolute Being, or as the one and whole essence that is everything that is, whether in us or outside us. This is what is true in the ontological proof. It amounts to saying that, if the law of causality is legitimate in its relations with our transcendent knowledge, the idea of God, which is infinite like its object, can be put in us only by God himself, or that God alone can be the cause of the notion that we have of God. It is in this sense that it is said: God is the master, it is God who raises us to God.

p. 430

But this notion is still vague and obscure, because it lacks fullness. To clarify it better and to develop it in its content, let us consider our knowledge once more from the point of view of its object. What are the objects of our knowledge? Properties and substances, and among substances the self and the not-self, and in the not-self, minds, bodies, beings formed by the union of a mind [p. 430] and a body, which we unite successively in the thought of a spiritual world, of a physical world, and of humanity.

Observation at first reveals to us, in childhood, only a small number of bodies. But as the mind gains strength, experience extends, and we recognize little by little the widely varied species of organic and inorganic bodies that furnish the earth. The earth itself then appears to us as a single body, as a star that travels through space, and that belongs, along with other planets, to one and the same solar system. To this system there are then added others, more extensive, which seem to be linked with one another by comets, and we arrive at last at conceiving the whole of nature, or the physical world, as a whole infinite in its kind, embracing an infinity of bodies spread through infinite space. This infinity is such that the astronomical distances that it has been possible to measure so far, which place the nearest of the fixed stars at millions of millions of leagues from the earth, are absolutely nothing in comparison with it. It follows from a calculation made by Herschel that light would take more than three thousand years to cross the space that separates us from a star of the sixteenth magnitude. Thus there are stars whose light has only just reached the earth, others whose light has not yet reached us, and others, finally, whose light, traversing from second to second the unfathomable depths of the sky, will never come as far as here. And on the other hand thousands of stars may have perished centuries ago without our ceasing to see them. What is the number of the stars? The Milky Way alone counts eighteen million of them, visible in the telescope. These abysses of the infinite appall the imagination, but please the reason. They diminish the importance of the earth, but exalt the grandeur of the world and the majesty of its author: Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei. Yet I do not affirm at this moment that nature is really infinite: it is a hypothesis to be verified.

p. 431

It is here above all that we recognize the insufficiency of observation.
