Most modern philosophers and scientists admit without hesitation the infinity of the world, and [p. 431] yet it is and always will be impossible to justify this affirmation by experimental means. For my part, I content myself with saying that we can and must conceive nature as infinite. For as soon as we posit in our mind a limit to space and to matter, we ask ourselves what happens beyond this limit, and we again glimpse, without end, other spaces and other bodies. Moreover, the principle of sufficient reason does not permit us to stop at a determinate number of bodies; for why this number rather than any other? The infinite alone is worthy of the divine intelligence and power. The laws of the motion of bodies seem to lead to the same result. “Since every globe never ceases to strive to dissolve itself, and is prevented from doing so only by the resistance of the surrounding globes, it is necessary that every globe be surrounded by other globes, and that consequently there be no outermost globes. Pascal had defined the universe thus: Center everywhere, circumference nowhere; it was a view of genius. If the universe had limits, it would be, however great its extent, only a material point surrounded by an empty and infinite space; a moment would suffice for it to enter into eternal dissolution (1).” The theological objections raised by this conception of the physical world have been foreseen, from the point of view of dogma, and are no obstacle for us (2). The philosophical objections are resolved without difficulty. Modern reason does not resist the attraction of the infinite; it plunges into it with enthusiasm, ever since it has witnessed the spectacle of universal motion and of the great heavens of Copernicus (3).

p. 432

The thought of the spiritual world develops in us parallel to that of the corporeal world. We are at first in relation only with a few minds; but, as [p. 432] our social relations multiply, we enter into communication, by means of speech and writing, with a steadily growing number of spirits who, united to bodies, inhabit or have inhabited the earth, and we end by suspecting that the spiritual world is infinite in its kind, like nature, its antithesis and its companion. Why should there exist only a certain quantity of spiritual beings, attached to our globe, while we conceive an infinity of bodies in space? Why a determinate number rather than any other? Has not each thing a sufficient reason? And then, what would be the purpose of the stars, if the forces and harmonies of matter were not to be known, tried, utilized, and governed by a society of rational beings? Whence comes, further, the identical constitution of all the minds that we observe here below? How can they all submit to the same laws of reason, and accept as true, as good and beautiful, whatever reason proclaims, as false and bad whatever reason condemns? These questions receive a satisfactory solution only if we rise to the notion of a universal spirit or reason, which manifests itself in an infinity of individual spirits, as nature reveals itself in an infinity of bodies subject to its laws.

(1) Azaïs, Précis du système universel. Paris, 1825.

(2) Traité de l’infini créé, attributed to Malebranche. See our Dissertation, Revue de Belgique, 1846. — Jean Reynaud, Terre et Ciel, 1854.

(3) F. Morin, de la Genèse et des principes métaphysiques de la science moderne, ou la Philosophie des sciences cherchée dans leur histoire. Paris, 1856.

p. 433

But we do not conceive only minds and bodies; observation establishes that minds are intimately united to bodies and thus form complex beings, among whom we distinguish men. The notion of humanity is reduced at first, for the child, to the notion of the family; then it extends to a group of families and becomes the city or the tribe. Many savage peoples stop at this elementary form of humanity; but civilized peoples constitute themselves into national bodies, according to the affinities of race. There the notion of humanity ends for the ancients, who regarded themselves as autochthonous, sprung from a national divinity and separated from foreign races, called barbarian, stripped of the qualities of man and destined for slavery. But, thanks to Christianity, prepared by the Stoic doctrine, the thought of humanity [p. 433] widens still further and now embraces all the peoples of the earth, without distinction of race, sex, or social position; for all descend from a primitive pair and form one family, under the government of one and the same heavenly Father; all are bound together in the fall and in the redemption. This great notion of humanity, which Christ inaugurated on earth, and which the Church applied to religious society, was also destined, in the course of the centuries, to transform civil society (1). It is the source of modern civilization. But is it the last term of the progression? No; after having conceived terrestrial humanity, we can and must still conceive universal humanity, spread through the whole of nature and peopling all the habitable globes sown in infinite space. Terrestrial humanity is then no more than a small fraction of infinite humanity, a branch detached from the human family, which accomplishes its pilgrimage on our globe, but whose ulterior destinies must be bound up with those of humanity as a whole. Why, once more, should there be only a determinate number of rational beings, from Adam down to the last inhabitant of the earth? Is the spectacle of life the exclusive privilege of our planet? What would the other celestial earths serve for? Why incommensurable heavens, if the intelligent beings can be counted? The principle of sufficient reason, in agreement with the state of our astronomical knowledge, therefore compels us to understand humanity as infinite in its kind.

p. 434

The system of Ptolemy, under whose influence Christian dogmatics was formed, sufficed for the needs of terrestrial humanity; the system of Copernicus, which has triumphed over traditional faith, demands an infinite humanity and broader dogmas. Hardly had the speculation of the infinite been introduced into philosophy when new ideas arose on all sides in science, in theology, and even in the controversies over optimism. Fontenelle, Huygens, Malebranche, Leibniz continue Descartes and [p. 434] sail under full canvas in the celestial regions discovered by Copernicus and traversed by Galileo. A revolution in beliefs was imminent. The biblical theories of heaven and hell no longer have a refuge in the world of science. The edifice so laboriously raised by St. Thomas lacks a foundation and crumbles. The demons are driven from the earth, the earth rises into the heavens, and the heavens, half opened, contain no trace of that marvelous abode of the blessed dreamed of by our fathers. We perceive at last that the Middle Ages had made nothing but a romance of the world, and that mythology had usurped the name of science. In the new conditions in which we find ourselves, everything has to be done over again. Since the world has changed its aspect, the destinies of humanity must change their face. Lalande, Laplace, W. Herschel, Chalmers, Brewster, and many others, relying on analogy, teach the habitability of the celestial globes (1). There is henceforth no other heaven and no other hell.

The objects of our knowledge are therefore nature, spirit, humanity; and these objects united form the world or the universe. Is that all? No: spirit, nature, and humanity, although each appears infinite in its kind, are only determinate things, opposed to one another; they are parts of reality, not the whole of reality. Now we cannot be content with the part; the part presupposes the whole, and the notion of the whole alone can satisfy reason. Hence a fourth object for thought, and this object is God. But is not this fourth object the sum or the collection of the first three? Is not God spirit, plus nature, plus humanity? No, God is not the world, God is not the totality of things; that is the error of pantheism; the application of the idea of cause obliges us to reject this doctrine.

(1) Laurent, Études sur l’histoire de l’humanité, vol. IV, le Christianisme. 2nd ed., 1863.

p. 435

At first sight it seems that the world is without a cause, by virtue of our premises, since we have supposed it [p. 435] infinite, and that the infinite as such has no cause. But a more attentive examination turns us away from this solution.

(1) Cf. Plisson, les Mondes, essai philosophique sur les conditions d’existence des êtres organisés dans notre système planétaire. Paris, 1847. — Babinet, de la Pluralité des Mondes, 1855.

p. 436

The world is a collective whole which, in itself, lacks unity, as a term superior to multiplicity: it is the totality of all finite things, spirits, bodies, and men, which we sum up in the thought of nature, of universal spirit, and of humanity. Each of these genera may be infinite, but it is only a genus, that is to say a part: it is a relative infinite, a thing infinite in itself, but not infinite in every respect. Nature is infinite as such, because it is the only being of its kind, because there is but one nature, which comprises an infinity of bodies spread through infinite space; but after all it is only nature, it is neither spirit nor humanity, it is not all. An infinite of this kind can coexist with other relative infinites, for each is restricted to its own sphere. Likewise, the world of minds is infinite, because it is unique in its kind and contains an infinity of spiritual beings; but these beings are never anything but minds, they are neither space nor time, they are not all. The infinity of the spiritual world therefore does not exclude the infinity of the physical world; for these two infinites apply to different orders; they are fractions of reality, each of which extends to infinity in its own domain, without encroaching on the domain of the other; they are, in short, distinct genera. Likewise again, humanity appears infinite, because it is unique and because it communicates its inexhaustible essence to an infinity of rational beings; but these beings are only men. Humanity is not the whole of nature, nor the whole of spirit, but constitutes a certain union of spirit with nature. Spirit, nature, and humanity are therefore determinate things, limited in relation to one another, opposed to one another and affected by negation. In a word, a relative infinite is an infinite that confines itself to one genus, to the exclusion of every other, an infinite that is not the whole of the infinite, an infinite that is still finite in certain respects. Now the principle of causality applies to everything that is finite or determinate, to everything that is part of something else. It therefore applies also to what is infinite only in one [p. 436] relative way, that is to say to the various parts of the universe. We can therefore ask, and we do in fact ask, why there is a world, why the world is composed of spiritual substances, of physical substances, and of complex substances, why it is not otherwise, and why evil is produced in it under so many diverse forms.

p. 437

Where, now, is the cause of the world? Shall it be said to be in the world itself? That is impossible: no thing is the cause of itself. How could the world that was to be made be caused by a world not made? ex nihilo nihil. The world, besides, is only an aggregation of things, and this aggregation does not act as a cause. Is an edifice the cause of what it contains? To say that the world has its cause in itself is to say that its various parts have their cause respectively in themselves and in the other parts: in themselves, that is nonsense; in the other parts, it is a circle or a violation of the relations of cause to effect. Spirit does not have its cause in nature, which is opposed to it, which is subject to other laws and possesses another essence, nor in humanity, which is subordinate to it. Nature does not have its cause in spirit, which is foreign to it, nor in humanity, which borrows from it a part of its essence. Spirit and nature may well sustain between them a relation of conditionality, because they are parts of one and the same whole, but not a relation of causality, because everything is free and spontaneous in the one, necessary and fettered in the other. There is no connection, but antithesis, between the world of bodies and the world of minds. And yet spirit is intimately united to nature in humanity. Where is the cause of this union? It cannot be wholly in spirit or in nature, for it surpasses at once the proper essence of nature and that of spirit. The human body may well find its cause in nature, and the human spirit in universal spirit; but man is not a spirit, plus a body, the sum of two heterogeneous substances; he is the being of union of spirit and body; as spirit he is influenced and modified by the body, and as body influenced and modified by the spirit; he is a single being, an organism and not an [p. 437] aggregate. This union of spirit and body cannot be explained either by the essence of spirit or by the essence of nature, for it constitutes a fact that is transcendent for the one and for the other. The notion of matter must account for the qualities of matter, but not for its relations with spiritual substances. Why, then, is the world not composed of pure minds and of pure matter? Why does matter unite with mind? The world does not give the solution of this problem.

The cause of the world is therefore not in the world, nor in any of its parts. It is therefore above the world. It must be sought, according to the law of causality, in a being or in a superior essence that contains at once spirit and nature, that serves them as a common basis, and thus determines their union in humanity. It is in the essence of this superior being that the reason for the whole constitution of the world must be discovered. But is this being God? Are there not intermediaries between God and the world? It is certain that we have no consciousness of such intermediaries, and that no one has ever pointed them out as distinct objects of knowledge. Yet our ignorance does not prove the non-existence of a thing. Modern discoveries ought to inspire greater circumspection in those who resolutely deny what they do not know. Let us say simply, then, that the question that has just been raised is insoluble at the point we have reached; it can be decided only in the science of God itself. For the rest, the solution of this point has no bearing whatever on the existence of God. If the proximate cause of the world is not the ultimate cause, it will be only a determinate thing which, according to the definition, will itself have its cause, and which will not be able to furnish the definitive explanation of the existence and composition of the world. What will be the cause of this cause? If it is again a particular thing, we cannot stop there, because, far from demonstrating the various orders of things, it itself needs demonstration. We must thus go back from cause to cause, until we come to posit the ultimate cause, which no longer has a cause, and

p. 438

Logic. — I. 28 [p. 438] which we call God. The reasoning by which it is supposed that the series of causes has no term constitutes the progress to infinity. It cannot satisfy thought, as Aristotle had already remarked, because it explains nothing; it only pushes the difficulty back indefinitely without resolving it, for the idea of cause, so long as it is applied to a determinate thing, always obliges us to rise to the indeterminate being, which is the reason of everything.

p. 439

The cosmological procedure therefore brings us face to face with God. It is impossible for us, in the full light of our consciousness, not to admit that the world has a cause, and that this cause is other than the world. But the world is, or can be, infinite in its various parts. What, then, is the cause of the world? It is assuredly an infinite thing, no longer infinite in a relative manner, but infinite in an absolute manner, since it is the last term of thought and must contain in itself all the genera of reality; it is the absolutely infinite being, that is to say, infinite in every respect and under every relation; it is the being that is all being. Relative infinites can exist together, because they are limited to one genus; but the absolute infinite is necessarily alone and unique, since it is everything. The relative infinites are in it and give fullness to its essence, as finite beings, spirits, bodies, and men, fill universal spirit, nature, and humanity. No finite outside the infinite; no relative infinite outside the absolute infinite. The absolute infinite is therefore without a second; it is all and contains all; it is only on this condition. Such is the thought of God. It is impossible for an enlightened consciousness not to conceive God as the being of all being: ens entium, omnitudo realitatis. It is the only thought that we lack when we have recognized the world as infinite in its various orders; it is the only one that completes and sustains the others, the only one that can serve as principle for all the rest; it is the ideal of reason, as Kant expresses it. The world, in fact, is only a collection of parts. This conception leaves a gap in our mind: the conception of God fills this gap. The world needs a cause, for it is limited under [p. 439] on each of its faces; this cause must be completely infinite, in order to explain the infinity of the things that we conceive in each genus; the only sufficient cause of the world is therefore the absolutely infinite being, who is God. It is the thought of God alone that tears us away from the thought of the limitation of things. We do say that space is infinite, because it is the whole of space and there is no other; yet space is only a genus. We say again that time is infinite, because it embraces everything that belongs to that order; but time also is only a genus. God is not infinite in this way; he is not merely all in a determinate genus, he is absolutely all: he is all that is real and positive in minds, all that is real and positive in bodies, all that is real and positive in the essences of all possible creatures, as Fénelon affirms. He has the whole being of all that is. The geometer who should say that space is infinite, but that there are still spaces outside of space, would be an object of derision to his colleagues. He would be less blind, however, than the theologians who maintain that God is the infinite being, but that there are still beings outside God (1). The infinite being signifies all being, ens omne: the infinite essence expresses the totality of essence, and whoever says the whole being excludes every restriction. Let us repeat it, then, with a learned bishop: God is all or he is nothing. If he is only a determinate being, we have no need of him: he is only a new genus added to the others, or an old genus arbitrarily raised to the rank of first cause. If he is all being, on the contrary, he is a necessary object of our thought, and only the fool can say in his heart: There is no God.

p. 440

The precise notion of God, developed in its content, is therefore the thought of the one, infinite, absolute Being who is and contains in his essence nature, spirit, humanity, and all finite beings. “In Deo sumus, vivimus et movemur. Ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia.” [In God we are, and live, and move. From him, and through him, and in him are all things.] It is the most [p. 440] full that we possess, or rather it is the single thought that comprehends everything, of which the other thoughts are only reflections and in which they are grounded, not excepting the intuition I and the idea of cause. We have no notion that is foreign to the notion of God; for in all the operations of the intellect we affirm something, we posit being or a determination of being. Whether one knows it or not, God lies at the bottom of every act of consciousness. The pantheist and the atheist alike proclaim God, but the one with discernment, the other without intending it.

(1) Du Panthéisme, examen d’un ouvrage de M. Tiberghien, by N. J. Laforêt, professor at the University of Louvain. Brussels, 1855.

p. 441

The thought of God must therefore not be formulated in a negative or restrictive manner. We must not say: God is this or that, but God is all. We must not say with the theologians: God is a pure spirit; nor with the materialists: God is only nature; nor with the positivists: God is humanity and nothing else; nor, finally, with the pantheists: God is all of these together. All these judgments are false, because they shut God up within the limits of one genus or of several genera. God is not a part of reality, but the whole of reality. He is consequently also the world, he is also spirit and nature and humanity; but he is not merely the sum of beings, he is the reason of all that is finite. God is not the totality of things, but the absolute unity of essence. The totality of things is the world; the principle or reason of the world is God. The principle is one, simple, indecomposable, for if it were a union of parts, it would be confounded with the world and we should have to seek anew the reason of this union. In the world there is antithesis and synthesis: the antithesis comprises nature and spirit, whose synthesis is humanity; but the thesis, the higher point of view of unity, is lacking there. The thesis is God. Nor must we say: God is the eternal and nothing but the eternal, or God is love and is only love; for God is also life and thought. God is nothing determinate; he is all in a pure and simple manner. The only name that befits him is being. God is Being; he is he who is, the ὄντως ὄν of Plato and of Aristotle. Whatever is added to being is useless or [p. 441] superfluous. Philosophy is only the explanation of this term.

Nothing, then, is to be taken away from the notion of God, except the determination that is found in the development of all the others. Determination is a limit and a negation; a determinate thing is a thing that is opposed to another and excludes it. God is coordinated with nothing and excludes nothing. He is the thesis, one and whole, the absolute thesis that has no antithesis. The thought of God is wholly positive; it is the only one that is negative in no respect. Spirit and nature are the negation of each other: God is the negation of all negation. There is something other than nature; there is something other than mind: there is nothing other than God. Everything that is is affected by negation, except God. Each genus repels every other and is external to it: God alone has no exterior. All is in him. He is also all that he contains in his essence; but since he is nothing determinate himself, since he is no more one genus than another, the limits that enclose finite beings on every side in the world, and that are the source of imperfection in all its aspects, are not the limits of God. Do the bounds that surround the celestial globes in space impair the simplicity and the infinity of space? Does the breaking up of colors alter the unity and purity of light? So it is that God is all in unity, and it is because he is all that he is above the negations, the conflicts, and the evil that attach to finite beings.

p. 442

Is it necessary, further, to ask whether the world is in God in an eminent manner or otherwise? In saying that God is not the world, but the reason of the world, we have laid down the principle of the preeminence or transcendence of God, but this principle can be exactly understood only in metaphysics. For the moment every distinction is useless. We must say simply with St. Anselm: “Ex ipsa summa essentia et per ipsam et in ipsa sunt omnia.” [From the supreme essence itself, and through it, and in it, are all things.] God is the whole, the one whole, the absolute and infinite whole, such is the first thought; and the immediate consequence is that God is infinite in every respect, absolutely [p. 442] infinite. He is therefore not infinite merely in intension, or in degrees of perfection; he is above every degree and every disjunction.

p. 443

We have thus completed the first part of the analytic procedure by which the mind rises progressively from the starting point to the principle. We have obtained a clear and precise intuition of God. We have recognized, in conforming to the laws of our spiritual organization, that our knowledge, considered in itself and in its object, necessarily has a cause, and that this cause, which contains in itself everything that we conceive of the finite or the infinite, is necessarily above the world. We understand God, and cannot help understanding him, when our intellectual dispositions are sufficiently developed, as the one, infinite, absolute Being, who is all and who is cause of all the parts of reality, of all the genera that we designate under the names of nature, spirit, and humanity. God as such is not a determinate being, higher than the others, but Being in its entirety, a necessary object of thought. The notion of God is absolutely full and positive; it is the unique notion, which embraces all the others and derives from nothing; it is the only one that is freed from all determination, all restriction, all negation. That is why this notion must spring up immediately in our mind, after a suitable preparation. Since God is deduced from nothing, we cannot either attach him to a higher principle by way of reasoning and demonstration. It is with the principle as with the starting point of science. It is not expressed in the form of a conclusion, or even of a proposition, since it is alone and unique, but in the form of a notion. It is the object of an intellectual intuition. We must see God by reason, as we see that the whole is greater than the part and that every phenomenon has a cause. This intuition is completely indeterminate, but it is susceptible of determination, for it is already distinguished from all determinate notions precisely because it is indeterminate. Since God is all Being, we are also [p. 443] beings in direct relation with him, and it is directly that we must grasp him. Now such is the notion that we had to bring to light and ripen before we could pronounce with full knowledge on the existence of God. Let us pass now to the application.

Has the notion of God, as we have just developed it, an objective validity, or is it only a fantastic product of our imagination? Does God, Being, the All-One, really exist, and are we certain of his existence? He who understands the question will resolve it without difficulty; he who has not yet understood it must abstain, until the thought of God illumines his mind. Certainty is an individual matter; it does not arise in all at the same moment, or in the same degree; it demands a certain culture of consciousness, proportioned to the greatness of its object; an uncultivated reason has no consciousness of rational things. For a thing to become certain or evident, it is necessary and sufficient that it be clear and precise. Now whoever sees God clearly must see at the same time that God exists. In fact, we conceive God as the being who is all; now what is all is also existence. Existence is assuredly something: it is a positive property; now nothing positive can be lacking to that which lacks nothing. What exists is more than what does not exist; now the Being of all reality could not be less than any other thing. In other words, to know God is to see the essence of God, or what God is. Now essence is inseparable from existence. Whoever posits essence posits existence in some manner, in thought or in reality; whoever posits infinite essence posits infinite existence. In the absolutely infinite being, essence necessarily involves existence, as Spinoza says: it is the profoundest thought that has been uttered on the subject of God, and it is worthy of remark that the author of this proposition long passed, and still passes, for an atheist.

p. 444

A finite thing possesses, in fact, only a limited and contingent existence; it may or may not exist outside us. But it is contradictory that an infinite thing should not exist and not have entire existence; in either case it would not [p. 444] be infinite any longer, since it would cease to be all. What exists in thought and in reality is more than what exists only in thought; the one has a complete and real existence, the other an imaginary and partial existence. Now nothing is more complete, more real, more positive than the being of all being; or, to put it better, the one and whole Being is the only one that is entirely positive and that is absolutely sufficient to itself. To conceive God, then, is to conceive that God exists. We cannot tolerate contradiction in our mind; now we should be in contradiction with ourselves if, on the one hand, we thought God as the Being of all reality, and if, on the other, we thought that God does not exist; for the second proposition is the negation of the first: God is not infinite if he does not exist; God without existence is deprived of something, he is less than we are, he is only one of the modifications of our mind; it is we who invent him, it is we who create the infinite, in spite of ourselves, in spite of the consciousness that we have of our limitation, in spite of the notion that we have of God. It is enough that such an aberration should have occurred once; to stop at it is to abdicate reason. Let us repeat it, then, with a well-considered conviction: the infinite Being can be thought only as existing; now we do think the infinite Being; therefore we must admit his existence.

p. 445

Is the existence of God thereby demonstrated? No; it is demonstrated, on the contrary, that the existence and the non-existence of God are equally indemonstrable, and that nevertheless we are obliged, by virtue of our spiritual nature, to accept the one and reject the other. God shows himself or reveals himself directly to every enlightened reason; but he is not demonstrated, because he is without cause, because he is himself the principle of all things, and consequently also the principle of demonstration. In order that demonstration may be possible and may not be prolonged to infinity, there must needs be one thing that can no longer be demonstrated, and this thing is precisely God. But by that very fact it is evident that God has no need of demonstration, since he is the object of an immediate intuition and since every attempt at demonstration [p. 445] of God is the negation of God, as infinite Being, as first and last cause. God is the only being who cannot and must not be demonstrated. But the non-existence of God is no more demonstrable; for the principle of this demonstration would have to be found, in the final analysis, in the very nature of the first cause, which is God. In every partial demonstration we must go back from cause to cause up to the whole. If God cannot be demonstrated, nothing else can be completely demonstrated except through God. Is this to say now that God is a frivolous hypothesis? Yes, for a frivolous mind, incapable of rising above finite things. For a serious mind, God is also the absolute principle of certainty and the source of all metaphysical certainty. This is what St. Augustine affirms in these memorable words: Deus in quo et a quo et per quem vera sunt, quæ vera sunt omnia. [God, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things are true that are true.]

p. 446

We must, no doubt, in order to understand God, begin by thinking, judging, and reasoning; we must analyze the self and venture upon the stage of the world, submitting ourselves to the laws of our intelligent nature, reserving the right to justify these laws after we have recognized God. But God is not for this reason any more open to dispute than all the other objects, sensible or non-sensible, of thought. Whatever we may think, we must obey the laws of our intellectual activity. Each being acts according to its essence, according to what it is, and conforms, whether it wills or not, to laws that it has not made, because they are the very expression of its essence. This necessity is common to all the works of the understanding and applies invariably to all the domains of science. He who would rely on this fact to criticize the result of our inquiry would therefore have to forbid himself to reason, or would put himself in contradiction with himself; for it is impossible for him to reason without following the laws of thought. Who could refuse his assent to these principles: each thing is what it is and is not another; every fact has a cause; the part presupposes the whole; a genus is a determinate thing; the finite is a part of reality; the infinite is the whole of reality; a collection of objects [p. 446] that are limited does not suffice to itself and does not appease the need of reason? He who would contest these fundamental truths would deny his own nature and would have to renounce performing any act of intelligence; for it is impossible for him to affirm a thing seriously without denying the contradictory term.

Let us remark, moreover, that these principles or laws of thought are only points of support and not arguments in our discussion. We employ them as levers, not as premises, because we cannot do without them and because terms are needed in order to understand one another. We do not invoke them to guarantee the certainty of our conclusions. Whether they be true or false, outside the limits of inner sense, the result we obtain is not affected by it; for we must always arrive at the notion of the whole that completes our other notions. The thought of the infinite and absolute Being is the necessary crowning of all intellectual culture. Now this thought derives from no other; it is independent of every preconceived opinion; it is not produced in our mind as the consequence of a reasoning; argumentation has no other purpose than to develop it methodically and to make it clearer. The notion of God as one and whole Being is therefore absolutely unassailable, from whatever point of view one places oneself; and it is solely on the strength of this notion, once well elucidated, and not on that of the course that has been followed, that we decide for the existence of God.

Our reasoning sums itself up in two points: we must conceive God as the Being of all reality, and in order to conceive him as such we must admit his existence. In other words, we can understand God only as Being, and Being only as existing. This reasoning applies only to God, because God alone is being in its entirety. We can imagine many genera without granting them objective existence. Only the Whole, without this quality, ceases to be what it is.

p. 447

Kant has not understood this distinction. He maintains that every judgment of existence is synthetic, because the predicate is not given with the subject, or because the subject can be conceived without contradiction as non-existent. This is true of all [p. 447] determinate subjects, of all the beings that are in the world. But there is a subject whose existence is necessary, or which cannot be conceived without contradiction except as existing: the infinite and absolute Being. The judgment God exists is analytic and not synthetic, for the thought of God carries with it the thought of existence. It is true that from a purely formal point of view, if we abstract from the nature of the notions, every judgment is possible, provided there are two terms and a relation. But God is not just any notion in our argument, it is a unique notion. We have regard to the matter of the judgment when we declare that everything that expresses a positive quality, such as existence, agrees necessarily with the idea of God (1).

I can therefore affirm against the skeptics, and every man who knows the value of terms can affirm with me, that God exists. I have consciousness of the truth of this proposition. Science is therefore possible, for it has a certain starting point and a certain principle. Science exists from the moment that God is recognized. From then on, too, man enters into full possession of his reason, his dignity, his independence. He no longer needs an external support: he finds within himself the authority that others seek outside. He is in direct relation with God, and can dispense with any intermediary or mediator for the accomplishment of his destiny. He is himself a minister of truth. To the subjective criterion of consciousness: as true as I am, he can add the absolute criterion, which completes the first: as true as God is.

(1) Kant, Critique de la raison pure. Des arguments de la raison spéculative en faveur de l’existence d’un Être suprême.

p. 448

CHAPTER THREE

CONCLUSION

p. 449

To establish the legitimacy of knowledge, it was necessary to show that science possesses a certain starting point and a certain principle. This demonstration has been made. The principle and the starting point are found in the knowledge of God and of oneself, which is the mark of wisdom according to Bossuet. The knowledge of ourselves raises us to God; the knowledge of God completes the development of our own consciousness, by linking the self to the principle of all things. At the origin and at the term of the evolution of thought, we find two intuitions that doubt can no longer breach, for both stand above the opposition between the subject and the object of the intellect. At the starting point, the self is as yet neither subject nor object; at the end, God is the common reason of the self and the not-self, the absolute principle of thought and of reality. How can these two truths be contested? He who doubts affirms himself; he who affirms anything must distinguish between thought and things, and ascend by the law of causality to the ultimate reason of knowledge. If there is anything, God exists. In examining the relation of these two intuitions, we become convinced that each of us must begin with his own self, for it is the self that aspires to know God, it is in the self that this knowledge must be made to germinate, and it is by the consciousness of its own limitation and dependence that the mind acquires the certainty of the existence of God. But once this certainty is acquired, we must also recognize that the intuition I is founded, like everything else, in the intuition God, which embraces all our particular thoughts and which alone can furnish a scientific explanation of them. In analysis we are content with the fact that the self relates to itself by inner sense, and the fact is certain, whether it has a reason or not. But in synthesis we ask [p. 449] why the self possesses this singular property, and the reason is found in God, in the relation of being to essence. If God did not exist, there would be no intuition at all.

p. 450

All science flows from the knowledge of God and of oneself. The affirmation of the self legitimates our immanent knowledge; the affirmation of God, our transcendent knowledge. To the development of the former the categories of being, of essence, of unity are applied; but this application is certified as correct by consciousness within the limits of the self. The same laws are found again in our transcendent knowledge, but in this new domain, foreign to the self, a demonstration of the validity of the categories becomes indispensable. We were able to neglect it for the question of the existence of God, but will it be the same for the question of the existence of the world? No, skeptical idealism retains all its rights. It may after all be that the external world is only a series of internal representations without objective basis. Doubtless we have already made use of the categories in passing from the self to the not-self and in preparing the notion of God; but it has been seen that this use, improper or not, has no influence whatever on the result of our researches, so far as the principle is concerned. The reason of this will now be grasped by considering the relation of the notion of God to the notion of the world. The infinite and absolute Being suffices to itself and can be understood in itself, whatever the judgments we pass upon the world. Whether the universe is composed of spirits and bodies, separate or combined, whether the substances that appear to us do not exist and others exist that are hidden from us—what does it matter to the notion of the principle? God will be none the less being without restriction and without condition, and it is as such that we affirm his existence. The conception of God is therefore independent of the conception of the universe and requires no previous verification concerning the transcendent reach of the categories. But the converse does not hold. The world is the collection of finite things that depend on the principle. The question is whether these things deduced from the principle are still [p. 450] such as they present themselves to our eyes when we observe them in themselves. Is there a real world outside us, and is there room in this world for the beings that we call spirits, bodies, men? Is the universe one or many, finite or infinite? All this depends on the categories that we apply to the objects of thought. We suppose that spirits are beings having a proper essence fundamentally distinct from the essence of matter; but is it certain that there exist, besides Being, beings, besides essence, essences, and that these beings differ among themselves and are other than God? The idealists are not of this opinion, and already in antiquity the Eleatics refused to leave the pure unity of essence and understood nothing of the multiplicity of things. The question has only a theoretical interest, but from this point of view it is harder to resolve than to pose.

These observations at the same time justify the course that we have followed up to this point in order to establish the legitimacy of our transcendent knowledge. The first question is that of God, as the principle of science. It seems that we have made a detour in rising to God in order to return afterward to the world. But we had no choice of means. Any other path engaged us in a begging of the question, since the world is founded in God and can be explained only by the principle. The world is demonstrated by God, but not God by the world. The world draws its truth and its certainty from God, but not the reverse. The cause can subsist without this or that effect, but not the effect without the cause. In going straight to the principle, we have followed the only possible method and have preserved ourselves from the deplorable illusion of a demonstration of God by the world, which has seduced so many thinkers.

The problem of the categories can now be approached with advantage. For this purpose we shall have to make a rapid excursion into the domain of metaphysics. We shall confine ourselves to what is necessary for the theory of knowledge, freeing our exposition of all geometrical apparatus, reserving the right to complete it later.

p. 451

Synthesis starts from the notion of God or of Being, which has been fully worked out by the dialectical procedure of analysis. From being essence is deduced, from essence unity, and so on. To God are applied in succession the fundamental categories that are contained in that of being, considering God first in himself, then in his content, and finally in his relations with his content, in conformity with the laws of knowledge. This point obtained, knowing that God is purely and simply all, and that he is identical with himself in all that he is, we reason thus: If the categories are the properties of Being, who is and contains all in his essence, they are also, by way of consequence, the properties of all that is in God, and therefore have an objective and universal validity. If God is being, he is in everything and everywhere as being; if God is essence, he is everywhere as essence; if God is one, he is in everything as unity; all that is in God therefore has being, essence, unity. If God contains the world in himself, and if the world in its turn contains finite things in itself, individualities, God also is, as being, as essence, as unity, the world and the individuals that develop in it, without being affected by the negation, the limit, and the imperfection that attach to finite things as such. Moreover, if God is infinite and absolute, he is still infinite and absolute inasmuch as he is also the world, inasmuch as he is and contains in himself finite and contingent beings. The infinite is the absence of limits, it is the whole essence; the absolute is the absence of conditions, it is the proper essence. Each thing will therefore have its proper essence and its whole essence as God has, and if God is truth, each thing can equally be known in truth according to its proper essence. In a word, all that is divine will be revealed in the world and will be a sign of God. Hence it is certain that the laws that we obey in knowledge are none other than the laws of reality; for the self and all finite beings, founded in the same divine essence, bear these laws impressed in their nature. The categories of being or the properties of God are the common type of the constitution of things, of the [p. 452] self and of the not-self. Hence the universal analogy; hence also the beauty that shines forth in the world, made in the image of God.

Let us verify these various points, considering God first in himself.

p. 453

God is being. This is the name given to him by the Bible, Plato, Aristotle, Fénelon, Bossuet, and most modern writers; it is the only one that fits him completely and expresses all that he is. All metaphysics issues from this fundamental proposition. Being is essence, for by essence I mean what being is. The second proposition is therefore this: God is essence. The divine essence is commonly designated by the divine or the divinity. It is important to bring no restriction to these categorical propositions; whatever is added to them diminishes their meaning. God is not such a being nor such an essence, but being and essence purely and simply. Essence is one, pure, homogeneous; God is one as being and as essence, for he is the divine, all the divine, nothing but the divine. This last determination is even superfluous with regard to God, for there is nothing else than being and essence. Who says being, says essence; who says essence, says unity. But the unity of essence manifests itself in two ways by two opposed or coordinate properties: inasmuch as he is one, God is himself the essence and he is the whole essence; in the first place, essence is the very essence or the proper essence of God and not of another; in the second place, the divine essence is the whole essence, which is restricted by no other. These attributes both derive from the unity of essence: if there were a second essence beside the divine essence, it could not be said categorically that the essence is wholly the essence of God; but if essence is one, it is all the essence, without any possible limitation, and at the same time it is the essence of God himself, without any condition or dependence. Limit and condition presuppose two terms: a being is limited by another being, an essence finds its conditions in another essence; remove every conception of a second term other than God, or remain in the notion of the pure and [p. 453] simple unity of essence, and you will necessarily exclude every limit and every condition from the divine essence. That is why the proper essence is characterized negatively by the absolute or the unconditioned, that is to say, by the absence of every condition, and the whole essence by the infinite, that is to say, by the absence of every limit. God is therefore the one, infinite, absolute Being. It is thus that he is defined in theology, and for the first time we see that this definition is rigorously scientific, because it is deduced without difficulty from the notion of being according to the order of the categories.

By virtue of the unity of essence, the infinite and the absolute are united in God: God is infinitely absolute and absolutely infinite. Union is not unity, but it comes from unity. It requires two distinct terms that are bound together, that do not separate or become strangers to one another, while preserving their distinction. It is the unity of essence that prevents this separation or that maintains the union. If essence is one, all is united in God, nothing is isolated. But union does not destroy variety; on the contrary, it supposes it, it exists only between things that are distinct. Unity without distinction is confusion; distinction without unity is separation. There is in God a principle of unity and of distinction, but there is no principle of separation or of confusion. Hence the formula: unite without confounding, distinguish without separating. The first distinction in God is the opposition of the absolute and the infinite, of the proper essence and the whole essence. This antithesis is the source of all the others. But the duality does not go so far as dualism, because the two terms are reduced to unity and only manifest the same essence under diverse forms. Dualism denies unity, as pantheism denies variety. Both fail to recognize the union or harmony of essence.

Let us pass to other properties, without dwelling on the categories of form. Let us seek the passage from the ontological attributes to the moral attributes of God. But here we need all the resources of the method as deduction, as intuition, and as construction.

Logic. — I. 29

p. 454

Let us begin with deduction. Since all is united in the divine essence, essence also is to being; in other words, being is related inwardly to its essence. And since essence is constituted or organized as unity of essence, as proper or absolute essence, as whole or infinite essence, and as harmony of essence, being must also be related to essence according to all the determinations of unity, of the absolute, of the infinite, and of union; in other words, the internal relation of being to essence must assume the four modes of essence: essence is to being under the higher character of unity, then under the opposed characters of proper essence and of whole essence, and finally under the character of the union between the two members of the opposition. The deduction is vague, because of its generality; it must be made clear by intuition.

p. 455

Let us return into ourselves and ask whether we know any property of this kind. I see one, and only one. What is intimacy, or inner sense? The inward relation of the self with itself, or of a being with its essence, a relation by virtue of which we take possession of ourselves and find that our essence, that our activity, that all that we are is ours and for us. And how is our intimacy manifested? It is one at first, above all opposition; then it is twofold and takes two names: self-consciousness and feeling of self, and these two forms end by uniting in the consciousness of feeling and in the feeling of consciousness. Intimacy has therefore four forms also, which develop under the characters of unity, of opposition, and of harmony. The correspondence appears complete; but what are the elements that predominate in the opposition of consciousness and feeling of self? Let us recall that consciousness is thought, and that thought is that faculty which has for its object the proper essence of things, and which determines itself as truth and as error, according as it grasps or fails to grasp things as they are in themselves, in their proper essence; that feeling, on the other hand, is that faculty which applies to the whole essence in a [p. 455] concrete manner, and which determines itself as pleasure and as pain, as joy and as sorrow, according as the object as a whole harmonizes or not with our nature. There is therefore between self-consciousness and feeling of self the same opposition as that which was pointed out in the deduction between the internal relation of being to essence under the character of proper essence and under the character of whole essence. Hence the correspondence is exact in every point between the terms of the deduction and those of the intuition, and nothing remains but to conclude by applying the one to the other in the construction.

p. 456

The relation of God to essence is therefore an intimate relation, God is in intimate relation with himself, God has intimacy or God is intimacy. This divine intimacy is one and whole, above all division, it is consciousness and feeling, it is the harmony of feeling and of consciousness. God is therefore God for himself (Deus sibi Deus), God is for himself such as he is, and all that he is. This is the root of all the moral attributes of God. But there is this difference between the divine intimacy and ours, that the former is complete, full and whole, while the latter is imperfect, restricted, affected by negation. It is because of this negation that our thought can manifest itself as error and our feeling as pain. But for the infinite and absolute essence there is no negation, no privation, no gap. The divine thought is therefore not truth or error, but pure truth, nothing but truth, and the divine feeling is not joy or sadness, but pure felicity, nothing but felicity. Hence these propositions: God is the truth, all the truth, the truth one and whole, infinite and absolute. In God consciousness is identical with truth, and truth returning into consciousness is identical with certainty. Aristotle had foreseen this doctrine in affirming that God is the thought of thought. This is the basis of the divine personality, which is itself the foundation of the moral order of the world. Personality is not individuality; it is the quality of a being that has complete consciousness and feeling of itself, that possesses itself and affirms itself as self. Man is [p. 456] a limited personality; God is the infinite personality; the intimate bond between these two personalities is religion. It is therefore wrong to say that every self supposes a not-self to which it is opposed; this is so within the limits of the world; but there is also an infinite and absolute self that has no contrary. If the infinite Being had no self, the self of man would be without reason and God would find in it his boundary. God is no longer a vague substance, he is he who is, and it is to him that prayer is addressed, as the inward movement of the mind and of the heart toward their center of attraction, toward the ideal of reason (1).

Truth is therefore not an invention of man; it is not made, it is. There exists a universal principle of truth, as the goal of science. Truth is God, and man can encounter it only by uniting himself with God in thought, by seeing things as God sees them, by cooperating with God in the action of the intellect. There are not two truths, one for God, the other for us. Truth is one and the same for all. No truth outside God. All truth is divine and every affirmation of truth is an affirmation of God.

Let us now see what God is, considered in his content, combining deduction anew with intuition.

p. 457

God is not empty unity, but the full unity of essence. What is there then in God? As the unity of essence manifests itself inwardly under the opposed characters of the absolute and the infinite, there must also be in the divine essence and in the divine being two distinct essences, two coordinate beings. Since the divine essence is one and indivisible, these two beings must each have as its share the whole essence, all the properties of God; but since these beings are opposed and contrary, the divine essence must also express itself [p. 457] in each of them under an original form. What then is the principle of their difference? It can be only the difference in the relation between the opposed qualities of essence, that is to say, the alternate predominance of the absolute over the infinite and of the infinite over the absolute. There are therefore in God two beings, each of which possesses the whole divine essence, but of which one is constituted from the preponderant point of view of the absolute or of the proper essence, and the other from the preponderant point of view of the infinite or of the whole essence. And since all is united in God, these contrary beings must also be united in Being. Hence a being of harmony, subordinate to the first two, which unites their opposed qualities, which expresses the divine essence from the point of view of union or equilibrium, and consequently without any predominance. This being of harmony is fully like God; it represents the synthesis of things, as the other two represent the antithesis or contrast. God, who is all being and all essence, is also each of these beings; but none of these beings is God, for all are determined according to the characteristic attributes of essence. God therefore remains distinct from all that is contained in him, he is above all determination, he is the indeterminate being, the all. But inasmuch as he is the indeterminate being and not this or that being, he also determines himself in subordinative opposition with the determinate beings that are in him. As such he is the Supreme Being, the first or highest of beings, he who is above all determinate beings.

This deduction is again obscure by its very nature, but intuition will make it understood. What are the things that analysis offers us? We know bodies, spirits, beings formed by the union of a spirit and a body, and we unite all these beings in the thought of a corporeal world, of a spiritual world, and of humanity. Above these three kinds of beings, we know God besides. These are all the beings that are the object of thought. They are four in number, like the terms of the deduction. One of them is common to the two series, namely God, the Supreme Being. Let us examine the others.

(1) Krause, Vorlesungen über das System der Philosophie, 1828. — Die absolute Religionsphilosophie, 1834–1843. — G. Tiberghien, Études sur la religion, Brussels, 1857.

p. 458

How do we conceive nature and spirit? As two orders of things that are opposed and contrary in every respect, but all of whose distinctive traits reduce to the reciprocal predominance of the proper essence or of the whole essence. Spirit is posited under the form of concentration, folded back upon itself in inner sense; bodies are posited under the form of expansion or extension, open to all influences from without, and making but one with the earth or with their globe. Spirit exists in itself and lives for itself with the consciousness of its absolute worth; bodies are things that are ignorant of their own worth and that are determined with a view to one another in the whole. Spirit acts of itself, spontaneously, voluntarily, without awaiting an excitation from without or without responding to it; bodies are inert, deprived of will, and manifest their activity only in relation with another, in the exact measure of the solicitations they receive. Spirits, in uniting among themselves, preserve their independence and are masters of their choice; bodies, in combining according to their specific affinities, penetrate each other entirely and lose even their distinctive qualities. Spirits develop freely according to their views or their caprices; now they sacrifice the whole to the part or one part to another, reason to sensibility, the understanding to the imagination, feeling to the intellect, now they observe the rules of the subordination and coordination of the faculties; they can unfold the series of their acts in a continuous and consistent manner or in a disorderly manner, interrupting the series where they will, without ever being bound by their antecedents; bodies, on the contrary, develop necessarily in their relation with the external medium, in the relation of all their parts among themselves, in the relation of each act with the past and with the future; nothing is arbitrary or capricious in the life of nature, everything there is continuous in time as in space, everything there is linked and chained to everything. Nature produces its works in all their parts at once, in the whole of all their microscopic details, without error or omission, when no external cause comes to [p. 459] disturb its action; spirit, on the contrary, composes its works in an abstract manner, according to its own notions, fitting one fragment to another, at the risk of going astray, even leaving its work unfinished, reduced to a mere form without ground, or to a part without a whole. All these differences between spirit and matter are expressed exactly in the conception of their laws, an inevitable result, since laws express the nature of things: on the one hand, freedom, on the other, fatality. Freedom and fatality are the two modes of accomplishment of laws that correspond to the proper essence and to the whole essence, that is to say, to autonomy and to continuity. The laws of the spiritual life, addressed to beings who find in themselves the motives of their acts, must be executed by the free will; the laws of nature, on the contrary, addressed to beings that bear the imprint of the linking of everything with everything, are executed ineluctably. Spirit can depart from its laws; bodies cannot. The organization of spirit and of nature therefore corresponds completely to the two terms of the deduction, in which the point of view of the proper essence or of the whole essence, of the absolute or of the infinite, predominates.

There remains the fourth term of the intuition. How do we understand humanity? Precisely as the being of harmony of creation, as the microcosm in which all the forces of the spiritual world and of the physical world are balanced, or in which animal life rises to its highest power and is intimately united with the highest manifestation of spirit, with reason, the sense of the absolute and of the infinite. Humanity is thereby constituted in harmony with all orders of things: it reproduces nature in science, it idealizes it in art, it adapts it to the ends of reason in industry, it reigns as sovereign over the globe, it can live in the intimacy of God by consciousness and by feeling, and cooperate with him in the realization of the good.

p. 460

The analysis of the objects of thought therefore coincides entirely with the deduction of the things that are in God. The application [p. 460] is therefore easy. God is one and is but once what he is. The beings that are determined in him, under the characters of the proper essence, of the whole essence, and of the union of these two qualities, are therefore the very same as those that we know intuitively under the names of spirit, nature, and humanity. Consequently, it is certain that God contains in himself two opposed beings, nature and spirit, and a being of harmony, humanity; it is certain that the world, in other words, is contained in God and is composed of three kinds, spirit and nature, which are coordinate with each other and subordinate to God, and humanity, which is the synthesis of the other two. These three beings are formed of the divine essence, which is the essence one and whole, but the divine essence is manifested in them under distinct forms which, considered as such, exclude one another, and it is the divine essence, thus determined or fixed in kinds, that becomes the proper essence of the world. The essence of things is founded in the divine essence, but it is not the proper essence of God; the latter is above the determination, the negation, and the exclusion that are always met with in the world. Inasmuch as he is above the universe, above nature, spirit, and humanity, God is the Supreme Being. The Supreme Being is a point of view of God. God is the all in an undivided manner; the Supreme Being is the all compared with the parts, inasmuch as it is distinguished from them, that is to say, inasmuch as the beings of the world are not God, but are in God, under God, and through God. These relations can be represented thus, according to the formulas of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis:

Supreme Being.

Spirit. Nature.

Humanity.

From this proposition some important corollaries are drawn for the theory of knowledge. There results first of all the certainty of the fundamental principles of cosmology.

p. 461

There exists a world, not outside God, but in God, and [p. 461] the world is determined in its various parts according to the divine essence. This is what permits us to affirm scientifically a relation of causality between God and the world, since causality expresses precisely a relation between two things of which one is determined in conformity with the essence of the other: hence the transcendent validity of the law of causality beyond the limits of observation. The causality of God is expressed in creation. The denial of this principle is one of the sources of skepticism; this denial is now recognized as false. Furthermore, the world is composed of three kinds of things, neither more nor less; spirit, nature, and humanity therefore have an objective existence, outside our thought, in the very essence of God, and consequently the contrary doctrines must be rejected. No intermediaries between the world and God. Materialism and idealism, which dispute the duality in the world, which reduce all substances either to matter or to spirit, are errors. Nature is not a phantom of the imagination, but a real being that has its reason in God; and spirit, whatever our senses may say, has no less reality than matter. The spiritualist philosophy, in agreement with common sense, is therefore also in conformity with the metaphysical principles of science. There are two orders of substances that do not derive from each other, but both derive from God; all is reduced to unity in the absolute. Spirit and nature are distinct from God without being separated from him, and are united with God without being confounded with him. This is what dualism and pantheism fail to recognize. For pantheism everything is confounded in the infinite, and God does not exist as Supreme Being above the world; for dualism everything is separated, and nature appears as the other or the contrary of God.

p. 462

It is demonstrated that spirit, nature, and humanity can be the object of legitimate knowledge, since they are presented to us in intuition such as they ought to be by virtue of their principle or such as they are in deduction. Skeptics like to persuade themselves that the subject and the object of thought are constituted in contradiction with one another, a bold hypothesis which it seemed impossible to combat [p. 462] and which in fact resists all the efforts of analysis. But this ground of doubt yields like all the others before the so remarkable coincidence of the direct procedure of intuition and the discursive procedure of deduction. This coincidence attests that the transcendent objects that constitute the world appear to us exactly as they are, as they ought to be, when their essence is deduced from the divine essence. Why should it be otherwise? If God is the unity of being and of essence, which follows necessarily from his existence, there is no contradiction in things. If God contains in himself spirit and nature, and if these two beings are harmonized in humanity, by virtue of the unity of essence, it is certain that thought and reality are organized with a view to each other. Spirit is for us the subjective world and nature the objective world. These two worlds, dominated by the higher unity of essence, which they express under two opposed aspects, are destined to unite in all their manifestations. Anthropology verifies this principle within the limits of observation: spirit and body in man are homologous organisms that correspond in all their determinations and that develop in parallel in life.

p. 463

The harmony of thought and of reality is henceforth a certain principle: thought is made to know things according to their essence, and things are made to be known in truth. It is in this sense that the proposition of Spinoza may be approved: the order and connection of ideas are the same as the order and connection of things (1), a formula transformed by Leibniz into the law of preestablished harmony. Consequently, what is one must be recognized as one, according to the unity and identity of essence. Spirit, nature, and humanity, each having but one and the same essence as God, cannot have contradictory attributes: the world is eternal or not, infinite or not, necessary or not, when it is considered under the same relation. It is against this truth that the criticism of Kant rises anew. Pure [p. 463] psychology has its paralogisms; theology, its illusions; cosmology, its antinomies. We have seen in the analysis of immanent knowledge and of transcendent knowledge what is to be thought of the objections of subjective or transcendental idealism against the certainty of the self and the certainty of God; let us see now, so far as the results acquired permit, what the celebrated antinomies of pure reason are worth.

(1) Spinoza, Éthique. Part Two, Proposition VII.

p. 464

Kant believes that a series of antithetical or contradictory propositions can be demonstrated concerning the world, which thus become, the one set as much as the other, equally certain or equally open to dispute. He proves, on the one hand, that the world has a beginning in time and a limit in space, and on the other, that the world is infinite as to space and as to time. This is the first antinomy. The proof of the thesis is drawn from the impossibility of making the synthesis of an infinite series of successive states or of an infinite series of coexistent parts. The proof of the antithesis is found in the impossibility of admitting an empty time outside the limits of the universe. According to the second antinomy, there exists something simple and there exists nothing simple in the world. The third bears on causality in its relations with freedom. On the one hand, physical causality does not suffice for the explanation of phenomena, a causality by freedom must be affirmed besides; for if everything happened by necessity according to the laws of nature alone, every state of the world would have its cause in a prior state, and so on to infinity, hence there would be no beginning, and consequently no sufficient reason for the states of the world. On the other hand, there is no freedom, everything is necessary; for a free cause would act absolutely without being determined by what precedes, which is in opposition to the law of causality. The fourth antinomy, finally, concerns the existence of God as author of the world. On the one hand, a necessary being is needed to explain the universe, otherwise we should have a series of conditions that would stop nowhere. On the other hand, there exists no necessary being in the world or outside the world, otherwise there would be a beginning without contingency [p. 464] and therefore without a cause; or else the series of changes would be without a beginning, it would be necessary in its totality, though contingent in each of its parts, which implies a contradiction.

The cosmological antinomies reduce to the opposition of the finite and the infinite, of time and eternity, of the simple and the composite, of necessity and freedom. The conflict of these elements has been regarded until now as the triumph of subjective idealism. The world, in fact, seems suspended between God and nothingness, at an equal distance from the one and from the other, and partaking of the nature of both. God is affirmation; nothingness is negation; the world is composed at once of affirmation and of negation. It is impossible to conceive the universe in a scientific manner without connecting it, by the law of causality, with the very essence of God. Now the divine essence is necessarily one and indivisible. The world, then, will be one, infinite, absolute, eternal, like God. And yet is not everything in the world multiple, variable, limited, and relative? How is this contradiction to be escaped? An author who carefully analyzes and discusses the principles of skepticism stops short before the cosmological problem and dares to voice only timid objections (1). Kant’s solution is well known. It consists in suppressing the world, in order to suppress at the same stroke the difficulties relating to the world. Time and space are in us, as forms of our sensibility, not outside in things; causality is a regulative law of our representations, not a constitutive law of beings; in a word, the objective is displaced and becomes subjective: this is the transcendental conversion of things. What matter, then, the apparent contradictions of the world? Criticism abandons them to the metaphysicians and shuts itself up in the self.

p. 465

This is not a solution, but a desperate expedient that betrays the insufficiency of the principles of criticism. The antagonism will be in the self instead of being in the world, and that is [p. 465] all; and it will further be necessary to justify the pretension of denying everything that reason affirms. Kant compared his reform to the astronomical revolution of Copernicus: it is not the sun that moves around the earth, but the earth that moves around the sun; it is not things that impose their laws on us, but we who impose our laws on things. The comparison is defective. Copernicus diminished the importance of our globe, but enlarged the notion of the world; Kant exalts the self at the expense of the universe. Subjectivism represents the system of Ptolemy far better than that of Kepler. Let us leave things where they are, since we can do justice to common sense. The question is not whether the self prevails over the not-self or the not-self over the self, but of explaining their accord. Two conditions are indispensable for the reconciliation of the cosmological antitheses: we must first possess the principle of science and deduce the world from the divine essence, in order to know what it must be according to its cause; we must next have an intuition of the world in its totality, in order to know what it is in itself or what it appears to be. Now Kant lacks both these conditions. On the one hand, he rejects the scientific knowledge of God and cannot connect the world with any higher principle; on the other, he disputes all intellectual intuition of reason, and seeks, for the imagination, only a total synthesis of all the determinate states of the world in time and in space, that is to say, an enumeration of parts to infinity or an infinite number, which implies.

(1) E. Maurial, le Scepticisme combattu dans ses principes; second part. Paris, 1857.

p. 466

The world is the expression of the attributes of God. God manifests himself as being and as essence in the world according to unity, according to the antithesis of the absolute and the infinite, according to harmony, in a word, according to all the determinations of his essence. Now the divine essence is one and indivisible. It cannot therefore be divided among the various beings of the world; it must be wholly in each, but realized only under distinct relations in conformity with the laws of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. If this is so, the world, regarded in its principle, must be one, [p. 466] infinite, absolute, harmonic or organized in itself and in all its parts. There is only one universe, as there is only one God, and in the universe only one nature, one spirit, one humanity. And as everything that is unique is also without condition or limits, or as the unity of essence manifests itself inwardly as proper or absolute essence and as whole or infinite essence, spirit, nature, and humanity are likewise infinite and absolute. And as the divine essence is further, from other points of view, eternal and necessary, the world is also eternal and necessary in its essence. All these deductions are exact and cannot be contradicted by any antinomic demonstration.

p. 467

There is, in fact, only one universe, since the universe is the ensemble of all that is determinate. When astronomers speak of the plurality of worlds, they mean by world an inhabitable star, a planet, a celestial earth, which is not contrary to the unity of the universe. If the theologians, on the other hand, still discuss the question of the possibility of other worlds, it is because they have grasped no essential relation between the world and God. The constitution of the world results from the constitution of God, and cannot be other than it is. Nor did the world begin in time; otherwise all the attributes of God that have reference to the world, including causality or creation, would have come into being with the world or would have existed before the world in a pure potentiality without act. Scientists are in agreement with Origen on the eternity of matter, but this eternity must extend to the entire world, considered in its essence, and eternity as such in no way destroys the law of causality. Only we must then rise above the sensible intuition of a temporal cause and of an initial point, to the intellectual intuition of an eternal cause that operates outside time. If God is the eternal and if he is cause, causality is eternal in God. An eternal creation does not offend reason and is better conceived than a creation that begins at a determinate moment. The theologians have always admitted it for the procession of the divine persons. Finally, if [p. 467] spirit, nature, and humanity are unique and like unto God, they are also infinite in their domain, as we had suspected in the analysis, without being able to decide the question. The world must be infinite if it is of the divine essence, and we have the intuition of an infinite world, if we will conceive it in itself, freeing ourselves from the conditions of sensible observation or of an intuition by the imagination. Let us leave the parts, let us not count the bodies and the spirits, let us see the whole, the whole in space, the whole in time, the whole in essence. If we had not this intuition, we should not have the intuition of God, of the self, of the principles of reason either. Finally, if the physical world and the spiritual world are infinite, humanity is so too, and from that moment terrestrial humanity is only a part of the whole of humanity, and our globe is no longer the only inhabited star. Here again is a vital question that the analysis could not resolve and that the synthesis settles without effort.

p. 468

Thus far we have encountered no antinomies in the world. The attributes of the universe are the reproduction of the attributes of God; this is quite simple, since the essence of the world is the very essence of God in the state of determination. But if we now consider this element of determination, we shall obtain other attributes that will seem contrary to the first and will have the effect of antinomies. Nature is one, infinite, absolute, we have said; yet nature is neither spirit nor humanity; how then is it one, infinite, and absolute? It is one in its kind: there is only one nature; it is infinite in its kind: it is the whole of nature, but not the whole of reality; it is absolute in its kind: it is without relation to another nature, but not without relation to something else. God, on the contrary, is purely and simply one, absolutely infinite and infinitely absolute, outside and above every kind.
